Musk wrote on Saturday that “using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be. Starshield, a different system, is controlled by the US government. What they decide to do is up to them. Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”
“Physically impossible”
Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor for Zelenskyy, denied the allegation in a Telegram post on Sunday. Beskrestnov wrote that all Starlink terminals located over Ukrainian territory, including territories occupied by Russia, were already subject to a movement speed limit of 70 to 90 kilometers per hour. He added that Starlink does not function over the territory of Russia.

In Serbia and Hungary, groundswells of youthful energy topple entrenched governments
Serbia has seen a dramatic shift after President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to student-backed candidates
BELGRADE, Serbia -- For over a year, residents of Serbia's capital were blocked from entering one of the city's most prominent parks, nestled between Parliament and the offices of the powerful right-wing leader, Aleksandar Vucic.
The reason: the park in Belgrade had been cordoned off and occupied by throngs of Vucic's most ardent — and violent — supporters, an effective enforcer squad for the authoritarian leader tasked with intimidating and sometimes assaulting members of a growing anti-government student movement.
But after Vucic stunned the Balkan country Sunday evening by conceding defeat in an election against student-backed candidates, ecstatic young revelers filled the streets of Belgrade and ripped down the cordons around the encampment known as Caciland. Before long, the barricades lay tossed aside and the tents within went up in smoke, along with Vucic's power.
The seismic shift came after two years of relentless organizing and sustained protests by the student movement, which accused the Kremlin-backed Vucic of increasing authoritarianism, connections to organized crime and runaway corruption.
It also echoed other bottom-up, youth-led protest movements that have recently challenged what they see as entrenched, unresponsive power structures in Europe and beyond. Close to home, in neighboring Hungary, they succeeded in ousting another entrenched leader.
Serbia's popular student movement grew out of anger at Vucic and his government since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Novi Sad. That set off the wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption and cronyism during renovation work at the station.
When Vucic conceded defeat on Sunday and tens of thousands took to the streets to celebrate, the scenes bore remarkable resemblance to the ouster of pro-Russian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in Hungary just six months earlier.
Where the far-right Orbán's 16-year grip on power had once seemed unshakable, growing anger over corruption and capture of the country's institutions coalesced around a political newcomer, Péter Magyar, who — like Serbia's students — spent two years relentlessly touring the countryside where Orbán was strongest.
Magyar campaigned heavily against corruption and in favor of bringing Hungary back into the fold of European Union democracies. When his center-right Tisza party won a landslide in the election, it was largely thanks to a groundswell of youth participation that delivered the highest electoral turnout in Hungary's post-socialist history.
Like Serbia's student movement, Magyar's activists and supporters offered a vision of restoring Hungary's institutions that had been hollowed out by Orbán, building a functioning state that responded to citizens' needs and adhered to the rule of law.
Both in Serbia and Hungary, many have expressed hope that ousting their autocratic regimes would open up a chance for a new generation of political representation and genuine democratic participation.
In social media posts on Sunday and Monday, Magyar congratulated Serbia's students, saying he was “delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle.”
“Surely I wasn’t the only one feeling nostalgic when I saw those pictures coming out of Serbia last night?” he wrote, alluding to the joyful celebrations in Belgrade and Budapest six months apart.
Since he came to power, Magyar has used his party's two-thirds parliamentary majority to gradually deliver on his promises to free the media, bring Hungary back into the EU sphere and punish members of Orbán's regime and their allies who had accumulated wealth under his patronage.
Serbia's youth movement now faces their own daunting task of restoring a ravaged democracy and institutions, but without the benefit of the constitutional majority that Magyar enjoys in Hungary. Their Students' List of candidates includes various experts in their fields but with little or no experience in politics or state jobs. The name of the future prime minister remains a mystery.
“Today we are celebrating … but tomorrow, the job starts,” said Radomir Saicic, one of the candidates on the students' ticket.
How the reform will play out will determine the success of the movement. Vucic's loyalists installed over the years in the security services, coupled with a well-organized propaganda machine, are likely to try to undermine the effort as Vucic on Sunday announced a struggle from the opposition against the new authorities.
Youth protests have recently rocked another Balkan country, Albania, where actions by student groups seeking education reforms have morphed into broader anti-government sentiment — largely centered on anger over a major development project linked to U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Sustained demonstrations against the long-serving socialist government have escalated into violent clashes on the streets of the capital Tirana, with protesters calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama — another Vucic ally — over allegations of widespread corruption. Riot police have responded with tear gas and water cannons.
Those clashes came as social unrest has set Europe's streets ablaze from France and Italy to Spain and Portugal, fueled by youth frustration over the state of public education, social services and the high cost of housing.
María Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain, said young Europeans are experiencing “a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control,” and that when specific conditions arise, “a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channeling that discontent and driving people into the streets.”
In a post-election analysis, Serbian professor Dejan Pavlovic wrote on X on Monday that the students' lack of political experience or involvement in any dubious business dealings had “become their greatest strategic advantage.”
Vucic, on the other hand, had become “culturally obsolete,” Pavlovic said, as the new generation with their own values and ways stepped into the scene.
The next challenge will be a presidential election that must be held by the end of the year. The students will have to avoid allowing political divisions that might split their movement. Some highly sensitive issues include relations with the European Union and Russia, but the primary focus will be dealing with corruption.
“Tentacles of Vucic’s octopus have spread around the entire country. Taking them out, dealing with them, is going to be one hell of a job,” warned political commentator Ivan Milenkovic.
Nonetheless, Pavlovic wrote, the Serbian students' success “challenges conventional assumptions about the resources necessary to defeat an entrenched incumbent” and will become the subject of scholarly research.

Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
Goodbye Raila
BBC Africa Eye investigates the killing of three mourners at Raila Odinga’s national farewell
Watch on iPlayer
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

Pope's South American trip to go ahead as planned after lung cancer surgery
- Published
The Vatican has confirmed that Pope Leo will go on his South American tour as planned, following his surgery for lung cancer.
He was diagnosed with lung cancer and underwent successful surgery in Rome on 13 October to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung.
The 71-year-old is scheduled to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on 6-17 November, the Vatican said, adding that the he was looking forward to it "with great joy and enthusiasm".
The Pope will follow the same programme as planned, visiting 10 cities on the tour.
"I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," Pope Leo said.
The Pope's trip will begin in Uruguay on 8 November, where he will visit the capital Montevideo, as well as other key cities.
He will then travel to Argentina from November 11-17, visiting a number of places including the capital Buenos Aires.
After that he will spend six days in Peru, where roughly 76% of the population are Catholic, and will include stops in Lima, Chiclayo, Cuzco and Pucallpa.
Peru's Cardinal Castillo, the Archbishop of Lima, has said the trip would involve young people, women who help run community kitchens and members of the country's indigenous communities, according to Vatican News.
The archbishop highlighted the Pope's close ties with the people of Chiclayo, where he lived for several years. The Pope has Peruvian citizenship.
The Catholic Church sent him to Peru as a missionary in 1985, when he was 30 years old.
He joined the Augustinian mission in Chulucanas, in the Peruvian department of Piura, and the following year, joined the mission in the city of Trujillo.
For almost three decades, he worked between the US and Peru.
Leo announced the news of his lung operation himself to the world on 11 October during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
He reassured pilgrims that the growth was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage" but that his doctors had advised him to have it removed.
The surgery lasted for 90 minutes, and he was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on 17 October.
The Pope's surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said he was in an "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition", and said there were "no clinical reasons" why the trip should not go ahead.
Tests showed the cancer was "localised".
Since his operation, the pope has been resting and gradually resuming his work. He has been "adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritise his recovery while continuing to fulfill the responsibilities of his ministry," the Vatican said.
Leo was "deeply grateful for the prayers and affection he has received from throughout the world," the Vatican said.
The Vatican said Friday that Leo would cancel a planned trip to Assisi on October 27th, on the recommendation of his doctors.

At a splashy event in New York City last week, General Motors unveiled its new tech roadmap centered on AI-driven vehicle development, advanced battery tech, high-powered car computers, and autonomous driving.
Sterling Anderson doesn’t think humanoid robots should be building cars
General Motors’ product chief breaks down the company’s software evolution, the physics of multisensor vehicle safety, and why personally owned autonomous vehicles beat robotaxis.
Sterling Anderson doesn’t think humanoid robots should be building cars
General Motors’ product chief breaks down the company’s software evolution, the physics of multisensor vehicle safety, and why personally owned autonomous vehicles beat robotaxis.
Some of this was old news: We already knew the automaker was developing hands-free, eyes-off driving automation and had been prototyping new battery chemistries. In a sense, the real purpose of the event was to showcase how all these pieces fit together. With its new “intelligence-defined vehicle” paradigm, GM is banking on artificial intelligence, centralized computing, and virtualized engineering to cut vehicle development timelines in half, aiming to compress a typical four- to five-year process down to just over two.
Yet, this high-tech overhaul arrives against a backdrop of steep industry headwinds and razor-thin margins for error. GM’s aggressive pivot comes as the automaker faces a wave of hyperefficient Chinese EV makers that are aggressively expanding globally. At the same time, softening EV demand in the US has forced GM to recalibrate its electrification hopes, balancing multibillion-dollar investments in next-generation battery plants with the ongoing costs of software development.
To be sure, for GM to bet its future on unproven software architectures and autonomous technology is a high-stakes gamble: If these complex AI systems falter or if development hits delays, GM risks burning through massive amounts of money while falling further behind agile rivals (like Tesla) that were built as software-first companies from day one.
After the event, I sat down with Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer, to talk about the company’s risky new ventures as well as how he plans to steer a century-old Detroit giant through an increasingly fast, software-driven world.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
So this was quite the massive announcement — just lots of disparate pieces. Is there a unifying theme here, would you say? And if so, what do you think it is?
The car’s getting smarter.
That’s it?
That’s it. I think so. Your vehicle is becoming a trusted, intelligent companion, and we’re doing that in a variety of ways. I think I might be one of the only guys who gets as excited as I do about what we’re doing in the development process and making that faster and better.
I don’t know how many people are going to come away with that takeaway in quite the spirit that I think it merits, but the level of tests and performance optimality that we can achieve when we can spin design decisions hundreds of times — that previously would have accommodated one — is huge. It’s really huge. I’ve been asked now by two folks I’ve met afterwards, “Hey, what about safety, and does speed come at the cost of safety?” The way we are getting speed is by virtualizing tests in a way that allows us to improve safety. Historically, I would have been able to afford X prototypes that I could send to crash tests, and it took me six months. Now, I kick off thousands of tests in the virtual world that give me feedback much quicker. So I get speed, and I get safety, better coverage, and better understanding. There’s a lot of cake being eaten, too, in this process.
“I kick off thousands of tests in the virtual world that give me feedback much quicker.”
— Sterling Anderson
What kind of AI models are you using? I know you talked about how data is sort of the currency here, so obviously there’s a lot that you’re pulling from your own customers, but there’s a range of products out there. What’s the dividing line between what to look for outside the company versus what to pull from inside?
It’s a good question. It depends on what we’re doing with it. In many cases, the transformer-based foundation models enable some of the generative design stuff I was talking about — we have enough data in-house based on decades of design files, analyses, etc., that we can get a pretty well-trained system to express our data well. But we have access to — and anybody has access in many cases to — a lot of data that informs us. The co-training of these models with data that exists beyond GM’s walls tends to make them better. So we do it with all of them.
You’ve talked about moving from deterministic code to probabilistic AI that learns from the structure of the world and from the data. How are you specifically embedding these models into the vehicles? How much is run locally versus pulling from the cloud?
For any safety-critical functionality, the inference is done onboard because we can’t deal with latency, possible dropouts, or whatever else. Some of these examples you saw from the team earlier today, like the OnStar AI interactions, aren’t safety-critical. You probably noticed, given the latency, that you had some round-tripping happening there because we don’t need to run those all onboard. Now, we’re thinking about distilling them down into onboard models just to deal with the latency, but that’s an on-the-edge user experience element, not a core safety consideration.
You talked a little bit during your presentation about how big GM is, which gives you advantages with data, but also a lot of inertia. Back in 2019, GM President Mark Reuss talked about moving toward the “digital brain” of the vehicle, and in 2021 you talked about Ultifi. Have things sped up now? Are you on the glide path at this point?
Yeah, and a big enabler of it is that common electrical system, including centralized compute. Historically, I know of very few killers to software speed quite like complexity. The moment a software team has a very large set of deployment targets that don’t share a common baseline is the moment you slow that team down enormously.
Rolling this out across our entire portfolio is specifically to enable software speed so we don’t have to continue to support vehicles of various configurations. As that hardware set rolls out, software engineers will suddenly be able to operate like they would if they were in a company with two models in production, which they just haven’t been able to in history.
GM is unique in having this huge portfolio of brands with distinct identities. How do you decide what to standardize across every vehicle versus ensuring a Buick remains a Buick and a GMC Sierra remains unique?
It’s a combination of things. First, the essence of each brand tends to manifest in aesthetics and interaction models. Aesthetics is something you can effectively skin via design, both in digital interfaces and physical sheet metal. We already do a fairly good job of commonizing the under-the-skin componentry because why wouldn’t we? For a given segment of vehicle, there’s a particular ride quality that tends to be best received by everybody.
Our T1-2 platform for our next-generation trucks is common between brands. Where you’ll see us differentiate is in the feature set, the aesthetics, and interaction patterns we effectively skin segment by segment. Sales has dedicated brand channels, but engineering is all one organization. That ensures we don’t ship heterogeneous, suboptimal cars for different brands just because a team that was slightly worse was assigned to one brand or another. I want our engineering team focusing all of their effort on what is the absolute best suspension, powertrain, or drive unit, and then we scale it across the portfolio.
Speaking of autonomy, we have autonomous vehicles on the road today — Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla Cybercabs. What are the challenges GM still needs to solve to get to a point where someone can take their eyes off the road comfortably and safely?
When you say “eyes off,” you mean autonomous?
Autonomously, yes. Hands off, mind off, eyes off. But at the same time, you wouldn’t be recommending people go to sleep in their vehicles yet?
We are designing them such that should they fall asleep, it won’t be unsafe, because we don’t have the luxury of ensuring that they’re paying attention. The reason you won’t hear me use terms like “eyes off” is because I hear people use those terms in reference to nonsensical levels of automation. What do you think your mind is doing when your eyes are on your phone? Where’s your mind? Let’s not draw these nonsensical distinctions. If you believe that your driver assistance system is super capable, you are already at risk of complacency — at risk of treating it like it’s an autonomous system. Our philosophy is: If we’re going to design an autonomous system, we’re going to actually design an autonomous system. The path of incrementalism that we’ll take will work for personal ownership, not the one that worked for robotaxis. Instead of regionally specific, speed-limited settings, we’re going to go toward road-type specific settings and expand outward from there. They both converge in the same place — self-driving everywhere at all times — but take different paths to get there.
With robotaxis today, we see problems around nuisance situations — like blocking intersections or emergency vehicles. Do you feel personal autonomy, as GM defines it, solves some of that because the driver remains an option to fall back on?
The form of the fallback matters. We will not fall back in a safety-critical dynamic situation. It’s just not reasonable to do that. What we can do in a non-safety-critical situation — where the vehicle is stopped and something odd is happening — is hand it back to the driver once we’ve reached a safe place. Having a human in the loop is very useful for that.
How do you structure that handoff to avoid driver complacency?
We’re not handing back dynamically. This is not an exchange of “you drive, now I’ll drive, oops, I don’t recognize this.” This is not Level 3. In the same way you put a robotaxi in a bounded region, we will put personally owned autonomous vehicles on a particular road.
When on that road, we will take the human to their destination and give a graceful countdown — like, “Hey, you’ve got 10 minutes left in this ride.” If they take over preemptively, great. Should they not take over, the system brings the vehicle to a safe state off the off-ramp and says, “I told you 10 minutes ago to take over. We’re stopped, and I’m not going any further.”
You have to operate under the assumption that bad actors will try to abuse the system — sitting in the back seat, like we’ve seen with Tesla users.
I get far more nervous when misuse happens in the context of a driver-assist system that wasn’t designed to handle every situation. If the vehicle accepts control, our system is designed to deal with more situations that can be thrown at it in that circumstance. So my anxiety level declines dramatically.
Features like OnStar AI ask for access to calendars, emails, and personal data. Given past FTC orders regarding GM selling customer data to third-party brokers without permission, how do you ensure customers can trust you with this data?
Privacy has to be designed in. With end-to-end encryption, we don’t see your data; you grant permission to an assistant that performs better with context. Data is only available to us at an aggregate, anonymized level. At an individual level, it is encrypted and under your control.
When you buy a car, going through dozens of terms and conditions leads to “click, click, click” without reading, which does a disservice to trust. We have dramatically simplified these authorizations down to a couple of clear choices that explain why the car needs data — like reading your calendar for smart routing. You can revoke permission, delete your data, or port it out at any time. You alluded to trust, which is foundational. Decisions made in the past by people who no longer work for this company have an overhang, but that’s not the company we are today. We earn that trust back by designing the architecture so that even if someone made a bad decision internally, the system technically wouldn’t allow them to access raw user data.
And the way we do that is by designing it. Look, even if we had someone stupid work for us again and do something like this, they couldn’t. They wouldn’t be able to access it.
“Look, even if we had someone stupid work for us again and do something like this, they couldn’t. They wouldn’t be able to access it.”
AI is cutting vehicle development times, but we’re also seeing hype around factory automation and humanoid robots from companies like Tesla and Rivian. Is GM heading in that direction?
If you want to be perceived as a robotics player these days, it seems you have to have a humanoid robot that does backflips. It’s weird. Advocacy for humanoids often comes from people who historically advocate for first-principles engineering, but humanoids are not born from first principles. They put form over function. The logic assumes the human form factor is optimal for a factory floor, but this form factor evolved to run away from lions on the African savanna! Production environments weren’t built for human forms any more than roads built for horses meant cars should have four legs. The most valuable real estate in a factory is the floor. Having bumbling humanoid robots clamoring in and out of vehicles is not where you start. You start with form factors that look alien — like an octopus hanging from a gantry that reaches into a moving vehicle line. We’re ignoring the “religion” of humanoids and focusing on underlying AI intelligence that can operate various specialized robot form factors for specific tasks.
Is GM building these robotics systems itself?
We already are. We actively work with heavy machinery suppliers like Fanuc, but we are actively developing many of our own solutions.
People are excited about cars getting smarter, but they also want them to be cheaper. How do these announcements lead to more affordable options?
LMR (lithium manganese rich) battery chemistry is a huge part of this. It delivers a range close to high-nickel packs at a cost closer to LFP. On a per-range basis, a customer will be able to buy a fourth-gen GM EV for less money than a competitor’s profitable model without relying on subsidies.
Additionally, commonizing our electrical architecture reduces wiring length and vehicle mass dramatically, making cars inherently more affordable. Virtualizing development cuts prototype costs, allowing vehicle business cases to clear at lower retail prices. This applies to ICE vehicles and hybrids as well, not just EVs.
Will this intelligence lead to higher subscriptions and paywalls?
Capability advances inevitably over time without raising financial costs — the device in your lap does far more than computers years ago for less money. Regarding subscriptions: I’m here to build great products. If customers like paying for services like a lease, let them; if not, don’t force them.
“The most valuable real estate in a factory is the floor. Having bumbling humanoid robots clamoring in and out of vehicles is not where you start.”
[GM spokesperson Chaiti Sen: For immediate features like OnStar AI, it will be included in our basic package. We aren’t going to paywall core baseline experiences or hand customers a bare “tin shell.”]
For your sensor suite, you’re using cameras, radar, and lidar. Do you see that remaining in perpetuity, or could you eventually scale back to a vision-only approach like Tesla?
If you scale back to vision-only, physics suggests you’ll be in trouble in certain situations. Radar is so cheap that dropping it doesn’t make sense — dropping it is a weird religious stance that ignores physics. Lidar operates on a similar wavelength to visible light and helps co-train camera systems to get better faster. Cameras can’t see through dense fog or measure instantaneous velocity like radar can. Having a multisensor suite provides obvious safety advantages that physics simply demands.

If your online algorithm detects your having even the slightest interest in growing mushrooms, you will, at some point, probably see an ad for the Lykyn. It looks like something out of a science fiction movie—a clear box with theatrical lighting, fog, and a giant mushroom displayed like an otherworldly specimen.
After trying the Lykyn myself for a month, I can confirm that it really does look like that in real life, and as someone who has tried many different mushroom-growing methods, I was impressed by how well the Lykyn worked as a legitimate fruiting chamber. The thing you’ll have to decide for yourself is whether it’s worth $300 to showcase a process that lasts only a week or two.
Some Assembly, Some Fog
Even though the company is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, Lykyn manufactures all fruiting chambers in Turkey and ships them straight from Istanbul for free. I worried about a delay, but my unit arrived in just 11 days, with none of the duty fees or other customs weirdness that seem to plague many overseas shipments these days. The speed was even more impressive given that I had the custom wood handle engraving add-on ($15), which puts your own text on the handle instead of “Lykyn.” (Mine had my name.)
The 13 x 13 x 15-inch unit, available in white or black plastic, arrives mostly disassembled—you will need to peel the protective film off both sides of each acrylic panel, slide them into plastic tracks on the base, add the corner posts, and fill the unit with distilled water. One panel doubles as a sliding door, and installing it was fiddly on my unit; I had to open and close it a few times to loosen it, and even now it still takes two hands to wrench it open. The Lykyn must be connected to 2.5-GHz Wi-Fi and a power source with its 5-volt USB-C cable (there is no provided brick), and the light—a little LED pad that sits on top—plugs into the base.
The only troubleshooting I had to do was with the ultrasonic humidifier, which emits an occasional cloud of fog (and is audible, but no louder than a typical humidifier), with extra humidity being pulled out by a fan. Despite my following directions, the mister produced no mist, and I kept getting notifications from the Lykyn app that the unit was out of water, despite the reservoir being visibly full. I eventually had to push the preinstalled wick farther down into its slot and “prime” the membrane on top with a little bit of water. (I later verified the Lykyn app’s humidity reading against my own hygrometer; the readings were similar within a couple of percentage points.) Other than refilling the water reservoir, the Lykyn needs no maintenance.
Brief but Spectacular Blooms
The Lykyn is a “smart” fruiting chamber, which means the humidity, airflow, and light schedules are controlled by settings for your specific species in the easy-to-use Lykyn app. There are also options to control these variables manually. (Note also that though the app shows the temperature, the Lykyn is not able to heat or cool.) While you can use any brand of fruiting block in the Lykyn up to 6 pounds, I tested my unit with the brand’s own 5-pound shiitake and pink oyster blocks, which came separately—no fruiting block is included with your Lykyn purchase. There are also no instructions on or with the blocks themselves, so be sure to check online for how yours needs to be prepared—some, like the shiitake, need to be taken totally out of their packaging, while others simply need an X cut into the side of the bag.
Having the block in versus out of the bag had a dramatic effect on the overall aesthetic of the Lykyn, which sat front and center in my dining room during the test. The bare shiitake block looked like a moon rock or quirky scientific specimen under the colorful lighting (which is customizable, but the default indicates the mushroom's “emotions," from green for “happy and thriving” to red for “stressed and worried”), while the black-bagged oyster mushroom block looked like … well, a black plastic bag. With the precisely controlled lighting and humidity, both mushroom blocks fruited within several days, compared with several weeks with other methods I’ve tried. This is especially impressive for shiitake, which are notoriously fussy in their requirements.

England-Republic of Ireland U15 World Cup game ends over alleged racism
- Published
England walked off the pitch during a match at the Under-15 World Cup after an allegation of racism by a Republic of Ireland player, which resulted in the game being abandoned.
Following an altercation between players from both sides, shortly before the end of the match in Azerbaijan on Monday, an England player approached his bench and made a complaint to coaching staff.
Match footage then showed England staff members relaying the complaint to the referee, alleging a racist slur had been said, and calling their players off.
Republic of Ireland were leading 4-1 at the time of the incident.
World governing body Fifa told BBC Sport it is investigating and gathering reports.
"Fifa is aware of an incident at the U-15 World Cup and Festival match between England and the Republic of Ireland," a spokesperson said.
"The match was abandoned by the referee following England's refusal to continue.
"The official reports are being gathered, and the matter will be referred to the independent disciplinary committee, who will decide in due course."
The Football Association and the Football Association of Ireland have been contacted for comment.
The aftermath of the incident
The alleged incident happened in the final minute of the Group C match in Baku.
Immediately following the allegation, England head coach Matt Thorpe was seen on the match coverage on DAZN asking for the referee to come over, before calling his players off the pitch.
After an initial report from Thorpe, the referee told England's coaching staff, "I cannot hear".
One of Thorpe's assistant coaches can then be heard telling the referee "we are reporting racism", before adding "we do not want to play".
When another official came over, talking about what would happen after the match, the assistant told him: "No, our players do not want to play".
He was later heard saying that a player was "upset".
Heated words were then exchanged between each set of coaching staff, with both saying they were trying to protect their players.
This is the first time the U15 World Cup and Festival has been played, and involves 189 countries and territories.
Matches are played in an eight-a-side format, on smaller pitches, with 20-minute halves.
England are scheduled to play their next match against Zimbabwe at 20:45 local time (16:45 GMT) on Monday, with Republic of Ireland facing Cambodia at the same time.

After personally trying dozens of couches for our buying guide, and hearing dozens of additional testimonials from my fellow testers on the WIRED Reviews team, I have a lot of strong opinions. And not every couch I've tested has been great, but even out of all the great ones, very few have stuck around. My favorite couch I've ever tried, the Eliot Sleeper Sofa from Joybird, is discounted right now, as are many of its aesthetically pleasing siblings as part of the Joybird Semi-Annual Sale. The sale is slated to end on November 1, so you should shop now for the best selection.
There are a few things to keep in mind. Joybird furniture is custom-made, so unless something is marked specifically as “Ready to Ship,” it isn't going to be dispatched as quickly as it would be from some other retailers. And while you can get 30 percent off site wide, the best deals are on best-selling items, on which you can save up to 40 percent. Most items are backed by a limited lifetime warranty and include free premium in-home delivery. You can order a free swatch kit to pick out your fabric, but unfortunately, it won't arrive in time for you to shop the sale. (Joybird usually has sales around Black Friday, too, so picking a fabric now could be good planning ahead.)
The Eliot Sleeper Sofa is so darn comfortable. It isn't so soft that you sink in and get locked there, but it's soft enough that you can chill for hours. It has a built-in pull-out mattress that has received rave reviews from myself and every guest I've ever had. Over the summer in a heat wave before I had an air conditioning unit, I found myself sleeping in the living room on the pull-out for a week. Somehow I managed to get good rest, despite the fact that my living room was approximately 100 million degrees. (Note that my model is the premium Tempur-Response memory foam mattress.)
It has some quirks; the buttons catch crumbs, the armrests aren't quite wide enough to rest a cup of coffee without some nerves involved, and sometimes I have to adjust the cushions. But I've taken enough fantastic naps on this couch that I can wholeheartedly recommend it, even if you don't get the hot pink velvet option. It's comfortable to sleep on when it's folded up as well. After more than a year of daily use, it still looks brand-new.
I can't speak to the quality of Joybird's chairs, beds, or accent furniture, since I haven't personally tried them, but I think the fact that I've kept the Elliot in my home since I reviewed it speaks for itself. If you need a furniture upgrade, this sale is worth checking out before it disappears.

India's cartoonists built an audience online - now their posts are being restricted
- Published
For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.
The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.
Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.
The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.
Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.
Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.
The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.
The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.
"Meta platforms have been restricting the reach of my cartoons for some years," Acharya told the BBC. "But when my entire profile was restricted in India, I was a little sad."
He wrote to Meta, Instagram's parent company, but received no reply. He says he was preparing to go to court when his account became accessible again in early October, only to be blocked again earlier this week for three days.
In a statement, Meta told the BBC that it may temporarily restrict accounts to comply with India's IT Rules but did not explain the specific reasons for restricting Acharya's account or Manjul's post.
Critics say the restrictions come as humour and satire play an increasingly visible role in political dissent in India, particularly among younger people.
Memes and Gen-Z humour helped fuel protests over education and jobs in July, which led to the resignation of India's education minister. Online debate has also intensified over a controversial revision of voter rolls that removed 130 million names.
The political significance of social media has not been lost on the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has urged ministers to strengthen their online presence and connect with younger audiences.
At the same time, technology policy expert Prateek Waghre says the government is increasingly using legal orders to regulate online content.
The Indian Express reported, external that government agencies sent nearly 195,000 blocking and content-restriction orders to platforms including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July through the federal government's Sahyog portal.
The figures, obtained through a right-to-information request, do not show how many posts were ultimately restricted or removed. The BBC has not seen the original response.
Waghre says that some platforms, particularly Meta, "seem more willing to comply", he says, while X appears more willing to push back. But limited public data makes comparisons difficult. Meta declined to comment on his assessment.
The government has also reportedly sought greater scrutiny of how social media platforms recommend content.
Earlier this week, several media outlets reported, external that authorities had asked Meta to ensure its systems did not steer users towards "a single or limited set of narratives" and strengthen checks on content that could "cause public disorder or incite violence".
The BBC has sought comment from India's IT ministry on the restrictions and reported instructions to Meta but has not received a response.
Of course, political satire has a long history in India - as do attempts to curb it.
Cartoons have been a fixture of Indian journalism since independence, with RK Laxman's Common Man becoming one of its most recognisable characters.
But cartoonists have also faced censorship. During the Emergency in the 1970s, when civil liberties were suspended and the press was tightly controlled, Abu Abraham continued drawing, even as dozens of his cartoons were stamped "not passed by censors".
In 2012, cartoonist Aseem Trivedi was arrested on sedition charges over cartoons allegedly mocking the Indian constitution. The charges were later dropped.
Today, concerns about restrictions on political expression extend beyond cartoonists. India ranks 157th in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, while critics accuse the government of putting growing pressure on independent media. The government rejects the criticism, saying India's media remains free and vibrant.
Comedians have also faced controversy over political satire. Kunal Kamra, known for his jokes about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his party, has faced threats, cancelled shows and legal action.
For cartoonists, however, challenging those in power is central to their work.
"We are among the default opposition," says Sandeep Adhwaryu, a cartoonist at a leading Indian newspaper.
"The nature of the craft is to oppose," he says, adding that cartoonists, like journalists, must question whoever holds power.
Acharya says he has followed that principle throughout his career. Before 2014, many of his cartoons targeted the Congress-led government and were shared by BJP leaders.
"I never faced official restrictions on my cartoons during the previous governments, though there would be some trolling occasionally," he says.
Now, with the BJP in power, much of his satire is directed at Modi's government.
Social media has allowed independent cartoonists like Acharya to reach audiences without relying on newspapers or other traditional outlets.
"We are not associated with newspapers or any mainstream media. That's why we can draw," says Manjul.
But that freedom comes with a new vulnerability - dependence on platforms that can restrict their work or cut off access to their audiences.
No one knows this better than Rachita Taneja, the creator of the hugely popular Instagram comic Sanitary Panels.
"My career would not have existed without the internet," she told the BBC. Yet she describes social media as a double-edged sword.
"At the end of the day it's a for-profit endeavour that answers to advertisers," she says.
Taneja says that Meta's compliance with Indian government requests reflects the company's commercial priorities rather than concern for users' rights. Meta declined to comment.
Even cartoonists working in traditional newsrooms face pressure. Adhwaryu says artists may soften captions, avoid certain subjects or think twice before submitting a cartoon. Over time, he says, such self-censorship can become normalised, even without explicit instructions.
Still, cartoonists have found ways to support one another.
When Acharya's Instagram account was first restricted, Taneja drew a stick-figure cartoon in solidarity. "Seeing people on the front lines creating communities, protesting, running campaigns, tirelessly fighting for their own rights and the rights of others is what keeps me going," she says.
Adhwaryu believes satire will continue to adapt. He compares cartoons and humour to a "shape-shifting virus".
"It keeps mutating in response to its environment," he says. "It will find its way."

Elon Musk gave his personal political committee, America PAC, more than $76 million in the first two weeks of October to boost Republicans in the final stretch of the midterms, according to a pre-election report the PAC filed Thursday evening with the Federal Election Commission.
The group spent nearly $43 million in the first two weeks of October, and entered the campaign’s last leg holding nearly $47 million in cash.
The Texas Senate race dominated the new spending. It drew $15.2 million, double what the PAC spent there all summer. That spending included $12.4 million to attack Democratic candidate James Talarico and $2.8 million to promote Republican Ken Paxton.
Daily filings since then show $9.1 million more against Talarico, bringing the PAC’s spending against him this cycle to nearly $28 million, about 40 percent of everything it has spent supporting or opposing candidates. The PAC also shifted toward online ads, spending $11.4 million on digital ads in the same two weeks, which is close to what it spent on mail and texting combined.
All told, Musk has given more than $445 million to Republican political groups this election cycle, according to WIRED’s analysis of FEC filings, making him the biggest known individual donor in the midterms. More than $165 million of that has gone to America PAC since July alone.
America PAC declined to comment.
Musk—who has several companies, including Tesla and SpaceX, based in Texas—has also been posting online about the race. On Wednesday, Musk posted on X that “there is something deeply wrong with Talarico,” then called him “a creep” and claimed, without evidence, that he “would vote to take away your kids and transition them.” Earlier this month, Musk amplified a false claim that Talarico had been treated at a mental health facility. Talarico shot back the same day: “There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator.”
The Texas race remains a toss-up. An Emerson College poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters, conducted October 17 to 19, found Talarico at 48 percent and Paxton at 46 percent, within the poll’s 3-point margin of error.
The stakes for Musk reach well beyond Texas. If Democrats win the House, the lawmakers in line to lead its committees have signaled they will investigate his role in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), his companies’ federal contracts, and what Zoe Lofgren, a California Democrat, called an “astounding” number of conflicts of interest. Unified Democratic control of Congress would pose even more problems for him.
Silicon Valley Democrats added another target on Friday: restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service in Ukraine. In a letter to the White House demanding an investigation, Representatives Sam Liccardo, Jimmy Panetta, and Ro Khanna vowed that the next Congress “will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk’s businesses.”

ముందుగా, ఈ విషయం గురించి ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, నిరసనల కోసం ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు ఇటువంటి పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేయడం గురించి ఎటువంటి విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా కథనాలు లభించలేదు.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, ఇందులో ఉన్న మనుషుల ముఖాలు, అక్షరాలు అస్పష్టంగా, అసహజంగా ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోని కృత్రిమ మేధ (AI) ఉపయోగించి సృష్టించి ఉండొచ్చని తెలుస్తోంది.
దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వీడియోను AI వీడియో డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్తో(ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరీక్షించగా, ఈ వీడియోను ఏఐతో రూపొందించినట్లు స్పష్టమైంది.
అలాగే, ఈ వీడియోను ముందుగా ‘Jaranor films’ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీ అప్లోడ్ (ఆర్కైవ్) చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియో AI ద్వారా చేయబడిందనే లేబుల్ ఇందులో ఉంది. ఈ పేజీ వివిధ ఏఐ వీడియోలను రూపొందిస్తుంది. గతంలో కూడా ఈ పేజీలో అప్లోడ్ చేసిన ఈఫిల్ టవర్పై పాలస్తీనా జెండా వీడియో గురించి మేము రాసిన ఫాక్ట్-చెక్ కథనాన్ని ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, నిరసనకారులను ఎదుర్కోవడానికి ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక AI వీడియోను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy
- Published
Israelis are heading to the polls for what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.
Polling published on Friday suggests incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu is in a near neck-and-neck race with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to become prime minister.
But neither of their political blocs are projected to win the 61 seats needed to form a majority government - meaning weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.
The campaign has been shaped by the issue of security - with the opposition bloc hammering Netanyahu for the unprecedented security failure that led to the 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken back to Gaza as hostages.
They have pushed for an independent commission of inquiry into the attacks - something Netanyahu has long resisted, insisting it would be biased against him.
Despite the opposition's attack lines, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security" - pointing to what he says are strategic victories in Israel's wars across the Middle East and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump.
Israel's proportional representation system means governments have always been coalitions - and the race to power can, and has, produced unexpected alliances. But this election looks especially tight - and lines in the sand have already been drawn.
Eisenkot, who leads the newly formed Yashar Party, is the main figure in the so-called "change bloc", a collection of parties who have ideological differences but share the goal of ousting Netanyahu.
Other leaders in the bloc include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security - and Yair Golan, a left-leaning former general.
For Netanyahu, a titan of Israeli politics who first served as prime minister in 1996, a return to power will hinge on another alliance with the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties that make up his current governing coalition - the most right-wing in Israel's history.
There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.
The opposition bloc also point to what they see as threats to democracy under Netanyahu, who faces an ongoing trial on corruption charges - which he denies - and is still pursuing contentious plans for reforms to the judicial system, which led to mass protests before the 7 October attacks.
On Sunday, Israel's Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu had pushed for last-minute military action that could trigger a confrontation with Iran prior to the elections - but was opposed by his own military chief Eyal Zamir. The following day, CNN reported that he had also tried to persuade Trump to carry out new strikes on Iran, but that Trump had refused to give the green light. Netanyahu denied both reports.
He also made headlines in the final days of his campaign for posting an AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb hitting Tel Aviv, warning that he is the only leader who can protect Israel "if the Iranians acquire nuclear weapons". Eisenkot called him "hysterical".
Another dominating issue has been conscription, with Netanyahu's government failing to enforce a Supreme Court ruling that ultra-Orthodox Jewish men in full-time religious study should be conscripted to the military - a highly divisive move as thousands of others have been conscripted to fight in recent wars.
Eisenkot takes a broadly similar position to Netanyahu on Gaza, and has pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through a US-led peace plan or, if necessary, military means.
Israel has continued to strike Gaza almost every day since a ceasefire was agreed last year, saying it is targeting Hamas operatives. The Israeli military has killed more than 74,000 people since the start of the war, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel has faced growing international condemnation over its conduct in the war, and relations with its allies around the world have deteriorated.
Eisenkot largely supports Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank - which are illegal under international law - but wants to crack down on extremist Jewish settlers whose attacks are at an all-time high, according to UN figures. He has also spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or a state-minus" for Palestinians - under ultimate Israeli security control.
The two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - has all but disappeared from mainstream Israeli politics.
Though some have speculated the Arab parties may end up informally propping up an Eisenkot-led minority government - Lieberman, a key prospective member, has ruled out being part of such an arrangement.
Red lines like these mean the electoral arithmetic is complex - but it remains to be seen what kind of concessions, deals and U-turns can be reached once the results come in.
An unprecedented 70,000 people have reportedly flown home from abroad to vote, while half a million are set to cast ballots for the first time.
At 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly.
Up and down the country, Israelis will gather to watch the results trickle in, with Netanyahu's Likud meeting in Jerusalem and Eisenkot's Yashar - formed only last year - assembling in Tel Aviv.
Hundreds of thousands of Israeli soldiers and reservists will also cast ballots, but many of those votes will not begin being counted until Wednesday - meaning there may be a late boon for the right-wing parties who are thought to have strong support from that demographic.
Though often framed as a run-off between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, it is possible another leader could take power, if they were to withhold their party's support for a coalition unless given the top job.
An outcome dreaded by many is political deadlock - where no bloc is able to reach a majority, and a minority government cannot be formed. In that scenario, new elections would be called, with Netanyahu to remain as interim prime minister.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties struggled time and again to co-operate.

Jordan says 'terrorists' killed in Syria in retaliatory strike over church attack
- Published
Jordan has struck what its military says were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation for an attack on a Christian funeral last week that killed nine people.
Syrian health officials told state media five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists", without giving further details.
Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government. Syria said it had not been notified of Monday's attack.
It comes after a nine people were killed and 34 injured in a shooting at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak on Friday.
In response to the strike, Syria said it had closed a border crossing with Jordan.
"The decision includes the complete suspension of passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, to ensure the safety of travellers and workers at the crossing," Syrian authorities said in a statement carried by state media.
It added that it had "opened direct channels of communication" with Jordanian officials and had launched "comprehensive investigations to establish the full circumstances of the targeting".
Nassib is the only passenger and commercial border crossing between Jordan and Syria.
Earlier on Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law over the church attack.
The Public Security Directorate (PSD) said the unnamed "terrorists" were found hiding in an abandoned house in Karak before dawn.
Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told state-affiliated TV the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack".

Trump's DOJ illegally fired ex-FBI director's daughter Maurene Comey, judge rules
The judge granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20

A federal judge ruled on Monday that the Trump administration acted illegally when it fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from her position as a federal prosecutor in New York last year.
Judge Jesse M. Furman determined that Maurene Comey, who served as an assistant U.S. attorney for ten years, was unlawfully removed in July 2025 despite handling major national cases and earning "the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike."
Comey is known for bringing criminal cases against Jeffrey Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell and music mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs during her tenure at the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's office.
Following her removal, Comey brought a lawsuit against the Justice Department and other officials, alleging her dismissal breached the First Amendment, the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause, and the constitutional separation of powers.
The judge highlighted her assertion that her firing stemmed from being the daughter of James Comey—whom President Donald Trump has long regarded as an adversary—or from assumptions regarding her perceived political affiliation and beliefs.
Furman rejected arguments presented by the government asserting that federal prosecutors could be removed at will because they exercise the president's "conclusive and preclusive" authority. He said that the government's claim that Congress lacks the authority to govern the dismissal of federal prosecutors "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."
Furman added: "Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system."
According to the ruling, the dismissal breached constitutional separation of powers, statutory provisions, Fifth Amendment due process rights, and the Administrative Procedure Act.
While reserving judgment on the First Amendment claim for further submissions, Furman indicated an inclination to throw it out as largely moot, given that Comey now works in private practice and is no longer seeking active reinstatement.
To "make her whole" and shield her from career harm resulting from the "unlawful termination," the judge ordered back pay and retroactive reinstatement covering the period between her termination and Dec. 20.
Her legal team, composed of Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali, and Margaret Donovan, praised the court's conclusion.
"This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law," they stated. "As the Court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.’ This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law."
The Justice Department did not immediately comment.
Under the Trump administration, the Justice Department has ousted numerous career employees, including agents and prosecutors connected to inquiries into Trump or seen as opposing the administration's goals, triggering several federal lawsuits.
Maurene Comey's dismissal was viewed as particularly personal due to her father's long-standing conflict with Trump.
The president removed James Comey from his post as FBI director in May 2017 while the agency investigated potential links between Russia and the Republican's victorious 2016 campaign. Trump has repeatedly demanded Comey's imprisonment over subsequent years, with the Justice Department pursuing action to varying degrees of success.
A previous criminal case charging James Comey with lying to Congress in 2020 was thrown out when a judge determined the prosecutor involved had been appointed unlawfully. A separate active indictment accuses the former FBI director of threatening Trump through an Instagram post showing seashells arranged in the pattern of "86 47"—a charge he is fighting to dismiss and which has drawn skepticism from multiple legal observers.

Arignar Anna Zoological Park in Vandalur will not be allowing visitors on October 22 and 23 as a precautionary measure following confirmation of H5N1 avian influenza infection in water birds by the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal, on October 2, 2026.
According to Forest Department officials, seven water birds in the zoo had died between October 3 and 7. Of them four were painted storks, one grey pelican, one grey heron and one oriental darter. As soon as the first bird died on October 3, the zoo officials cordoned off the area.
Immediate preventive measures, including disinfection, sanitisation, and strict implementation of biosecurity protocols, were undertaken in accordance with the Government of India’s guidelines, officials said. However, the zoo remained open as no further bird mortality or sickness has been reported since October 9.
Now that the confirmation has come, the zoo management has to follow the protocols laid out by the Centre and so the zoo would remain closed on Thursday and Friday, officials said.
This temporary measure is intended to facilitate intensive sanitisation, strengthen biosecurity measures, and ensure close monitoring of the situation. The public are requested to cooperate with the precautionary measures, a press release from the zoo said.
According to the protocol, as soon H7 avian influenza is confirmed, visitors’ entry needs to be stopped forthwith.
The movement of the vets and labourers should be restricted and in no case they should move from infected pens to healthy pens. The management of the healthy sheds should be done by a separate team. Maximum possible number of birds is to be sampled, while sampling a water body, birds arriving at different locations be taken into consideration, it should be ensured that different species are proportionately represented.
In addition to sampling of birds, environment samples like water, soil are to be collected and sent for testing, the guidelines state. The control actions to be initiated are same as for domestic poultry. However, endangered and precious captive birds confirmed as non-infected could be exempted from culling, say officials.
Sampling has to be repeated every 15 days for at least four times and if consecutive two samplings from the last positive result are found negative then the opening of the zoo for public could be considered by the competent authority, according to the action plan for prevention, control and containment of avian influenza.

More dads taking paid family leave for a new baby, sometimes as much as moms are
Dad shift: Men now file majority of paid family leave claims in key states
Karlo Campana is usually outnumbered these days. He has three young kids under age 4.
On a recent Saturday, he played a mini-game of basketball with his two older kids in their Southern California home, shooting a ball into a hoop on the door, while his baby boy watched from his bouncy chair.
Campana took paid time off in May after the birth of his son — just as he did for his daughters.
It's sometimes called "bonding" or "family" leave, to distinguish it from the paid leave ("maternity" or "disability" leave) that mothers can take to physically recover from childbirth.
"You need that adjustment period," he said. Campana, who works at an ad agency, said having the time off not to think about work — or worry about losing income during that time — was crucial for him and his family during a sleep-deprived period.
"My wife isn't doing it on her own," he said. "She doesn't feel like she's alone on this journey. She feels like she has support." He jokes that by kid No. 3, he thought he had nailed diaper changes without too much mess — but he was wrong.
"The benefits are I get to spend time with each of them when they were in the infant stage, the baby stage, and I get to hold them and, you know, change the poopy diapers," he said. " It's like the funny moments of, like, being a parent, like, 'This is it right here, you're in the thick of it.'"
Campana is among a growing number of fathers who take leave to bond with a new child in the states that offer paid family leave programs — and are part of a larger cultural shift that has seen dads handle more caregiving duties.
In California — as in several other states — men make up about half of bonding claim applications. Last year, men even surpassed women — as in Colorado and Washington — for the first time in the state's history. This trend comes at a time when the federal government has said it wants Americans to have more babies, and families report affordability is an obstacle in raising them.
There's no federal law guaranteeing paid parental leave, but California is one of 14 states, plus Washington, D.C., that have passed legislation to enact paid family leave programs — and in many of those places, more dads are opting in.
"We're in a very different place in terms of our understanding of gender roles, of paternity leave, of dads' roles than we were 20-plus years ago," said Molly Weston Williamson, policy director at Paid Leave for All, an organization that advocates for paid family leave policies.
California's program offers, within a year, up to eight weeks of paid bonding leave for parents after a birth, adoption, or foster care placement. That's on top of six to eight weeks of paid disability leave that moms get to recover after birth.
Campana said he initially wasn't sure if he should take paternity leave because of lingering gender stereotypes.
" I felt guilty, for sure," Campana said. " I think dads maybe feel they need to be the provider. They need to be the ones that are only helping their family by bringing money or working."
Campana said that when he was growing up, his father worked three jobs. "It was hard for him to be present, and I think that's the one thing now — it's like, 'No, be present. Be there for your kids.'"
Research has shown that paternity leave confers benefits beyond allowing a father extra time to bond with a new child: It has positive effects on the whole family, including better health outcomes for both parents.
Paid parental leave has also been linked to lower odds of postpartum depression and a decrease in infant mortality rates.
In California, men accounted for 51% of bonding claims filed in 2025. It's a massive shift from when the state program started in 2004, and men made up about 18% of claim applications.
States fund their paid family and medical leave programs with different combinations of employer and employee contributions; California is among six states where family leave is entirely funded by employee payroll deductions.
In addition to changing gender norms, Williamson said other factors are likely contributing to the increase in claims by men in the state: greater awareness about the program, and recent changes to the benefit.
In 2025, the state boosted the amount of income a worker can recoup while on family leave. Now, in California and in other states, the leave benefit can be as high as 90% of their regular salary.
"That makes it a realistic option for a lot more families, and I think we're seeing dads and moms responding to that change," Williamson said. Still, she said, there's a lot the new data about dads isn't telling us.
"We're getting one particular vantage point into this data, which is useful and valuable, but it's only telling us sort of part of the story, and we'd need other kinds of information to better understand the full picture," Williamson said.
"Is it that more dads are working and therefore are potentially eligible for these benefits? Is it that women are deciding not to take leave?"
While private employers can offer their own paid leave as a benefit, this data also reflects only people who took leave through California's paid family leave program.
A spokesperson for the California Employment Development Department, which administers the state's family leave program, said the department couldn't provide definitive reasons for the increase in male bonding claims.
One thing is clear: The growth in these states comes as more parents are feeling strained economically.
President Trump has said, "We want more babies," and has promoted policy initiatives like expanding access to in vitro fertilization and offering investment accounts for newborns.
"People really are very worried about the affordability of kids," said Jeremy Pope, a professor of political science at Brigham Young University, and a principal investigator of the American Family Survey.
According to the latest survey in 2025, 7 in 10 Americans said raising children had become unaffordable, according to the survey. It was the biggest single-year jump since the survey started more than a decade ago.
"I don't think they want government involved in the decision to have kids," Pope said. "But they worry a lot about how much it costs and they would like to see ways of making those costs smaller or getting help with those costs."
The Pew Research Center found in a recent survey of full-time working parents who are not self-employed, 84% said paid parental, family, or medical leave would be "extremely or very helpful" to them, but only half said it was available to them.

This update is available today for Halide Mark III users, and Lux Optics suggested that further Duo-focused features are in the works.
