'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
- Published
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.
Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.
The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.
She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"
Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.
In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.
The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.
The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.
A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.
The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.
At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.
The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.
The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.
At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

Ukraine is mounting grenade launchers on ground robots, allowing its forces to bring useful firepower closer to Russian troops without sending in soldiers to pull the trigger.
Grenades have long been important in Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion, particularly in close-quarters trench combat, but the battlefield is changing.
Troops increasingly fight in smaller force concentrations from scattered defensive positions rather than heavily manned continuous trench networks. Meanwhile, the growing "kill zone, which is swarming with drones, makes it harder for troops to approach these front-line positions. While infantry remains critically important, drones and robots are bridging the gap and taking over more and more missions, from logistics to medevac to assault.
Defense manufacturers told Business Insider that grenade launchers are increasingly being mounted on uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs, allowing soldiers to strike Russian positions from a safer distance.
Oleg Fedoryshyn, the director of R&D for the Ukrainian robotic and defense company DevDroid, told Business Insider that grenade launchers are useful because soldiers "don't need to see the enemy to hit him."
A soldier in hiding is easier to hit with a grenade launcher than, say, a machine gun, which is a line-of-sight weapon.
Now, soldiers can mount them on ground robots so that they don't have to put themselves in harm's way. A soldier-carried grenade launcher might have a range of a few hundred meters, but using a robot, an operator can be tens of kilometers away.
DevDroid's TW-40 ground robotic system has a range of 70 kilometers on paved roads and up to 50 kilometers off-road, making it effective in the kill zone. And the mounted grenade launcher has a reach of 1.5 kilometers.
Ukraine has been using soldier-carried and truck-mounted grenade launchers since before Russia began its full-scale invasion in February 2022. The robots deliver similar firepower without risking human lives.
Ukraine's Third Army Corps, for example, said in September that it used grenade launchers on robots to "dismantle enemy positions" in its Operation Vivaldi, characterizing it as "a new tactic."
"Equipped with dual Bullspike grenade launchers, the UGVs attacked Russian positions before detonating directly inside the enemy's shelters. The occupiers believed they were under assault by an entire assault squad; in reality, they were being pulverized by the Third Assault Brigade's robots," the brigade wrote on Telegram.
It said that robots were able to strike, put psychological pressure on Russian forces, and clear the position "all without putting our infantry at risk."
"This is a tactic never before seen in the history of warfare. The robots were controlled by operators from a secure shelter located tens of kilometers away from the front line."
Robots armed with grenade launchers are another example of how this war is blending elements of old warfare with new, advanced technologies. In this war, it's not uncommon to see drones dropping grenades or electronic warfare sharing the battlefield with artillery.
In addition to grenade launchers, robots can also fire other weapons, such as RPGs and American-made M2 Browning machine guns.
DevDroid's goal with its systems is "to change all roles that we can change to save people's lives," Fedoryshyn said.
That goal is shared by Ukraine's soldiers, defense industry, and leadership. Oleksandr Yabchanka, the head of the robotic systems for Ukraine's Da Vinci Wolves Battalion, told Business Insider that Ukraine is constantly working to increase the distance between troops and the fighting.
"Our philosophy is, above all, to preserve our personnel," he explained. "We strive to position our fighters as far as possible from the line of contact and the zones of highest risk — the so-called 'kill zones.'"
Other manufacturers say they're seeing a shift in how soldiers use armed robots in combat.
Defense firm Frontline Robotics makes the Buria autonomous remote weapon station, which allows soldiers to fire grenade launchers and other weapons remotely. Early last year, Ukrainian forces were hiding them in prepared locations to stop Russian advances.
"But right now, everything has changed," Mykyta Rozhkov, chief business development officer, told Business Insider, pointing to the growing drone saturation on the battlefield.
Now, it's being mounted on UGVs, creating small tanks that can advance toward Russian positions without exposing troops.
DevDroid's Fedoryshyn said robots armed with grenade launchers are most effective when paired with robots carrying machine guns and aerial drones that can spot targets and direct fire.
Robots can be used to transport gear, evacuate the wounded, blow up enemy positions, lay mines, and fire various types of weaponry. Their use has increased dramatically. Ukraine's defense ministry said in June that it had contracted over 22,000 uncrewed ground vehicles so far in 2026, nearly twice as many as all of the previous year.
The Da Vinci Wolves' Yabchanka said that he sees that "many units have begun employing UGVs. This usage has already become widespread. Ground-based robotic systems are becoming an integral part of combat operations for most units deployed along the line of contact."
As UGV use grows, Rozhkov said that Frontline Robotics' goal is to "provide different robotic solutions to get people outside the danger zone. So just to keep the line with the robots."

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the "Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability" initiative on Sept. 30.
Fox News reported the 90-day requirement on Oct. 25 and quotes department spokesperson Sean Parnell throughout the article. Though Parnell shared the report on X that day, he has not confirmed the 90-day requirement.
In October, a claim circulated online that the Pentagon had announced an initiative called FORTRESS that would require military bases in the U.S. to be able to operate for at least 90 days without relying on civilian power, fuel, water or supply lines.
For example, one Facebook user who made and posted a video about the alleged measure wrote (archived):
The Pentagon just Built a 90- Day Survival Plan.
Under FORTRESS (Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability), every major U.S. military base is being ordered to operate for 90 days with no civilian power, fuel, water, or supply chains, using portable nuclear reactors, microgrids, and stockpiles. The military is hardening itself for a grid-down war. Civilians are on their own.
Snopes readers contacted us to ask about the initiative, while similar posts about FORTRESS and what it entails also circulated on Instagram and Reddit (archived, archived).
FORTRESS is a real Department of Defense initiative and social media posts detailing what it involves are broadly accurate. The acronym stands for "Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability." Though the measure itself is new, it also includes some energy and manufacturing-related programs that already exist within the DOD.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced FORTRESS during a speech in Quantico, Virginia, on Sept. 30. His speech and a department memo released that day describe the initiative as an "insurance policy" for the United States.
On Oct. 25, Fox News reported more details about the measure (archived), mainly saying it would require U.S. military bases to "keep operating for at least 90 days without outside support."
Fox News reported Defense Department spokesperson Sean Parnell has led the initiative. Parnell is quoted throughout Fox's report, which he posted to X (archived) that day. His posting of the article, however, does not explicitly confirm the 90-day operating requirement. Therefore, we've rated this claim mostly true.
Snopes contacted the DOD for official confirmation of the 90-day requirement and any additional information it could provide about the FORTRESS initiative. We await a reply to our inquiry.
FORTRESS merges existing DOD programs
The Sept. 30 department memo says FORTRESS would focus on five pillars: "Energy independence; supply-chain and defense-industrial base resilience; a strategic defense reserve; installation hardening and cyber resilience; and resilience in space and spectrum."
Hegseth explained the changes the initiative would bring as follows (at 32:07):
Every major military installation in America is going to generate its own power independent of the civilian grid. If an adversary takes down the grid by cyber attack, by sabotage or by any means, our bases stay lit. Our aircraft keep flying. Our command centers never go dark.
We're bringing our critical supply chains home: the rare earths, the specialty metals, the semiconductors, the propellants mined in America, refined in America, built in America by American workers.
We are building long-overdue strategic reserves deep enough to fight through disruption. Think munitions, fuel, medicine, blood. Deep enough that if the world's supply lines break, and in a real war they're going to break, America keeps fighting anyway.
We're hardening every installation on American soil against cyber intrusion, sabotage and drones.
And we're securing the high ground and the airwaves, our satellites, our spectrum, our ability to see, to navigate and to talk to one another.
Fox News reported that a "central concern" that FORTRESS would address is the military's reliance on the civilian power grid. Under the first pillar of "energy independence," Fox News said the measure would see the U.S. military developing its own sources of power such as "portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids."
Around a month before the DOD made FORTRESS public, the department had already announced five vendors to build and operate nuclear microreactors at Fort Benning, Georgia; Fort Bragg, North Carolina; Fort Campbell, Kentucky; and Fort Drum, New York; and Fort Hood, Texas, as part of the Janus Program.
That program aims to supply U.S. military bases with "the energy resilience necessary to project combat power globally, without relying on potentially vulnerable external grids," according to the DOD, and seeks to build at least 20 microreactors.
FORTRESS would reportedly also use another existing DOD program — the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network — to identify domestic factories that could switch to manufacturing for the military in a crisis even if normal supply chains are disrupted.
Hegseth said during his Sept. 30 speech that FORTRESS was not meant to spread concerns about war on American soil. Rather, he said (at 33:56):
We'll make certain that America cannot be starved out, shut down or cut off. A fortress is not a place where you hide from. It's a ground you stand on, the foundation you fight from, the strength that lets you reach anywhere in the world, precisely because you are fully prepared at home.
It is unclear how the initiative would affect civilian disaster preparedness. Writing in The Wall Street Journal on Oct. 9, Tim Echols, who has served on the Georgia Public Services Commission since 2011, suggested the initiative could benefit consumers. Echols wrote that "the learning curve for building nuclear is paid for by the government" through microreactors for U.S. bases, whose technology could also apply to civilian power grids.
Echols also suggested that lessening demand for electricity in cities that provide substantial power to military bases would allow those power companies to retire older units and replace them with more-efficient ones.
Conversely, the user who made and posted the aforementioned Facebook video suggested FORTRESS would leave civilians "on their own" by taking away investment from shared resources.
The U.S. government provides disaster preparedness advice for civilians on Ready.gov.

Ghost of Yōtei studio Sucker Punch reportedly lays off 24 workers
The developer released a well-received expansion for the game just a few weeks ago.
More video game industry workers are out of a job after Sucker Punch Productions carried out layoffs. The Ghost of Yōtei developer let go 24 workers on Monday, as Aftermath reports. The developer is said to have roughly than 200 employees, though exact counts aren't available. Regardless, it lost a significant number of its staff a little over a week before parent company Sony reports its latest quarterly earnings.
"After carefully observing the challenges in the market and reviewing the team needs for our next project, we've decided to make some staffing reductions. Several positions across Sucker Punch will be eliminated as a result," the studio told staff in a memo obtained by Aftermath. "We know this is a lot to take in, and we want to assure you that we did not make this decision lightly. We have given this a lot of attention and worked to support our affected colleagues during this transition as well as we can. [...] There's no getting around that this is a hard day. Next week we will go into more details about the future."
Ghost of Yōtei was released in October last year and it racked up 3.3 million sales in its first month. Sucker Punch released a well-received expansion just a few weeks ago.
Unlike its predecessor (which sold 13 million copies in its first four years), Ghost of Yōtei does not appear to be coming to PC. A port was seemingly almost ready before it was reported earlier this year that Yōtei, Saros and future first-party single-player games would remain exclusive to the PS5.
This is yet another blow for workers in the video game industry, which has laid off tens of thousands of employees over the last few years. Just last week, EA closed BioWare and cut around 400 jobs.
There are certainly more layoffs on the way. Xbox said in July it would shed around 3,200 workers over the following 12 months, with hundreds of those still to come. It most recently laid off 268 workers in September.
Meanwhile, the fate of Arkane remains uncertain. It was reported last week that the studio had until November 13 to find a buyer or face closure. However, Microsoft has given Arkane, which is said to be in the final stretch of development on Marvel's Blade, more time.
"We have extended the consultation period by one additional month as we explore options, including finding a partner to support the studio through the development work still ahead," a company representative told PC Gamer on Friday. "This is a defined extension, and we remain committed to keeping the Works Council informed throughout the process."

In a major defence acquisition push, India on Monday cleared procurement of a range of military platforms and weapon systems, including light multi-role helicopters, long-range Kamikaze drones and radars, at a cost of ₹2.12 lakh crore to boost the combat prowess of the defence forces.
The procurement proposals were approved by the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), the defence ministry's highest decision-making body on military procurement. It was chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh.
The DAC accorded Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) or in-principle administrative approval to various capital acquisition proposals of an estimated cost of about ₹2,12,000 crore, the defence ministry said.
For the Indian Army, approval was accorded for the procurement of high mobility vehicles (HMVs), self-propelled tracked gun system, gun shot response system (GSRS), light multi-role helicopters (LMRH), very short-range air defence system (VSHORADS) and counter unmanned aerial system (C-UAS), it said.
The DAC also cleared the acquisition of other unmanned aerial system, surveillance aerial vehicles, integrated surveillance and strike system and long-range Kamikaze drone system for the Army.
While the HMVs are expected to enhance operational capabilities, logistical support and mobility in challenging terrains, the self-propelled tracked gun system will provide mobility and firepower to mechanised formations.
The GSRS will serve as a force multiplier, providing real-time situational awareness, the ministry said.
It said the LMRH will be used by both the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force for a range of purposes including reconnaissance and surveillance, combat, search and rescue of troops, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief.
The VSHORADS will engage new-generation small-size aerial threats, while C-UAS will enhance the survivability of tanks in the modern battlefield. The surveillance and drone systems will enhance the surveillance and targeting capabilities of the Indian Army, according to the ministry.
For the Indian Navy, approval was given for the procurement of active offboard decoy system (AODS) and other major naval platforms. The AODS will enhance the credibility of anti-missile defence, especially against modern anti-ship missiles of adversaries, the ministry said.
The indigenously designed and constructed major naval platforms will possess modern-day warfare capabilities and enhance the combat capability of the navy, it said.
The DAC approved procurement of helicopters, air defence systems and weapons and mobile X-band Doppler weather radar system to enhance the air defence and warfighting capabilities of the force.
"The procurement of special utility helicopters will help the Indian Air Force to meet the important air transport requirements. The X-band Doppler weather radar system will provide high-resolution, localised weather surveillance in forward areas," the ministry said in a statement.
Out of the total AoNs accorded, approximately 82 per cent of the procurements will be made from the Indian industry, it noted.

Rama Rao Malla, the son of a farmer from Anakapalli, went on to earn a B.Ed., an M.Sc. and a Ph.D. in biochemistry from Andhra University. During Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Prof. Malla, of the Department of Life Sciences at the Gandhi Institute of Technology and Management (GITAM) (Deemed to be University), is leading research to develop a blood test for one of the most aggressive forms of breast cancer.
The first graduate in his family, Prof. Malla has been a teacher for more than three decades. He joined GITAM early in his career in 2001 and, after completing postdoctoral work at the University of Illinois College of Medicine, returned to set up the university’s cancer research laboratory in 2011. He has guided 14 doctoral scholars and completed several projects on breast cancer, with four more under way, he says.
His current research focuses on triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), which lacks the receptors for oestrogen, progesterone and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), the targets of certain cancer therapies. Patients are treated mainly with chemotherapy, to which many develop resistance. TNBC accounts for 10% to 15% of breast cancers, he says, and is increasingly being diagnosed in women in their mid-30s and 40s. Mammography may miss small tumours, particularly in younger women. “If we can identify this cancer at an early stage, we can successfully eliminate the tumours by surgery,” he says.
The project, titled “Exploring Serum Exosomal microRNAs as Minimally-Invasive Biomarkers for Early Diagnosis of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer”, has been sanctioned under the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)’s “Follow-on Nischayak Anveshan” Extramural Grants programme, with Prof. Malla as the principal investigator. He says the project has an outlay of more than ₹2 crore over three years.
The study will examine exosomes, nanosized vesicles released by cells, including tumour cells. Their microRNA content can reflect that of the cells from which they originate. The researchers will compare serum samples from patients with early-stage TNBC, provided by the Mahatma Gandhi Cancer Hospital & Research Institute (MGCHRI) and the GITAM Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (GIMSR), with samples from healthy women. Sequencing and digital polymerase chain reaction (PCR) will be used to identify candidate microRNAs, and a machine-learning model will be trained to distinguish patients with early-stage TNBC from healthy individuals. The ultimate objective is to develop a kit-based test.
“We hope we can achieve something after three years that will be useful for society,” he says.
The co-investigators are P. Kiranmayi, P. Vasudevaraju, A. Krishna Chaitanya and M. Srivenkatesh of the GITAM School of Science; K. Viswa Kalyan of GIMSR; and V. Muralikrishna of MGCHRI.
The World Health Organization advises that any abnormal breast lump should be examined by a health professional, even if it is painless.

Heavenly Creatures killer Pauline Parker dies in Orkney, aged 88
- Published
To her neighbours and friends, Hilary Nathan was a quiet, religious woman who ran a riding stable in the small Orcadian island of Burray.
But her death in an island care home last week at the age of 88 closes a chapter on an extraordinary life that began 70 years ago on the other side of the world with a sensational murder trial.
As a 16-year-old and under her birth name of Pauline Parker, she was convicted alongside her schoolfriend Juliet Hulme of the murder of her mother Honora Parker.
The case shocked New Zealand – and the rest of the world.
The court heard the girls had become inseparable at Christchurch Girls' High School. Fearing that they'd be separated following the divorce of Juliet's parents and a planned move to South Africa, they plotted to kill Mrs Parker, who they believed stood in their way.
They lured her to a park and bludgeoned her to death with a brick inside a stocking.
By the time filmmaker Sir Peter Jackson was born in 1961, both girls had served five years in prison, been released, given new identities, and left New Zealand for good.
"It was known for its tabloid sensational aspect. I know a lot of English tabloids flew to Christchurch, New Zealand, to cover the case of the 'evil schoolgirl killers'," he told the BBC's Late Show in 1995.
"Repeating that stuff would have been easy, but that's not what we wanted to do. We wanted to understand more about Pauline Parker and Juliet Hulme, and what made them become friends."
His film Heavenly Creatures starred Kate Winslet as Hulme and Melanie Lynskey as Parker. It showed how their intense friendship spilled over into a strange shared fantasy life which culminated in the brutal murder.
The defence argued insanity, but both girls were found guilty of murder and only avoided the death penalty because of their age.
In 1960, having served five years in separate prisons, they were given new identities and moved away from New Zealand.
The court ordered that they should never meet again, and yet they lived part of their lives about 80 miles (129km) apart.
When the film came out in 1995, Juliet was living in Portmahomack in Rosshire, where she'd become a crime writer living under her new name, Anne Perry.
She told the Late Show that she didn't plan to see the film.
"It would be too harrowing," she said. "What was close to the truth would be distressing and what was far from the truth would be even more distressing."
"It's a bit like being stripped naked in the High Street for everyone to come and look and pick and poke. I'd rather put my clothes on and go back home, thank you."
During filming, Kate Winslet said she had no idea where the two women were, and after Anne Perry's identity was revealed, the actress expressed the hope that Pauline Parker would be able to retain her anonymity.
"These are two women who, for the last 40 years, have had to overcome so much in order to get on with their lives and just survive," she said.
"I hope she is never found."
But in 2011, Parker was found by lawyer and true-crime author Peter Graham, who had written a book about the case called So Brilliantly Clever, its title taken from her diary, which was used as evidence in court.
She, like Juliet, had come to the UK, where she had settled in a small village in rural Kent and opened a riding school. By 2011, and now known as Hilary Nathan, she had moved to Orkney, running another stable.
For both women, religion and small tight-knit communities provided a haven. According to an interview her sister gave to the New Zealand Women's Weekly, Nathan was a devout Catholic who led a reclusive life.
Perry was a Mormon, enjoying the support of her own community when reporters began to arrive after Heavenly Creatures was released.
She said: "The media descended on Portmahomack. I was horrified, especially since my mother lived in the village. It's not just the people the film is about, it's all the people around them. I felt it might ruin my family."
Although her books were hugely successful in America, she never really found the fame she merited here in the UK, partly because of her reticence to do any promotion.
Prime Suspect creator Lynda La Plante expressed interest in a TV version of Perry's books, but the author vetoed the plan for the same reason.
In 2001, I visited Perry in Portmahomack for a rare interview for Newsnight Scotland. At that stage, she was a glamorous author, with a back catalogue which had sold 15 million copies around the world.
"I think after 51 years, you can let it go," she told me. "It's not who I am now. It's not who I have been for decades."
We didn't talk about the murder directly, but you don't have to look far in her books for insight into what happened and how her life had turned out. Her detective, the Victorian policeman William Monk, suffers from amnesia, and sometimes wonders exactly who he is.
"Monk sees himself as just himself but because of his memory loss, he has to deal with the fact that he may be someone else. That comes from my own sense that other people view me as a monster," she admitted.
"Of course it affects what I write. I have far more compassion and understanding for people who do wrong things than I'd ever have if I hadn't been in that position.
"The questions of right and wrong and compassion and forgiveness concern me in a way they wouldn't have, had I not had the life I had."
Anne Perry died in Los Angeles in 2023 at the age of 84.
Hilary Nathan's death last week brings their strange story to a close.
How they reinvented themselves out of the world's harshest headlines, and found redemption in the smallest of Scottish communities.
"I would say if you had something which harrowed you, or caused you to feel shame, you should never give up," Anne told me.
"There's more forgiveness, understanding and help out there than you might think."

A video (here & here) purportedly showing US Senator Richard Blumenthal calling India a failed state with a collapsing economy is being shared on social media as a genuine video. Let’s verify the authenticity of this clip.
Claim: The video depicts genuine footage of US Senator Richard Blumenthal calling India a failed state with a collapsing economy.
Fact: The video is an AI-generated deepfake. The original footage is from a September 2026 press conference where the Senator merely urged India and China to stop buying Russian oil, and he did not make any derogatory statements about India. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the original, full-length footage (here & here) from 17 September 2026. The video shows a bipartisan press conference following a House vote on a Russia and Iran sanctions bill.
In this video, Senator Blumenthal urged India and China to stop buying Russian oil and to seek alternative sources. However, he did not make any of the comments heard in the viral video. We then analysed the viral clip using AI video detection tools (here & here), which confirmed that the footage had been digitally altered.
Furthermore, a PIB Fact Check also confirmed that the video is a deepfake and that the Senator made no such statement.
To sum it up, the viral video is an AI-generated deepfake, and Senator Blumenthal never made the derogatory remarks about India being a failed state.

The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site.
The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing
Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.
The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. On the retailer’s website, an item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart. Using Meta’s Muse, The Verge was able to instruct the AI agent to continuously re-add The RealReal listings in a shopping cart as soon as the 20-minute hold had expired, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing products for hours or longer.
After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge’s story. The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out, Friang said. Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages, Friang said, adding that the company will continue to strengthen protections as AI-powered online shopping evolves.
Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Technology companies are selling agents as personalized assistants for billions of people — always-on, compliant entities that will schedule meetings, throw parties, and purchase things for human users. So far, agents and shopping seem to go hand in hand; Meta said in its Q3 earnings call this month that it was the most common use case for Muse so far, and that purchases were over $200 on average. Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents: The company said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days.
But robots shopping for things instead of humans has the potential to upend the balance of the web as we know it. For one, if humans stop visiting websites directly and instead access the web through chatbots, businesses become one step removed from their customers. Retailers — most notably Amazon — have recognized that reality could disrupt their bottom line, especially advertising revenue, and have blocked agents from shopping on their sites.
An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website. There is, of course, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive. An agent in contrast does not care. It is perhaps precisely the type of busywork a fashion-forward person might pay an actual personal assistant to do on their behalf. Now, a capability like this is at the fingertips of millions of consumers, and they are just beginning to learn how to take advantage of it. Retailers, too, are playing catch-up.

They also serve science, who are not scientists. One of science’s most egregious instances of epistemic dominance, where a powerful institution overrode and exploited a marginalised individual - was Henrietta Lacks – donor of the famous, immortal HeLa cell line. Cells extracted from her, without permission, transformed medical research, but her story was ignored, erased and obscured for decades. The scientific world that generously used this unique cell line for successful research into virology, vaccines, genetics and even cancer care, but the erasure of the donor of those cells was historic in its completeness.
Lacks, an African American tobacco farmer from southern United States, sought treatment at the ‘coloured ward’ in Johns Hopkins Centre for cervical cancer, way back in 1951. While it was common for medical professionals, in those days, to take samples and cells without the express permission of the patient, particularly if it was an African American woman, these cells were different. Johns Hopkins used the cells from her tumour to culture a line of cells that was extraordinarily durable outside the body. Usually human cells die outside of the body. Anonymised by a laboratory acronymn, Lacks’ cells (HeLa) turned out to be the first human cells to successfully grow, divide, and survive indefinitely outside the human body.
HeLa was a miracle that scientists had chanced upon. With HeLa, they could mass produce human cells in a standard format that could be used for biomedical research, and would underpin several breakthrough discoveries, that would revolutionise medical care. No one knew, however, of the immense exploitation behind this miracle cell line, and the profound lack of consent in procuring the samples.
Lacks, who died at merely 31 years, and was buried in an unmarked grave, remained invisible, not even a footnote, completely uncredited and her family entirely in the dark about her contribution to the world of science. Henrietta Lacks’ family first learned about her cells in nearly quarter of a century later, when scientists reached out to them, requesting blood samples once they suspected that the HeLa cell line had contaminated other research samples. This came as a bolt on the family, who could not fathom how cells from their mother had survived this long outside of her, and how this strange situation had come to be. While the academic world and several sections of the corporate world benefited richly from the HeLa cell line, Lacks’ own family had remained entrenched in poverty and struggling to make ends meet. The struggle of the family to come to terms with this exploitation, and the battles they had to fight with the system and science itself is well curated by Rebecca Sloot in her best selling book The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks.
In the 1950s, bioethical norms, particularly around informed consent were either non existent, or, at best, weak. But, in this particular case, Lacks was a black farmer from a rural unit, being treated in a segregated section in a large hospital. Consequently, an entrenched rascism, still alive in the southern United States in the 50s, and class bias contributed in good measure to the shabby treatment of this very valuable patient. Unhesitatingly and boldly, Sloot dragged this out into the open, through the book, knocking on the consciousness of the world and science, biomedical research, urging a discussion, a debate and at the end of it, a nod to what happened. It took years before these units would shamefully acknowledge the great injustice meted out to Lacks’ and her family.
The book, published in 2010, drew attention to the larger debate of patient rights and bodily autonomy. Sloot also underlined the fact that donors need to be acknowledged, heralding a new woke world of bio ethics, laboratory practices and the responsibilities of researchers. No longer could a moral failure be allowed to take patients for a ride, rules and regulations should replace the conscience and a situation like this would hopefully never happen again.
But this story does not end this way. After nearly 75 years of fighting this battle, the Lacks’ family finally found some closure. Reparation was finally achieved with the family settling with Johns Hopkins and other associated institutions in a landmark agreement that firstly acknowledged harm had been done, and also included measures to compensate the family and honour Lacks’ role in science. This included significant financial recompense, and involving the family into research using HeLa cells.
This agreement did reinforce the supremacy of informed consent practices, thus refining research ethics policy, but it also expanded the involvement of the patient and the community in research work. The Lacks’ family success is a milestone of sorts in biomedical research, with calls now being made to improve how institutions and labs credit how their biological materials, and also look at reparative action for families historically exploited by science.
Lacks’ story is a cautionary tale for science. It’s a reckoning with what has historically gone wrong, to set some wrongs right , and make sure the violations of the past are not repeated, but do inform the future, so that scientific progress can proceed without losing respect for human dignity. For this stupendous achievement, we have Henrietta Lacks to thank. From being denied even the footnote in history, she has created a brave new world in science.

Quick Answer
The Fitbit Edge is a $179.99 fitness tracker with a 1.34-inch AMOLED display, built-in GPS, ECG, replaceable battery, and up to seven days of battery life. It also offers Google Maps navigation, Gemini-powered coaching, advanced health tracking, and a special Stephen Curry edition.
The fitness world may be in a “to screen or not to screen” state, with fitness bands without screens gaining popularity, but Google is clearly keeping its Fitbit feet in both screen and screenless fitness trackers. Days after launching its Fitbit Air screenless tracker in India, the Search giant has launched the Fitbit Edge, a fitness tracker with a display that sits right in the middle of the Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5, both in terms of pricing (it starts at USD 179.99, well above the USD 99.99 of the Fitbit Air but well below the USD 399.99 of the Pixel Watch 5) and display size. Only time will tell whether it will hit the golden middle ground between “lots of display” and “no display at all,” but while we wait for the Fitbit Edge to hit stores later this month (and indeed, hopefully arrive in India soon), here are twelve points worth noting about the latest Fitbit in fitness town:
Table of Contents
A big display in an increasingly no-display zone
In a fitness band world that seems to be aiming to become more and more screen-less, the Fitbit Edge comes with a big-gish display for a fitness tracker. It has a 1.34-inch AMOLED, always-on display, which is 46 percent bigger than the one on the Charge 6, its predecessor. It is also much brighter and has Gorilla Glass 3 protection. Fitbit actually claims it is the brightest and biggest display on a Fitbit fitness tracker. Should the Fitbit Air be jealous?
Wear it without Wear OS: Fitbit OS onboard
It comes from Google and also has a display on board like the Pixel Watch 5, which has led many to assume that the Fitbit Edge must be running on Wear OS, but that is not the case. The Fitbit Edge actually runs on Fitbit OS. And like all Google fitness devices, it also uses the Google Health app to keep track of your data and give you fitness inputs. While this means you get relatively less distraction and only basic notifications, it also means you do not get access to third-party apps on the device.
Bye bye Haptic, Hello real button!
One of the biggest headaches of the Fitbit Charge 6 was its pressure-sensitive, haptic touch button, which many of us struggled to use (it almost had a vibe of its own). Thankfully, the Fitbit Edge fixes that and brings a physical button on the side for controls. We couldn’t be more glad. The haptic control on the Charge 6 was a bit of a pain and messed up what was (and still is) a superb fitness tracker.
A battery that can be removed and replaced
Most modern devices have given up on the concept of a removable battery, which was sad because once the battery of a device died, it tended to render an otherwise perfectly good device useless, unless one went in for complex engineering. That, however, has been changing thanks to regulations from the EU, and the Fitbit Edge comes with a removable battery. Which means you can simply remove the battery and replace it if its health deteriorates, increasing the life of the fitness tracker.
Very Air-y battery life
In terms of battery life, the Fitbit Edge rather surprisingly has the same battery life as the display-less Fitbit Air – about a week. However, keeping the always-on-display feature on reduces this to a rather low two days.
Metal frames that can take an ECG…and save your life (in select countries)
The Fitbit Edge’s metal frame can be used to take a 30-second manual ECG. This can highlight heart rate irregularities and can also spot signs of AFib. The tracker also has an optical PPG heart rate sensor that continuously tracks one’s heart and pulse rate and alerts the user if their heart rate is unusually high or low. The catch is that the ECG is only available in select countries, but it is still great to see an ECG on a fitness tracker – a feature seen generally in premium smartwatches.
Take it swimming
Much like its screen-less sibling, the Fitbit Air, the Fitbit Edge too is pretty sturdy. The device comes with 5 ATM water resistance, which means you can easily take it along for your swim sessions. The device also features IP68 dust and water resistance, and as we mentioned earlier, Gorilla Glass 3 protection.
Comes with GPS and is stair-worthy
The Fitbit Edge has an improved and built-in GPS, something the Air lacks, so you do not need to carry your phone along to cover outdoor workouts and activities. It has multi-constellation support, which is paired with a new antenna and chip, making the device up to 40 percent better at tracking locations than the Charge 6. The Edge has another edge over the Air – an integrated altimeter, which can detect changes in altitude, and comes in handy not only while counting stairs but also during hikes and trekking, where you can accurately measure altitude change.
Get Google Maps directions on your wrist:
The Fitbit Edge might not have Google Wear, but it works in sync with Google Maps on your phone and can show you turn-by-turn directions on your wrist. The feature requires you to have an active Bluetooth connection between your phone and the Fitbit Edge, and directions will start popping up on your tracker screen when you start walking, running, cycling, or even driving. That big display really helps!
Quick Notifications, quicker actions but no call support:
The Edge has a mixed relationship with your smartphone. It is a few steps ahead of the Air in terms of notifications, or some might say behind it in terms of a distraction-free experience. You get basic call, message, and app notifications on the tracker, and also get quick reply and navigation access on it. However, you cannot use it to handle calls because the device does not have a mic or a speaker. You can accept a call from the tracker, but it will be directed to your smartphone.
Google Health Guardian’s on your wrist
Earlier limited to the more expensive Pixel Watches, Google’s Health Guardian is available on the Fitbit Edge. This comes with cardiovascular tracking and alerts, alerts for potential breathing and pulse issues, and tracking of trends in the background to create monthly reports on blood pressure and even insulin resistance. It also unlocks premium features of the Google Health app, like personalized coaching and deeper tracking and analysis.
Gemini present, but cannot be summoned:
The Fitbit Edge comes with personalized Gemini coaching to help you meet your health and fitness goals. But complete access to all of Gemini’s features requires a subscription, and you cannot summon the AI assistant on your tracker – you have to use your phone for it.
And one more thing: There is a Stephen Curry edition:
The Google Fitbit Edge comes with a special edition, designed in collaboration with 4-time NBA champion Stephen Curry. It pairs the regular tracker with a Satin Pyrite aluminum case and also features a custom moisture-wicking, water-repellent, recycled polyester yarn band. Also on board are special basketball watchfaces. Mind you, all that extra goodness will set you back by an additional USD 40 – the Stephen Curry edition starts at USD 219.99.

Army debunks fake AI video on China, Rijiju demands Congress apology
NEW DELHI: Bhartiya Janata Party on Tuesday hit out at the Congress for circulating an AI-generated video falsely attributing claims about Chinese control of areas in Arunachal Pradesh to an Indian Army officer, escalating the political face-off over the clip.Leading the BJP's counterattack, Union minister Kiren Rijiju accused the Congress of sharing the fabricated video featuring Lieutenant General Girish Kalia and demanded an apology for allegedly tarnishing the Army's image.In a post on X, Rijiju demanded an apology from the opposition party, writing, "Congress Party must apologize to the nation for spreading fake AI video to tarnish the image of Indian Army."
"This is a treacherous act and is on par with the vile deeds of our enemies. The Congress Party is running a despicable campaign on behalf of India's enemies," the Union minister added.The row erupted after Congress shared a post on Monday alleging that China had captured the three areas in Arunachal Pradesh.Congress leader Ritu Choudhary on X wrote: "Shameful! Lieutenant General Girish Kalia (GOC, Spear Corps) says that China has captured Asafila, Longju, and Taksing circles in Arunachal Pradesh.
Despite demands for logistics (supplies), there are reports that the army is being deployed against 'Gen Z' instead of China," Choudhary wrote.
The Indian Army's fact-check unit also debunked the viral video, saying it had been digitally altered and contained fabricated remarks attributed to the officer.In a post on X, the Army said: "A digitally altered video is being circulated with fabricated remarks attributed to Lt Gen Girish Kalia, claiming that China has taken control of Asaphila, Longjou and Taksing Circle in Arunachal Pradesh and that the Indian Army has been denied essential supplies. The misleading video attempts to portray fabricated statements as a leaked admission by a senior Indian Army officer. The video uses Synthetic Generated Information to falsely attribute remarks to Lt Gen Girish Kalia. The original footage relates to a press briefing delivered by then GOC 28 Infantry Division, Maj Gen Girish Kalia, in Kupwara, Jammu & Kashmir, on 27 October 2023. He addressed infiltration attempts across the Line of Control, reporting 10 foiled attempts, the elimination of 27 terrorists and the recovery of warlike stores and narcotics.
He made no such statements about Chinese control over Arunachal Pradesh or denial of supplies to the Indian Army..."
The Army clarified that the original footage was from a press briefing held in Kupwara, Jammu and Kashmir, on October 27, 2023, when then Major General Girish Kalia spoke about infiltration attempts across the Line of Control. According to the Army, he reported 10 foiled infiltration attempts, the elimination of 27 terrorists and the recovery of weapons and narcotics.The Army said the officer had made no statements about Chinese control over areas in Arunachal Pradesh or the denial of supplies to Indian troops.

Authorities investigating whether first Kenyan and Nigerian Ebola cases crossed paths
JOHANNESBURG – The first Ebola patient confirmed in Nigeria may have crossed paths with the first Kenyan Ebola patient at a Ugandan airport, health officials said Thursday.
Nigeria announced its first case of Ebola in more than a decade on Tuesday. Nigerian health authorities said the patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a diplomat based in Abuja who had vacationed in Uganda in September and returned to Nigeria earlier this month.
She is being treated and 44 people she had close contact with have been quarantined, Dr. Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told a press briefing on Thursday.
Authorities are now investigating what the source of her exposure was.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, is the fourth on the continent to record an Ebola case during the current outbreak, but it's the first in West Africa and the furthest away from the epicenter in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Congo's current Ebola outbreak began in May in the country's east. It has become the fastest spreading on record. At least 4,600 people have died and about 9,700 have been infected in Congo.
Neighboring Uganda initially recorded about 20 cases but was declared Ebola-free in August.
The first case in Kenya was recorded in early October and since then eight other cases have been confirmed in the east African nation.
The first Kenyan patient, who has since died, travelled from Congo to Kenya, via Uganda.
Officials are now investigating whether that person crossed paths with the Nigeria case at the Entebbe International Airport in Uganda – as they were there on the same day.
Dr. Mankoula said the center was probing whether there had been "some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport."
Ebola is spread through direct contact with an infected person's bodily fluids or contaminated items. It causes severe fever and can be deadly. However, generally people are not considered infectious until they start showing symptoms.

The Hague: India’s commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal on Monday said Europe was adding to businesses’ regulatory burden just as the global economy seeks simpler rules and greater freedom to operate.
“We are deregulating. Sadly, you need to take a lesson or two from us on that. With Europe adding to the regulatory burden of businesses. I tell you, whenever I say that, I become the darling of the business world. In your countries,” Goyal said at the India Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague.
Goyal, on an official visit to the Netherlands, also positioned India as a trusted partner for businesses, saying the country does not steal data, technology or ideas.
His remarks follow a visit to Germany last week, where he said European manufacturers would need trusted partner countries to produce goods that were becoming increasingly expensive to make in Europe. He also called out the European Union’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), which imposes a carbon cost on certain carbon-intensive imports, calling it “inviting disaster.”
Goyal said businesses globally wanted less compliance, simpler procedures and less paperwork. “Because really, it's the world wants deregulation. The world wants more freedom to operate. Business world is looking for less compliance burden. Simpler processes. Simpler procedures. Less paperwork. And we can do that.”
His comments come as India pursues its Jan Vishwas initiative, which seeks to improve the ease of doing business and living by replacing criminal punishment for minor, technical and procedural violations with monetary penalties, warnings or administrative action.
The Netherlands’ foreign trade and development cooperation minister, Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, defended the European Commission’s approach, saying it was pursuing an agenda of deregulation while maintaining rules needed to protect consumers. Regulations that were unnecessary and hindered trade, however, needed scrutiny, he said.
Sjoerdsma also ruled out a rethink of CBAM, describing it as an essential instrument for ensuring the world adheres to the goals of the Paris climate agreement.
India, for its part, has secured commitments including a forward-looking most-favoured nation assurance under which any flexibilities granted to a third country under the CBAM regulation would also be extended to India.
The India-EU trade agreement is expected to be signed by the end of the calendar year, with implementation targeted for the following spring.
“We hope that this will be signed in December and we hope that implementation will follow as soon as possible, preferably the next day, but we all know it takes a little more than that. So I don't have my crystal ball as to the exact date, but let's hope that this gets implemented spring next year. Spring next year. But preferably sooner,” Sjoerdsma told reporters.
Trade between India and the EU in goods totalled €118.4 billion in 2025, with the bloc importing €69.5 billion worth of goods from India and exporting €48.9 billion to India. Annual bilateral trade in goods and services amounted to €180 billion.
Goyal also highlighted India’s energy infrastructure and its appeal as a destination for investment in data centres, linking the country’s scale with its pitch as a trusted business partner.
“We are sitting on the world's second largest single national grid today….One grid with 70% clean energy providing a huge opportunity for data centres for example. And we are a trusted nation. We don't steal data, we don't steal technology, we don't steal ideas,” he said.
“The new global growth equation will be shaped by countries that combine scale with trust, technology with inclusion and ambition with responsibility,” Goyal added.
Bilateral trade between India and the Netherlands, meanwhile, fell 16.2% to $23.26 billion in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), from $27.75 billion in the previous year. India recorded a trade surplus of $11.74 billion, with exports worth $17.5 billion.
Sjoerdsma said closer ties between the two countries were increasingly important as global trade became more politicised and unpredictable.
“I think it's also important that we place the relationship between the Netherlands and India within this global context, because if you look around, trade has become more politicised, has become more unpredictable, and that means that if you want to build on this relationship, if you want to strengthen your economic relationship, if you want to strengthen trade, you have to increase the level of trust. And I think nothing speaks trust better than the strategic partnership that we have, the continued business that we see.”
Ramita Mishra contributed to the story.

Odisha tribals protest doctor’s arrest; police allege anti-mining violence role
Odisha tribals protest arrests of two anti-mining activists, alleging a crackdown on opposition to Vedanta’s proposed Sijimali bauxite mine.
Hundreds of tribals held a protest in southern Rayagada district in Odisha on Monday to demand the release of Dr Randall Sequeira and karate instructor Laxman Naik. The two were arrested in connection with clashes over Vedanta’s proposed bauxite mining project, with protesters alleging that the police action is aimed at suppressing local opposition to mining.
The protesters, organised under the Niyamgiri Suraksha Samiti (NSS), gathered outside the Muniguda tehsil office and demanded the withdrawal of cases against activists and an end to alleged attempts to facilitate mining in the Niyamgiri hills. They have planned another protest in Sijimali on Tuesday.
Police said the two are accused of violence, criminal intimidation and other offences. Sequeira faces charges including attempted murder, rioting and offences under the Arms Act, while multiple provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) have been invoked in the case.
“Both were arrested for their alleged involvement in threatening members of the public and other serious offences. Sequeira has eight criminal cases registered against him, while Naik is named in 16 cases. Both were produced before a court following their arrest and their bail pleas were rejected, after which they were sent to Rayagada sub-jail,” said Raj Prasad, Rayagada Superintendent of Police. “Dr RandallSequeira was not providing medical services to the people but was engaged in instigating tribals against the state government. Why would police arrest any innocent person, especially a doctor?” said Akhileswar Singh, South Western Range DIG.
Police said the two were arrested by Kalahandi police from a rented house in Bhawanipatna at 11pm on October 16 and handed over to Rayagada police. They were arrested in connection with clashes on April 6 and 7 in Kantamal village of Kashipur where activists held a protest against the construction of a road linked to the proposed Sijimali bauxite mine.
DIG Singh said that the two men, accompanied by 25-30 people, had visited the home of two women in Kantamal who supported the mining project and threatened them to withdraw their support. According to police, one of the women had complained that her family was confined in their house for three days and denied food and water. She also alleged that she and her children had received death threats and that she was pressured to withdraw a police complaint.
But the arrests have triggered protests among activists who said Sequeira had provided free medical care to people in remote tribal villages for several years.
The 39-year-old doctor, who completed his MBBS at St John’s Medical College in Bengaluru and an MD in internal medicine from Sawai Man Singh Medical College in Rajasthan, came to Kalahandi in 2017 and later began visiting remote villages to provide healthcare.
“He treated patients suffering from malaria, tuberculosis, fever and other ailments in areas where access to hospitals is very limited. During the Covid-19 pandemic, he and his associates provided medical assistance. We believe he has been falsely implicated,” said Govind Naik, a resident of Sijimali village. “He had treated people injured during the police lathi-charge and the use of tear gas during the Sijimali agitation on April 6 and 7,” said Suna Majhi of Sarambai village.
Sequeira’s father, Alex Sequeira, who travelled from Mumbai to meet him in jail on Monday, said his son had spent the last six to seven years providing healthcare and creating awareness among the poor and marginalised communities in the remote areas of Kalahandi, Koraput and Rayagada.
The proposed Sijimali bauxite mine, auctioned to Vedanta in March 2023, has faced sustained opposition from local activists who fear that mining will damage forests, water sources and traditional livelihoods. The project seeks to tap an estimated 311 million tonnes of high-grade bauxite reserves spread over 1,549 hectares and involves diversion of 709.72 hectares of forest land.
Clashes between protesters and police in April left several people injured, including at least 40 police personnel, according to the document. While activists have accused the administration of trying to silence the anti-mining movement, police said that the arrests were based on complaints and evidence of alleged criminal offences.

Sir Arthur Conan Doyle created one of the most beloved fictional detectives of all time in Sherlock Holmes, spawning countless novels, films, TV series, and so forth featuring the sleuth. Far fewer people know about the real-life inspiration for Holmes: a renowned surgeon at Scotland’s University of Edinburgh named Joseph Bell, who taught Doyle when the author was still a young medical student. Bell is the subject of a new, eminently readable biography, Sleuth-Hound: The Case of the Real Sherlock Holmes, by medical historian Lindsey Fitzharris.
In 2020, Fitzharris hosted a documentary for the Smithsonian Channel, The Curious Life and Death Of…, exploring famous deaths, ranging from drug lord Pablo Escobar to magician Harry Houdini. Fitzharris performed virtual autopsies, experimented with blood samples, interviewed witnesses, and conducted real-time demonstrations in hopes of gleaning fresh insights. And last year she and her husband, caricaturist Adrian Teal, collaborated on an illustrated children’s book, Dead Ends! Flukes, Flops, and Failuresthat Sparked Medical Marvels.
With Sleuth-Hound, Fitzharris returns to the Edinburgh of The Butchering Art, of body snatchers and surgeons’ discovery of ether, which was also the Edinburgh of Arthur Conan Doyle and Joseph Bell. Bell was notorious for his peculiar method of diagnosis: he was able to infer a patient’s occupation and personal habits, as well as any ailments, just by looking at them. For instance, Bell once figured out the route a patient had taken walking to the infirmary by identifying the type of clay on the patient’s boots—an incident Doyle used in The Sign of the Four. Bell was also something of a medical detective, working with a local police surgeon on some of the most famous murder cases of his day.
Ars caught up with Fitzharris to learn more.
Ars Technica: What drew you to writing an entire book about Joseph Bell?
Lindsey Fitzharris: I’ve known about Bell because I’m a medical historian and I knew that he was an inspiration for this character, but nobody had written a big commercial book on him. There was a book in 1982 by a guy named Ely Liebow. So people in the Sherlockian world, they know a bit about Bell through him, but I really wanted to bring a medical history lens to it.
When I sold the Sleuth-Hound proposal, I had never read the original Sherlock Holmes tales. I decided to put off reading them initially because I knew enough about Bell to know that it became an irritating comparison; he found it rather reductive at the end of his life. I really wanted to bring the real man behind the myth to life in Sleuth-Hound, not just as the inspiration for Sherlock Holmes, not just as this parlor trick, but as this complex character. I’ve been talking to a lot of Sherlockians who have been really surprised at how much Bell is Sherlock, but also how much he isn’t Sherlock. That’s an interesting discussion as well: why Conan Doyle focused on this one aspect of him.

Ars Technica: What are some of the ways Bell is and isn’t Sherlock?
Lindsey Fitzharris: He had this Sherlockian way about him where he could tell everything about a person before they ever spoke a word: a callous, a stain, a limp, all were clues to Bell if you only knew how to see it. But in a lot of ways he wasn’t Holmes. For instance, he was a deeply empathetic character. He was very feeling for his patients. And he also was a family man. His wife dies when he’s in his 30s, and he doesn’t remarry his entire life. He holds the torch for her. She dies in childbirth, and he raises his three children alone.
My husband is a caricaturist, and we have this discussion about how he can only caricature people he doesn’t know well. That’s because caricature is about those first impressions. I think Conan Doyle knew Bell in his capacity as a student, but he didn’t know Bell the man. So he took the most recognizable flashy trait of Bell and transposed that onto Sherlock Holmes. The question I pose at the end of the book is, would Holmes exist if Conan Doyle had known Bell better, or would he exist in the same format?
Ars Technica: Did Conan Doyle’s contemporaries recognize the similarities?
Lindsey Fitzharris: Those who knew Bell recognized it immediately. Robert Louis Stevenson reads Sherlock Holmes. He writes to Conan Doyle and he says at the end of the letter, “One thing bothers me, could this be our old friend Joe Bell?”
But Bell was a lot more complex, and I really wanted to bring that medical history lens, because this isn’t just a story about his relationship with Conan Doyle and the inspiration for Sherlock Holmes. It’s about the development of forensic medicine. It’s about the moment that medicine enters the courtroom for the first time. Bell wasn’t just the inspiration for Holmes; he was actually doing what Holmes was doing in practice. He was working officially with a police surgeon named Henry Duncan Littlejohn, who was fascinating in and of himself. He was a pioneer of fingerprinting and courtroom photography. They end up partnering and working on some of the biggest high-profile cases in Scotland in the 19th century.
Ars Technica: I was frankly shocked about the baby farming case; I had no idea that was a common practice.
Lindsey Fitzharris: It’s such a crazy story. The thing that I want people to contextualize here is that there was no birth control. So there were a lot of women having a lot of children, and they were deeply impoverished, and they didn’t have enough money to feed these children. So they turned to the baby farmer. In theory, the baby farmer took the child and then took a fee from you, the mother, with the promise that they would farm out the child to somebody who could take care of the child. That was how it was supposed to work. There were no legal routes for adoption in the 19th century, so they turned to the baby farmer.
The case in Sleuth-Hound, the baby farmer, Jessie King, ends up taking the fee and then just killing the infants. This was a horrific case. The chapter opens with these boys finding this bundle of rags and using it as a football and kicking it around. And then they open it, and it’s the decomposing remains of a child. Littlejohn and Bell work on the case. They perform the postmortems; they testify in the trial.
One of the dark themes of this book is that a lot of early forensics was built on the brutalized bodies of women in particular. Jessie King was killing infants, but this is a crime that is particular to women—women trying to get their children into families that could afford to feed them. A lot of the crimes are committed on women who never receive any justice, but the science outlives what their bodies taught these early forensic investigators like Bell and Littlejohn.
Ars Technica: Case in point: the infamous Chantrelle murder case and how it coincides with the rise of toxicology.
Lindsey Fitzharris: The Chantrelle case is so fascinating to me. Eugene Chantrelle was this respectable gentleman who lived in Edinburgh. He was a French tutor, and his wife Lizzie is seemingly poisoned by a gas leak, a broken pipe in the flat, and she’s removed from the property and later dies. But it turns out that Chantrelle was abusing her the entire marriage.
