We think Littlejohn brought Bell onto the case. Bell and Littlejohn discover that it was opium poisoning, and they test the vomit on her nightgown, and they’re able to tie him to this crime. Bear in mind, Bell worked like Sherlock Holmes. He worked in the shadows. So in these earlier cases, it was very difficult to know if Bell really did work on them.
But there’s a really intriguing clue at the end of this story. Littlejohn investigates, [Eugene Chantrelle] is convicted, and he is hanged for this murder. On the scaffold, he allegedly looked around at the audience, locked eyes with Littlejohn, and shouted, “Give my regards to Joe Bell. He did a good job putting the noose around my neck.” This was such a Sherlockian moment. How did Chantrelle know that Bell had worked on this case? We don’t have any records that actually confirm this except that he allegedly said this on the scaffold.
The other extraordinary aspect of this story is that Chantrelle was drinking buddies with Robert Louis Stevenson, so he becomes one of the inspirations for Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde: this respectable person on the outside and very sinister and evil on the inside. The prosecutor told Stevenson that this was not Chantrelle’s first victim and that he had killed four or five other people with his opium and cheese parties.
Ars Technica: Your book launch should feature an opium and cheese party.
Lindsey Fitzharris: (laughs) And ether drinks. You’re invited. The Victorian period was wild because there were a lot of poisons that you could just get over the counter from your pharmacist. Chantrelle had trained as a doctor at one point and had bought a huge amount of opium just before the murder. Even the chemist thought that this was strange, but he assumed that Chantrelle was a doctor. So poison was a big problem in the Victorian period. Some of it was legal, it was hard to detect. Forensic medicine was just developing. I call it the golden era of murdering because you probably had more of a chance in the 19th century of getting away with it.
Ars Technica: Sleuth-Hound is written in a deceptively novelistic style, but you’ve clearly done very extensive research on this. What sources did you find most helpful?
Lindsey Fitzharris: One of the things that happened was that Bell’s diary became available, that had been locked away for over a century by the Bell family. Perhaps they were waiting for enough time to pass. I almost called the book Sleuth-Hounds because I do also think Littlejohn taught Conan Doyle as well. Bell gave Conan Doyle the method, and Littlejohn gave him the world of forensics. He was a professor of forensics in Edinburgh at the time. We can flesh out what Bell was doing because we know that they worked together often on these cases.

You do get dialogue through the murder trials, because there’s so many documents and court records that go along with these trials. There are a lot of letters, diaries. Nothing’s made up, but sometimes I had to take educated guesses. For instance, Conan Doyle is a terrible narrator of his own life. He constantly is contradicting himself, even in his own memoirs. It was difficult figuring out when he came into contact with Bell for the first time. I believe it’s in the winter of 1878, and I provide a lot of context for that in the back notes of the book.
I’m a historian. It’s got to be armed to the teeth with sources. But I want people to be able to pick up the book, not know anything about Sherlock Holmes, not know anything about medical history or forensics, and just be able to enjoy it. Medical history is the most universal way into the past. I make the past relatable. I tell you what that was like a hundred years ago.
My superpower in 2026 is that I’m one of the few people who can make you feel good about living today. Progress is not a straight line necessarily, but if you had that medical crisis a hundred years ago, it would’ve been a lot worse. I’ve been through cancer myself. Today is the best day to be alive and to get that diagnosis and tomorrow will be a little bit better, because I’m an optimist when it comes to medicine. I’m hoping that chemotherapy or radiation treatments will become obsolete. They’re brutal. And there’s a cancer vaccine on the horizon.
Lindsey Fitzharris: I know. We have short memories. We don’t remember. It’s weird to me as a medical historian because I remember it all. I remember the times when parents lost their children to preventable diseases. It’s coming back, and it’s sad to see that repeat. If I could just show people the diaries and the letters of brokenhearted parents who lost child after child to measles or polio and all of these diseases we can now treat and prevent. I put up pictures of smallpox on social media, and people think it’s AI. They can’t believe that something like that existed. It’s the only human virus we’ve ever eradicated. It should be celebrated. So I’m always out there banging the drum. I hope that we steady the ship a bit and people learn from the past again.
Jennifer is a senior writer at Ars Technica with a particular focus on where science meets culture, covering everything from physics and related interdisciplinary topics to her favorite films and TV series. Jennifer lives in Baltimore with her spouse, physicist Sean M. Carroll, and their two cats, Ariel and Caliban.

Quick Answer
The Logitech MX Keypad makes managing AI tools, apps, and everyday tasks easier with nine customizable LCD keys, app-specific shortcuts, and one-click automations. It’s compact, reliable, and highly flexible, but at $99.99 (INR 15,999), it’s best suited for those who regularly use AI tools and shortcuts.
AI has fundamentally changed how I interact with devices. Ever since I started using an AI dictation app and a few other AI tools to get things done, I barely type anymore. Instead, I press a button on my Mac or on Android, say what I want, let AI transcribe it into text for me, and press enter. AI agents that have full access to my computer do everything.
On smartphones, you can easily ditch the keyboard if you want to and replace it with a single mic icon, like most AI dictation apps do today. But on devices like a Mac with a physical keyboard, that is not possible. Even so, I found myself using mostly one key more than any other: the Fn button, a shortcut I use to type with voice typing and to instruct AI applications and agents on my Mac what they need to do.
All this time, I have really wished I could replace my entire Mac keyboard with just a handful of buttons that do one specific job. That’s pretty much the idea behind the Logitech MX Keypad. However, it doesn’t replace your keyboard; it sits next to it and lets you perform actions with a single click. It comes with nine customizable LCD keys. You can assign shortcuts, launch apps, and trigger specific actions with a single press, making it easy to perform the most-used actions with just a single click.
The best part about the Logitech MX Keypad is not the buttons but the idea behind this approach, and how well they executed it.
I have been using the Logitech MX Keypad for more than a week now, and I honestly love this approach and the thought process behind it. In this review, I will share my full experience with the device and how useful it is for me as a vibe coder and someone who hates remembering shortcuts.
Table of Contents
Logitech MX Keypad Review: The Missing Controller for AI-First Workflows
The idea of getting things done with fewer interactions is not new; we have had this for years, and we refer to it as shortcuts. And this isn’t the first time someone has created a separate device for it. In 2017, Elgato released the Stream Deck, a similar 15-key LCD controller for streamers that allowed users to switch between scenes, launch applications, and automate actions with a single button press.
And Logitech, the company behind this product, also isn’t new to this idea as well. Back in 2024, when AI was just a buzzword, the company announced the MX Creative Console, which has similar ideas of controlling apps and easy-to-access shortcuts with just a button. Fast forward to 2026, when AI usage has grown, the company recently introduced the Logitech MX Keypad, the same idea, but now as a keypad designed to sit next to your keyboard.
Logitech MX Keypad Design and Appearance: Compact and Well Built
The Logitech MX Keypad has a two-piece design. One is the keypad itself, and the other is a detachable stand; you can prop it up using the stand, or you can place the keypad itself directly on the surface, where its slightly slanted design makes it easy to access. It also comes with a slanted surface that makes it easy to interact with. It also comes in two colors; I received the Graphite color. There is also a Pale Grey variant that looks best if you have a premium desktop setup.
The base has a rubber finish so it won’t slip off smooth tables and stays firmly in one place, and the keypad itself is slim and lightweight and connects to Mac or Windows via a USB-C cable. The same cable powers the device, so you don’t need a separate power source, though I wish it had wireless connectivity and a built-in battery. But since it uses only one USB cable, you can tuck it to the back and keep the setup clean. Both are solidly built.
The Keypad comes with nine customizable keys with their own individual LCD displays, along with two left and right navigation controls in the button array, aligned to the left, and with a Logi logo to the right. On the back, the USB-C cable connects to the device and is also removable. The buttons have a glossy, smooth finish; they aren’t tactile, but I like the soft, jelly-like click when pressed.
The LCD button displays are sharp; the icons and the action text are sharp and easy to read, even in brightly lit desktop setups. They are also full-color displays, so you can choose different themes based on your needs and preferences. And at just 91.7 × 77.9 × 25.5 mm, it also doesn’t take up much space on your desk.
Logitech MX Keypad Specs and Features: Nine Keys That Do a Lot More
The Logitech MX Keypad has nine physical LCD buttons, where each button can be assigned a different action or shortcut. But you are not limited to just nine shortcuts. You can set up 15 individual pages for each app, which allows you to set up 135 shortcuts for each app and switch between them using the switch arrows below.
For most users, this setup should be enough to perform frequently used shortcuts and actions, and the Logi Options+ app also lets you create and assign multiple shortcuts for each app, so you have set up multiple shortcuts and switch between them daily.
In my testing, I didn’t notice any latency between pressing the button and seeing the action happen on your Mac. Since it’s designed for developers, it also shows live actions, including the running status of your AI model.
For instance, when using Claude, the Keypad shows the live running status of the AI model. You can also stop the task directly from the keyboard with a single press; you can also create a new chat; approve Claude to perform actions with a single click, which is the most common in AI agents where you need to manually click Allow every time the model needs your permission to perform a task if you set it to manual approval.
If you don’t want to use these controls, you can customize the buttons and assign completely different tasks that suit your workflow. In addition, the Logi Options+ app supports various system shortcuts, including clipboard shortcuts such as pasting copied text, clearing the clipboard, formatting text, and other useful actions like making text title case, and more. You can also control volume, use automation to run multiple actions with a single click, and more. Even without AI tools, you can set up automations for everyday tasks.
Logitech MX Keypad Everyday Use: The Little Things Make It Work
Devices like the Logitech MX Keypad should make your work easier rather than adding extra burden. If the team behind this hasn’t thought about these tiny interactions, using the device becomes a burden for the user.
First, it automatically switches profiles based on which app you are using. Even if you set multiple custom profiles, the app instantly switches to the app you are using without having to manually switch between different sets of shortcuts.
In my testing, it works, and the keypad instantly switches to the shortcuts I set for each app, even for the app I custom-built. It also works with other apps and software, including the latest AI applications like VS Code, Claude Code, your browser like Chrome, or the usual shortcuts you can use on the Mac’s home screen.
Another thing that I initially thought would be extra work is manually turning off the device if I shut down my Mac. Thankfully, Logitech has thought of that too: the Keypad automatically powers off when you shut down your computer and turns back on automatically when you start. Although they may seem like tiny details, these thoughtful interactions make the Logitech MX Keypad easy to use instead of adding to your workload.
Logitech MX Keypad Interface and App: Reliable and Easy to Customize
The app also offers plenty of customization options, which I cover in detail in this section, but one handy feature is the ability to adjust key brightness, which can come in handy if you are working in dark environments.
Although many people say Logitech device companion apps are buggy and unreliable, that hasn’t been my experience with the Logi Options+ app I installed on my Mac. The app worked for me without any issues throughout my testing and was surprisingly reliable.
It also has one of the cleanest UI experiences for an accessories provider. The app lets you completely customize your Logitech MX Keypad. By default, you have a general profile that appears when you turn on your Mac and are on the home screen. You can also create multiple general profiles and switch between them too.
You can also create and customize profiles for each individual app. Logitech already offers popular shortcuts for some popular and most-used apps like Google Chrome, Slack, and more. So you don’t need to set everything from scratch. If you cannot find the action you are looking for, you can create your own shortcut and add it to an app profile.
There is also a dedicated Logitech Marketplace that lets you access various shortcuts created for apps by the community. AI apps like Claude and ChatGPT aren’t available by default, but they are available in the Logi Marketplace. Even if an app isn’t available in the marketplace, you can build your own plugins and custom profiles using the Logi Actions SDK. Logitech also partnered with GitHub to offer 3 months of a GitHub Copilot Pro+ subscription for free and include all shortcuts for the VS Code app.
And since you have everything under your control, you can create custom profiles for the personal applications you have created on your device.
This level of flexibility makes the device stand out, even for power users who want to perform everyday tasks with just a button instead of constantly switching between apps, navigating menus, and repeating the same steps.
Logitech MX Keypad Compatibility: Mac and Windows Only, with Some Setup Required
And for those wondering whether it works with Android, iPhone, or even iPads, no, it doesn’t. To use it, you need the Logi Options+ app installed on the device, which is currently limited to Windows and Mac. You also need to download an additional file, such as a .crx extension, to work in Chrome and go through multiple steps to set it up for the first time. Once setup is done, it works flawlessly. But if you are a developer, you can also technically build a workaround to control an Android app or other devices.
Logitech MX Keypad Review Verdict: Worth It if It Fits Your Workflow
Overall, the Logitech MX Keypad is a well-crafted device that makes a lot of sense for people who spend much of their day with AI tools, whether they are developers, students, or creative professionals.
It is not just about triggering shortcuts with a single press but also about tiny details that make it easy to use. Also, at $99.99, it can be a neat and useful addition to your desktop that is genuinely useful. Remember that it will take a bit of time to get used to its input style, and sometimes you will even forget it’s there if you don’t make it part of your workflow. At $99.99 (INR 15,999), it’s a worthwhile addition to your desktop.

Delegations meet in Iran with Mideast on edge over potential for renewed fighting
High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held talks in Tehran for a meeting aimed at preventing renewed fighting in the Iran war
CAIRO -- High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war.
Many in Iran are anxious about a possible return to all-out war. Israeli and American leaders have been sharpening their threats before elections in both countries, while Iranian leaders have remained defiant.
The war in Yemen and strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also discussed, according to two regional officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak with reporters.
The four countries agreed Monday to continue talks on expanding cooperation among them, particularly about regional peace and security, a statement said. No details were given about a date or place for a future meeting.
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, attended the talks, hosted by Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that Iran supports any agreement that would deepen regional cooperation, resolve differences and make greater use of the shared resources and capabilities of Islamic countries.
Delegations from the other Middle Eastern countries sought to avoid further turmoil in the region.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan warned in a televised address on Monday that renewed attacks on Iran would destabilize the region and hurt countries that aren't party to the conflict.
“It is our hope that all parties will refrain from any actions that could drag our region into a new spiral of violence,” Erdogan said.
Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find “ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability.”
Qatari mediators also traveled to Tehran on Sunday, working in coordination with the United States, as part of efforts to de-escalate regional tensions, according to a regional official speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks.
Pakistan and Qatar helped broker an agreement in June aimed at having Iran fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, ending a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and opening negotiations on a broader settlement addressing Iran’s nuclear program. The deal unraveled quickly, however, as both sides renewed attacks.
With worries about renewed fighting before Israel's election on Tuesday and the U.S. midterm election on Nov. 3, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said over the weekend that Iran hadn't closed the window of diplomacy and that messages were being passed to the U.S. through intermediaries.
With negotiations long stalled, he said that the U.S. appears to be persisting in unilateral demands and that U.S. President Donald Trump and other American officials repeatedly use the phrase “complete surrender,” which Baghaei said no Iranian accepts.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, repeated his warning on Sunday that Iran or its proxies could launch an attack before the election to disrupt the vote, citing intelligence.
“The (military) is ready both to defend and to strike,” he said in a video statement. “You will suffer disproportionate blows far greater than you can imagine.”
Israel’s Channel 12 reported Sunday night that Netanyahu and his military chief of staff clashed over an instruction by Netanyahu to carry out an “action” that the army believes could quickly trigger a resumption of the conflict with Iran.
Netanyahu’s office later described the report as “fake news.”
In Tehran, when asked whether Iran was planning attacks, Baghaei on Monday said that “the Israeli regime is highly skilled at carrying out false-flag operations.”
“The Islamic Republic of Iran will not hesitate to exercise its inherent right to self-defense to protect Iran’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence,” he said.
Yemen has become a widening front in the Iran war that began in February, with the Houthis increasingly launching attacks on Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government battling the rebels.
The conflict has intensified since forces from the internationally recognized government and Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that largely stopped the fighting in Yemen’s civil war.
Early Monday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said that the rebel group had fired ballistic missiles at military gatherings and weapons depots belonging to Saudi-backed government forces in Aden and Lahj provinces. He said that the attacks destroyed military equipment and caused casualties, but didn't provide evidence. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify the information.
Houthi media said that airstrikes targeted a solar power system and a water well in Sanaa, but offered no proof. In the port city of Mokha, recently seized by the Houthis, residents said that rockets hit several buildings, including a hospital.
Doctors Without Borders, or Médecins Sans Frontières, said Monday that three strikes hit Mokha, one landing just 150 meters (nearly 500 feet) from Mokha General Hospital, where its teams work in maternity and pediatric wards.
The statement came after the Houthi-run Health Ministry accused Saudi-backed forces of targeting the hospital. The Saudi-backed forces haven't commented.
All staff and patients were safe, MSF said, adding that the strike damaged the hospital building.
Days earlier, a missile struck near Aden’s airport as an MSF plane carrying humanitarian workers was preparing to take off, forcing staff to seek shelter instead of boarding, the organization said. Aden’s airport is the main entry point for humanitarian workers, supplies and medical equipment to the southern parts of Yemen.
Houthi-run al-Masirah channel also reported strikes in Saada, in northern Yemen, and in southwestern Taiz province, where the rebels and Saudi-backed government forces have been fighting for weeks.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said that an operation in Houthi-controlled territory destroyed five tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and other missile storage.
Meanwhile, Egypt’s parliament on Monday approved a request from President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi to provide military support to Saudi Arabia to help defend against Houthi attacks.

Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or
- Published
Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth consecutive year.
Putellas, 32, captained Barcelona to Champions League glory as part of a quadruple in 2025-26, before joining Women's Super League (WSL) side London City Lionesses in July.
She joins Spain team-mate Aitana Bonmati on three Ballon d'Or Feminin crowns - her former Barcelona colleague won the award in 2023, 2024 and 2025 after Putellas did so in 2021 and 2022.
The past six Ballons d'Or have been won by the Spanish pair, with Norway's Ada Hegerberg (2018) and Megan Rapinoe of the United States (2019) the only non-Spaniards to claim the prize.
Putellas' latest victory caps a remarkable return to the pinnacle of world football after suffering a career-threatening anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in 2022.
"All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn't matter if you're a boy or if you're a girl," Putellas said.
"Doesn't matter where you come from. Don't listen if someone tells you, you can't do it. Believe in yourself."
She collected the most votes from an international panel of journalists across Fifa's top-50 ranked countries, with Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor coming second and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw third.
Meanwhile, England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or, becoming the first English player to do so since Michael Owen in 2001.
The numbers don't lie
While Barcelona are always overwhelming favourites to win the three competitions on offer in Spain, Putellas' performances last season showed that she is still among the world's elite.
Nicknamed 'La Reina' - meaning the queen - Putellas scored 21 goals and provided 13 assists in all competitions, ranking her third and second respectively among players across Europe's top five leagues.
Seven of those goals came in the Women's Champions League as Barcelona claimed a fourth continental title in six seasons.
Only Pernille Harder (eight), Alessia Russo (nine) and Ewa Pajor (11) scored more, all of whom are strikers by trade.
But Putellas' contributions to Barcelona's attacking play went far beyond scoring goals herself.
In Liga F - which Barcelona won for a seventh consecutive season - she finished joint-sixth for assists (seven) and fourth for open-play chances created (40).
Across Europe's top five leagues, only Claudia Pina (199), Vicky Lopez (183) and Georgia Stanway (168) recorded more sequence involvements ending in an open-play shot than Putellas (151).
In all competitions, she created more chances (89, 19 of which were big chances) and completed more passes ending in the final third (965) than any other player in Liga F, the Champions League, Copa de la Reina and Supercopa de Espana.
Only Bayern Munich's Klara Buhl created as many chances as Putellas in the Champions League last season (36), the most by a player in a single edition of the competition since Caroline Graham Hansen in 2021-22 (38).
From watching Iniesta to winning it all
Putellas was born and grew up in the Catalan municipality of Mollet del Valles, about 12 miles north-east of Barcelona.
She began playing football in the street, and soon became a Barcelona fan and a regular attendee at Camp Nou.
With matches always on the TV at home, former Spain and Barcelona star Andres Iniesta and Brazilian duo Rivaldo and Ronaldinho quickly became her idols.
After attending a summer football camp run by Xavi and playing for local side CE Sabadell, Putellas spent a year at La Masia, Barcelona's famous youth academy.
Spells at Espanyol and Levante followed the disbandment of her girls team, before she eventually returned to Barca in 2012.
Cue the start of a 14-year career with her childhood club during which she won 38 trophies, including 10 league titles and four European cups.
But after winning the Ballon d'Or for the first time in 2021, one of the toughest moments of Putellas' career came when she suffered an ACL injury on the eve of Euro 2022, ruling her out of the tournament.
Though she retained the Ballon d'Or later that year, it took a while for her to return to her best level. Playing only a bit-part role in Spain's triumphant 2023 World Cup campaign would have stung.
After scoring in the 2024 Champions League final and improving further the following season, in 2025-26 she shouldered much of Barcelona's creative burden as Aitana Bonmati missed five months through injury and ended the season a quadruple winner.
If that was not enough, the midfielder scored twice in a 4-0 thrashing of England in June that secured Spain's place at the 2027 World Cup at the Lionesses' expense.
With her contract at Barcelona expiring and keen for a fresh challenge, Putellas made the decision to leave her childhood club. She, and her fans, were distraught.
She had several offers from England, Mexico and the United States, but joined the ambitious project of US billionaire Michelle Kang at London City Lionesses in July.
"I'm just always looking forward to better things and that's why I'm here too, because I always need to be moving as a person and a player," Putellas told BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast in August.
With three goals and one assist in seven WSL games for her new club, it is clear Putellas is still deserving of her nickname.

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

Most parents worry about exposing their kids to too much screen time, but it can be tough to find alternatives that children find entertaining and that might be beneficial. Enter Qubitunes, a screen-free play stage and speaker for kids. Content comes in wooden cartridges that you slot in the top, and kids can place wooden character pieces on the circular soundstage, divided into four sections, to change the audio it plays.
This seemingly simple design allows for interactive stories that change based on the characters and spots your kids choose, music that can be layered up with different instruments, and themed games and quizzes. I’m a huge fan of Qubitunes, and it has a deserving place in my guides to the best STEM toys and speakers for kids. As Black Friday and gifting season approaches, the Qubitunes starter kit is one toy to keep an eye on for discounts.
I played with Qubitunes for hours when it arrived and really enjoyed it. The stereo speakers are decent, there's a headphone port, and it can be recharged via USB-C for up to six hours of play. It has since gone into my wife’s classroom, and it’s usually the first thing picked when kids have finished their work and it’s choosing time. It’s very popular with 7- and 8-year-olds, but kids aged 3 years and up (all the way up to adults) will potentially get a kick out of this.
There is a caveat: the need to purchase content separately. These add-ons cost between $10 and $20 each. Stories, games, and other options come in wooden blocks that slot into the device so you can download the content. You need a Wi-Fi connection for the initial content download and firmware updates, but then you can play offline. They usually come with three or four character blocks and a labelled bag to keep them in.
My top pick is the Little Maestro set ($20) featuring players in an orchestra covering Mozart, Vivaldi, Beethoven, and Bach. There are also stories about quirky characters, such as The Groblies ($20), a fun cooking game called Bernard’s Kitchen ($20) with different ingredients, and various themed soundscapes and quizzes. I prefer activities where there’s some creativity or a learning game involved, but the stories and soundscapes are good for very young kids. The interactive nature of these sets elevates the experience beyond passive listening and provides replay value, as kids experiment to discover what happens when they move and replace pieces on the stage.
Qubs has also recently released a Maestro expansion ($10) with four new composers, a Jurassic Sounds Dinosaur Game ($20) with facts and T-Rex roars, and versions of Little Red Riding Hood and Hansel & Gretel, among many others. If you like the idea of sustainable, screen-free toys, the maker Qubs also made a clever wooden car STEM toy called Cody Block ($70) that introduces kids to basic coding concepts, and it’s on sale right now, down from $100.

Weak monsoon, crop failures, force farmers to cut spending
India’s weakest monsoon in over a decade raises concerns about farm output, winter sowing and rural spending
Farmer Ramesh Valvi, 34, hoped to buy a ₹4.5 lakh tractor for his three-hectare farm in Maharashtra’s Mandvi village. He saved ₹60,000 and hoped to earn another ₹50,000 for the ₹2 lakh down payment. Valvi planned to arrange the remaining amount from his brother, a construction contractor.
The plan is now on hold as Valvi’s maize and tur crops failed after rains stopped. ₹40,000 he invested in his land is also lost. Valvi expects to only break even, leaving little room for the tractor purchase. There is not enough water even to drink, and he sees little chance of sowing a rabi crop in the winter, unless water becomes available.
With no income expected from another harvest, he expects to use his savings to feed his family. His remaining hope is compensation through crop insurance. Valvi’s predicament echoes many as India’s weakest monsoon in more than a decade raises concerns about farm output, winter sowing and rural spending.
The effects are beginning to show in fertiliser and farm machinery sales, while low reservoir levels threaten to extend the damage beyond the monsoon crop.
The weak monsoon
The southwest monsoon, which delivers 70% of Indian rains, started weak. The country registered its fifth-driest June since national statistics began in 1901. There was a 39.8% fall from the long-period average. Rains picked up briefly bringing some relief in July but plunged again in August, recording a 16.3% deficit and the hottest August since 1901 as El Nino conditions strengthened.
The monsoon ended with a 12.6% downfall, the fourth-lowest since 2001. There were also sharp regional variations. East and northeast India received 25% less rainfall than normal. Southern peninsular India had 24% less and northwest India 6% less rain. Key agricultural states also recorded poor rains. Bihar had a deficit of 32%, Punjab 41%, Marathwada 39% and Kerala 28%. Overall, 17 meteorological subdivisions, covering 42% of the country’s area, recorded deficient rainfall during the season.
The decadal weak monsoon has left parts of the country with inadequate soil moisture just as farmers prepare for the rabi season. The weak monsoon has also left reservoir storages down. Despite higher storages recorded at the beginning of the season due to above-average rains last year, reservoir levels depleted to 68.6% of capacity on October 15, against 90.8% a year earlier and against the 10-year average of 82.1%.
According to a Barclays report, over 37% of districts had severe or extreme soil-moisture deficits. Rain-fed areas are particularly vulnerable because they have less access to irrigation. For farmers who have lost their kharif crops, a failure to sow rabi crops could mean another season with little or no farm income.
Fertiliser sales slide
The lack of rain affected not just Valvi’s crop but also how much fertiliser he could apply. He usually applies it four times during the crop cycle, but managed only two rounds this year because there was not enough water. The fertiliser he did apply failed to spread into the soil properly, he said, and pests attacked the crop.
National fertiliser sales have also weakened. Industry estimates suggest sales of complex fertilisers fell by more than 20% in April-September from a year earlier. Urea sales also declined, despite higher domestic production and imports.
Poor rainfall may have discouraged farmers from spending on inputs, though supply constraints and higher raw-material costs have also affected some fertiliser categories. With little water available even for drinking, Valvi does not expect to sow a rabi crop. His savings, which he had set aside to buy a tractor, will now go towards feeding his family. He is hoping for compensation through crop insurance to help him tide over the losses.
Muted tractor demand
India, still being a largely agrarian economy, has a significant percentage of the population dependent on agriculture for a healthy income. Prospects for that have turned sour this year owing to the bad monsoon.
Tractor retail sales fell 12.58% month-on-month to 76,906 units in September, according to the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, but were still 13.75% higher than a year earlier. On a year-on-year basis, sales were down 18%. A Barclays report said the effect of crop losses on tractor purchases could become clearer in early 2027, as lower farm earnings prompt some farmers to delay expensive purchases.
For Valvi, that decision has already been made. With his kharif crop gone and the next sowing uncertain, the money he set aside for a tractor will instead go towards food.

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.
From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.
The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.
A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.
“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.
Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.
As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.
Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.
Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.
“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.
As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.
“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.
Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.
The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

Parents of spinal muscular atrophy(SMA)-afflicted children coming to the SMA clinic at SAT Hospital had been counselled several times about the government introducing the generic version of Risdiplam, instead of the Evrysdi brand by Roche, said V.H. Shankar, Head of the Department of Medical Genetics, who is also in charge of the treatment of children with rare diseases at the hospital, here on Friday.
Dr. Shankar, who attended a press conference along with Health Minister K. Muraleedharan, said several meetings had been held with the parents of SMA-afflicted children, during which time all their queries on the efficacy of the generic drug were clarified.
He was answering queries on whether the parents had been told about the introduction of the generic drug for SMA and whether their concerns had been assuaged adequately by the authorities.
Dr. Shanker said he himself had spoken at several of the meetings with the parents. He added that the new generic drug Natsmart was given to six children and the parents were clearly told that the drug being dispensed was not the same brand (Evrysdi) that used to be dispensed earlier.
He said the technical committee had evaluated the decision to shift from Evrysdi to Natsmart several times. The purchase procedure was initiated in February 2026 itself.
Chairperson of the technical committee and Director of Medical Education K.V. Viswanath said the medicine bottles bore the sticker “Physicians’ sample/ for clinical trials”, which is just an indication that the bottles were not for open sale.
The SAT Superintendent had earlier clarified that they were awaiting the government supply of Natsmart, when on Monday, patients had arrived at the SMA clinic seeking the medicine. He had also clarified that rather than asking them to come another day, the hospital had contacted Natco and secured some samples from them to be given to the SMA patients.
The government supply arrived on Tuesday evening itself, but by which time, the campaign that clinical trial medicines were being given to SMA patients was already raging.
Former Health Minister, Veena George, had demanded on Thursday at a press conference that the government should explain how “drugs meant for clinical trials” had been supplied through the hospital. She also alleged that after the controversy broke, the parents had been “threatened” into returning the medicine bottles by the SAT Hospital authorities.
Mr. Muraleedharan said the authorities took back the medicines and replaced it with the lot from the government supply to put the controversy and concerns at rest. He said the doctors at SAT Hospital had spoken to the parents and explained everything and the so-called “concerns” were the creation of some news channels. He said it was also possible that the controversy was deliberately raked up by some along with pharma majors.
He said the government intended to purchase only the generic version of Risdiplam so that the treatment can be provided to more patients.
Meanwhile, many public health experts have expressed concern over the manner in which the issue is being politicised by the Opposition, which has continued to perpetuate the concerns and misgivings of parents of SMA patients by raising the allegation that “clinical trial drugs” were distributed to children.

The story so far
An initiative launched by Keralam government to make the treatment for Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) accessible to more patients is now courting controversy.
SMA is a rare, life-threatening genetic disorder that progressively weakens muscles, severely impairing both mobility and respiratory function. While a complete cure remains elusive, the launch of Risdiplam, marketed as Evrysdi by Roche Pharmaceuticals, the first at-home, oral treatment for SMA, gave hope to thousands of SMA patients. Risdiplam was found to have a significant effect on the progression of the disease, by slowing down motor degeneration, improving physical milestones and stabilising respiratory function.
Risdiplam was launched in India in July 2021, making it the first and only approved drug in the country to manage SMA. But the drug’s astronomical cost made it inaccessible to most families.
Keralam, which has been giving Risdiplam free of cost to eligible children since 2022, made a switch to the less expensive generic version of the drug in October this year . But since then, a section of parents of children living with SMA children have urged the government to switch back to the expensive, branded version.
Last week, when the generic drug was dispensed for the first time at SAT hospital, a Centre of Excellence for Rare Diseases in Thiruvananthapuram, a sticker on the bottle which said “Physicians’ sample/for clinical trials” reopened the branded versus generic debate and a new allegation, that drugs meant for clinical trials were being used on children
How Keralam began SMA treatment
Keralam was the first State to give Risdiplam free of cost through government hospitals in 2022 and an SMA clinic was subsequently opened at SAT hospital. Though initially Risdiplam was given free only to children under 12, in 2026 the government announced an extension of coverage to genetically confirmed SMA Type 2 patients up to age 25, with ₹30 crore allocated in the State budget for this. However, as of now, 109 Type 1 and 2 children with SMA below the age of 12 are being given Risdiplam, free.
Risdiplam, under its trade name Evrysdi, used to cost ₹6.3 lakh for a bottle (current price ₹4.44 lakhs), which the State was getting at a negotiated price of ₹5.4 lakh per bottle. Under the patient assistance programme, Roche used to give 11 bottles free of cost to the State for every four bottles it purchased. The State’s annual requirement was estimated at around 2,500 bottles and the annual financial commitment was around ₹23 crore. The State, therefore, was up against enormous cumulative expenditure as more children became eligible and existing patients required continued treatment.
The decision to switch to generic
A technical experts committee in Keralam met several times to evaluate if the generic alternative, Natsmart, which has all regulatory approvals, and which was ready for commercial distribution in October 2025, could replace Roche’s Evrysdi. Natco Pharma, through a historic Delhi High Court verdict, had won the right to marker the generic alternative of Risdiplam at a dramatically reduced price of ₹15,900 per bottle, against Roche’s Rs. 6.3 lakhs per bottle.
A bottle of Evrysdi on which Roche holds a patent, typically lasts 12 days, meaning the annual maintenance cost for a patient would amount to a crushing ₹60-70 lakh. With Natsmart, the generic alternative, the cost would be under ₹5 lakh. In February 2026, the Keralam government gave the go ahead for Natsmart, and purchase processes were initiated.
What are parents’ concerns?
Parents and advocacy groups including the Cure SMA Foundation of India claim that the branded medication, Evrysdi, has a proven, long-term track record of safety and efficacy, while the new generic version lacks dedicated human bioequivalence or long-term clinical studies specific to paediatric patients. They claim that a sudden switch to an unverified or less effective generic formula could reverse the critical motor and survival progress already achieved by children who are currently stable on the original drug. They have been continuously petitioning the government asking that their children be allowed to continue on Evrysdi.
What do doctors say?
Public health experts have hailed the government’s decision to switch to the generic drug. They say that arguments challenging the efficacy of the generic formulation and alleging a lack of ‘bioavailability’ are entirely unscientific and baseless.
Bioavailability denotes the rate and extent to which an administered pharmaceutical substance enters systemic circulation through the digestive tract. A bioequivalence study normally compares the rate and extent of absorption of the generic with the reference product. The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises this as an important way to establish interchangeability. However, bioequivalence studies are not required for every generic medicine. The WHO’s guidance on generic medicines explicitly recognises circumstances in which equivalence studies can be waived. One such circumstance is when the generic and reference products are pharmaceutically equivalent oral solutions containing the same active ingredient at the same molar concentration, subject to the applicable requirements for excipients.
In this case, both products contain Risdiplam. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) approved Natsmart and the regulator’s position is that a bioequivalence study is not required for this particular oral solution. Public health experts also say that the absence of a conventional bioequivalence study does not necessarily mean the regulator approved the drug without adequate evidence. A regulator may accept a scientifically-justified waiver.
Doctors also point out that Natsmart is being prescribed by many premier teaching hospitals in the country and several patients are already using it in Keralam too, for the last five months, without any complaints.
Public health is about maximising access to people, and unless credible scientific evidence demonstrates that the approved generic is less safe or less effective than the original molecule, regulatory approval should remain the primary basis for procurement decisions in publicly-funded health programmes, experts have argued.
The current controversy
The current controversy centres around an alarm raised by parents of children with SMA, after they pointed out that the bottle of Natsmart dispensed to them was labelled, ‘Physicians’ sample/for clinical trials’. Though the authorities clarified later that these were drug sample bottles they were forced to source directly from Natco and not part of the government supply (which was delayed), the issue has become something for Opposition parties, particularly the CPI(M), to latch on to. It has also served to perpetuate fears and misgivings about the generic drug among SMA families.
What is happening at present?
SAT Hospital authorities, who are responsible for the SMA clinic, have now decided to hold a meeting of families to assuage their concerns. They say that several meetings had been held earlier too, to reassure parents about the switch from Evrysdi to Natsmart. However, the new controversy over ‘clinical trial’ drugs may have undone some of the previous work. The labelling issue is clearly separate from the concerns about the switch to generic medicine and the families’ demand for scientific evidence and transparent communication is valid, authorities admit.

The Uttar Pradesh Cabinet on Tuesday (October 27) approved the establishment of a 69.52-acre robotics and artificial intelligence (AI) park in Greater Noida, with the project projected to generate more than 1 lakh direct and indirect jobs and contribute around ₹2,000 crore annually to the state’s economy at full scale.
The proposed platform for Robotics and AI Growth Through Technology and Innovation (PRAGATI) Park aims to promote indigenous robotics manufacturing, accelerate AI-based technology development and attract investment and research in the sector, Finance Minister Suresh Kumar Khanna said after a Cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath.
The project will be developed in two zones, with different investment and ownership structures.
The proposed park will cover 69.52 acres, divided into an eight-acre zone to be developed under a public-private partnership (PPP) model and a second zone spanning 61.52 acres for private investment.
The first zone will be developed and operated through a special purpose vehicle (SPV). The Greater Noida Authority will hold a 26% equity stake, while the selected industrial partner will own the remaining 74%, Khanna said.
The second zone will be developed by private enterprises through investments in industrial units and related activities. The state government will have no capital liability for developing this zone, he added.
The financial structure for the first zone includes an equity contribution of ₹21.1 crore from the Greater Noida Authority and an interest-free loan of ₹126.2 crore from the state government for 30 years.
The combined value of these two amounts is ₹147.3 crore.
The lease premium for the eight-acre plot will be reimbursed to the Greater Noida Authority through the state government's IT and Electronics Department under the prescribed arrangement, according to an official statement.
The SPV will also receive a service charge equivalent to 5% of the revenue generated from development charges on land allotments in the second zone, along with applicable goods and services tax (GST).
The industrial partner will be selected through a quality-based selection process. Subsequent steps will include registering the SPV, allotting land, executing the lease deed and undertaking construction-related work.
Commercial operations in the first zone are targeted to begin within 36 months of the SPV’s registration. The deadline may be extended to a maximum of 48 months if required, according to project details shared at the media briefing.
A committee will review the project's progress.
The park will house shared infrastructure and specialised facilities, including robotics testing and certification centres, rapid prototyping facilities, AI computing infrastructure, motion-capture systems and data laboratories.
Startups and entrepreneurs are expected to gain access to advanced testing and prototyping facilities, as well as graphics processing unit (GPU)-based computing infrastructure, at affordable rates.
The park is also intended to strengthen companies’ ability to test robotics products against global standards and obtain certifications such as CE and UL.
At full scale, PRAGATI Park is projected to generate more than 1 lakh direct and indirect jobs and contribute around ₹2,000 crore annually in gross value added (GVA) to Uttar Pradesh's economy.
The project is expected to create employment and skill-development opportunities for young people and technical workers across robotics, AI, prototyping, testing and advanced manufacturing.
It also aims to strengthen domestic technology development and manufacturing, reduce dependence on imports and help Indian companies build products for global markets.
The employment and economic contribution figures are projections for the park at full scale, rather than confirmed outcomes from an operational facility.

After two months of discomfort, a man in South Korea went to an eye clinic where doctors pulled 11 living, wriggling worms from his eyes. They apparently made the most of their time on the man’s peepers; at the time of extraction, many of the female worms were pregnant. The man narrowly avoided having them spew their loads of living larvae directly into his eyes.
The man in this case was a 71-year-old crop farmer. He told doctors that for the previous two months he had the sensation of having something stuck in both his eyes, which were also red and blurry. When ophthalmologists took a look, they quickly saw the problem: multiple mobile, whitish roundworms. His eyes were not in good shape either, as one might expect. The blood vessels in the membrane over the eye, the conjunctiva, were enlarged, making his eyes look red. And the cells of his cornea—the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye—had eroded, potentially after the helminths’ hanky-panky.
According to a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the doctors gave the man a topical treatment to numb his eyes and then began plucking out the worms one by one with fine forceps. They collected 11 adult worms, which ranged in size from 11 to 22 mm.
Examining the worms under a microscope, the doctors identified them as Thelazia callipaeda nematodes, which are widespread across Asia and have also established in parts of Europe. These parasites primarily infest the eyes of cats and dogs but can sometimes make their way into human eyes inadvertently.

NASA plans to launch three massive rockets for the Artemis 3 crewed lunar test mission
Blue Origin, SpaceX and NASA are launching heavy-lift rockets within a short timeframe for the mission.
Earlier this year, NASA made some major changes to its Artemis program that would push back the next crewed moon landing to 2028. Artemis 3 was supposed to be the agency's first crewed moon landing since the Apollo 17 in 1972, but under the overhauled program, it will now involve testing at least one moon lander instead. Now, the agency has revealed its detailed plans for Artemis 3, which will launch three spacecraft on three different heavy-lift rockets from Florida within the span of two weeks.
Artemis 3 will officially begin when Blue Origin launches the New Glenn with a test version of its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander into low Earth orbit, about 273 miles above Earth's surface. After that, NASA will launch Space Launch System (SLS) with the Orion crew capsule on top, carrying NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas, as well as European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano. Orion will settle into an orbit at an altitude of around 345 miles before rendezvousing with Blue Moon Mark 2. The New Glenn launchpad exploded back in May during a hotfire test, but the company is working to make it usable again by the end of this year.
The crew will make sure everything is in order for a couple of days before they open the hatch between the two spacecraft and enter Blue Origin's lander. They will verify its ability to maintain proper atmosphere and pressure and test its software, flight-control systems and life-support functions. The astronauts will then return to Orion, which will undock from Blue Moon Mark 2 so it can position itself for the next rendezvous.
The last part of the mission will see SpaceX launching Starship version 3, which had its first flight back in May. It will fly with a docking system mounted at the vehicle's forward end, so it can also dock with Orion. This rendezvous will be shorter and last just two hours. The crew will not go inside the Ship capsule and will only verify how Orion interacts with it, docks and undocks when they're linked in space. Once the rendezvous is done, the crew will have around five additional days that they can spend in orbit before they head home.
NASA says the separate docking approaches will "demonstrate how Orion interfaces with two very different commercial lander architectures during a single mission." Artemis 3 will also help NASA evaluate the new Orion Crew Survival System suits, custom-made for deep-space missions. It's not quite clear when Artemis 3 will launch, exactly. NASA Watch reported last month that NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman sent an agency-wide memo admitting Artemis 3 is three months behind schedule. In the best-case scenario, the mission will launch in the summer of 2027 so the agency can have two moon landing opportunities for Artemis 4 in 2028.

Geneva – His Excellency Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, today signed several funding agreements totaling € 25.5 million to support critical health priorities.
The agreements include € 4.5 million of funding for the Core Voluntary Contribution Account (CVCA) of WHO; these are fully flexible funds which allow WHO to allocate resources to key priorities outlined in its General Programme of Work. An additional € 15 million will be used to deliver on specific key priorities, such as One Health, the advancement of universal health coverage, and primary health care, communicable and noncommunicable diseases, the medical countermeasure initiative, and the country readiness strengthening through WHO’s office in Lyon.
A large part of the contribution (€ 6 million) is aimed at covering the humanitarian response on several fronts: € 2 million will go towards enhancing mental health initiatives in Ukraine; € 0.35 million is to support the response to the cholera outbreak in Malawi; € 1 million will support WHO’s humanitarian response in Gaza, with an additional € 2 million dedicated to strengthening the technical and human activities of the WHO Office in the occupied Palestinian territory. Finally, € 0.65 million will go to the Contingency Fund for Emergencies, to be used as needs arise.
“As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health. France's financial contributions and agreements, signed today, provide flexibility and align well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, power and perform for health” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General.
France’s WHO Framework Agreement for the period 2020-2025 ensures sustainable funding for priority health programmes, aligned with WHO priorities.
Some of the joint 2022-2023 collaboration priorities include the work of the WHO Academy, based in Lyon, stronger health systems towards universal health coverage, health emergencies – in particular the International Health Regulations (IHR) and health emergencies preparedness – and reducing health inequalities.
These priorities align with the France Global Health Strategy 2023-2027, published in October 2023.
“Committed to global health, France supports the WHO’s action in crises and for the benefit of the most vulnerable,” said Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations.
In 2020-2021, the Republic of France contributed over US$ 143 million to WHO, (including assessed and voluntary contributions), with 76% of the contributions in flexible and thematic funds. Flexible funds allow WHO to assign resources when and where they are needed most, ensuring that key priorities are funded, and a better flow of funds, enabling a more agile delivery of WHO’s objectives as per the General Programme of Work.

The mistake iPhone Duo buyers can easily avoid
The iPhone Duo is costly, and fixing it comes at a high price as well.
The iPhone Duo is finally available, and you might be interested in one after reading our iPhone Duo review. There can be some justification for its mighty $2,000 price tag if you see it as combining an iPhone with an iPad mini. If you want to be a little more productive on the go when you don't have your laptop, here's your answer. It should also be a killer ereader and YouTube player.
With such a high barrier to entry, it can be tempting to skip iPhone Duo add-ons of the sort you'd normally pick up alongside a new phone. You probably already have enough cables and chargers. Heck, you might even think to skip a case if you're careful about how you hold and stash your new foldable.
One extra you probably shouldn't dodge, though, is AppleCare+ or AppleCare One. While it adds hundreds of dollars to your phone's lifetime price, the penalty if something goes wrong could be even more severe. It's inherent to the nature of foldable phones, at least as they are in 2026.
Why AppleCare could save your hide with the iPhone Duo
With a foldable phone, there's a whole extra screen to break, and the out-of-warranty repair costs for that can be astronomical. While the outer display is only 5.4 inches, Apple's service pricing page estimates a repair cost of $379 for it. The main attraction — that 7.6-inch, nano-textured inner screen — is listed at $999 for repairs. That's more than a new iPhone 17, or even an iPad mini with max storage.
As if that weren't enough, there's at least a $199 charge for repairing the back glass, while battery service and fixing the rear cameras are $229 apiece. There's also a blanket $1,499 cost for "other damage." Presumably, that's for the hinge, bending damage or anything involving the guts of the phone, such as its storage and processor. There's little else that could justify spending more than the base price of a MacBook Air.
Conversely, AppleCare+ is $20 per month or $200 annually, while AppleCare One is $20 per month for individuals or $50 per month for families. If you already have an AppleCare One family plan, or an individual plan with an older iPhone you're replacing, your new Duo would be covered at no additional cost. Otherwise, you're looking at either $400 or $480 for two years.
Before Apple's reduced AppleCare service fees, which range from $19 for cover layer fixes to $99 for "other" damage, those subscriptions are less than half the cost of repairing the inner display. Remember that AppleCare+ also covers theft and loss (with a $149 fee), not just accidents. That ongoing expense could save you another way if you're a frequent traveler or prone to setting your phone down and walking away.
Could you get away with just an iPhone Duo case?
If your only major concern is dropping your Duo, then possibly. Many cases, including Apple's, add a raised edge around the displays and the camera bump, allowing them to absorb some impact before the force is transferred to anything vulnerable. It's also worth noting that the front display uses toughened Ceramic Shield 2 glass, developed in tandem with Corning. It's not invincible, but with a case, my iPhone 16 Pro's display has survived multiple drops despite using first-generation Ceramic Shield material. On top of that, the Duo has Ceramic Shield back glass, plus a titanium frame and hinge cover.
The problem, once again, is that inner display. Because it needs to bend, there's no Ceramic Shield protection whatsoever. You could thus be in serious trouble if you drop your phone when it's completely open. We've also yet to discover how durable its hinge is or how well its nano-texture surface will hold up against fingernails, debris and an Apple Pencil. Scratches are a real threat on other foldables, and it's doubtful that Apple has come up with a perfect antidote.
Compounded with risks like theft and loss, it's hard to ignore the peace of mind extended AppleCare brings, making it a virtual necessity. If the added costs sounds too pricey, you're better off skipping the Duo entirely. Forking out another $2,000 for a replacement Duo likely isn't in the cards for most people.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memo warning military personnel against using nonpublic information to make bets on prediction markets, saying the wagers could give important clues to enemy countries.
“Do Not Compromise Military Operations for Personal Financial Gain,” said the subject line of an October 20 memo published yesterday by CBS News. Hegseth’s memo was sent to senior Pentagon leadership, Combatant Command leaders, and Defense Department field activity directors.
Hegseth wrote:
Our enemies watch movements in these markets. When an American Service member, intelligence professional, or other Department civilian engages in a financial transaction on a military outcome, they create a signal. That signal can be aggregated, correlated, and exploited by hostile foreign intelligence services to anticipate our movements, targets, and timing. The lives of our Service members often depend on the enemy not knowing what is coming. The men and women who carry our flag into harm’s way deserve a Force that protects them—not one that exposes them to the enemy for personal gain.
In April, a US Army soldier was arrested and charged with using confidential information to make $410,000 in Polymarket bets on the timing of the military’s capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. An August report by the Anti-Corruption Data Collective said the group found 152 suspicious wallets that placed longshot bets on military and defense markets and won a combined $8 million.
Betting can warp judgment, Hegseth says
Hegseth’s memo said the prohibition applies to “all financial platforms,” including traditional betting services and prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi. Defense Department personnel may not make any financial transaction informed by nonpublic information, regardless of whether that information is classified or unclassified, Hegseth wrote.

Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
- Published
Algeria is to send troops to Niger in its first foreign deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973.
The deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister, as the country seeks support against armed groups, some of which are linked to al-Qaeda or Islamic State.
Algeria has economic interests in Niger, including a planned gas pipeline that would carry Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.
The deployment comes as the two neighbours rebuild ties after a diplomatic rift in 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers.
Algeria's upper house of parliament held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on the proposed deployment. According to AFP news agency, 148 of the 174 senators voted in favour. It was later backed by the lower house of parliament.
However, the timing and number of soldiers to be deployed have not been announced.
The move would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision allowing overseas military deployments and a significant shift in Algeria's long-standing policy against sending forces abroad.
"We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure," Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after the vote.
Algeria's state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has also signed an agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry to explore for oil in the Kafra region. Two exploration wells are estimated to contain 168 million and 100 million barrels, respectively, Reuters reported.
Relations between Algeria and Niger have not always been smooth in recent years.
Algeria condemned the 2023 coup that ousted Niger's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum, and brought Gen Abdourahamane Tchiani to power.
Tensions rose again in 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border. Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers in solidarity with Mali, a close ally which is also under military rule.
Relations have since improved. Tchiani visited Algeria in February 2026, and in late August, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sent fighter jets to Niger to help suppress a coup attempt and also donated four military helicopters.

The 56th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu examines early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, concerns about the reliability of cancer research and challenges in accessing treatment for children with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss how Alzheimer’s disease can affect younger people, the implications of unreliable cancer research, and concerns raised by families over a generic SMA drug.
The episode begins with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease and how the condition can present differently in younger people. The discussion looks at changes in memory, behaviour and everyday functioning, and the challenges of recognising the disease when symptoms appear earlier in life.
Another segment examines cancer research articles flagged for suspected links to paper mills. These businesses produce and sell research papers, sometimes using fabricated data, manipulated images or other questionable research practices. The discussion looks at how unreliable publications can undermine scientific progress, affect future research and complicate efforts to assess the evidence behind medical findings. It also highlights the need for careful investigation, as an article being flagged for suspected links to a paper mill does not, by itself, establish research misconduct.
The episode also looks at concerns raised by families of children living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) in Keralam over a generic drug used to treat the rare genetic condition. The concerns have brought questions about the safety, quality and effectiveness of medicines into focus. The discussion examines the importance of reliable information about treatment, regulatory oversight and the challenges families face in accessing medicines for rare diseases, where treatment costs can be a significant barrier.
The final segment revisits the history of Alzheimer’s disease through the case of Auguste Deter. In 1901, German psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer began documenting the symptoms of Deter, a 51-year-old woman who experienced changes in memory, behaviour and her ability to carry out everyday activities. Her symptoms differed from cases he had typically encountered. After her death in 1906, Alzheimer examined her brain and identified changes that contributed to the understanding of the condition later named after him. The segment explores Deter’s experience and the role of clinical observation and patient documentation in the history of medical research.
