India's largest share sale could end cheap mobile internet for millions
- Published
India's biggest telecom giant, the Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms, is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday.
Despite a bruising spell for Indian markets, its historic $3.2bn initial public offering (IPO) - the country's largest ever - has drawn overwhelming demand from top global fund managers, domestic institutions and mom-and-pop retail investors.
Bids outstripped the shares on offer within hours of subscriptions opening on 21 October.
Owned by Asia's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, Jio is one of India's most consequential companies, with half a billion people subscribing to its cheap mobile data. But its meteoric rise has also been dogged by controversy.
The company burst onto India's crowded telecom scene in 2016, offering throwaway tariffs that got millions of Indians hooked to the internet.
But its launch led to a huge disruption in the telecom sector. A market once crowded with 17 operators shrunk to an oligopoly of just three, with critics accusing the deep-pocketed company of waging a price war that pushed rivals out of business.
More recently, Elon Musk criticised Ambani, calling him the "real boss of India", suggesting that Jio was trying to thwart Starlink's entry into India. Reliance dismissed the allegations saying it welcomed competition from Musk.
For all the scrutiny it has faced over the last decade, Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution, spawning a huge digital economy and democratising online payments, food delivery and e-commerce in Asia's third-biggest economy.
Within three years of its launch, customer data usage rose fifty-fold and data prices crashed.
This aggressive discounting helped Jio rapidly amass some 553 million mobile subscribers by 2026. It also cemented its dominance in other segments, capturing 50% of the wireless broadband market and more than 40% of fixed broadband.
Jio also carries 60% of India's wireless data traffic and boasts of the largest 5G subscriber base outside China, according to brokerage Emkay Global, which has described the company as the "digital engine of India".
But analysts say its stock market debut - which will see its promoters dilute their shareholding by about 3% - could mark a turning point in Jio's pricing strategy, potentially bringing an end to years of ultra-cheap tariffs.
"The era of Jio using cheap tariffs as a market-share weapon is drawing to a close," said Nitya Shah, co-founder of KamayaKya Wealth Management.
"A listed Jio must answer to minority shareholders… which structurally reduces its incentive to keep pricing suppressed."
Jio's future growth will no longer be driven primarily by adding subscribers through discounted plans. Instead, it will depend on "earning more per subscriber - through the migration to 5G, successive tariff revisions, and the extension of fixed wireless broadband into homes fibre has never reached", brokerage company Motilal Oswal said in a note.
The listing could also pave the way for Jio's competitors to raise prices, as fears of being undercut by a cheaper rival begin to recede.
"The biggest beneficiary of this shift could be Vodafone Idea," says Shah. "It is a moment the sector's weakest balance sheet gets its strongest tailwind".
For Indian consumers, any further increases would come on the heels of an industry-wide tariff hike a few years ago. Analysts say another round of price rises could trigger a fresh churn in the market as price-sensitive customers switch to the cheapest plans available.
While consumers may have to brace for higher bills, Jio's IPO offers investors a bet on India's seemingly insatiable appetite for data - and the growing ecosystem of digital services the company offers across entertainment, cloud computing, gaming and financial services.
India has emerged as the second-largest consumer of mobile data in the world, driven by lower tariffs and rising penetration of smartphones.
Jio's monthly data use per customer has climbed from 28.7 GB in 2024 to 42.3 GB in 2026 - up by 52% in two years. As per some estimates, usage is expected to surge further to 65GB by the end of this decade as disposable incomes rise.
All of this will give a tailwind for Jio to drive long-term growth in average revenue per user.
"Penetration of most digital services remains well below China and the US, which leaves significant headroom [for growth]," according to Emkay Global.
The listing is also likely to enhance transparency and provide investors with a "clearer market valuation" for the company, according to Moody's rating agency, as Jio is currently part of Reliance Industries, which has businesses spanning oil refining and retail.
But as much as its central and growing role in India's economy has excited investors, the buzz about the IPO also comes from the fact that this is the first share sale from the Reliance conglomerate in over two decades.
The company - which started as a small spice and polyester yarn trading venture in 1958 before expanding into textiles, petrochemicals, refining and eventually to retail, telecom and digital services - is known for its track record of long-term wealth creation, and enjoys legendary status among mom-and-pop investors.
Dhirubhai Ambani, the founder of the Reliance empire, is said to have played a foundational role in popularising equity investing and taking it beyond the preserve of traders and wealthy families in the 1980s and 90s.
In its early years, Reliance built a vast base of individual shareholders by turning its annual general meetings into grand spectacles of big announcements, dividend payouts and celebrations of public share ownership. Over time, this helped forge a fiercely loyal investor base, many of whom developed a deep emotional bond with the company.
And while Reliance Industries' stock has fallen nearly 20% over the past year, its longer-term track record continues to inspire confidence.
"The company has given average annualised returns of around 30% consistently for thirty years," Kranthi Bathini of Mumbai-based WealthMills Securities told the BBC.
"That's why there's anticipation that the same magic can be replicated with the Jio IPO."

Justice delayed: Acknowledging women pioneers in science
For a discipline so wedded to reason and fact as science is, it has fiendishly guarded its gender bias. Over centuries, pioneering women in science have been ignored, their achievements overlooked or usurped by male colleagues, their names left out of scientific publications; they have been underpaid and undervalued, denied promotions and advancements in careers, sometimes consigned to housekeeping roles about the office in order to keep their jobs.
In a compilation of such women in scientific research through the ages, Rosalind Franklin would probably be right on top of the list. It was Franklin’s X-ray diffraction image that lore says, was crucial to discovering the DNA’s double helix structure, enabling advances in genetics and molecular biology, with vast applications in medicine. And yet, when the Nobel Prize for Physiology in 1962 was announced, the names on that list were Watson and Crick, shared with Wilkins. It was decades before her true role in this path-breaking discovery came to be known to the world.
Today, Franklin stands testimony to the power of women, as she is representative of the ‘woman wronged by science’, but not just that – her achievements in science (in other fields) have broken new ground that researchers have since travelled on. As we unveil the achievements of women in science, particularly those whom their present refused to acknowledge, it is important to get her story out there, more so since she was vilified and mocked by the very men who benefitted from her work.
At King’s College
Franklin was a British chemist and X-ray crystallographer. In 1951, she joined the team at King’s College London, biophysicists led by John Randall, and Maurice Wilkins as his deputy (who would later share the Nobel prize), that were using X-ray diffraction to study the structure of the molecule, recount Matthew Cobb and Nathaniel Comfort, two researchers looking into the past of Watson and Crick to craft their biographies, in an article in Nature.
Franklin, had already been trained in this technique, having used it earlier to study the structure of coal, which she advanced by many lengths with her work. Cobb and Comfort detail in their article: “Franklin was able to exploit a discovery that Wilkins had made earlier — DNA in solution could take two forms, what she called the crystalline or A form, and the paracrystalline or B form. Franklin found that she could convert A into B simply by raising the relative humidity in the specimen chamber; lowering it again restored the crystalline A form.” A B form X-ray image it was that provided great clarity on the actual structure of the DNA.
Photograph 51
The distorted story of Franklin’s role was spread, thanks in good measure, by Watson’s best selling book The Double Helix. In the book, Watson infantilised Franklin, claiming that she did not realise the importance of the photo she took – the life altering, or life-explaining Photograph 51. Let’s refer to what Kings College London records about this photograph: “Photograph 51” is an X-ray diffraction image of DNA taken by Rosalind Franklin, together with her PhD student Raymond Gosling, at King’s College London in May 1952. In fact, the camera was set up to take the photograph on Friday 2 May and it was developed on Tuesday 6 May: as Franklin reported in her lab notebook, the DNA was exposed to X-rays for a total of 62 hours to take Photograph 51.”
Photograph 51 was reportedly infinitely clearer than any of the earlier images, and also with other data from Rosalind’s work during her time at King’s it was possible to make the leap to the double helix structure, notes the college’s website. This entire body of work was key to building the structure of DNA but never properly acknowledged until much later, after her death. Records have it down that James Watson was shown this photograph (without her permission) and it reportedly spurred both him and Francis Crick to attempt to build a model, which was then feted across the world as a path-breaking discovery.
Cobb and Comfort however challenge Watson’s narrative: “[It] contains an absurd presumption. It implies that Franklin, the skilled chemist, could not understand her own data, whereas he, a crystallographic novice, apprehended it immediately.” While implying that the whole story constructed around the Eureka moment from Photograph 51 was probably an exaggeration, they add: “Moreover, everyone, even Watson, knew it was impossible to deduce any precise structure from a single photograph — other structures could have produced the same diffraction pattern... In fact, it was other data from Franklin and Wilkins that proved crucial, and even then, what really happened was less malicious than is widely assumed.” However, malice, wilful sexism, or a casual miss, the fact remains that Wilkins was co-named for the Nobel, while Franklin was not.
On the website of the Rosalind Franklin Institute, set up in Franklin’s honour Professor Patricia Fara, president of the British Society for the History of Science (2016-18), Clare College, University of Cambridge, writes on the life and work of Rosalind Franklin: “Since her early death at the age of 37 [of cancer], Rosalind Franklin has become mythologised as the victim of male prejudice, the unsung heroine who took the crucial X-ray photograph enabling James Watson and Francis Crick to build their double helix model of DNA, and was unjustly deprived of a Nobel Prize. She would neither have recognised nor endorsed this soundbite description. Franklin regarded herself first and foremost not as a woman, but as a scientist, and her DNA research occupied a relatively brief period in her successful career working on a variety of topics. In particular, on top of her famous investigations into DNA, she also made foundational contributions to modern understandings of coal, graphite and viruses.”
Since her death however, Franklin’s story has been freed from the cloisters it was trapped in. It has traversed the mythical seven seas and seven mountains to sound in the corners of the world. Several honours have since been heaped on her, in recognition of her immense contributions to science in a short life. Not least of them, was a 1989 Swedish stamp features an image of the DNA double helix based on Photograph 51.

The video is authentic but does not show recent gatherings, as some people falsely claimed. It features clips of larger "No Kings" rallies that occurred on Oct. 18, 2025 — almost one year ago to the day.
This week, people shared a video displaying a collage of aerial clips allegedly showing "No Kings" gatherings, specifically the Oct. 17 "No Kings: Vote Early" event. Cities featured in the video included Minneapolis, Philadelphia, Washington, D.C., Chicago, New York, San Diego and Boston.
The NoKings.org website describes "No Kings" as a movement against kings, dictators and tyrants, primarily focused on U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration. A footer on the homepage explains, "No Kings events are nonpartisan and are designed to increase participation from all eligible voters."
As an example of posts currently spreading the "No Kings"-labeed video, a Facebook user's repost of it (archived) on Oct. 17 received millions of views. The post's caption read in part, "When citizens stand together and make their voices heard, the country should pay attention." That same user later claimed (archived) the video showed moments from Saturday's event and that "the news is ignoring it, and social media is censoring it."
In sum, our research found the video clips were authentic but also about a year old. Therefore, we've rated the video miscaptioned.
Others reposted the same video on Bluesky, Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Those users either claimed the clip showed last Saturday's gatherings or displayed comments from people who believed that it did. Some commenters falsely suggested the video was an AI-generated fake.
The video was a montage of clips of "No Kings" rallies that took place on Oct. 18, 2025. On that day, the progressive activist group Indivisible — one of nine partner organizations mentioned on the NoKings.org website — posted the video on Bluesky, Facebook, Instagram and other platforms. Others prominently posted the video on or around the same day.
Snopes emailed Indivisible to officially confirm that the organization was the first to post the video and whether they compiled it themselves. We'll update this article if we receive further information.
Reverse image searches for each city in the video found matching clips or photos from the 2025 rallies, including for Minneapolis (at 2:42), Philadelphia (at 1:46), Washington, D.C. (at 0:17), Chicago (at 1:15:10), New York, San Diego and Boston.
Fact checkers reported at the time that some users falsely alleged the 2025 Boston footage broadcast by MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) really originated in 2017.
Earlier this year, some people also reposted the October 2025 footage to falsely represent "No Kings" demonstrations as occurring on March 28.
Saturday's 'No Kings: Vote Early' gatherings
The most recent "No Kings" event on Saturday, dubbed "No Kings: Vote Early," reportedly featured smaller demonstrations than past "No Kings" occasions — with a singular focus on the upcoming midterm elections — including community gatherings such as block parties and cookouts.
The Indivisible organization posted an authentic video that they said showed glimpses at some attendees participating across the U.S.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d'Or: Bayern Munich striker becomes first English winner of award in 25 years
Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d'Or at London ceremony; Bayern Munich striker becomes first English winner of award in 25 years; England captain hit 73 goals for club and country last season; ex-Tottenham forward beat Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe and Barcelona winger Lamine Yamal to prize

Harry Kane has become the first English winner of the Ballon d'Or in 25 years after being honoured at a ceremony in London.

- The claim that North Korea's supreme leader Kim Jong Un is dead is unfounded.
- The rumor stems from U.S-based Chinese dissident Wanjun Xie, who has a history of spreading false or unverified claims on social media.
- Snopes found no verifiable evidence confirming Kim had died. North Korean state media posted photograhs claiming to show Kim touring a garment exhibition on Oct. 19, but we could not verify when they were taken. If Kim were dead, there would likely be more speculation and reporting from South Korea and reputable news agencies worldwide.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the North Korean permanent mission to the United Nations and await a response.
In October, rumors spread online that North Korea's supreme leader Kim Jong Un had died from a serious health condition.
Some posts claimed he died after a brain hemorrhage led to a coma, while others said he died from myocarditis, a heart condition.
Snopes readers also asked us to verify Kim's condition and whereabouts.
(X user @xie_wanjun)
Snopes found no verifiable evidence confirming Kim had died. North Korea's supreme leader has been the frequent subject of death hoaxes in the past.
North Korean state media posted images that they claim show him visiting a garment and footwear exhibition on Oct. 19, but we were unable to definitively confirm when they were taken. Furthermore, we could not independently verify claims about Kim's health or medical history. Until we know more, we've left this claim unrated.
Snopes reached out to the North Korean permanent mission to the United Nations to learn more and will update this story accordingly.
The earliest example of this rumor originated from U.S-based Chinese dissident Wanjun Xie, who also claimed on X that Chinese President Xi Jinping was dead. Xie alleged that due to poor medical facilities in North Korea, Kim went to Beijing, China, to receive treatment.
As seen above, Xie shared a video claiming to show a North Korean news announcement of Kim's death. This video is from 2011, not 2026, and shows a North Korean newscaster announcing the death of Kim Jong Il, Kim's father and predecessor.
On Oct. 20, North Korea's state news, Korean Central News Agency, released images of Kim on an official tour. The news release read:
Respected Comrade Kim Jong Un, General Secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea and President of the State Affairs of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, went round the venue of a garment and footwear exhibition in light industry on October 19.
He was accompanied by leading officials of the Party and the government.
Comrade Kim Jong Un was greeted on the spot by senior officials of the Light Industry Department of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea.
A series of photographs published by Rodong Sinmun, the official newspaper for the ruling Workers' Party of North Korea, showed Kim and his daughter Kim Ju Ae inspecting garments and shoes on display.
(Rodong Sinmun)
(Rodong Sinmun)
(Rodong Sinmun)
There were no obvious signs of AI generation or manipulation in the images, but Snopes could not definitively confirm when they were taken. Signage in the background indicates the photos may have been captured sometime in 2026 without pointing to a specific date. While this does not prove that Kim is alive, there is no evidence of his death either.
Xie has circulated unverified claims before, including ones stating Xi had stepped down or been ousted from power in China. There is no evidence to support such claims amid news that Xi is preparing for a possible meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
If there were authentic sources discussing Kim's death, this news would have been widely covered by reputable news outlets like The Associated Press or Reuters. That was not the case.
According to BBC News, if Kim had died, China would likely be tightening security along its borders in anticipation of refugees. North Korean defectors to South Korea also would have received information through their whisper networks. 
News reports over the years have said Kim is a heavy smoker, overweight and has cardiovascular issues, but there's no evidence he suffered a brain hemorrhage or has myocarditis, as posts suggested.
As we've previously reported, North Korea is a black hole for independent media coverage so verifying any information coming in or out is difficult.
For further reading, Snopes has dug into numerous rumors about the dictator over the years.

From the bright minds that brought you FTX Arena and NBA Top Shot NFT maketplace (where sales last month dropped to $762,781, which is a 99.66 percent decrease compared to the February 2021 peak of $226,350,843), the NBA announced Monday that it has new “preferred” prediction market deals for Kalshi and Polymarket, as well as a memorandum of understanding with the US CFTC about how to manage the relationships. It also announced an expansion of its DraftKings deal to include prediction markets, and says that more expansions will be announced with others soon.
The NBA’s response to gambling scandals is to add more gambling partnerships
The NBA announced a new integrity framework, along with prediction market deals for Polymarket, Kalshi, and DraftKings.
The NBA is already facing scandals after Jontay Porter pleaded guilty to conspiracy over a gambling and manipulation scheme in 2024, Malik Beasley is reportedly in negotiations over a plea deal on similar charges, while former player Terry Rozier and coach Chauncey Billups are under indictment on charges of allegedly rigging prop bets and participating in rigged poker games, respectively.
NBA Head of Media Distribution & Partnerships Scott Kaufman-Ross proclaims that “Protecting the integrity of the game is our top priority,” as it establishes its integrity framework for the Kalshi and Polymarket deal. Under the new arrangements, prediction markets will be able to use official league data and IP, while promising limitations on “permissible markets” and information-sharing on suspicious trades and investigations.
That last bit will probably be important, as prediction markets have already drawn insider trading activity for everything from US military activity in Venezuela to Trump’s teleprompter. Currently, New York attorney general Letitia James is just one of many state AGs suing Kalshi and the others as senators investigate reports pointing out how DraftKings and others use AI to target the gamblers who are more likely to lose, while restricting bets from those who win.

For people living with peripheral artery disease (PAD), walking even short distances or doing routine household tasks can become difficult because of leg pain. The condition develops when arteries supplying blood to the legs become narrow, usually because fatty deposits build up along their walls. With less blood reaching the muscles, walking can cause pain, cramps or heaviness that ease with rest. In advanced cases, pain may persist even when a person is sitting or lying down, and poor circulation can lead to wounds that do not heal.
Treatment can be challenging too because movement is an important part of managing PAD, while pain makes it difficult to stay active. Structured exercise, medicines and control of risk factors such as smoking, diabetes and high blood pressure can help manage the condition. When blood flow is severely reduced, procedures may be needed to prevent damage to the feet and legs. PAD can also affect overall cardiovascular health, increasing the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Managing pain
Pain, cramps, heaviness in the calf or thigh that develop during walking and ease with rest are known as intermittent claudication. This happens when narrowed arteries cannot supply enough blood to meet the muscles’ increased needs during activity.
Venu S., consultant vascular surgeon, Prashanth Hospitals, Chennai, says structured walking programmes can help patients gradually increase the distance they can walk. Patients are generally advised to walk until the discomfort becomes moderate, rest until it settles and then resume walking. Sessions commonly last 30 to 45 minutes and take place several times a week, with supervision where possible.
He says patients who follow a structured programme for about three months may be able to walk twice as far, or more, before pain begins. The pace and duration should suit each patient’s ability. Those who find walking difficult may need an adapted exercise programme under medical supervision.
Balaji V., senior consultant, vascular surgery, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai, says quitting smoking, eating a healthy diet, staying physically active and controlling blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol are also important parts of treatment.
Exercise should not mean pushing through severe pain. Pain that does not settle with rest needs medical assessment. Pain in the feet or toes while resting, particularly at night, can indicate a serious reduction in blood flow and requires prompt medical attention.
Diagnosis and treatment
Diagnosis usually begins with a review of symptoms and medical history, followed by an examination of the legs and feet, including checking the pulses. Doctors may measure the ankle-brachial index (ABI), which compares blood pressure at the ankle with that in the arm, to assess blood flow. A Doppler ultrasound scan can help identify narrowed arteries and assess circulation. In patients with severe symptoms or wounds that do not heal, a CT angiogram may be needed to locate the blockage and plan treatment.
Medicines aim to relieve symptoms, slow the progression of arterial disease and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. Antiplatelet medicines such as aspirin or clopidogrel help prevent blood clots. Statins lower cholesterol and help stabilise fatty deposits in artery walls. Medicines to control blood pressure and diabetes are also important. Cilostazol can help some patients with walking-related pain walk farther before symptoms begin, but it is not suitable for people with heart failure. Select patients may need additional medicines to reduce cardiovascular and limb-related risks.
Experts say treatment often needs to continue long term, even when symptoms improve. Patients should not stop or change prescribed medicines without consulting their doctor.
Diabetes can damage nerves and reduce sensation in the feet, allowing cuts and wounds to go unnoticed. It can also affect smaller arteries, making some blockages harder to treat. High blood pressure and cholesterol contribute to arterial damage and the build-up of fatty deposits. Kidney disease can cause calcium to build up in artery walls and delay wound healing. Heart disease can occur alongside PAD because both may result from the same underlying process.
During follow-up, doctors assess changes in walking distance and symptoms and may repeat ABI measurements or Doppler scans to check blood flow. Blood tests can help monitor cholesterol, blood sugar and kidney function.
Preventing complications
When symptoms remain disabling despite medicines and exercise, doctors may consider a procedure to widen the narrowed artery. The decision depends on the location and extent of the blockage, the severity of symptoms and the patient’s overall health.
Angioplasty uses a small balloon to widen a narrowed artery. A stent may be placed to help keep it open. Experts say newer techniques can also help treat complex blockages.
Intravascular lithotripsy uses shock waves delivered through a specialised balloon to modify heavy calcium deposits in the artery, making it easier to widen the vessel. Atherectomy devices can remove fatty deposits in selected cases, while thrombectomy devices are used to remove blood clots. The appropriate method depends on the type and location of the blockage.
For extensive disease, bypass surgery creates an alternative route for blood to reach the affected part of the leg. The choice between a procedure performed through a blood vessel and surgery depends on the blockage, the patient’s condition and the likely benefits and risks.
Pain at rest, wounds that do not heal or gangrene can indicate that the leg is at risk and require urgent medical assessment. A wound that has not healed within two weeks, a cold or discoloured foot, or a black patch on a toe or heel should not be ignored. Sudden, severe leg pain accompanied by paleness, coldness, numbness or weakness is a medical emergency because it may indicate a sudden blockage of an artery.
Regular foot checks are particularly important for people with diabetes, who may not feel an injury developing. Recognising worsening symptoms and seeking timely care can help preserve mobility and prevent serious damage to the feet and legs.

Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.
The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.
All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.
Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.
“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he feared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled. “We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.
Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.
Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.
Africa’s third largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.
The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.
Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said by phone from Al-Junaid town in Al-Jazira: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.
“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.
Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.
To the east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”. “Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss,” he said.
Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and its currency has lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.

Microsoft researchers say an AI tool that diagnoses patients step by step, as doctors do, was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases, according to a study published on Thursday in Science.
The model identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked of a patient, as well as the exams and tests that should be ordered, using an “orchestrator” that organises how AI will tackle a problem by employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, according to the report.
Existing medical AI models typically take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient’s symptoms, lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis.
With the orchestrator coordinating the steps to reaching a diagnosis, the AI model first decides what to ask about the patient’s history and what is significant in the physical exam. Based on what it learns, it decides which tests to order, considers the results, and orders further testing as appropriate.
All the while, it is updating its working hypotheses and plans, the research leaders said in an interview.
Tasked with diagnosing more than 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas, the model employing the diagnostic orchestrator was more than twice as accurate at “working up” the patient and determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet.
The tool also outperformed human physicians when presented with scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions.
Assessments comparing these types of older systems to human doctors usually use multiple-choice questions, the researchers said.
“AI has become very good at getting a 100% pass rate on those,” said Dr. Dominic King, the corporate vice president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, whose team is developing the new technology.
“But of course, that’s not real-world. No patient ever came to see me with a nice summary.”
The researchers also found that diagnostic processes cost less when the orchestrator designs the work-ups than when human doctors do.
“We’re not just measuring the accuracy of the systems. We’re also measuring how judiciously and carefully it goes through a diagnostic work-up,” said Harsha Nori, head of AI at Microsoft AI Health.
In a collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, the researchers will next test the tool’s ability to triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms.

I'm just a girl: TVK minister Keerthana slams trolls over wearing gold jewellery at Tirupati
Tamil Nadu Minister Keerthana responded to social media criticism over the gold jewellery worn during her Tirupati visit. Her remarks underscored her resolve and acknowledged support from Vijay and the public.
Tamil Nadu minister Keerthana has hit back at social media users questioning the gold jewellery she wore during a recent visit to the Tirupati temple, saying she would not allow criticism to undermine her confidence or deter her from her work.
The controversy erupted after pictures of Keerthana's temple visit circulated on social media. Some users compared her jewellery with the assets declared in her election affidavit, claiming she had disclosed owning only three sovereigns of gold but appeared to be wearing nearly 10 sovereigns during the visit.
'YOU CANNOT DIM A WOMAN WHO KNOWS WHY SHE STARTED'
Responding to the criticism, Keerthana took to social media and alleged that her words, actions and personal choices were being subjected to excessive scrutiny.
"I'm just a girl. And perhaps that's why they feel entitled to dissect my every word, question my every move, and put my worth under a microscope," she wrote.
Taking a swipe at her critics, the minister said even the gold she wore was being scrutinised alongside her speeches, but maintained that such criticism would not shake her resolve.
"But let them. You can dissect my words, question my worth, and scrutinise my every move. But you cannot dim a woman who knows why she started," she said.
KEERTHANA THANKS VIJAY FOR SUPPORT
The TVK minister also credited Tamil Nadu Chief Minister and party leader Vijay for standing by her, while thanking people who continued to support her.
"I stand tall with the support of Hon'ble Chief Minister Vijay Anna and the love of the people who believe in me. I don't need to prove my worth to every critic. Time will do that," she wrote.
Concluding her post, Keerthana said she had nothing to hide and used the analogy of gold undergoing testing to respond to the scrutiny surrounding her jewellery.
"Gold doesn't fear the laboratory. It has nothing to hide. And neither do I," she said.

OpenAI announces new discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics
It formed groups of experts to examine and explain the results.
Just a few weeks after OpenAI released manuscripts with over 700 pages of solutions and progress for 372 major math problems, the company has announced even more discoveries. This time, the discoveries don't just cover math results, but also results for computer science and physics problems.
For this release, OpenAI has experimented with three different strategies. It has published the math results, so researchers can look them up and make their own efforts to explain them. But for the computer science and physics results, it formed an external group of expert collaborators. OpenAI asked the group working on the computer science results to explain them in their own writeups and materials, while also releasing the AI output to the public. Meanwhile, OpenAI has deferred the release of the physics materials to the group handling them. The company is welcoming feedback "on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful."
OpenAI has added two new manuscripts on GitHub you can access right now. One establishes Sogge's local smoothing for waves in every spatial dimension, which is a conjecture about the behavior of solutions to the wave equation. The other shows proof that the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which is an assumption in computer science that some problems are just too hard to solve quickly, is false.
As OpenAI notes, ETH is widely believed to be true and has been the basis on hundreds of papers across a wide variety of fields, including databases and computation biology and geometry. If it is indeed false, then we could, in theory, find better algorithms to solve problems in those fields more efficiently. The scientists who proposed ETH are now part of the group OpenAI has asked to examine and explain the results generated by its models.
Finally, the physics results involve proof of interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions. The group examining the physics results has yet to publish anything about it, but it has provided an email – YANGMILLS4D[@]gmail.com — for all questions about its efforts.
The company says it will not seek any academic credit for its models' discoveries. Instead, the people in each group will get credit for the writeups and materials they create. The groups will also be in charge of making sure that the AI-generated results appropriately credit all the researchers, techniques and ideas the company's models drew on.

Android Auto and CarPlay have transformed the way people drive.
Rather than putting up with whatever infotainment systems car manufacturers have put together, we're now able to interact with our phones from our car dashboards—with our contacts, our music, our podcasts, and our mapping apps all available. And the list of supported vehicles just keeps growing.
Both the Google and Apple solutions for this are really simple to use too. Most of the time they'll connect up automatically once you've done the initial setup. What you might not realize, though, are the demands that Android Auto and CarPlay put on your phone. Your handset is essentially doing all the regular phone stuff and then powering a large tablet-like display at the same time. That typically includes constantly updating a map in real time.
With that in mind, your Android phone or iPhone can quickly start to lose battery life and heat up when it's connected to your vehicle, which you've perhaps already noticed. To keep your handset cool and your battery in good shape, here's what you need to do.
Go Wired if You Can (but Watch the Charging)
Wireless Android Auto and CarPlay are convenient, just like wireless charging is convenient, but it puts more stress on your phone. If you've got the option of a wired connection, that's preferable—but that introduces a new potential heat problem, which is that your phone will always be charging up.
To counter that, you can set charge limits (Battery and charging from Android Settings, Battery > Charging from iOS Settings), or simply make sure your phone is kept in a cool, dark spot of the car.
This wired option has the added bonus of letting you switch to airplane mode on your phone, which will go a long way to limiting heat. Again there's a trade-off though: No one will be able to reach you, and you'll need to have your maps, music, podcasts, and whatever else you need downloaded to your device in advance.
If you do stick with wireless Android Auto or CarPlay, try to avoid charging your phone at the same time, especially on the wireless pad built into the car’s dash (which generates more heat). You don't want to end up with a dead phone half way through the journey, so you may have to compromise at certain times.
Think About Where Your Phone Is Placed
As mentioned above, where your phone is in the car makes a real difference to how hot it's going to be. If you have your phone's interface up on your car dashboard, then you don't necessarily need to have it fixed to the dashboard, too, possibly under direct sunlight. The glove compartment will do just fine.
If you have a mount for your phone, think about attaching it in front of one of your car's air vents. Blasts of air conditioned air will significantly reduce how hot your handset gets, working like a DIY cooling system.
You might also want to think about taking the case off of your phone for the length of the trip, if your phone is fitted with one. Your handset is less likely to be dropped or knocked while you're driving anyway, and a case can trap the heat in.
The rules aren't too different to keeping your phone cool generally, though with the added wrinkle of needing to keep it connected to your car somehow. Make sure the cabin in general is at a comfortable temperature, though you're probably already doing that for your own sake. The bigger thing to remember is to avoid leaving your phone behind in a vehicle that's going to heat up in the sun if you're stopping off somewhere.
Limit the Work Your Phone Has to Do
If your phone is hooked up to Android Auto or CarPlay, then it's probably got some work to do—whether it's getting you to a destination or streaming music. However, you can still reduce heat by keeping phone tasks down to a minimum. If your calls and (voice-activated) messages can wait, leave them until the end of the journey.
We mentioned offline syncing above, but it doesn't have to go along with airplane mode. If you sync your tunes, podcasts, and maps to your phone ahead of time, your handset has less work to do while you’re driving since it doesn’t need to pull data from the cloud while also constantly searching for a wireless signal as you travel. Less stress on the modem means less heat overall.
Both Apple Maps and Google Maps let you download maps ahead of a trip. In Apple Maps, tap your profile picture, then Offline Maps, then Add Offline Map and find your location. With Google Maps, tap your profile picture, then choose Offline maps > Select your own map to choose the coverage.
There may be times when your phone has to be charging, wirelessly connected, making calls, in direct sunlight, and streaming music over a cellular connection, but try to keep these times to a minimum. Check regularly on how hot your phone is getting while connected to Android Auto or CarPlay, so you can take action if needed.

Nike CEO Elliott Hill said he protects family time by scheduling them like work commitments.
Hill, who came out of retirement to lead Nike in 2024, said he follows a structured routine when he is not traveling.
"What time I try to get to sleep, what time I try to wake up. I get a workout in every morning, too. That helps keep me grounded and keeps me balanced," Hill told host Greg Byrne on the "You Got Byrned" podcast.
He said he makes a point of identifying what matters most to him and scheduling time for those priorities.
"I sat down, and I actually listed what was important to me: family, friends, my own personal — and then work — growth, and I put commitments underneath each one of those, and then I built them into my calendar," Hill said.
For example, he said he knew his work schedule meant he would miss his two kids before they headed to school, so he found other ways to show up for them.
"I knew I wasn't ever going to be there for breakfast with the kids because I was an early bird, and I was going to be in the office," Hill said. "But I did say I'm going to be home for dinner, and I had my admin build it into my calendar so that I would leave in time to be home for dinner."
He also blocks off parent-teacher conferences and other school events on his schedule, and said he would shift work trips when they overlap with those commitments.
"It all comes down to being very deliberate about what's important to us. Writing it on a piece of paper was very, very helpful, and then being planful enough to build it into your calendar. That's how I've always managed the balance," Hill said.
Hill joined Nike as a sales representative intern in 1988 and spent more than three decades in the company in a range of roles. He retired in 2020 after leading Nike's commercial and marketing operations, then returned in 2024 as CEO.
Other business leaders have also shared the systems and habits they rely on to stay organized.
Leah Solivan, a venture capitalist and the founder of TaskRabbit, told Business Insider in April that she uses six color-coded calendars to stay on top of her day.
The cofounder and CEO of Fishwife, Becca Millstein, told Business Insider in September that she does not hold company meetings without a written agenda.
Allie K. Miller, the CEO of Open Machine, told Business Insider in early October that she'll take regular "Claude walks," during which she'll walk for an hour while talking to AI or taking a call.

Lancashire consider Anderson farewell amid fan unrest
- Published
Lancashire will look into organising a farewell for bowler James Anderson amid fan unrest over his departure from the club.
It was announced last week the 44-year-old, England's all-time leading wicket-taker, has been released by the county he first represented in 2001.
The topic dominated a tense meeting between the club hierarchy and members at Old Trafford on Monday evening, with many members angered by the decision.
Some raised their upset at the fact the end-of-season decision had denied fans the chance to thank Anderson for his service to the county and celebrate his career.
The club, represented by new chief executive Richard Kenyon and incoming director of cricket Paul Farbrace, agreed to look into a solution.
Farbrace joined the meeting via video from his holiday in the United States and is understood to have taken ownership of the decision when taking questions from members.
The former England assistant coach, who left his role in charge of Sussex before joining the Red Rose county, reiterated his explanation from Lancashire's public statement on Sunday - that he wants to build a squad capable of winning the County Championship within the next four years and does not believe Anderson, who turns 45 next year, will play a part in that.
One attendee among about 200 members at the meeting told BBC Sport the atmosphere in the room remained mixed.
Other members suggested Farbrace had gone some way to calming the unrest.
Anderson was Lancashire's captain in the County Championship last season and while the county finished second bottom in Division Two, continuing a poor run of results in recent years, he remained one of their best performers.
He took 50 wickets and was named their Championship player of the year.
A number of counties have expressed an interest in signing the veteran for next season.
Anderson first played List A cricket in 2000 as a 17-year-old for the Lancashire Cricket Board against Suffolk.
He made his professional debut for Lancashire a year later and was in the England team by the end of 2002.
In addition to his 911 international wickets - an England record and a record for all pace bowlers - Anderson claimed 443 first-class scalps for Lancashire, along with 83 in List A cricket and a further 50 in T20s.
When his England career was abruptly ended in 2024, Anderson opted to continue playing with Lancashire in 2025.
At the time, he said he felt he could play for three more years.
In his first public comment since the decision on Sunday, he expressed his sadness at the situation but stopped short of retiring.

Ritwik Banerjee, a professor and chairperson of the Economics area at IIM Bangalore (IIM-B), has been appointed associate editor of the Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization (JEBO), an ABDC A*-ranked journal. JEBO publishes theoretical and empirical research on economic decision-making, organisational processes, human behaviour and economic change. Banerjee has been a professor at IIM Bangalore for more than a decade. He holds a bachelor’s degree in economics and a master’s degree in economics from Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). He earned a second master’s degree from Iowa State University in 2009 and later completed a PhD in economics at Aarhus University in Denmark. In 2009, Banerjee started working as a research associate at ICRIER. In 2013, he worked as a consultant at the World Bank Group and, in 2015, became a visiting scholar in economics at Harvard University. Between 2014 and 2015, he was a postdoctoral research fellow at Aarhus University. He later joined the Indian Institute of Management Calcutta as an assistant professor. In 2019, he became a visiting scholar at the United Nations University World Institute for Development Economics Research. Later, he became a Fulbright-Nehru visiting scholar at the University of California, Berkeley. Since 2016, he has been at IIM Bangalore and has worked in different roles. Between 2016 and 2019, he worked as an assistant professor. From 2019 to 2025, he was an associate professor and, since November 2025, has been a professor. His research lies at the intersection of behavioural and development economics, with extensive use of experimental methods. His work examines issues including corruption, inequality, education and discrimination. His broader research interests span behavioural economics, social preferences, social norms, social identity, status and reference dependence. He also investigates public economics, development economics and public policy, applying psychological insights to questions of corruption, affirmative action, self-confidence, competition and gender. The story so far:
On October 6, the National Medical Commission (NMC) issued guidelines on advertising and public communication by doctors and hospitals. Intended to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, they cover hospital hoardings, social media and artificial intelligence (AI). Beyond curbing deception, they raise another question regarding how much can doctors and hospitals say to the public about their work and achievements?
What is prohibited?
Claims of “guaranteed cures”, “100% success” or being the “best” are barred. Similarly, fake reviews, manipulated online rankings, misleading celebrity or influencer endorsements, and offers encouraging unnecessary treatment are deemed unethical practices. The guidelines rightfully prohibit AI-generated or manipulated patient images, voices and testimonials. But section 8.1(i) prohibits advertisements that create “unnecessary demand” for medical procedures or promote “fear-based marketing”. Without objective criteria, such expressions leave considerable room for subjective interpretation and inconsistent enforcement.
Hospitals may publish factual details of services, charges, accreditation and doctors’ credentials. Yet Section 8.1(iii) restricts advertising professional achievements and success rates, and Section 8.1(v) prohibits promotional “before and after” surgical photographs, except for specified scientific or educational purposes. Such blanket restrictions risk regulatory overreach, particularly when authentic, appropriately contextualised images could help patients understand surgical outcomes. Section 9.2 also restricts the use of doctors’ photographs for self-promotion, including on letterheads and signboards. These restrictions apply only to registered medical practitioners under the NMC’s jurisdiction.
Why the information asymmetry?
Patients rarely possess the same medical knowledge as those treating them. Even amid an abundance of AI-enabled health information, choosing a surgeon or assessing a hospital’s safety record remains difficult. Verifiable professional achievements, including the number of surgeries performed, years of experience and treatment outcomes, could help patients make informed choices. While such figures can be misleading without context, they are fundamentally different from unsubstantiated claims to be the “best” or to guarantee success, which the guidelines already prohibit. Rather than restricting genuine professional accomplishments, requiring their accurate and transparent disclosure could better serve patients’ right to informed choice. The answer may lie in better disclosure, rather than less information.
Is commercialisation unethical?
The guidelines seek to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, while Clause 8.1(ii) restricts promotion, suggesting commercialisation of medical practice. But in India, profit-making healthcare is lawful, as section 2(c) of the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, recognises privately operated hospitals, and section 3(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, enables lawful commercial enterprises, including hospitals. Government policy also permits 100% FDI in hospitals.
Article 19(1)(g) protects citizens’ freedom to practise a profession or conduct business, subject to reasonable restrictions. In the case Tata Press v. MTNL (1995), the Supreme Court recognised commercial speech under Article 19(1)(a), including the public’s right to receive information, while permitting restrictions on misleading advertisements. The current guidelines appear to treat commercialisation itself as a problem, without clearly distinguishing legitimate business interests from practices that mislead or exploit patients.
Are government schemes exempt?
Central and State government schemes undertaken in the larger public interest are exempted, and can advertise. Flexibility for vaccination drives and other health programmes is understandable. But the exemption is broad. Safeguards should remain equally important whether a campaign is run by the government or a private hospital. Patients seeking private healthcare may independently praise or criticise doctors. But the guidelines remain silent on hospitals and practitioners using unsolicited patient testimonials for promotion. What if a patient voluntarily posts an account and a hospital subsequently shares it? The distinction remains unresolved.
Other unclear aspects
Graded penalties are intended for violators, starting with a warning and mandatory ethics training for the first violation, and increasing to a 6- to 12-month suspension for subsequent violations. At the same time, repeated offences could lead to removal from the register for one to three years. State Medical Councils will enforce these provisions after issuing show-cause notices and considering doctors’ explanations. Appeals can be made to the NMC’s Ethics and Medical Registration Board.
The guidelines remain unclear about who can initiate complaints and the evidence required. It addresses genuine concerns, but its broad and ambiguous provisions may create confusion over compliance and leave considerable room for subjective enforcement, particularly affecting smaller hospitals. Protecting patients from misleading advertisements and commercial exploitation is necessary. However, treating commercial intent itself as inherently suspect serves little purpose. Clearer distinctions between legitimate professional communication and unethical promotion would better serve both patients and healthcare providers.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

A three-year long study in Bengaluru of over 10,000 frontline workers has brought to light reduced lung function among BMTC bus drivers, traffic police, pourakarmikas and construction workers — sections most exposed to polluted air.
The study, done by the VAAYU Occupational & Environmental Respiratory Illness Clinic (VOERIC), screened 4,517 BMTC drivers, 3,285 traffic police personnel, 2,169 construction workers and 379 pourakarmikas.
Vulnerable sections face highest health risk
All the groups that were screened showed higher-than-normal prevalence of early lung-function abnormalities.
Among the occupations, pourakarmikas were found to have the highest proportion of workers with the PRISm pattern, an indication of reduced lung capacity. Around 45% of them showed indications of reduced lung function.
BMTC workers and traffic police followed, with 29.5% and 28%, respectively, showing reduced lung function. Among construction workers, 15% showed a PRISm pattern.
Around 2.6% of BMTC drivers, 2.3% pourakarmikas, 2.1% construction workers, and 1% traffic police personnel reported signs of obstructive airflow.
The survey also found that 88.2% of the BMTC drivers never used a mask, as was the case with 55% traffic police, 37.9% construction workers, and 16.3% pourakarmikas.
Comorbidities
The subjects were also analysed for comorbidities, and the results revealed a grim situation, with high levels of obesity reported among the sections.
Pourakarmikas had the highest proportion at 62%, closely followed by BMTC drivers, 60.7% of whom were found to be obese/overweight. For traffic police, the figure stood at 51.3%.
The figures are much higher than the India reference figure of 28.6%.
The study also flags that diabetes prevalence among BMTC drivers was 18.2%, higher than the Indian average of 11.4%. Among traffic police personnel, the prevalence was 14%.
The physically active nature of the work and the relatively young demography among the construction workers translated to lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases. The average age of construction workers was found to be 31.3± 10, 98.3% of whom worked for more than 8 hours daily.
The concerns with higher incidences of diabetes, uncontrolled blood pressure, overweight and obesity across occupational groups has reinforced the need for a comprehensive approach to worker health including cardiometabolic screening
“While the findings demonstrate a significant burden of health abnormalities, further longitudinal research is required to establish the extent to which occupational exposures contribute to specific respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes. VOERIC plans to start this as cohort along with government support,” a statement from VOERIC said.
“Air pollution is considered the new tobacco. It is an emerging risk-enhancing factor for heart attack and brain stroke,” said C.N. Manjunath, leading cardiologist and Bengaluru Rural MP, at a round table where the results from the study were published.
Speaking about the importance of reducing traffic congestion, scientific garbage disposal and adoption of necessary measures during road construction to reduce dust, in tackling air pollution, he acknowledged the importance of policy intervention backed by data.

Kenya's Health Ministry announced the country's second Ebola death on Friday (October 23, 2026), saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
The Ministry said medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life", but she died on Friday (October 23) evening.
Her family was notified, and the Ministry said it would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
The remaining seven Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities. No new infections were reported.
Kenya announced its first ever Ebola case on October 6 after a 40-year-old Kenyan man who was living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3. He was driven by a relative to Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for Ebola on October 5 and died the same day.
Authorities have identified some 135 contacts of the first patient, placing 118 in quarantine. Eight tested positive while in quarantine, including four health workers and four close family members.
The Health Ministry said some contacts who completed the 21-day quarantine period without developing symptoms would be released starting Saturday (October 24).
'Nigerian patient did not travel to Congo'
In Nigeria, authorities said on Friday (October 23) that they were yet to verify how the country's first Ebola patient contracted the disease. The woman tested positive for the virus upon her return to Nigeria's capital of Abuja from Uganda.
The woman — married to a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria whom she had been travelling with — did not visit Congo and "is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda", Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, or FDFA, told The Associated Press on Friday (October 23).
Her husband has not shown any symptoms and remains in isolation, the FDFA added.
Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Pate told reporters on Friday (October 23) that the Nigerian patient "appears to be closely related" to the first case in Kenya in terms of the nature of their infection. "That may or may not change the understanding of the route of transmission given that the virus itself takes time to change," Mr. Pate said.
The Africa CDC earlier said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3.
U.S. introduces new protocol for all travellers
United States health officials this week said that all passengers boarding an international flight to the U.S. — no matter from where — must sign a statement attesting that they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. The US has been screening travellers from Ebola-affected countries during the current outbreak.
Travellers who were in Congo in the three weeks leading to their trip will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations, including Americans, the U.S. CDC said on Thursday (October 22).
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May.
