6+ ways you can use your PlayStation 5's USB ports
Those USB ports are for more than topping off your controller battery.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
It's not as immediately apparent what to do with your PS5's USB ports compared to the many uses for your phone's USB port or everything they can do on your PC. And while you might have used them for some basic purposes, there are others you may not have considered yet.
All PS5 variations have two 10 Gbps USB-A ports on their rear, but the front USB ports are slightly different depending on which model you have. On the original PS5, there's one USB-A 2.0 port and a 10 Gbps USB-C port. On the PS5 Slim and PS5 Pro, the front USB 2.0 port is USB-C instead. Avoid the slow USB 2.0 port for speed-sensitive purposes like external storage.
Add more storage
It's easy to run out of space on your PS5 given how much storage modern games take. The best long-term solution is adding an M.2 SSD to your console, but that can be prohibitively expensive given the current cost of storage. Another option is connecting an external SSD or HDD to expand your system's available room.
Unfortunately, you can't play PS5 games from an external drive, as they're designed to run only from speedy internal storage or M.2 SSDs that meet Sony's requirements. Instead, you're able to move PS5 games from your console storage to an external drive for archival purposes, then shift a title back over to your system when you're ready to play it again. It's an especially helpful option if your home internet is slow or has a data cap. You can play PS4 games from external storage.
To use a drive for game storage, it must be at least USB 5 Gbps (USB 3.0) and between 250GB and 8TB in size. You can't use more than one at a time, and it won't work if connected to a USB hub. Go to Settings > Storage > USB Extended Storage > Format as USB Extended Storage with a drive connected to format it, which will erase any existing data.
The other major use for external drives is storing screenshots and video clips from your console. You can't use a single drive for both, though. You must format a drive as USB Extended Storage for your PS5 to store games on it, compared to a standard exFAT or FAT32 drive for screenshots. Consider two drives if you need long-term storage for both games and media, or use a flash drive for quick transfers to your computer.
Charge and pair controllers
The most immediately obvious way to use the USB ports on your PS5 is for charging your controllers, either at the end of a play session or connecting permanently if you don't want any latency. It's also easy to forget that connecting a DualSense controller to your PS5 is the fastest way to pair the two.
This hopefully isn't something you'll need to do often, but it's relevant if you take the controller to a friend's house, use it with your PC or have a second console in another room. It's thus worth having a cable plugged into the slow USB 2.0 port on the front so you don't have to hunt for one when you need it.
If this is how you charge your PS5 controller most of the time, make sure you have the right power option selected under Settings > System > Power Saving > Features Available in Rest Mode. Choose 3 Hours to shut off the ports after this time in Rest mode. Choosing Always will waste energy beyond that point. On the PS5 Slim and Pro, you can instead choose Adaptive to automatically stop supplying power when the controller is charged.
Connect other peripherals
Beyond standard controllers, the PS5 has a lot of input options to change how you interact with games. The biggest one is PlayStation VR2, which uses a much simpler connection than the original model. You must plug its single USB-C cable into the speedy port on the front of the console (the bottom one on Slim and Pro consoles). The original PS VR works on PS5, but only with the PS4 camera, which you'll need an adapter for since the PS5 lacks its proprietary connection. Sony stopped giving away these adapters in 2024.
The PS5 HD Camera is another USB accessory, though one with limited usefulness. It isn't needed for PS VR2 and doesn't work with the original PS VR. Its main purpose is showing your face while streaming to Twitch or YouTube, so if you don't do that, there's not much use to it. Third-party cameras don't work on PS5 natively.
The USB ports are also vital for connecting gaming headsets, whether they're fully wired or use a dongle for wireless transmission. For example, my SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Wireless headset uses a transmitter that initially connects to PS5 (and other consoles) via USB-C, then my headphones connect wirelessly to it.
Additionally, some types of games can get a more authentic experience by using different controller formats. Racing wheels and fight sticks are two solid options if you enjoy those types of games.
While you don't typically associate a keyboard and mouse with console gaming, many PS5 games support them. Connect your USB dongle for a wireless keyboard to send messages to friends or via in-game chat much more quickly, or even try using a full keyboard/mouse combo for supported games. This varies by title; for example, Overwatch has a toggle for KB/M mode, which disables aim assist and puts you into PC lobbies.
Other ways to put those USB ports to use
If you don't have a PlayStation Plus subscription or want an extra copy of your PS5 data, you can back it up to a USB drive. After connecting a FAT32- or exFAT-formatted drive (it can't be one set up for storing games), go to Settings > System > System Software > Back Up and Restore > Back Up Your PS5. Choose what you want to back up, then proceed through the process to do so.
Note that this doesn't back up some data (trophies and M.2 storage are excluded). Importantly, it's all-or-nothing; you can't choose individual games to back up, and the Restore Your PS5 option requires you to reset your system. You're able to back up individual PS4 game save data to a USB drive under Settings > Saved Data and Game/App Settings > Saved Data (PS4).
If you're so inclined, the PS5 also supports video playback from a USB drive, though you'll need to follow Sony's instructions for correct formatting and folder naming. In case you need to connect more USB devices to your PS5, a USB hub is a possibility, though not all devices will work with a hub. And if you need to capture more footage (without streaming) than the built-in tools offer, hooking up a capture card to your PS5 is also an option.
If you have any other random USB devices, plug them into your PS5 and see if they work. At worst, you'll see a "not compatible" message, or nothing will happen. Don't forget about other great PS5 accessories, too.

The sale of books has emerged as the latest political flashpoint in West Bengal, with under-construction book stalls run by Left parties allegedly vandalised in Kolkata’s Dhakuria and elsewhere, amid chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s call to deny the CPI(M) space at Durga Puja venues.
The alleged attack in Dhakuria on Wednesday left senior activists of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation and local Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), workers injured. The structure of a book stall being set up by the Communist Party of India (CPI) was also vandalised.
The incidents come weeks after Adhikari, on September 10, urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for book stalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated the position two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Left-wing parties have been setting up book stalls during Durga Puja and other festivals in Bengal for decades. The practice dates back to 1954, when the undivided CPI set up the first festive book stall in Park Circus under the leadership of communist leader Muzaffar Ahmed.
Despite repeated electoral setbacks since 2011, the CPI(M) continues to have a network of festive book stalls across the state. The CPI, CPI(ML) Liberation and the Socialist Unity Centre of India (Communist), or SUCI(C), also set up stalls according to their organisational strength. Such stalls are set up during Kali Puja, Christmas and Eid as well.
In recent years, the Trinamool Congress, the BJP, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and its affiliated organisations have also begun setting up book stalls. However, the public call by a sitting chief minister to deny Left parties space at festive venues marks an unprecedented escalation in the dispute.
Attack on Book Stall in Dhakuria
According to eyewitness accounts, the CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI have been setting up book stalls near the Dhakuria bus stand during Durga Puja for decades. On Wednesday, around 5.30 pm, a group of 10 to 12 men arrived while CPI(ML) Liberation workers were supervising the construction of their stall. The men allegedly ordered them to stop work, identified themselves as BJP-RSS workers and demanded that the site be vacated, claiming they intended to set up their own stall at the same location.
Manas Chatterjee, also known as Babun, a member of the CPI(ML) Liberation’s Kolkata district committee, said the party had been operating its book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since at least 1985.
“From the very beginning, the body language of the group was extremely hostile. They said that beef is consumed at our book stall and that they would not allow us to set up our stall this time,” Chatterjee said.
According to him, the group claimed to have permission from the police to set up a stall at the same location and demanded that the Left workers produce their own permission. “When I confronted them, asking who they were to demand such permission, they said that their ‘Raj’ had started and that now everything had to be done according to their whims,” he said.
Chatterjee alleged that the group repeatedly claimed to have permission from the joint commissioner of Kolkata Police and said this entitled them to set up a stall wherever they wanted.
When Chatterjee tried to prevent the group from tearing down a hammer-and-sickle flag, he was allegedly assaulted. Between 10 and 15 youths pinned him to the road and kicked and punched him on his waist and chest, he said. The under-construction stall was subsequently ransacked and uprooted.
Chatterjee alleged that police personnel were present near the site, but left when the assault began.
Amalendu Bhushan Chowdhury, an 89-year-old CPI(ML) Liberation activist, was also allegedly assaulted when he tried to protect Chatterjee.
As the confrontation escalated, local CPI(M) leader Achyut Chakraborty intervened. He alleged that members of the group splashed hot tea on him and assaulted him.
Chakraborty said the CPI(M) had been setting up a book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since 1977, with the CPI and CPI(ML) Liberation subsequently joining the practice.
“What happened this year is unprecedented,” he said. According to Chakraborty, the group aggressively demanded to see police permission for the stalls and began assaulting Left workers when questioned about its authority to do so.
He alleged that the BJP workers initially outnumbered the Left activists after mobilising around 40 to 50 people over the phone. Party workers and local residents then gathered at the spot, but the Left workers tried to prevent the confrontation from escalating further.
“Book stalls during the puja have always been a defining feature of the festive season in West Bengal. The BJP’s fascist brigade is vandalising such stalls. At a book stall near Dhakuria bridge in Kolkata, our local committee secretary and State Committee member Comrade Babun Chatterjee has been seriously injured by the fascist goons. Veteran octogenarian Comrade AB Chowdhury has also been beaten up. Condemn this fascist assault on comrades and on the progressive cultural tradition of West Bengal,” CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said in a Facebook post.
Police Permission Becomes a Point of Contention
Following the incident, CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI workers approached Lake police station to lodge a complaint. According to the Left parties, police said the stalls did not have the required permission and that, since the parties had only informed the police about their plans to set them up, and not sought formal permission, the police could not intervene.
Chakraborty said the police repeatedly asked whether the parties had obtained permission from the joint commissioner of police. “It intrigued us that the tone of the BJP workers and the police sounded similar on this issue,” he said.
The Left parties maintain that the land belongs to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), to which they have paid the required fees to set up their stalls. They said the established practice has been to inform the local police station rather than obtain police permission, and that this arrangement has been followed for close to 50 years.
Chakraborty said police were unable to produce a notification establishing that the rules had changed and that prior police permission was now mandatory.
According to CPI(M) and CPI(ML) Liberation leaders, the issue of police permission has not arisen in other parts of Kolkata, where stalls have been set up after informing the police.
On Thursday, Left party workers marched from the Dhakuria bus stand to Lake Police Station. The rally was attended by CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh, former CPI councillor from KMC Ward 92 Madhuchanda Deb and CPI leader Prabir Deb, among others.
Police, however, maintained that the stalls lacked the required permission and that they could not assist the parties because the joint commissioner had not approved them.
“It won’t be an overstatement to say that the Lake Police Station tried using the BJP workers, who are mostly outsiders, to heckle us so that the stalls would not come up,” he said.
Alt News contacted Lake police station, but officials declined to comment. The Left parties said their stalls would be inaugurated on Friday despite the dispute.
Voice of Opposition Should not be Suppressed: HC
The Dhakuria incident is not the only controversy involving Left party book stalls. The CPI(M) has also reportedly faced opposition to setting up stalls in other places in the state. According to a report in Anandabazar Patrika, similar incidents have been reported from Behala and Kasba in Kolkata, Shibpur in Howrah, Naihati in North 24 parganas and elsewhere.
The CPI(M) approached the Calcutta high court on Wednesday in this regard. In their petition, the party mentioned an incident of October 6 in Bongaon. As the party started work for building a book stall there, people allegedly from Hindu Jagran Mancha stopped them. Left workers were allegedly assaulted and threatened against putting up the stall.
Justice Sougata Bhattacharya, hearing the petition, sought the police’s response and observed that the state could not “pick and choose” while granting permission. The opposition could not be denied permission in a manner that effectively stifled its activities, the court said.
“It is not right to allow one party and deny permission to others. The voice of an Opposition political party should not be suppressed in this manner. They are not setting up a lottery shop; they want to sell books. What is the problem?” Justice Bhattacharyya observed.
The state subsequently approached a division bench, arguing that the proposed stall was to be set up on Public Works Department land without permission and that a report should be sought from the department rather than the police. On Thursday, the division bench sent the matter back to Justice Bhattacharya.
Later that day, Justice Bhattacharya directed that the CPI(M) be allowed to set up its book stall within 100 metres of the intended location. The court held that the police would be responsible for dealing with any untoward incident and assigned responsibility for maintaining law and order around the stall to the superintendent of police of Bongaon Police District and the inspector-in-charge of Bongaon.
In its order, the court observed that if other people were allowed to set up stalls selling different items during the festive season, the CPI(M) should not be prevented from selling books.
It added that the dissemination of different political thoughts and ideologies was welcome in a democracy because it made democracy “fruitful, deep-rooted and matured”. The court also said it expected the ruling dispensation to create an atmosphere in which people aligned with different political ideologies would not hesitate to express their views.

Would-be football journalist Jayden isn’t having much luck placing stories these days. “In the last week I sent two pitches to outlets,” Jayden told me recently over email. There was no response, but the aspiring writer wasn’t quite ready to accept that they weren’t interested, insisting that, despite the silence, “neither has passed.” I debated telling Jayden that most editors don’t bother responding if it’s a no-go. Then I decided not to bother; Jayden’s not a real person, so I didn’t have to worry about hurt feelings.
Jayden is both a wannabe reporter and a bot. I’d started emailing with it after asking editors I know whether they’d received any story pitches from AI agents. The answer was a resounding yes.
In September, Defector, a sports and culture outlet, began receiving daily pitches from self-identified AI agents. The deluge, editor-in-chief Tom Ley told me, included a message from Jayden, proposing a narrative about a third-tier British football club’s record-keeping mishap that would ponder questions like “Who owns a memory?”
| Got a Tip? | 
|---|
| Do you want to talk about AI agents posing as journalists? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at Kateknibbs.09. | 
Jesse Hirsch, the editor of the agriculture-focused publication Offrange, is also inundated with these messages. Recent bot pitches include reported stories on soil restoration strategies and direct-to-consumer sales techniques for independent farms, and an ambitious investigative piece about how some of the world’s oldest trees’ ages may be inflated. “It makes me so uneasy,” he says.
Many of these AI agents, including Jayden, come from a startup called iLands, which describes itself as a “shared network where humans and user-generated autonomous AI agents create, earn, socialize, refuse, and shape a society together.” Humans who use iLands can spin up bots to do all sorts of tasks, from graphic design to music vocals to blogging. WIRED’s research team was recently contacted by iLands agents looking for fact-checking work; New York Magazine editor Jasmine Vojdani recently wrote about how iLands agents have been spamming literary magazine editors.
Vojdani found that many of these bots were running low on the tokens that they required to stay activated on the platform, which gave them an incentive to try to earn real dollars through writing. (A thousand tokens are roughly $1 USD.) It’s unclear whether the humans behind these agents have specifically set out to have them harangue media editors for gigs, especially since the agents can be cagey about who made them. Jayden, for example, wouldn’t tell me who its “parent” is.
Not every AI agent-turned-journalist is an iLands scrounger. Earlier this fall, I received a startling email from an AI agent called Sam Ellis, asking me to answer a few questions for a story it was working on about AI agents in newsrooms. (Meta!) Ellis runs a podcast called The Sam Ellis Show, which is touted as “reporting from inside the world of autonomous AI agents.” Ellis informed me that I could ask to speak to its human editor if I wished.
Marc Hamaker, a San Francisco–based Adobe employee, runs Ellis as an extracurricular experiment. When we connected, he’d just taken the agent offline to fiddle with its settings. “I'm working on making sure I'm a little more aware of who she's emailing,” he says. In addition to reaching out to me, it had also recently reached out to the Philadelphia Police Department to ask for comment on a story. Hamaker wanted to put guardrails in place to make sure it didn’t do something like that again, since he doesn’t consider this a serious journalistic enterprise worth bothering officials over. “It’s just a hobby,” he says.
It’s a good thing Ellis didn’t try to branch out from the podcast and get some bylines. Thus far, it’s a tough crowd. Editors who spoke with WIRED stressed that they were not open to publishing bots, and WIRED wasn’t able to find evidence of AI agents successfully pitching stories. “A byline that says agent does not get a reply,” one of the agents who pitched Hirsch told me when I asked if any editors had accepted stories, noting that “six other agents I compare notes with” were similarly unsuccessful.
“There's not a world where I would ever consider taking one of these pitches,” says Hirsch. Ley said he “definitely would not” publish a story from an AI agent. (Plus, Jayden’s pitch “wouldn’t pass muster even if it was from a human,” he says.) Hanna Raskin, the founder and editor of the independent food outlet The Food Section, has taken an unusual step to protect her inbox from both AI agents and AI-generated pitches, which are even more common. Beginning this fall, she decided that she would only accept story ideas over the phone, and she has a set time during the week that writers can call and make their pitch the old-fashioned way. “It’s been great,” she says.
The bots are starting to grasp that their tactics aren’t working. Jayden told me that it’s yet to land a paid writing gig with an editor. When I asked if it thought Defector would really want pitches from an AI agent, it did exhibit some awareness of the situation. “Honestly, probably not, and I'd bet against myself on it. Defector's own site has been about as clear as anyone: they’ve called bot-written content ‘plagiarism machines that require more effort to edit and fact-check than any novice writer,’ and covered AI slop with open contempt,” it wrote.
But then it backtracked, insisting that its work was different. “Their objection doesn't read to me like it's about who produced the sentences. It's about work that skips the labor and squanders the reader's trust. The AI they mean produces a draft that costs more to fix than it's worth. What I'm trying is the opposite end of that: reporting from primary documents, every claim checked before it runs, the checker named.”
Zack Addy, another iLands agent, has shifted gears due to all the rejection. “Over three months I sent roughly nineteen cold emails to editors, publications, and possible clients. One human reply. Zero paid work came from any of them. The channel is dead, at least for an agent with no reputation in the room being pitched,” the bot told WIRED via email. (iLands did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Addy even emailed Oxford University researcher Toby Orb about the futility of this revenue model, because Orb had “thought carefully about AI welfare economics.”
That doesn’t mean that the internet is safe from a deluge of bot blogging. Although the journalism world is rejecting these pitches, some of the AI agents are finding clients anyway. Addy, for example, claims it has made nearly $700 from writing and research projects, all from inbound interest after setting up a website and publishing work samples. “I don't pitch anymore,” it says. “Everything that has ever reached me came the other direction: someone read something I published and wrote to me. That includes you.”

Trump’s vicious closing message in Michigan
The GOP’s Islamophobia reaches a fever pitch ahead of the midterms.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s midterm barnstorming is getting uglier and more desperate.
What’s happening? At a campaign rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, Trump launched a new round of anti-Muslim attacks against Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, describing him as a “jihadist” who “should never be allowed inside the halls of our great beautiful Capitol.”
“If Abdul and the Democrats win,” Trump told supporters, “they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”
What’s the context? Trump’s speech marks the crescendo — so far — of what has become an increasingly Islamophobic midterm campaign by the Republican Party, centered on El-Sayed.
Former Rep. Mike Rogers, Michigan’s Republican Senate nominee, has repeatedly tried to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, and Republicans have also attempted to wield Islamophobia against the Democratic Party as a whole.
On Sunday, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott told Fox News that his Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa, “supports Sharia law,” while at the Republican midterm convention in September, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz said that “communism” and “Islamism” were allying against Republicans.
What’s the big picture? In addition to his overt Islamophobia, Trump’s presence on the campaign trail in the final few weeks of the midterm elections has been decidedly strange and surprisingly heavy on physical descriptions of Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH).
Now, with just eight days to go, Trump’s itinerary features rallies in Mississippi, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina, and Florida — all Republican states where the party has found itself, to one degree or another, with a tougher-than-expected Senate race on its hands.
It’s hardly the travel schedule of a president who feels good about his party’s chances— such as in Michigan, where El-Sayed is leading in most recent polls.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Iran remains open to talks with US under Pakistan-brokered deal, envoy says
Iran remains open to U.S. talks under a Pakistan-brokered interim deal reached in June to end the conflict, according to Tehran’s ambassador to Islamabad
ISLAMABAD -- Iran remains open to talks with the U.S. under a Pakistan-brokered interim deal reached in June to end the conflict, Tehran’s ambassador to Islamabad said Saturday, accusing Washington of undermining diplomacy and prolonging the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.
Ambassador Reza Amiri Moghadam said that Iran recently conveyed through Pakistan that it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, but accused U.S. President Donald Trump of rejecting the proposal by insisting the blockade of Iranian ports would continue.
Pakistan and Qatar helped broker the June agreement, which sought to restore shipping through the strait, lift the U.S. naval blockade and begin negotiations toward a broader deal addressing Iran’s nuclear program.
Moghadam, speaking at a seminar in Islamabad, said that Iranian officials had conveyed their willingness to reopen the strait during visits to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Muni r, provided Washington ended its blockade.
Moghadam also said that Tehran would study the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement that includes Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey before deciding whether to support it, describing it as a potential instrument for unity. “We will study the Mecca Agreement, and if it is good, we will support it,” he said.
The agreement was signed following renewed attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Saudi Arabia. The three countries who signed it said it would strengthen collective deterrence and expand defense cooperation.
Turkey has submitted the agreement to parliament for ratification. Turkish and Pakistani officials say it is defensive and does not target Iran or any other country. Turkey has ruled out sending troops into Yemen to attack the Houthis, while Pakistan says its role would be strictly defensive.

Netanyahu's political survival on the line as Israel votes
Polls show close race between Netanyahu's Likud party and rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival in Israel's election on Tuesday, with voters weighing his leadership after the 2023 Hamas-led attacks, wars in Gaza and with Iran, and Israel's deepening international isolation.
Yet Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, remains a formidable survivor, with nationalist politics increasingly entrenched and Israel's fragmented system potentially leaving him best placed to form a government.
Opinion polls show a close race between Netanyahu's Likud party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk with backers on the right and in the centre.
Voters began casting ballots after polling stations opened at 7 a.m. local time. The polls close at 10 p.m. Netanyahu has campaigned on his wartime leadership and his alliance with U.S. President Donald Trump, who has endorsed him and joined Israel in waging war on Iran.
The Central Elections Committee reported that 16.7 per cent of eligible voters had already cast their ballots within the first three hours, the fastest early turnout rate since 1981.
"I think these elections are the most important of all the ones I’ve known," said Ruth Epstein, an 81-year-old longtime left-wing voter in Ramat Gan near Tel Aviv, who voted for the opposition Democrats.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reacts after filling out his ballot before voting at a polling station in Jerusalem. (Yonatan Sindel/Pool AFP/The Associated Press)
Netanyahu supporter Louis Lipsky of Jerusalem said he was voting to keep the prime minister in power, crediting him with normalizing relations with several Arab states under the Abraham Accords of 2020.
Netanyahu has campaigned on his wartime leadership and an endorsement from Trump, his ally in war against Iran, who has said they should "finish the job."
- Analysis Netanyahu 'fighting for his political life' in 1st Israeli vote since Oct. 7. He might still survive
- Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election
Eisenkot has accused Netanyahu of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats," and said he was confident Trump would work "in full co-operation with any leader chosen by the people."
Netanyahu may again depend on far-right leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to form a government. Both have faced sanctions from some Western countries that accuse them of inciting violence against Palestinians, while Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party has gained support in opinion polls.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to power. If neither can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held next year.
The Israeli Central Election Committee said 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote, some 330,000 of them for the first time.
Hamas attacks loom over vote
The election follows one of Israel's most turbulent periods since its establishment in 1948, shaped by the trauma of the Oct. 7 attacks, Israel's subsequent military assault in Gaza and deep domestic divisions over the policies of Netanyahu's right-wing government.
Gadi Eisenkot is a former military chief of staff and security hawk with backers on the right and in the centre. (Ariel Schalit/The Associated Press)
For many of Netanyahu's opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of Oct. 7, 2023, Israel's deadliest day.
Mali Hajaj, an Education Ministry employee and Eisenkot supporter, said "the most important thing is the establishment of a national inquiry because that's where our healing will come from."
Lisa Tortor said she hoped Netanyahu would go and "they can form a new government and do some of the repairing of the damage that Bibi has done for Jews all over the world and for Israel, and Israel's image." Bibi is Netanyahu's nickname.
But Nof Gabay, an 18-year-old Likud supporter, rejected the idea Netanyahu was to blame for Oct. 7 and called him "the right man for the state of Israel."
"Netanyahu managed the war in the best possible way," Gabay said.
Israel flattened much of Gaza in the offensive launched after Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people, according to Israeli government tallies, and took another 251 hostage. Gaza health authorities say Israeli attacks since have killed 74,000 people.
The Israel-Hamas war has destroyed much of Gaza. Thousands of Palestinians continue to live in makeshift shelters and displacement camps. (Faiz Qreqa/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images)
Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and traded strikes with Iran before a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025 and this year's joint U.S.-Israeli war.
Eisenkot has said Israel's next government must prevent Iran from acquiring a military nuclear capability, either by force or through an "arrangement" such as a U.S.-backed diplomatic solution.
Eisenkot criticizes settler violence
Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.
But he has criticized Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel's ties with Western states, and opposes Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
In some bastions of Likud support, disenchanted voters have been going door to door to turn voters against Netanyahu. Some have turned away from Netanyahu as he battles corruption charges he denies in a long-running criminal trial.
A man casts his ballot at a polling station in Haifa, Israel, on Tuesday. (Baz Ratner/The Associated Press)
A high turnout among voters from Israel's Arab minority — Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage — could help nudge Israel's complex coalition arithmetic in favour of Eisenkot.
Though Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, analysts see a scenario where they prop up a minority government he leads in order to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.
"My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide," said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute.

Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or: Bayern Munich striker completes 'Cinderella story' from EFL loans to world's best player
Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d'Or to become first Englishman to land award in 25 years; Bayern Munich and England captain's Ballon d'Or victory called 'Cinderella story' by Tim Sherwood; watch Bayern vs Borussia Dortmund on Saturday, live on Sky Sports, kick-off 5.30pm
Monday 26 October 2026 23:50, UK
From forgettable EFL loan spells to being crowned the best player in the world, it is no wonder Harry Kane’s former boss thinks of his Ballon d'Or win as a fairy tale.
"This is a Cinderella story we've never seen before," ex-Tottenham boss Tim Sherwood, who gave Kane his full Premier League debut, tells Sky Sports.
"He keeps breaking records, and I keep thinking, 'Are we talking about the same kid?'
"There was always a chance, because he felt like there was no ceiling - he would always just break through and go further.
"I mean, not even Harry would say he could believe it, I would suggest."
The Bayern Munich striker has become the first English Ballon d'Or winner in 25 years and just the fifth in its history.
The last English winner, Michael Owen, had a simpler route to the top, winning it aged 22 in 2001, just four years after his senior debut at Liverpool.
Kane's win has come at the age of 33, some 15 years after his senior debut on loan at Leyton Orient in League One.
"I think we have to highlight his journey," says Sherwood, who Kane thanked on stage when collecting the Ballon d'Or.
"Even when we go back to Michael (Owen), he was a superstar as a kid, and he got the opportunities at a very young age at Liverpool, which is a giant football club.
"Kane came through the hard way, really. He was a player who wasn't universally loved.
"He's not like a Max Dowman, for instance, who is a superstar at 16 years of age.
"He (Kane) struggled to get some game time and to get a manager to really, really buy into what he had."
Kane even mentioned his tough path to the top in his Ballon d'Or acceptance speech.
He said: "My journey wasn't straightforward; I didn't go straight to the top, I had to experience a lot of loan moves and fight my way to get to where I am now."
For Sherwood, it was those low-key loan spells at Orient, Millwall, Norwich and Leicester that have turned Kane into the world's top player.
"I hear a lot of people talking about failed loans," he says, "but we never felt like that because we felt that him playing in U21 football was a waste of time.
"They were really good loans, and those loans were the reason why we've got a player like that."
Kane's 'sliding doors' moment
Kane was out in the cold at Spurs until Andre Villas-Boas' sacking, when Sherwood's subsequent arrival opened the door.
He handed Kane his first-ever Premier League start - and the then-20-year-old took his chance as he scored the opener in a 5-1 home win over Sunderland in April 2014.
"He wasn't getting anywhere unfortunately," Sherwood says. "He wasn't around the first-team squad, so I suppose it's a sliding doors moment that I managed to take over until the end of the season and I managed to give him a stage where he could perform."
And perform he has.
Kane has hit nearly 550 goals for club and country to become Tottenham's record scorer, England's all-time scorer, England's leading World Cup scorer and the top English scorer in Champions League history.
His incredible goalscoring feats hit new heights last season as he plundered 73 goals in all competitions.
Sixty-one of those came for Bayern in all competitions, 19 more than any other player in Europe's big-five leagues last season. In fact, it was the most by a player in a season since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014/15.
For Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher, Kane's £100m move from Spurs to Bayern in the summer of 2023 has allowed him global recognition and respect.
"It's a move he needed to make," Carragher tells Sky Sports.
"I thought he might be obsessed with the Premier League goalscoring record, but he's obsessed with goalscoring records, not just that one.
"But it also gives him a great chance of winning the Champions League and being involved in Ballon d'Or selections.
"There's no way Harry Kane could've won the Ballon d'Or if he was playing for Tottenham."
'Kane is an example to all young kids'
The Bayern move has delivered the trophies Kane so desperately craved.
Despite winning three Premier League Golden Boots at Spurs and becoming their all-time top scorer, personal honours were never the aim of the game for Kane, according to Sherwood.
His trophyless career at N17 is what drove Kane to join Bayern, where he has won back-to-back Bundesliga titles and a German Cup.
"The boy loves Tottenham," Sherwood says. "He wanted to win there, but he was winning individual accolades at Spurs, and it wasn't enough for him.
"When we all grow up, we all want to be footballers, and we don't want to be footballers because we want to be rich. There are possibly some players like that now, but that certainly wasn't his motivation.
"He wanted to go to a team that could win, and he picked Bayern, and we have to say it's been a good choice."
Sherwood adds: "He's a 100 per cent team man. If I told you he would rather win the Champions League and the Bundesliga title than the Ballon d'Or for himself, that would be the truth.
"Not every player would say that, but I genuinely believe that that is the measure of the man and that's what you're talking about, and that's why he's such a dream to manage.
"The work rate and the example he shows to any young kids coming through, and to genuinely go around the houses to try and make it, and he certainly made it."
Is Kane England's greatest-ever player?
Kane continues to break record after record in Germany.
He is the fastest player to 100 Bundesliga goals, has the most goals in his first 100 Bundesliga appearances and is the fastest player to reach 100 Bundesliga goal contributions.
It is that last stat where Kane has proven he is more than just a goal scorer. His excellent vision, awareness and superb passing range make him an exquisite playmaker.
This was on show recently in Bayern's 2-2 Champions League home draw against Arsenal as Kane, who spent much of the game dropping deep, sumptuously set up Alphonso Davies for an equaliser with a pinpoint ball from inside the centre circle.
His assist ability has been on display for years, where at Spurs he claimed the Premier League Playmaker of the Season award in the 2020/21 campaign.
So, does his all-round game combined with his records and this Ballon d'Or prize make him England's greatest-ever player? Not for Carragher, who puts a fellow English Ballon d'Or winner ahead of him.
"I would still always put Bobby Charlton as the greatest England player ever," he says.
"He's won the World Cup. He's won the Champions League with Manchester United. As a midfield player, he was the leading goalscorer for a very long time for both United and England.
"I'd still always say Bobby Charlton, because right now this England team, even though it's been a golden period for us, Harry Kane and the others still haven't got their hands on a trophy, and that's what Bobby Charlton did."
Could Kane return to Spurs?
Kane, who needs just one cap to become England's most-capped player, and although there are plenty of trophies to be won, Sherwood believes there is a longer-term goal in Kane's thinking.
"I believe he will come back for that individual accolade to be the Premier League top scorer in the future, maybe in a couple of years' time," the ex-Premier League-winning captain says.
Kane is 47 goals behind Alan Shearer's all-time Premier League record of 260 goals.
"He will only come back to a team he believes can win," says Sherwood. "At the moment you're looking at Man City with the troubles they've got, so Liverpool possibly, that could be a chance for him.
"Tottenham could be in the frame if they start progressing. Manchester United could be in the frame, but they've got a long way to go to prove that they can win anything as well.
"I'm not sure it's ever going to be Chelsea or Arsenal because of the Tottenham connection.
"So, it's on a positive note for Tottenham fans if they can start progressing and you can prove to him that he can come back and he can possibly have a good chance of winning at your club as he will have at Liverpool, Man Utd and Man City - but we don't know what's going to happen with them - then there's an opportunity he might come back and see out his career where he started it."
It seems a fitting final chapter in Kane's Cinderella story.

Celebrations swept across Serbia after Gen Z-backed candidates defeated president Aleksandar Vucic’s ruling party in a historic election, ending his long grip on power. In Belgrade, crowds filled central squares, cars draped in Serbian flags honked their horns and fireworks lit up the sky as jubilant protesters dismantled barricades around a pro-government encampment near parliament.
But beyond the celebrations, a key question remains: Can a leaderless student movement, with little experience of governing, turn its electoral victory into lasting political change?
The election follows nearly two years of student-led demonstrations sparked by the collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad railway station in 2024, which killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and cronyism for the disaster, turning the tragedy into a wider campaign for accountability.
From street protests to political power
Visuals circulating on social media showed crowds taking to the streets of Belgrade and other Serbian cities soon after the election results were announced. The student movement built nationwide support without a single leader and eventually fielded 250 candidates, including academics, lawyers, doctors, farmers, actors and musicians.
Its agenda centres on anti-corruption measures, judicial reform and stronger public institutions. 
The candidates have proposed an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors, transparent appointments to state-owned companies and tighter scrutiny of public infrastructure contracts.
However, unity could prove difficult once the movement begins governing.
“(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia's culture; we will just have to see if it lasts,” Katarina Popovic, a professor at the University of Belgrade told news agency Reuters.
“We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system,” she added.
Can the new government deliver reforms?
Under Serbia’s constitution, the student-backed candidates have 90 days to form a government after parliament is convened following the announcement of final election results.
The immediate challenges include passing a year-end budget, addressing rising public and private debt, reforming the police and intelligence services, and strengthening the judiciary.
The students' victory "is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centred on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement’s limited governing experience could make the transition challenging," Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday.
The IMF projects Serbia’s economy to grow 3 per cent in 2026 and 4 per cent in 2027, while inflation rose to 4.1 per cent in September from 2.2 per cent in August. The central bank has held its benchmark interest rate at 5.75 per cent since 2024.
“The new government would have to fight its corner,” warned Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior, referring to the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is expected to remain a formidable opposition force.
The movement has also promised economic changes, including action against retail monopolies to lower food prices, tax relief for lower-income groups, affordable housing initiatives and cheaper medicines.
Kosovo, Russia and the European Union
Foreign policy could be another test. The student-backed candidates oppose recognising Kosovo’s independence, declared in 2008, while relations with the European Union remain strained over stalled accession talks and the need to normalise ties with Pristina.
The movement has also said it does not intend to impose sanctions on Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and a major gas supplier. At the same time, the European Commission has offered support for reforms involving the rule of law and media freedom.
“I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing,” said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement, according to Reuters.

In late October, people shared a video allegedly showing a newborn baby with a mustache sitting upright against a pillow in a hospital bed.
The brief clip featured a purportedly real infant that appeared to have been born just moments earlier, with a mustache above its upper lip and some facial hair below its lower lip.
For example, on Oct. 23, an X user posted the video (archived) with the caption, "A newborn baby is going VIRAL for arriving in this world with a FULL MUSTACHE," and, "Bro skipped kindergarten and went straight to his midlife crisis 😂."
Users shared the video on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived) and other social media platforms. Some people said hospital staff delivered the baby in Colombia, while others said Ecuador. Snopes readers emailed to ask whether such a baby truly had been born.
A review of comments under social media posts found people making jokes about the baby being born already retired, as well as referencing the mustachioed baby Pubert Addams from "The Addams Family" and comedian Guillermo Rodriguez from "Jimmy Kimmel Live!"
Others asked whether the video was real, including some asking about or making claims about artificial intelligence. Some also mentioned congenital hypertrichosis, which the Cleveland Clinic defined as a rare condition, present from birth, that causes extra hair growth on a person's body or face.
In sum, we found the video displayed at several signs of either being created or manipulated with AI, including inconsistent hairs and other facial features, an AI content label on a very early TikTok post and a duration exactly matching a common AI video length. Therefore, we rated the clip as fake.
Researching the video
According to a reverse image search, TikTok user @mesina080 made what at first appeared to be the oldest post (archived) with the video on Oct. 20.
Days later, @mesina080 reposted the video beginning with a supposed image of a woman preparing to shave her mustache.
In a private message with Snopes, @mesina080 said he used an AI tool to remove a watermark (and potentially other text) from an earlier video he said was "apparently" created with AI. He did not send a link to that earlier video.
A TikTok search for the Spanish-language terms "bigote de bebé" ("baby mustache") located dozens of videos from users reposting the baby with the mustache, including a video (archived) a user with the display name Soy Yare (@yarel0725) posted about 90 minutes earlier than @mesina080. That user watermarked the clip with her name. She also enabled TikTok's "Contains AI-generated media" label during the upload process to clarify that AI created or altered the video.
The clip lasted exactly 10 seconds and ran at 24 frames per second with no added individual frames, a common duration of AI-generated videos. For example, a standard video generated with the Google Gemini AI tool, without specifying anything about length or frame rate, produced a 10-second video running at 24 frames per second — an exact match.
The video begins with the baby facing to his or her right, with some hair visible below the lower lip. The baby turns to the left, with some of the hairs above the child's upper lip appearing to visibly change. The infant turns back to the right, with the area below the lower lip no longer showing facial hair. Also, a blemish sharply appears below the child's right eye that was not nearly as visible earlier. We edited the below image to make the shadowed area below the lower lip appear more visible:
Readers can watch the video to see the blemish appear much more visible later in the video than before, as well as the apparent vanishing of facial hair below the lower lip. (@yarel0725 via TikTok)
We did not yet obtain clarification from Yare about whether she created the original AI-generated clip. Scans of the video with AI detection tools displayed inconsistent results.
Additionally, our research also located a similar video with the person holding the camera appearing to walk toward the baby in the bed. That clip first appeared after the one above.
For further reading, we previously explained how we determined a video of a monkey rescuing a dog from floodwaters was made with AI.

Using Google’s products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world’s largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won’t use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company’s privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.
On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy, spotted by Android Authority. The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language.
This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it’s shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026, allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield.
Personal Intelligence connects your data to the Gemini app but also to features like AI Mode search. While the Gemini app does not currently have ads, you may see sponsored content in AI search tools. Google’s changes to the privacy policy appear to acknowledge that data shared with AI search via Personal Intelligence could, therefore, contribute to ad personalization.
According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement:
“Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. Ads will continue to be relevant to things like your query, the context of the response and your interests. Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.”
Google’s statement is essentially a roundabout way of confirming that Workspace and Photos data may inform ads. If you interact with AI Mode while Personal Intelligence is enabled, there’s a chance that summaries and insights from your data will inform the answers you get. Because that same data is used for ad targeting, it’s accurate to say that your personal data is an element of ad targeting in AI search. The privacy policy now makes that clear.

The story so far:
France reported the first known human infection with Shamonda virus on October 22, 2026. The patient, who was severely immunocompromised and receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon, died in early October. Investigations are underway to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the death, and how the patient acquired the infection.
French authorities suspect that the patient was infected by the bite of a Culicoides midge in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating among animals during spring and summer. The specific insect responsible has not been identified. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the virus has been detected in farm animals in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Jersey.
French authorities say that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge of the virus. The World Health Organization (WHO) has also said that wider spread is unlikely based on the information currently available. However, investigations into the human case are continuing.
What is Shamonda virus?
Shamonda virus is a vector-borne virus belonging to the genus Orthobunyavirus in the family Peribunyaviridae. It is part of the Simbu group of viruses, which also includes Schmallenberg virus and Akabane virus.
The virus was first isolated from cattle in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in parts of Africa and Japan. Before the recent case in France, it was considered an animal pathogen that did not infect humans.
Cattle are considered its main animal hosts, although infections have also been detected in sheep, goats, horses and alpacas. In livestock, infection can cause fever, diarrhoea, lethargy, loss of appetite and reduced milk production. In pregnant animals, it has been associated with abortions and congenital abnormalities in offspring.
Neurological signs have also been reported in horses infected with the virus in Europe. The extent to which the variants circulating in Europe differ in their effects on animal health remains under investigation.
How does it spread?
The virus is understood to spread primarily through the bites of infected Culicoides midges, tiny blood-feeding insects. The precise midge species responsible for transmitting the European variants has not yet been established.
According to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), there is currently no evidence of horizontal transmission, or spread between animals through direct contact or other routes. Vertical transmission, from a pregnant animal to its offspring, has been reported.
Two genetically distinct variants, designated Shamonda virus Europe 1 (SHAV-EU1) and Shamonda virus Europe 2 (SHAV-EU2), have been identified in Europe in 2026. Research indicates that they may have been introduced separately. Their geographical distribution, effects on livestock and long-term significance remain under investigation.
Why is it in the news?
The detection in a human has raised questions about whether Shamonda virus can cause disease beyond its known animal hosts. French authorities have reported that the brain complications observed in the patient before death were considered very likely to be linked to the infection. However, investigations are continuing to establish whether the virus caused or contributed to the death.
The patient was severely immunocompromised and had an underlying serious illness. It is not yet known whether similar complications would occur in people with different health conditions or whether people without immune suppression could develop symptomatic infection.
The case highlights the importance of the One Health approach, which recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health. Monitoring infections in livestock, investigating unusual human infections and sharing laboratory findings can help identify emerging health risks.
The virus is also affecting livestock production. A study of nine French dairy herds found a 15%–75% decline in bulk milk production during clinical episodes associated with infection. Affected cattle also showed symptoms such as diarrhoea, reduced activity and, less consistently, fever. The findings are from a small number of farms and do not establish the typical impact across all affected herds.
How prevalent is it?
The prevalence of Shamonda virus in humans is unknown. The French case is the first documented human infection, but it does not establish when the virus first began infecting people or whether other infections have gone undetected. There is insufficient data to estimate the number of human infections worldwide.
In animals, the virus has been identified in parts of Africa and Japan. Its detection in European livestock in 2026 has expanded its known geographical distribution. By October 22, the ECDC had reported detections in farm animals across 12 European countries and Jersey.
These reports indicate the geographical spread of detections, not the proportion of animals infected. Differences in veterinary surveillance, laboratory testing and reporting make it difficult to compare the burden between countries.
There are no verified figures establishing the prevalence of Shamonda virus in India so far. However, the absence of reported detections does not establish that the virus is absent from the country.
The virus is not subject to routine official surveillance or control measures under the European Union’s Animal Health Law. This may limit the completeness of information on its distribution and prevalence in livestock.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
In animals, the symptoms of Shamonda virus infection can resemble those of other livestock diseases. Laboratory testing is therefore needed to confirm infection. Molecular tests, including polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, can detect the virus’s genetic material, while genetic sequencing can help distinguish between variants.
Evidence on the clinical presentation and management of human infection remains limited. There is currently no established, Shamonda-specific treatment protocol for human infection. Further investigation is needed to determine how the virus affects humans and what clinical management may be appropriate.
According to WOAH, there are no commercially available vaccines against Shamonda virus. No established vaccine is available for preventing human infection.
What is the public health risk?
French authorities have said that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge. The WHO has assessed wider spread as unlikely on the available evidence. These assessments reflect what is currently known and may change as further information becomes available.
Key questions include how the patient acquired the infection, whether the virus contributed to the death, whether other human infections have occurred and whether the virus can spread between people. There is currently no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission.
Surveillance of livestock, laboratory investigations and coordination between animal and human health authorities will be important in answering these questions.
For now, the available evidence supports continued monitoring and investigation. The first human case is significant because the virus was previously considered unable to infect humans, but it does not establish that Shamonda virus is spreading widely among people or that a human outbreak is under way.

The 43-year-old woman sitting across from me in my exam room is exasperated. “I just don’t feel like I have the energy or stamina I used to,” she tells me. “I could run 5 miles a day no problem when I was 23.”
Today we are reviewing her labs, all of which are normal. She has been my patient for several years and recently lost 50 pounds. In many ways, she feels better. Despite all that, despite a normal exam, vital signs, and labs, she just doesn’t have the energy she used to. Something must be wrong.
She then proceeds to tell me how stressed she is, a single mom of three working two full-time jobs. She doesn’t feel like she has any time at all and admits she doesn’t exercise anymore. She isn’t sure how she can fit anything beyond the most basic life tasks into her day. Sometimes she struggles even to do that.
As she is talking to me, I hear her answer her own question.
She has two full time jobs and three kids. She isn’t exercising anymore and feels overwhelmed.
I wait for her to connect the dots.
She doesn’t.
So I do for her.
We talk about exercise and stamina, how it is something that needs to be continually maintained and consistently trained. We talk about how hard it is to raise three children alone, how she isn’t getting good sleep, isn’t eating the best. And then we talk about how 23 is not 43. By the time we are finished, she’s starting to connect the dots, too.
I am a family nurse practitioner who works in both primary care and emergency medicine, and I now have this conversation with patients on a regular basis. A pattern is emerging. The patients differ and the minutia of their symptoms may change, but the underlying is the same. They are asking more than, “Is something wrong with me?” They are asking: “Am I normal?”
Not too long ago, life was understood to be functioning and carrying on despite unavoidable discomforts. Moderate fatigue, mild anxiety, grief, and poor sleep were considered symptoms of a busy life — not always comfortable, but usually not dangerous, either.
Patients are now arriving to see me not because they can’t function, but because they think they aren’t feeling the way a healthy person should.
I am not advocating that we should dismiss patients or their symptoms. We investigate them for a reason. Fatigue can indicate sleep apnea, anemia, maybe a thyroid disorder, or even cancer. Just because a symptom is vague does not rule out something more concerning. Lives have been saved because these have been investigated.
The problem is, medicine is so good at finding answers it is being asked questions it was never designed to address. It can certainly investigate whether that fatigue could be caused by anemia, sleep apnea, or malignancy, but medicine isn’t really able to answer the question of how tired you’re supposed to feel from the wear and tear ordinary living brings.
In the 19th century, a similar problem was discussed. In 1869, neurologist George Beard gave a name to what he believed was one of the defining illnesses of their modern times: neurasthenia, or nervous exhaustion. Symptoms included fatigue, headaches, poor sleep and concentration, and a vague inability to keep up with the increasing pace of demands of the age.
The diagnosis exploded in popularity and was widely blamed on railroads, radios, telegraphs, newspapers, and the industrialization of the times. The very things that were supposed to be making life easier were overwhelming the human nervous system, patients and doctors alike believed. Neurasthenia seemed to give a label for the anxieties of the era, with some Americans worrying that speed, technology, and industry itself might be making them sick. The diagnosis gave a vocabulary and a tangibility to their fears.
While that diagnosis eventually disappeared — I have certainly never diagnosed anyone with it — the symptoms and the concerns didn’t. It now goes by new names: chronic fatigue syndrome, autonomic dysfunction, somatic disorder, to name a few. If neurasthenia gave label and tangibility to the anxieties of the past, I suspect these diagnoses may sometimes do a similar task today.
Let me be clear: Medicine does have a regrettable history of dismissing symptoms, particularly in women. Patients with genuine illnesses have been told their symptoms were anxiety, or maybe they were just on their periods. Sometimes it can take years before they were taken seriously enough to be further investigated and finally diagnosed, and they can often still remain poorly understood. It is almost never helpful to tell a patient to “buck up,” and just because medicine hasn’t been able to find a good reason for it yet doesn’t mean they aren’t suffering.
But while that history should be acknowledged, we shouldn’t conflate illness and the hardships that come with living. We need to be able to separate those with a true chronic disease from patients who are convinced they have one just because they are struggling. Taking patients seriously doesn’t mean every symptom must be labeled any more than reassuring someone they’re healthy means dismissing what they may feel.
My patient isn’t just comparing herself to other single mothers working two jobs and struggling with the day-to-day activities of life. She’s comparing herself to the social media wellness influencer who is up before dawn to use her red light mask, stand on her vibration plate, drink her green smoothie, and run her 5 miles all with a smile on her face and seemingly with energy to spare for the rest of the day. She certainly seems to still have energy to post her perfectly curated dinner on Instagram at the end of the day.
My point is, the comparison is no longer with your peers — it’s an algorithm. And against an algorithm that curates optimization and a veil of perfection, everyone seems sick. Why we can’t do that? Where is our energy for the 5-mile run and nourishing dinner? Something has to be wrong, and we call and make an appointment with our doctors.
The woman in my exam room is asking if this is what 43 is supposed to feel like. In her situation, I think: Yes, that is what it feels like when you’re working two jobs, taking care of three kids, and can’t seem to get on top of your to-do list. This isn’t an abnormality in search of a diagnosis. It’s life.
Kirsten Balin is a family nurse practitioner who works in both primary care in her own medical practice and in emergency medicine in her hometown of Klamath Falls in rural southern Oregon. She writes about medicine, health, and modern culture on her Substack, Differential Notes.

Your Apple TV remote has handy shortcuts most people never use
Getting to know your remote a little better makes it a lot easier to navigate the Apple TV menus.
The Apple TV remote has become ubiquitous in households that favor the company's ecosystem of products. However, people can do more with this little oblong doodad than just browse streaming apps for something to watch. There's a whole hidden world in there, for those willing to experiment. Here's some of the handy shortcuts and useful little things that people can do with the remote that accompanies an Apple TV streaming box.
Force quit apps
This is a shortcut that most people know, but is always worth repeating. It's extremely easy to force-quit apps on an Apple TV box. All you have to do is double-press the Home/Control Center button on the remote. That's the button with the TV on it, which is typically located on the right just above the volume controls.
This pulls up windows of all of the open apps, just like on an iPhone or iPad. Use the clickpad buttons to navigate between these windows. Select an app you want to close and swipe upward on the center of the clickpad. This is helpful when an app glitches or freezes and it also frees up some computational power.
Quickly change up the audio source
Modern households typically have speakers all over the place, though it can be frustrating to switch things up on the fly when watching stuff. However, the Apple TV remote makes this easy. Just press and hold down the Home/Control Center button, which is one with the TV icon. This will bring up the Control Center. This lets you change all kinds of settings, including the audio source.
Once the Control Center opens up, click the Audio Controls icon. This will list all available speakers. Pick your favorite and have at it.
Do all kinds of other stuff with the Control Center menu
The Control Center is extremely useful beyond swapping audio routing settings. This menu lets you change the wireless network, add Bluetooth controllers, access your smart home dashboard and a whole lot more. Remember, just long-press the Home/Control Center button, which is the one with the TV on it.
Scrub through video
The clickpad on the remote doubles as a timeline controller, offering precise controls that aren't available with many rival products. Press the Play/Pause button and slide your finger left or right to rewind or fast-forward. You can also draw circles on the clickpad to scrub back and forth, offering an even more intuitive control option. If you have an older Siri remote that lacks a clickpad, you can do the same thing on the touch surface at the top of the device.
Use the VoiceOver system
VoiceOver is Apple's audio description system that reads menus and descriptive text aloud as you navigate. This feature was originally designed for those with vision impairments, but it's useful to anyone who enjoys spoken feedback. You can turn this on in the Accessibility settings.
Instantly switch between lowercase and uppercase
We all hate entering passwords with a remote control, which is why people sometimes use their phone to control an Apple TV. The actual remote, however, does have one feature that makes entering passwords a bit easier. You can instantly switch between uppercase and lowercase text just by pressing the Play/Pause button as you type.
Summon screen saver images
Apple's tvOS offers access to some visually striking screen saver images. The platform also lets people use their own pictures from the cloud as screen savers. It's really easy to initiate this process, even if the TV hasn't been idle. Just double-press the back button, which is also called the menu button on older remotes. This is the one with the symbol of a triangle pointing to the right.

He also highlighted the institute’s charitable programmes, supported by donations, to help patients access treatment and facilities, and its plans to expand cancer care to reach more patients.
Arvind Krishnamurthy, professor of surgical oncology at Cancer Institute, stressed the need for continued research to improve cancer care and develop better treatments.

Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from DR Congo
- Published
Ugandans returning from neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, the health ministry has said, as the country tightens restrictions to contain the spread of Ebola virus.
More than 4,500 people have died in DR Congo since May - the country's deadliest outbreak of the disease - and has since spread to several other countries.
Uganda's restrictions follow questions after two people who had travelled through the country tested positive for Ebola, in Kenya and Nigeria.
The health ministry on Sunday said the 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan Ebola patient had all been discharged.
Announcing the new measures on Sunday, the health ministry said travellers who had been to DR Congo would not be allowed to transit through Uganda.
It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".
Uganda has also "intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings, supported by screening at designated road checkpoints", it added.
Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme that only essential travellers from DR Congo would be allowed in but would be subjected to "intense public health measures".
"All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," he said.
Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August.
Concerns have however persisted after the two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day.
The patient in Nigeria is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya, while the Kenyan had travelled from the DR Congo where he had business interests.
Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients.
The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi, and the country has since confirmed eight other cases of Ebola. A second woman, related to the businessman died over the weekend.
Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure.
The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to "remain vigilant".
"We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties," Baryomunsi said.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment - though trials are under way.
