During a lengthy news conference on Friday, NASA provided a detailed overview of how it plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface as soon as 2028 as part of its Artemis Program.
Although much of the information behind these plans has been previously reported at Ars Technica and elsewhere, this marked the first time NASA has laid them out in detail and acknowledged some substantial changes in the architecture.
Most notably, for SpaceX’s Starship vehicle, the revised plan calls for the Orion spacecraft to dock with the Starship lunar lander in high-Earth orbit before transiting to the Moon. And for Blue Origin, the mission architecture includes four launches of the New Glenn rocket, but no spacecraft-to-spacecraft refuelings. Additionally, the Blue Origin plans allows for the possibility of its Blue Moon lander rendezvousing with Orion in low-Lunar orbit.
During the presentation on Friday, NASA officials said they continue to anticipate launching the Artemis III mission—a demonstration involving docking with both Blue Moon and Starship near Earth—by “summer” 2027. And they are still tracking toward a 2028 launch of Artemis IV, which would involve an actual landing on the lunar surface.
“This is an achievable path we are on right now,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said. “We have the mandate, we have the resources, and the support from our stakeholders to be able to execute, and that’s what we intend to do.”
It is commendable that Isaacman and his leadership have taken a hard look every element of the Artemis Program and sought to make changes where they can help the lunar lander companies execute and accelerate their plans. But can they hold to those dates?
The SpaceX plan
The biggest ask SpaceX engineers had in meetings with NASA in early 2026 was removing the requirement to dock with Orion in a near-rectilinear halo orbit around the Moon. This required more energy and had other difficulties associated with it. When NASA canceled the Lunar Gateway earlier this year, it solved this problem for SpaceX.

Amazon launched a flurry of new consumer devices this month. Behind the scenes, rising memory costs are adding pressure to its already money-losing hardware business.
An internal planning document obtained by Business Insider shows Amazon forecasting a $612 million gross loss this year for its first-party devices business, compared with a leadership target of a $438 million loss.
The document said rising memory costs were "putting pressure" on the business's profitability, forcing "difficult trade-offs" among sales volumes, average selling prices, and gross profit.
The projected $612 million loss was at the gross profit level, meaning it did not account for all operating expenses, such as R&D, sales and marketing, and administrative costs.
The figures offer a rare glimpse into the pressure on Amazon's hardware business as it absorbs rising component costs. Other tech hardware companies, including industry leader Apple, face similar pressure from surging memory chip prices.
An Amazon spokesperson declined to comment.
A new wave of AI devices
Despite the pressure, Amazon continues to expand its consumer hardware lineup. Even if the company loses money on device sales, it can make money in other ways, such as subscription services, as more customers use its gadgets.
In October alone, the company introduced new Kindles, Alexa-powered tablets, Ring smart locks, and AI wearables under its Bee brand. The August planning document identified Bee and new smart glasses as strategic products still in an investment phase.
Amazon has historically used low-cost hardware to pull customers into a broader ecosystem of shopping and digital content. Rising component costs could make that strategy more expensive, forcing the company to raise prices.
The clearest shift is in Amazon's tablets. Earlier this month, the company phased out Fire tablets after 15 years and replaced the budget-friendly lineup with pricier Alexa Tablets powered by Alexa+. The new devices cost between $229.99 and $499.99, a notable increase from previous generations.
Not just Amazon
The planning document was prepared in August, the same month Amazon raised prices on products including Echo speakers, Kindle e-readers, and Fire TV devices.
The pressure extends beyond Amazon. Apple has raised prices on some Macs and iPads, while Microsoft and Sony have increased console prices. Dell, HP, and Lenovo also face higher memory costs.
The AI boom is helping drive the squeeze. Huge data center investments have increased demand for memory chips, while manufacturers have devoted more capacity to high-bandwidth memory used in AI servers. That has tightened supplies and raised prices for components used across consumer electronics.
Amazon is experiencing both sides of the boom. It expects roughly $220 billion in capital expenditures this year, largely to expand AWS data centers for AI demand, while higher component costs squeeze its consumer hardware business.
The rising cost of Alexa+
The August planning materials show Amazon reassessing both Alexa+ revenue and operating costs. They called for updated forecasts, expansion through enterprise sales and advertising, and more detailed AWS cost modeling.
Amazon is now confronting the cost of operating Alexa+ at scale. Business Insider reported in July that internal forecasts put Alexa+'s AWS cloud costs at roughly $1.7 billion in 2026, nearly triple the prior year's figure. Amazon was working to lower those costs by relying less on Anthropic's AI models and routing more requests to its own, cheaper systems.
A separate project called Moonraker, intended to give Alexa more advanced AI-agent capabilities, was projected to require more than $100 million in GPU spending this year. Amazon internally considered delaying or scaling back the initiative as one option for easing cost pressure, Business Insider previously reported.

Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering, which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might expect, the biggest section of the filing by far is given over to “risk factors,” which are all the things that could squash Anthropic’s big plans. Or, in this case, humanity itself.
While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.
“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)
Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.
The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights—but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.
Or, as the Anthropic filing puts it: “Risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models.”
The prospectus repeatedly makes the point that RSI could lead to AI models that develop faster than the company’s safeguards, and that the company may not even realize it has lost that race until it’s too late. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
It also gets specific about what might happen after that. “As AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the prospectus says, “there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” This is Skynet territory.
Speaking of robots, Anthropic flags concerns about those as well. “When our models direct physical equipment,” the filing says, “errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible.”
You might think, given the apparently existential stakes, that serious consideration would be given to whether RSI should be pursued at all, much less embraced. In an industry as competitive as frontier AI, though, it’s become fait accompli. Here’s how Anthropic describes that same process elsewhere in the prospectus, this time in a section about the startup’s “core advantages:”
“We refer to this recursive dynamic as ‘closing the loop,’” the prospectus says, “and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI.”
Failure to “close the loop,” Anthropic later says, could result in “falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities.” In other words, the same systems that are causing all that existential concerns are the ones Anthropic sees as critical to its success.
Every AI company is dealing with this same tension. When former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral for loudly resigning, he put curbing RSI at the top of his wish list for the industry. Employees at Google DeepMind and elsewhere have had similar revelations. There are multiple bills in Congress, including one cosponsored by Bernie Sanders, that propose a ban on RSI. At the same time, these are for-profit companies, and there are trillions of dollars at stake.
It’s a tricky dynamic to navigate. Recursive self-improvement could become a runaway train that destroys humanity. But until then, just look at how fast it can go.

68-point swing and a Tonga win - how England avoid World Cup exit
- Published
Sixty-eight. That is the magic number for England.
For Brian McDermott's side to reach the semi-finals of the Rugby League World Cup, a specific series of events needs to happen next weekend.
On the backfoot since being humbled 30-12 by Tonga in their opening game, England responded with a crushing 82-0 victory over France to keep their dreams alive.
It means England need to beat co-hosts Papua New Guinea in their final group match in Wollongong next Friday – then hope Tonga beat Samoa, two days later in Sydney.
If Samoa win, England will be eliminated because of their inferior head-to-head record against Tonga.
But if Tonga win, it comes down to points difference between England and Samoa.
England's difference, after the Tonga loss and France win, is +64. Samoa, following hefty victories over the French and PNG, is +132 – which is 68 better than England.
So, 68 is the number to remember. If England beat PNG by 68 points or more, then any Tongan win is good enough for McDermott's men. Less than 68, and they must hope Tonga are really inspired by Pacific rivalry to put one over their island neighbours.
England hope the numbers go in their favour to avoid an unwanted first. In 16 previous Rugby League World Cups, staged in varying formats, neither England nor Great Britain have ever finished outside the top four. And every time the format has included semi-finals, they have got there.
Group B-C: The remaining games
- Fri, 30 Oct: England v Papua New Guinea: Wollongong, 09:05 GMT
- Sun, 1 Nov: Lebanon v France: Parramatta, Sydney: 06:40 GMT
- Sun, 1 Nov: Tonga v Samoa: Parramatta, Sydney: 09:05 GMT
'I'm not sure what else we could have done'
"What we have done today is enormous, given the context," McDermott told his post-match media conference in Perth.
"Knowing we had to win big - and we have had candid conversations about that this week - we have done that without getting hot. Everything was measured and planned.
"Whatever the results next week, we have to finish strong - if we go home next week, we will be disappointed, but I'm not sure what else we could have done."
McDermott's final comments may allude to the controversial format of this men's World Cup, which features an unbalanced group stage that has not helped England's prospects.
Pool A has four teams - Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and the Cook Islands - fighting for two semi-final places in a round-robin format. Simple enough.
But Pools B and C are combined into one six-team league, from which only the top two will make the semi-finals. England, drawn in Pool B, play the three Pool C teams - Tonga, France and Papua New Guinea.
It means while England are competing with Samoa for a semi-final place, they will not actually play each other.
It also means that while New Zealand lost their opening fixture against Australia, their path to the semis remains simple – win their final two group games.
England too had to win their last two pool matches but also needed snookers.
There is some reason behind the maddening format, introduced after France – who were supposed to host a 16-team men's World Cup last summer – pulled out because of money troubles.
Australia stepped in with New Zealand and Papua New Guinea, with the number of teams involved shrunk from 16 to 10 to cut costs.
This format also means every team plays three group games, there are no fallow weekends and the whole tournament can be done in a relatively tight five weeks.
- England thrash France to keep alive World Cup hopes 
  - Published4 hours ago
- 'We had to change after Vegas' - but England suffer another humbling 
  - Published36 minutes ago
'We have given ourselves half a chance'
But it is unquestionably harder on sides in Groups B and C. The fact Australia and New Zealand are in Group A won't help the perception of the tournament being skewed towards the southern hemisphere giants.
"We were the best we could be," England captain George Williams said of the France win. "The situation has been difficult, but we have given ourselves half a chance."
It also leaves England fans with a nagging feeling their side are only producing their best when they are already halfway home.
After a sluggish, disconnected showing against Tonga, England were slow starting against France before finding their mojo - no tries until the 23rd minute; by the final whistle they had run in 14.
England's UK based players took nearly 48 hours to travel out to Perth. BBC Sport understands that the tournament organiser planned England's travel itinerary for the World Cup.
The convoluted route featured a bus journey to London, then flights via Singapore and Sydney rather than straight to Perth, where they played their first two games.
McDermott's side did not play a warm-up fixture and completed just two full training sessions before taking on Tonga.
"We have been together for only five field sessions; we are building something here," said McDermott. "The tries we scored before half time were what we are chasing.
"With a long build up, we could have achieved some special things."
Ifs, buts and maybes. All England can do now is aim for 68 points, and hope.

Ex-West Brom & Stoke striker Berahino retires at 33

Former Premier League striker Saido Berahino has retired from football at the age of 33 to concentrate on his role as a coach with Burundi's national team.
The Midlands-bred Burundi international made his name with boyhood club West Bromwich Albion, where he had one especially prolific season of 20 Premier League and cup goals in 2014-15 before joining Stoke City for £12m in January 2017.
But, having already faltered at Albion in his latter days under Tony Pulis, Berahino flopped badly for Stoke, who went on to suffer relegation from the Premier League in April 2018.
After being given a second chance by then Stoke boss Gary Rowett, he scored five times in 2018-19. But he soon fell out of favour again until he was released by mutual consent with still three years remaining on his contract.
Having left Stoke in August 2019 for Belgium, Berahino played at Waregem and Charleroi before being signed by former Baggies boss Darren Moore at Sheffield Wednesday in August 2021.
He has since played in Cyprus, India and Slovenia, as well as for his native country, having previously been capped by England at all age levels up to and including under-21.
Berahino was twice called up for England's full squad by then manager Roy Hodgson - but was not picked to play.
Berahino's 'Letter To The Game'
Berahino reserved special thanks for his first club, for whom he scored 36 goals in 121 appearances in all competition, including a hat-trick on his first start, as a 20-year-old, against Newport County in the EFL Cup in August 2013.
In a statement, entitled 'A Letter To The Game', posted on Instagram, Berahino wrote: "I want to thank West Bromwich Albion for believing in me when I was a boy.
"Those years at the club, the goals, the fans, the moments, they will always be special. There were highs and lows, mistakes and lessons. I learned that the game can lift you up and test you at the same time.
"The time has come to hang up the boots. My body and my heart are ready for the next chapter. I am proud and grateful to now serve the Burundi national team as a coach. Giving back to the country that made me, and helping the next generation, feels right.
"To my family - you have been my strength. To the fans who stayed with me through every chapter - I will never forget your support. This is not goodbye to football. It is simply the end of one story and the beginning of another.
"Football has given me everything. From the streets of Bujumbura to The Hawthorns, from the Premier League to places I never imagined I'd play - this game carried a young refugee kid through life."

'Maxxing' selected as Dictionary.com word of the year
- Published
Americans have gone all in on "maxxing", making it the 2026 Word of the Year for Dictionary.com.
Short for maximising, the term "can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible", Dictionary.com said in a statement.
It's a major departure from two years ago, when the site, after analysing US social media trends, news stories, and search data, chose demure as word of the year. Last year's was "67".
"Maxxing is the linguistic manifestation of a culture increasingly preoccupied with getting the most out of everything," said Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group.
Digital media used "maxxing" nearly 19 times more in August 2026 compared to the 2025 monthly average, Dictionary.com found. The site also considered affordability, data centre, odyssey, and the shortened form of uncle, "unc", as potential words of the year.
On social media, many people in Generation Z and younger - those under 30 - post extensively about their maxxing efforts to achieve all sorts of perfection.
Influencers focused on fitness and wellness post about "proteinmaxxing" and "fibermaxxing". Those giving their full attention to improving sleep habits say they are "sleepmaxxing".
The influencer Clavicular has gained thousands of followers as he chronicles his extreme "looksmaxxing" - working to meet a set of prescribed criteria for attractiveness, with particular importance given to jawlines, eyes and physique.
"Whatever we're doing, we want to push it further," Johnson said. "But its expanding uses also reveal how people are responding to that impulse. Some embrace it. Some exaggerate it for laughs. Others subvert it entirely to describe stepping back from the relentless pursuit of more."
People were playing with the term - and idea - for decades before Clavicular started posting videos.
In the opening song for the 1990s television show The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, for example, Will Smith raps: "Chillin' out, maxin', relaxin' all cool."
"Unfortunately, by the time the dictionary gets a hold of it, that probably means that it's reached critical mass," says teacher Lauren Cella.
Cella, a content creator known for her viral Gen Z history lessons, says she and her students have been using "maxxing" for some time as a suffix.
"They're actually, in their own way, reinventing grammar, which I think is super cool," she says.
Maxxing gives the students permission to "optimise to meet a goal" or do something others might think of as "cringe", and allows them to own it, she says.
"It's a fun, harmless way that kids are expressing themselves and sharing different goals that they have," she says.
Linguist Vanessa Croft, who teaches English, says the internet and digital media make language move at "warp speed", even faster than radio, film or television ever did. As swiftly as new terms are added to the lexicon, they can just as quickly fall out of favour.
"By the time millennials and Gen X or Gen Y start using the terms, Gen Z and Gen Alpha aren't using those terms anymore," she says.
While she and her secondary-school aged students are still "maxxing" too, they are now using it "almost ironically", she says.

Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.
Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.
The 38-year-old migrant worker, born into a poor Muslim family, was not alone. Since last year, 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – have been removed from India’s electoral roll through a process known as SIR, or special intensive revision. In the nearly eight decades since India’s independence, never have the voter rolls shrunk by such a huge amount over such a short time.
The Narendra Modi government has called SIR a legitimate exercise to clean up the electoral rolls. Overseen by the election commission, tens of millions of dead and duplicate names have been removed. Yet so have the names of millions of living Indian citizens.
Critics allege that the pledge to “purify” India’s voter roll of illegal immigrants has instead been used for more sinister purposes – disenfranchising tens of millions of Muslims, other minorities, and poor and lower caste communities, who are largely not BJP voters.
In a matter of weeks, nationwide anger at SIR has boiled up and spilled out on to the streets of India’s biggest cities, presenting a formidable challenge to the government. Over the weekend, Delhi was transformed into a high-security fortress of barricades, roadblocks and tens of thousands of police and paramilitaries who detained thousands of people, as they attempted to stop youth-led protests calling for the man who oversaw SIR, the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down immediately.
On Monday, opposition parties – who have decried SIR as a “weapon for vote theft” by the Modi government – drew tens of thousands of supporters as they marched through the capital and presented a petition to the supreme court, demanding Kumar’s resignation. The youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, who were behind the call for Saturday’s action, have vowed to “fight on” in their protests against SIR.
Opposition and civil society leaders allege that SIR has already given the BJP an electoral advantage in states such as Bihar and West Bengal, claims the party denied. Others say the exercise has had even more concerning implications: under changes to SIR unilaterally implemented by Kumar, the election commission has become the arbiter of Indian citizenship, a sweeping overreach of its remit.
The consequences are already playing out in West Bengal, where Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) recently came to power and began a crackdown on “illegal” immigrants, complete with several new detention centres. Civil society groups say Muslims excluded by SIR are being targeted.
Fakir was among them. Just three months after the voter list was published – and while her hearing to challenge her exclusion was pending – she was picked up by police and accused of being an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant.
In July she was pushed over the border to Bangladesh, a country she had never been to nor had any connection with, and remains stuck there. “I have all the documents to prove I am an Indian citizen,” she said in a tearful phone call from the Bangladesh border village where she has been sheltering. “I fell on their feet and begged the police not to send me to Bangladesh but they pushed me over the border.”
A Bangladesh border guard officer confirmed Fakir’s account. “We checked all her documents and are convinced that she is an Indian citizen,” they said. In September, her family submitted a petition to the supreme court challenging her deportation. The Indian government was given a month to respond.
“All I want is to return to my family and my home in India. I am waiting desperately for that day,” she said. The backlog of millions of voters in West Bengal challenging their exclusion means it could be years before Fakir’s case is heard.
Those across West Bengal who have been stripped of their votes speak of their terror of being accused of being an alien in their own land. Some have had benefits taken away. Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui, 80, from the North 24 Parganas district, said his grandfather had been a freedom fighter for Indian independence and three generations of his family were on the voter rolls. Yet after SIR, Siddiqui described his “humiliation” on finding his name gone.
“With my name erased from the voter list, I am in constant terror. What if they send me to a detention camp?” he said. “I cannot bear to think about being separated from my children and grandchildren at this age, especially when all my ancestors have been buried in India.”
Critics say the problems began in 2023, when the Modi government changed the process for appointing the three-body election commission, giving majority control to the government for the first time. Within a matter of months, the Modi-led panel had appointed Kumar as the election commissioner in spite of opposition objections.
“For decades, the election commission was one of our more credible, independent bodies, but now that has been eroded,” said Ronojoy Sen, a senior fellow at the South Asian Studies Programme, National University of Singapore.
By the following year, the new election commission body had begun SIR, starting in Bihar, where it immediately raised concerns among human rights groups after more than 6 million names were removed. Not long after the revisions, the BJP won a landslide victory in the Bihar state elections.
Despite concerns over SIR rumbling on for months, it did not spark national protests until the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two members of the election commission had raised 14 objections to how voters were being excluded from the rolls, but they were unilaterally overruled by Kumar.
“India has always been a flawed democracy but at least citizens felt they had the right to vote and that elections were regular and fair,” said Sen. “SIR has taken away that right. From how it has been conducted, it’s difficult to see how the motive was anything other than to enhance the election prospects of the BJP.”
Three former election commissioners have openly criticised SIR as a “hostile exercise” that has undermined the sanctity of the country’s electoral rolls by focusing on the exclusion – rather than inclusion – of voters. OP Rawat, a former chief election commissioner, described changes to the voter registration form as “wrong and illegal”.
Ashok Lavasa, who was an election commissioner between 2018 and 2020, called for the SIR to be scrapped. “An unfair procedure has been imposed on millions of people in the country, and you have the judiciary which has validated that,” he said last month. “How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?”
None have been more vehement in their opposition than SY Qureshi, who was chief election commissioner between 2010 and 2012. “This is a national harassment exercise designed to throw Muslims off the electoral roll,” he claimed. “The only way to restore the credibility of India’s elections is to restore those deleted voters.”
The BJP has denied any political involvement or motive in the SIR process, accusing the opposition Congress party of “jealousy” over its recent electoral victories and saying any deleted voters can simply re-enrol. The BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the allegations were “disinformation” and part of an opposition campaign “being orchestrated to create an atmosphere of division and anarchy”.
Nonetheless, the election commission has appeared to accept some flaws in the process. Late last week, it belatedly put a cap on the number of voter deletion forms – which allow people to submit objections on behalf of others – after incidents in which people submitted thousands of forms targeting legitimate Muslim voters.
Public anger, meanwhile, has continued to build. In Delhi, where the SIR exercise left millions of people off the draft list, protests are expected to continue this week.
A Delhi resident for 30 years, Prashant Tandon, 60, said he could not believe it when a notice came to his door, questioning his life as a voter. “If someone doubts my citizenship, they should produce evidence against me,” he said furiously, adding that he would be protesting alongside the young people. “I should not have to prove that I am an Indian citizen.”

Serbia's political veteran Vucic outplayed all opponents. Then came the students
Serbia’s populist leader Aleksandar Vucic has dominated politics in the Balkan country for 14 years
BELGRADE, Serbia -- Serbia's populist strongman Aleksandar Vucic dominated the Balkan country's politics for 14 years. Then came the students.
The long-ruling authoritarian leader on Sunday conceded the defeat of his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party to a grassroots movement of university students in a parliamentary election. The students had led protests for almost two years before unseating him in a historic change of government.
The 56-year-old political veteran easily outplayed political opponents in the past and thought he could do it again. Ahead of Sunday's ballot he pulled a maneuver in the style of his ally Russian President Vladimir Putin when he resigned the presidency to pursue a bid to become the prime minister.
Vucic then launched a fierce campaign involving favorable around-the-clock coverage on state media and attacks on opponents. He handed out cash to voters and promised higher pensions, new roads and cheaper medicines.
It didn't work. The diverse youth movement's message that rampant corruption, cronyism and organized crime under Vucic were eating away at the country resonated widely with voters.
The student protests first started in 2024 after a collapsed canopy at a renovated train station in Serbia's north killed 16 people, triggering claims that graft-fueled negligence led to poor construction work and eventually to the crash.
Defiant, Vucic on Sunday blamed his defeat on foreign interference.
“I want people to know,” he said. “This was the verification of a revolution that they carried out directly with support of different European countries and the deep American state, the one that is also against President (Donald) Trump.”
During a political career spanning more than 30 years, Vucic morphed from being an extreme nationalist who supported aggression against non-Serbs in the former Yugoslavia to a populist who shifted his preferences to balance between global powers and influences.
During the wars in the 1990s, Vucic was one of the radical party leaders who advocated the creation of a “Greater Serbia” that would include territories in Croatia and Bosnia where minority Serbs live. Those policies are widely blamed for bloody conflicts that killed over 100,000 people and displaced millions.
Vucic was known for fiery speeches, including one in Serbia’s parliament where he said that for each Serb killed in the Bosnian war, 100 Bosnian Muslims must die. He later said that he didn’t mean it literally.
As information minister in the late 1990s, Vucic oversaw media critical of then-President Slobodan Milosevic slapped with heavy fines or shut down. He shifted away from ultranationalism to a proclaimed pro-EU stance on the eve of his party’s electoral win in 2012.
In office, Vucic positioned himself as pro-European and pro-Russian, and as an admirer of Trump. Ahead of the decisive ballot, however, Vucic re-embraced his hard right roots and turned to Putin again as he struggled to restore his shaken voter base.
Vucic defied the EU last month by allowing a hero’s funeral in Belgrade for Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb army commander convicted of genocide by a U.N. court in the Netherlands.
“It is no coincidence that Vladimir Putin said he hopes that I will be the prime minister,” Vucic boasted days ahead of the ballot, ditching the proclaimed pro-EU position that helped his populist party come to power in 2012.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov expressed hope Monday that the post-Vucic government will retain friendly relations with Russia. Vucic had refused to join EU sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine despite formally seeking membership for Serbia in the 27-nation bloc.
“We highly value the contribution Mr. Vucic has made to the development of our bilateral relations," Peskov said.
“We intend to continue doing everything possible to help the development of our relations with Belgrade,” Peskov said. "But, as you know, it takes two to tango.”
Konstantin Kosachev, a deputy speaker of the upper house, the Federation Council, said that the Serbian elections’ outcome could signal that “there would be one sovereign country less in Europe.”
But Konstantin Malofeyev, a hawkish tycoon who sponsors a virulently nationalistic media outlet, welcomed Vucic’s defeat, denouncing him as a hypocrite who has tried to maneuver between Russia and the West.
“The Serbian people have delivered a historic verdict on the Vucic regime,” Malofeyev said on his Telegram channel. “The era of political hypocrisy and duplicity is drawing to a close."
In the past 14 years, Vucic served as a deputy prime minister, the prime minister and president.
As president for nearly 10 years, Vucic turned the largely ceremonial post into the center of power in the country. He was known for frequent addresses to the nation and appearances in pro-government media.
“He is a competitor who has mastered a technology of governing that is based on stick and carrot, and the idea that nobody but him is right,” Dejan Pavlovic, a professor in the Faculty of Political Sciences at the University of Belgrade, told The Associated Press recently.
Pavlovic described Vucic’s 14-year rule as a “textbook regime” of autocracy, with his party extending its control over the media, judiciary and other institutions, leaving nothing to chance.
“Cover it all: control the media, control the judiciary, control all institutions,” he explained.
In the highly organized ruling SNS party, Vucic commanded ultimate authority and loyalists were rewarded through lucrative deals with the state and protection from prosecution, Pavlovic said. Vucic, he said, “created a whole new elite in the Serbian society and that elite knew how to be thankful.”
Elections under Vucic were increasingly marred by reports of voting irregularities, violent incidents and complaints that his control over pro-government media and use of public funds to bribe voters gave his party an unfair advantage.
During the student-led protests, Vucic fenced off a central park outside his office in Belgrade and installed tents with groups of supporters as an apparent human shield. Investigative reporters identified some of the camp residents as people with criminal backgrounds and tied Vucic to criminal clans, which he refuted.
As he conceded defeat, Vucic vowed to keep fighting.
“Our structure is very firm, we are very united and strong, and we are used to being in opposition,” he said in a Sunday night speech.
Former President Boris Tadic believes Vucic would not have conceded in case of a less convincing student victory. But under the circumstances, “he could not avoid it.”

Woman treated for Ebola in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
Nigerian authorities continued monitoring 52 people who had been in contact with the woman, while Switzerland will take over her care

A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria has been flown home to Switzerland alongside her husband, as health authorities continue to track 52 people who were in contact with her.
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Pate said the patient, who was the country’s first case in the present outbreak, departed the capital, Abuja, early on Monday with his authorisation. Her health had improved significantly, leaving her stable, conscious and capable of communicating, he said.
"This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place," Pate wrote on X. Her spouse, a Swiss diplomat stationed in Nigeria, has displayed no symptoms.
Mohamed Janabi, the World Health Organization’s regional director for Africa, explained that the evacuation occurred because the pair are Swiss citizens, adding that local medical teams had stabilised her after managing the acute phase of the disease.
Switzerland is taking over her treatment and monitoring her husband, while Nigeria tracks the remaining 52 contacts.
"With the evacuation of the patient and her husband, Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases," Janabi stated, emphasising that continued caution is essential. Pate confirmed that containment efforts stay in effect and asked Nigerians to remain alert.
The woman tested positive after returning to Abuja from Uganda. Nigerian authorities said Friday they had yet to establish how she contracted the virus.
Switzerland’s foreign ministry said that she had not visited Congo and was believed to have been infected while traveling to Uganda with her husband.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had both traveled through Uganda’s Entebbe International Airport on Oct. 3. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but later declared itself free of the virus.
Kenya has recorded nine cases, including two deaths, since confirming its first case earlier this month.
The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus.
The latest figures from Congo’s health ministry show more than 9,900 cases, including more than 4,800 deaths, since the outbreak began in May.
The WHO has said the outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to surpass the death toll of the deadliest: West Africa’s 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed 11,000 people. Nigeria was among the countries affected, recording 20 cases before its outbreak was declared over after three months.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has issued notices to Nestle India and Zydus Wellness over “misleading claims” in certain products and has asked the companies to provide scientific proof to support their advertisements.
In a social media post, the FSSAI said notices were sent to Nestle India for misleading claims and non-compliant promotions involving two food products ‘Lactogen Pro 1 Powder’ and ‘Nan Excella Pro Stage 1’.
The regulator also issued notice to Zydus Wellness Product Ltd citing misleading claims and advertisement on its food product Complan.
In the notice issued for Lactogen Pro 1 powder, the FSSAI said the company has claimed, in its labelling and advertisement material, that the product “contains whey protein, which is a part of milk protein that is easy to digest”.
The food safety regulator has asked Nestle to furnish scientific substantiation for the claim regarding whey protein being easy to digest.
In the product Nan Excella Pro Stage 1, the FSSAI said that the claim “5 HMOs [human milk oligosaccharides] helps support normal immune system” was considered to imply that the product was suitable for supporting the immune system.
“The claim was considered non-compliant with provisions prohibiting claims relating to the prevention, alleviation, treatment or cure of any disease, disorder or particular physiological condition, unless specifically permitted under applicable regulations,” the regulator said.
In the case of Complan, the FSSAI said the product label displays images of two children and claims include “2X Faster Growth”, “Supports Concentration and Memory” and “Pro Immunity+ 34 Vital Nutrients”.
The claims were found to be in violation of the FSS (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018.
The regulator has asked Zydus to provide scientific justification for such claims.
The advertisement claim “Growth Comes in 4 Flavours” was found to violate regulations of the FSS (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018.
The companies have been directed to show cause within the stipulated period as to why action should not be taken against them, the regulator said.

Justice delayed: Acknowledging women pioneers in science
The debate in the scientific world has often been about glory. Who deserves the glory for a discovery, for an invention, for defining a procedure, a drug, a vaccine? Does credit ever attach to the patients who were experimented upon, the participants of a clinical trial, people who gave of their time and body in order that science may advance, in order that people who come after them do not suffer. Codes of ethics are mutable, they keep changing, and the grant of credit in science also operates on this arc. This story is a page from such an omission, a blunder. Nearly 150 years later, some form of reparation was attempted.
For the world, for the longest time, perhaps even till today, J. Marion Sims was the ‘Father of Modern Gynaecology.’ Sims reportedly earned the title for his ‘groundbreaking surgical innovations, notably the development of a cure for vesicovaginal fistula.” For his achievements, Sims not only received the soubriquet, but also statues and memorials and hospitals and wards named after him. The number of girls on whom he perfected his techniques were not even a footnote in the glorious history he covered himself with.
Among them was Anarcha Westcott, a teenage mother, a patient who developed a terrible vesicovaginal fistula, tears or holes that develop between the bladder and vagina, sustained after three days of labour. The tears made it impossible to control her bowel or bladder and the condition caused her immense pain and suffering. That is how she came under the ‘care’ of Sims, if care could be used to describe what he went on to do.
Anarcha was a young African American woman wrested down in slavery. Sims reportedly believed that African American women do not feel pain, so he experimented on her repeatedly (we know of two others -- Betsey, and Lucy), operating without anaesthesia (though it was available). Sims himself records that he had performed nearly 30 procedures on her, consent was a casualty of the times, before he perfected his technique using silver to suture the fistula, that prevented infection.Before this, a vesicovaginal fistula was considered untreatable, and women would continue to suffer the rest of their life.
Anarcha did not disappear after this though. J. C. Hallman, in his 2023 book Say Anarcha- A Young Woman, a Devious Surgeon, and the Harrowing Birth of Modern Women’s Health, did extensive research to uncover that far from disappearing after the Sims experiments, she went on to serve in Sims hospital, as a midwife, nurse, and ‘doctor woman’ to her own people, women who were also slaves. Many decades after Anarcha died, a groundswell of support arose for her from women who objected to the way she was quietly erased from history, and instead calling for her to be celebrated as the “mother of gynaecology.”
Say Anarcha excavates history, deconstructing the biographical smoke screen of a surgeon who has falsely been enshrined as a medical pioneer and bringing forth a heroic Black woman to her rightful place at the center of the creation story of modern women’s health care. She was more than a medical ‘specimen’, she worked at Sims’ slave hospital near Montgomery, Alabama. She trained and served as a surgical nurse and went on to help other women, also being experimented upon at the hospital.
More recently, efforts have been made to honour her contribution to gynaecology. The American college of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists have dedicated two days – February 28 and March 1—to Anarcha, Lucy and Betsey. Recognition also saw expression in art: At Harvard’s Hutchins Center exhibition in 2023, a prominent exhibit was artist Jules Arthur’s paintings of Anarcha, Luch and Betsey through her work titled “Call and Response: A Narrative of Reverence to Our Foremothers in Gynaecology“.
Artist Michelle Browder created a 15-foot public monument honouring them as “the mothers of gynaecology“ in downtown Montgomery. Tangentially, it was also seen as a victory that Sims’ statue was removed from Central Park in April 2018 and relocated. Hallman’s book was preceded by a documentary Remembering Anarcha.
Unfortunately, Anarcha’s story is not merely a historical wrong. It serves to remind health practitioners and policy makers that several inequities still govern access and affordability of high quality care; that for women, it could be tougher than it might be for men. For that, we will have to keep saying her name, so it will be a reminder. Say her name, say Anarcha.

I know we’ve had a lot of “You Can See Everything” content in this newsletter, but allow me one more plug. A recent STAT letter to the editor included a message from the former director of a Phoenix lab. “Venipuncture yields several milliliters of excess serum or plasma, from which we can perform repeat tests, which are often requested by clinicians when they receive what they believe is an aberrant result,” he wrote. “More often, results lead to further requests from the ordering doctor, which we can perform since we store excess serum or plasma for up to one month and can do without requiring the patient to come back to the draw station. RFK Jr.’s new NIH center on vaccine injuries actually has a much broader mission
Earlier this month, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a new National Institutes of Health center focused on patients with vaccine injuries. Chelsea Cirruzzo’s reporting reveals the center’s actual mandate is broader, focusing on the long-term symptoms that people experience after an infection. (Long covid is a good example of this phenomenon.)
The goal of the center, a senior official told Chelsea, is to get to the bottom of why some people’s immune systems have more robust responses than others, and to learn more about diseases, as well as ways to make vaccines more safe and effective.
Her story has other details too — the center itself is actually a new research study within the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases that plans to enroll several hundred participants who have vaccine injuries or post-infection symptoms. There is no clinical element to the center, and even people concerned with Kennedy’s vaccine skepticism have praised the center’s director. Read more here.
A virus that afflicts cows makes the jump to a human
For the first time, a human has been infected with the Shamonda virus, according to French officials. The man who got sick was severely immunocompromised and later died. (Investigators are currently studying whether the virus contributed to his death.)
Shamonda virus is spread by bites from a type of fly called a midge. It mostly infects cattle, though cases in horses, sheep, and goats have been reported as well. The virus has circulated in Africa and Japan since the 1960s but was only documented in Europe this year. It can cause fever, miscarriages, and neurological symptoms in animals.
Officials have said they believe the patient, who lived in Lyon, was infected by a midge bite, and that he showed some neurological symptoms. European officials said they’re watching for additional cases, but the World Health Organization says broader transmission is unlikely. In other words: No need to panic.
A podcast full of memories honoring Helen Branswell, from those who loved her
Take yourself back, for a moment, to March 2020. Covid was in the news, but barely. Many of us were still continuing with our lives, following the virus on the margins.
But STAT reporter Helen Branswell knew better. In a beautiful new Readout LOUD, STAT Executive Editor Rick Berke recounts the story of a Covid-19 panel he moderated at Harvard on March 7, 2020. Rick asked the panelists about the then-novel coronavirus, and Helen offered this clear-eyed assessment: “Having written about the possibility of something like this for years, I still find myself really startled that it’s happening.”
“For Helen to be startled, I took that really seriously,” Rick said on the Readout LOUD. She could see before anyone what we were in for, and went on to cover the pandemic with remarkable authority and clarity.
As we shared in this newsletter, Helen passed away earlier this month from complications of cancer. The whole podcast, which includes interviews with her family, STAT staffers and public health officials, is worth a listen.
Christina Applegate’s MS misdiagnosis was all too familiar
For the last several years, actor Christina Applegate has spoken out about having multiple sclerosis, shedding light on the debilitating illness. Except it turns out Applegate does not have MS after all. She shared on a recent podcast that she’d been misdiagnosed.
Lindsay Karp knows what that feels like. In a new First Opinion, she writes about her own 13-year journey to get a diagnosis for the debilitating weakness, pain, and fatigue she’d been living with, and why MS diagnoses are so complicated. Read more.
Days of our … diabetes conference
The drama continues for the American Diabetes Association, which created an uproar it’s still unwinding after armed guards escorted five doctors and scientists out of its June conference for the high crime of distributing an editorial outside a hall where a Trump administration official was speaking.
In a new report, the ADA offers background on the evictions, writing that they had received a written threat before the event that there would be “protest and disruption” at the conference. Liz Cooney has the “threat,” along with all the details, in her story.
If that’s not enough to convince you to read, may I draw your attention to the lede of Liz’s story: “Since five members of the American Diabetes Association were ejected from its scientific session in New Orleans on June 5, the professional organization has released two explanations, one apology, one summary of its review of the events, and one notice of further review.” It just gets better from there.
Am I sick or is this just what 40 feels like?
The patient wasn’t sick, exactly. Her labs were normal, and her vital signs were strong. But she felt tired. Is something wrong, she asked?
Nurse practitioner Kirsten Balin said she’s having more conversations like this, with patients who are aging, working too much, and just feeling kind of … off. “Not too long ago, life was understood to be functioning and carrying on despite unavoidable discomforts. Moderate fatigue, mild anxiety, grief, and poor sleep were considered symptoms of a busy life — not always comfortable, but usually not dangerous, either,” she writes. “Patients are now arriving to see me not because they can’t function, but because they think they aren’t feeling the way a healthy person should.”
At the heart of it, Balin writes, they’re asking: How bad is healthy supposed to feel? Find Balin’s answer — and her advice for sorting illness from “the hardships that come with living” — here.

Fintech startup axiTrust is in talks to raise around $5 Mn in fresh capital in its Series A funding round, people aware of the matter told Inc42 on the condition of anonymity. The fresh round is likely to be led by Singapore based Argor.vc, and will see participation from axiTrust's existing investor General Catalyst. Questions sent to axiTrust didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story. The fresh round has come almost a year after the startup raised $2.6 Mn in its seed funding round led by General Catalyst. Other investors including Atrium Angels, YAN Network and Supermorpheous are also on the fintech startup’s cap table. The fresh capital will help the startup build digital infrastructure to accelerate adoption of its surety bonds offering. For context, surety bonds are insurance-backed guarantees that assure a buyer or project owner that a business will fulfil its contractual obligations. Instead of blocking the capital as collateral, they allow the buyers to pay a premium to secure the guarantee, helping free up working capital and reduce financial strain. Founded in 2024 by Aditya Tulsian (CEO), Rajeev Chari (COO), and Mukund Daga (CRO), axiTrust issues, underwrites and manages digital surety bonds, providing an alternative to traditional, collateral-heavy bank guarantees. As per the startup, more than ₹15 Lakh Cr of MSME working capital is locked up as collateral for bank guarantees, and replacing these traditional guarantees with insurance-backed digital surety bonds can free that capital, expand credit access, and improve trust in business transactions. From digital underwriting and AI-based risk assessment to cashflow-based lending and embedded finance, they are filling long-standing gaps that traditional banks could not address efficiently. These solutions are helping businesses and consumers access credit with fewer delays, lighter paperwork, and better transparency. Investors are actively backing such startups because the lending market in India is massive, still underserved, and primed for digital disruption offering both strong growth potential and meaningful financial inclusion. As per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, the fintech sector saw funding of $243 Mn across 13 deals. Of these, the heavy lifting was done by lendingtech startup Centricity ₹280 Cr round and Navi’s $100 Mn pre-IPO funding.

The survey provided a state-wise breakdown of the average monthly cost per worker for trips to and from a fixed workplace.
Comparing the urban regions of Delhi and Bihar, the survey showed that Delhi recorded the highest average cost among all the states/UTs at ₹2081. Meanwhile, the cost in Bihar (urban) was recorded at ₹702.

The average monthly expenditure on commuting to a fixed workplace is ₹785 per worker, according to data from the National Household Travel Survey for July 2025 to June 2026.
According to the survey, urban workers incur a substantially higher average monthly cost of ₹1,044, compared with ₹612 for rural workers.
It also revealed gender disparity in worker travel spend. The survey showed male workers spend an average of ₹835 per month on fixed-workplace commutes compared to ₹533 per month for female workers.
The survey collected data on regular trips of one kilometer or more performed by Indian people. It aimed to collect information on the modes of transport they use, trip purposes, travel frequency, average cost of regular trips, and other related parameters.
Covering both rural and urban areas across all States and Union Territories of India, this nationwide survey will be a comprehensive benchmark for understanding characteristics of household travel behaviour in the country.

Twenty-one-year-old Saouhum Sharma, a 4th-year History honours student at Hans Raj College, joined the October 12 rally led by Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi to the Supreme Court. By the end of the day, a knife had been slashed across his throat.
The Assault
Sharma and three friends met at Barakhamba Road at 2 pm. They subsequently met more friends and made their way to Mandi House.
“It wasn’t too chaotic at first,” he told Alt News. “We got the call from some Indian Youth Congress (IYC) people who were leading the protest around the area that Rahul Gandhi and everyone was reaching the Supreme Court; we should also reach the Supreme Court. The route from Mandi House to the Supreme Court is a straight road. So we decided to just start walking there. It was two groups of IYC workers and us.”
By 5.40 pm, the group had made some headway towards the Supreme Court when they encountered police barricades. “Some of the IYC people tried to topple the barricades but could not. So we went through a cut onto Sikandra Road.”
As they walked along Sikandra Road, they came across around 15 men standing beside a jeep. Sharma said some appeared to be Hindutva workers, based on what they were wearing.
“They were donning some markers of Hindutva workers. A couple of ‘gamchas’, one in a saffron-coloured T-shirt. Nothing overt, but definitely visible,” he said.
Initially, the men were provocative rather than violent, Sharma recalled. “They were whistling at the female IYC workers — whistling and calling after them. They called a few of them ‘chikni’. They were calling them while standing 20 metres ahead on the side of the road; arms around each other’s shoulders. From afar, they did not look like they would interfere because we outnumbered them. So we didn’t really think of turning back.”
However, as the group approached, the men began taking saffron flags with long poles out of the jeep. “They still weren’t exactly being violent, just provocative.”
Asked whether the men identified themselves as members of any organisation, Sharma said they did not. The flags, too, did not name any organisation, he said. They were generic saffron flags bearing images of an angry Hanuman or the Ram Mandir.
“The men decided to swing the poles, and the IYC workers got a bit agitated, and a bit of a brawl ensued between them; the IYC workers got into an argument with the goons,” Sharma said.
Amid the confrontation, a young man, whom Sharma estimated to be 18 or 19, entered their group. He was not wearing any of the visible markers that Sharma had associated with the men beside the jeep.
“Then this one guy, he was probably 18-19 years old, made his way inside our group. He wasn’t wearing any of those identifiable markers. So we couldn’t tell that he was from the other group. He stood beside me for about five seconds and then… it happened quite quickly.”
“He pulled out a barber’s knife. My friend saw it and dragged me towards herself at which point he swung the blade. He missed my face, and it grazed my neck. He walked away after that.”
Sharma said it took him some time to realise what had happened. “I felt a sting in my neck and realised I was bleeding. At that point, we walked away from the group and decided to head home.”
Encounter with Police
After walking around 500 metres from the spot of the assault, Sharma and his friends encountered a police official on Sikandra Marg, who spotted the blood on Sharma and called out to them.
“He was drinking chai by a police vehicle, wearing a light green vest. There wasn’t a lot of police presence at that point, as we were a little far from the protest site. He offered to give us a ride after he saw the blood,” Sharma said.
As the group considered the offer, the officer turned to the driver seated in the vehicle and asked him to detain them, Sharma alleged. “We got scared, turned him down and left. He insisted at first but didn’t follow us when we left. We immediately left the vicinity of the protest site, went to the Jama Masjid metro station and left.”
According to Sharma, the police official was not wearing a name tag.
“Thankfully, the cut wasn’t that deep as he missed my face and the knife only grazed my neck. After returning, I cleaned the wound a bit and then got a tetanus shot,” he said.

Nepal is set to receive $20 million from the United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund following devastating August floods that killed around 1,500 people and left more than 5,000 missing. But the allocation covers less than 1% of the country’s estimated reconstruction costs, raising questions about whether global climate finance is reaching vulnerable nations at the scale they need. The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) agreed to set aside the money through an emergency procedure at a meeting on Thursday, October 22, the Nepalese government said. The assistance is intended to “help address the severe damage caused by climate-related disaster”, the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment said in a statement, as per Reuters. The allocation marks a significant step for the fund, established to help developing countries cope with climate-related destruction. However, the money has not yet been disbursed. Nepal must submit a detailed proposal for approval by the fund’s board before payment can be made. The disaster began on August 26, when an avalanche of ice and rock near Nepal’s border with China’s Tibet region triggered destructive flooding downstream. According to official data cited by Reuters, the floods affected around 60,000 people across 15,000 families and damaged critical infrastructure, including roads, bridges, schools and 13 hydropower plants. Nepal estimates infrastructure losses at approximately $2.7 billion, while the overall cost of recovery and reconstruction could exceed $4.7 billion. Nepal sought assistance from the FRLD in a letter sent in August, less than a week after the floods. Prime Minister Balendra Shah, in his maiden address to the United Nations in September, described the disaster as a warning to the world and linked it to climate change, despite Nepal’s negligible contribution to global emissions. Nepal had also called for international recognition of the damage caused by climate change. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal clarified later in September that the government had not formally sought compensation from India, China or the United States. The FRLD emerged after years of demands from developing countries, which argue that they face disproportionate climate risks despite contributing relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions. The fund is intended to help countries address climate-related losses that cannot be avoided through mitigation or adaptation alone. With reconstruction needs estimated at more than $4.7 billion, the proposed $20 million contribution is unlikely to make a substantial difference to the overall recovery bill on its own. The decision comes ahead of COP31, the UN climate conference scheduled to take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. The iPhone Duo may be a bit of a risk right now, but there’s a new mid-size Apple touchscreen device that might do the job. Starting at $699, the 8th-gen iPad mini price has gone up, but there are some big changes. Apple says the refreshed 8th-gen iPad mini marks the most significant update ever for its petite tablet, featuring an OLED screen and the A20 Pro chip that we first saw in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.
The new iPad mini has roughly the same footprint as the 2024 release, but the display is slightly larger thanks to a 24 percent reduction in bezel thickness. The device is almost a full millimeter thinner than the last iPad, coming in at just 5.4 mm. The chassis is also IP67 rated for water and dust protection. The 7th-Gen iPad mini didn’t have any official IP rating.
The 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR display (up from 8.3 inches) moves on from the IPS technology of the last-gen device to adopt OLED. That means dapper blacks and a much higher peak brightness—1,200 nits versus just 500 nits for the previous mini. It can also manage 1-nit minimum brightness so as not to sear your retinas in a dark room. There will also be a nano-textured matte display option. The display experience on the new mini should be much more in line with what we’ve come to expect from Apple’s Pro-level devices.
The 2-nanometer A20 Pro chip was a noticeable upgrade in the iPhone 18 Pro, and it will be even more significant in this tablet. The previous model had a 3-nanometer A17 Pro chip, which was already a year old when it appeared in the iPad mini. In the iPhone 18 Pro, we found the A20 Pro significantly improved graphics performance thanks in part to a 50 percent increase in memory bandwidth.

Around 3 a.m. on August 15, 1995, policemen on night patrol on Sivagnanam Road at T. Nagar in Chennai stopped two men on a cycle-rickshaw. A constable noticed a handbag and tried to examine its contents. In a flash, one of the men bit a cyanide capsule tied around his neck and almost instantly dropped dead. In the confusion, the other man rode away on a cycle kept nearby with the bag. The police found a Vellore tailor shop’s label on the dead man’s shirt. A few hours later, at the Egmore Railway Station, a policeman in plainclothes, who had worked in the ‘Q’ Branch, noticed a group of 11 waiting to board a Madurai-bound train. He found their Tamil accent different. Suspecting something, he quietly approached the Railway Police. As a posse of policemen walked towards the group, two of them bit cyanide capsules. One of them died and the other was later hospitalised. A few women constables of the Government Railway Police overpowered some of the fleeing men. Angry at being caught, some of them bit the women in a vain bid to escape.
Common link
It did not take long to conclude that the men involved in the two incidents shared a common link. All belonged to the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), the Sri Lankan Tamil outfit, which was banned in India in 1991, following the assassination of former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi. It emerged that 43 hardcore LTTE militants, including four women, all of whom were housed in a special camp in the Vellore Fort, had escaped after digging a 153-foot-long tunnel in the Tippu Mahal. The tunnel was dug from one of the bathrooms to the moat. “Two batches of six militants each escaped on the night of August 13, while a group of 11 slipped out after midnight on Monday. The rest fled afterwards,” reported The Hindu in its August 16, 1995 edition.
The daring escape had sent shock waves as the camp was well-guarded: it had five watchtowers and two companies of the Central Reserve Police Force to assist the Tamil Nadu Police. Chief Minister Jayalalithaa immediately convened a meeting with Chief Secretary N. Haribhaskar and Director-General of Police V. Vaikunth to work out a strategy to recapture the militants. The Superintendent of Police of North Arcot-Ambedkar district (as Vellore was known then) was suspended, along with officers in charge of security at the camp. The government announced a reward of ₹10,000 for anyone sharing information about the escaped militants. It ordered a judicial inquiry headed by Justice T.N. Singaravelu, a retired judge of the Madras High Court. This was not the first time that the LTTE militants had escaped in Tamil Nadu. In November 1992, 18 militants had escaped from the Tippu Mahal itself. In January 1991, the police opened fire in the Vellore camp, when 400-odd militants attempted to break open the window bars and attack the policemen. Some of them had climbed the terrace of the Tippu Mahal and threw stones and bricks at the policemen standing below. An attempt to set ablaze Sub-Inspector Kannappan after dousing him with kerosene was foiled. A militant, Indiran, 21, was killed in the police firing.
Yet, this was the first time that the militants had escaped by digging a tunnel. “The elaborate planning was proved by the fact that the escapees organised themselves into groups and fanned out to different areas. While one group was believed to have arrived in the city by train, another did so by bus. The direction the other groups took was not known,” wrote The Hindu in a report, ‘LTTE escape: Many questions unanswered’. It said, “People in Vellore expressed surprise and disbelief when reporters told them about the militants’ escape by digging a tunnel using old and rusted pipes and other improvised tools. They were anxious to know whether the tunnel had been dug beyond the rampart wall of the fort. How could they do such a job when the fort had a very deep rocky foundation? they wondered.”
‘Pressmen reluctant’
When journalists wanted to have a look at the tunnel on day one, the police refused permission, citing the judicial inquiry. However, on August 19, journalists from Madras were taken to inspect the tunnel, which had just an 1-1/2 foot x 1-1/2 foot entry point on the first floor of the Tippu Mahal. The exit point of 3 feet x 3 feet was located in between the fort and the moat walls on the western side. “Both the entry and exit points looked so hideous that pressmen were reluctant to pass through the tunnel despite the readiness of the police to allow them. Commandos Sathya and Perumal told this correspondent that they could crawl through the tunnel within three minutes, though the route was zigzag at some points,” read a report. Many of the escaped militants were captured later.

Nadal’s appearance in a tennis exhibition Las Vegas early next year will be his first on a U.S. court since he retired two years ago.
The 22-time Grand Slam champion will headline “The MGM Slam presented by Capital One” at T-Mobile Arena on February 27, organizers announced Monday.
Nadal previously played a Vegas exhibition against Carlos Alcaraz in 2024, during his last year on tour.
“I remember how impressive it was to feel the energy of a full arena in a city like Las Vegas,” the 40-year-old Nadal said. “Now I return in a different stage of my life, without the pressure of the tour but with the same passion for this sport. I have always loved competing, and even if my professional career is finished, that feeling never really goes away.”

Most people worldwide could be categorised as having a high genetic risk for three of 28 common conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and schizophrenia, even if they might not develop them, a new study has found.
Researchers, led by the UK's University of Exeter, described the 'average' human genome, finding that everyone, regardless of their current health status, could be considered at risk for numerous conditions based on their genetics alone.
Every person's genome, or the average human genome, contains around five million variants, or DNA locations that differ between individuals, the findings published in the journal Genome Medicine reveal.
The locations include around 10,000 variants that alter gene sequences, which can have positive or negative effect, ranging from lactose intolerance to drug response, though are often biologically neutral, they show.
Each person also carries between one and three rare variants previously shown to cause serious genetic diseases, and another 50 rare variants that are currently of uncertain clinical relevance, the researchers found.
The team analysed data from two major population biobanks -- the UK Biobank and the US' All of Us -- that include whole genome sequencing, covering nearly one million individuals.
Senior author Caroline Wright, from the University of Exeter, said, "Whole genome sequencing has become such an important tool in diagnosing genetic disease, and we're increasingly moving towards genetic screening for predicting disease."
"Yet most people are unaware of just how much genetic variation is present in every genome. Actually, variation is the norm. For the first time, our study outlines what to expect in the average human genome, which can benefit clinicians and patients across the word in understanding, interpreting and contextualising genomics," Wright said.
The researchers also analysed numerous polygenic risk scores, which consider all known genetic factors to calculate a person's future risk of developing a disease.
"... applying polygenic scores (PGS) for 28 common diseases within UKB (UK Biobank), we estimate that the average person is in the top 10 per cent for (nearly) three conditions, and around one in five people are in the top one per cent for at least one PGS," the authors wrote.
"Importantly, we found that everyone carries a small number of genetic variants linked to disease, although many of these will not actually cause disease in that individual," Wright said.
The senior author added, "It is therefore crucial to consider context when interpreting findings from genetic testing, including symptoms or family history of disease as well as other clinical and environmental risk factors. Our findings also provide important context for professionals who are interpreting genetic testing results or commissioning genetic screening programmes."
Although the studies are large, participation is skewed towards people of Western European origin, and the researchers acknowledged the need for data from more diverse populations to further improve understanding and impact.

The Black Cats have been eliminated in six of their last eight League Cup fourth round ties - the most recent in 2021/22 - and are struggling to find the magic touch they had last season.
But form doesn't always translate onto the pitch and knockout football is a different beast altogether. At home, Sunderland will feel they are a match for anyone - and will not want to get stung again on Wednesday.

The Carabao Cup often gives teams a chance to rotate their squad in order to remain fresh for the upcoming Premier League games. That is less likely to be the case here. Instead, it could act as a preview of their league meeting on Monday night.
