Revival Rugs is turning 9 this month, and evidently, the birthday girl is feeling generous. The rug retailer is taking 20 percent off everything sitewide (exclusions may apply, as always). But don’t dillydally—the party ends Sunday, October 25.
Sure, Black Friday is around the corner, and there will be deals aplenty. But will they be sitewide and stackable? Revival’s 20 percent stacks, meaning it also applies to marked-down and clearance items. Will the rug you’ve been eyeing for months still be available in November? Are you willing to risk it? I wouldn’t.
Why We Love Revival Rugs
Revival is a retailer we love here at WIRED, mainly because of its lovely selection of hand-knotted and handwoven wool rugs at reasonable prices. The company imports rugs from Turkey, Morocco, and India, and also works with its own supplier in Oakland, California. Revival also offers a variety of washable rugs, à la Ruggable (which, by the way, is having its own October Hosting Sale). Not every Revival rug is machine washable, but many are easy to maintain with spot cleaning and a low-suction vacuum.
WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell has the Bronto Hand-Tufted Rug in her toddler’s bedroom, and they are both fans. Farrell appreciates how soft it is and how it makes the room feel playful without looking tacky. Meanwhile, her son is mostly here for the giant dinosaur, which, honestly, is fair. WIRED operations coordinator Molly Higgins has the Garland Washable Area Rug in her living room, where its Turkish-inspired folk-art pattern adds plenty of color and disguises everyday stains. WIRED commerce director Cooper Fleishman just bought a vibrant marmalade wool rug for his new office from the Birthday Sale; sadly, it’s sold out, but this tonal design is a close cousin.
As with any sale, there are a few exclusions. Swatches and gift cards aren’t included, and be sure to read the terms and conditions for more information.

On the first day of its war against Iran, the United States killed 123 children when it targeted and struck an elementary school.
Can machines be war criminals?
A law professor explains how AI-assisted weapons subvert our justice system.
The strikes, ultimately approved by humans, were facilitated by the US’s Maven Smart System, an AI-enabled software platform developed by Palantir Technologies that allows the military to aggregate, organize, and process battlefield data. Operators fed Maven intelligence classifying the elementary school as an Iranian military facility, and the system, in turn, marked it as one of the priority targets for day one of the war. Though the site was formerly part of a naval military base, it had been converted into an elementary school in 2017 and had remained one since. The intel handed to Maven did not reflect this.
This mistake resulted in what some reporters have called “one of the single worst massacres committed by the US government since the Vietnam War.”
Such scenarios may become more common as militaries continue to deploy a once-theoretical technology — AI-assisted or autonomous weapons, capable of making both targeting and launch decisions on their own — on real battlefields around the globe. And they raise a troubling, unresolved question: When human beings and machines collaborate in violating international law, who is to blame?
In this case, the government and private sector are pointing the finger at each other. Some US Central Command personnel, according to Pentagon officials who spoke to Bloomberg, expected Maven to flag stale information or inconsistencies in the underlying intelligence assembled for potential targets. Meanwhile, a Palantir spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company “is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies,” while also denying that the evidence indicated that its software was at fault in the strike.
This debate underscores the fact that AI and autonomous weapons are raising a new host of unresolved issues within the law, even as they’re actively assuming positions on the battlefield. In institutions where the line between human and machine decision-making continues to blur, how do we assign responsibility for war crimes? And, are the laws in place suited for the job?
In institutions where the line between human and machine decision-making continues to blur, how do we assign responsibility for war crimes?
To unpack some of these issues, I spoke with international law expert Allen Weiner, a senior lecturer at Stanford Law School, where he teaches courses on the law of armed conflict. Before teaching at Stanford, Weiner practiced international law in the US Department of State for more than a decade. We discussed the difficulties in attributing criminal responsibility, achieving justice for those harmed by lethal autonomous weapons, and much more. The conversation below has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
How do autonomous weapons challenge traditional understandings of responsibility when it comes to the law of armed conflict?
For most of the 20 years I’ve been teaching at Stanford, there’s been a real fascination and fixation on the problem of autonomous weapons. But the truth is that up until pretty recently, nobody really had any [of them]. It was more of an idea than a problem. It’s only in recent years that we have begun to see the deployment of tools that seem to have the capability [to make decisions themselves], so this does raise the question about compliance with illegal orders and where in the chain responsibility lies.
There are different theories about this. Some people say that if we’re engaged in an illegal attack, that has to be because of the programming or the code, so the manufacturers are somehow responsible for committing war crimes.
Other people would say no, that’s not the case, especially if the military has said the tool is not allowed to make very substantial autonomous judgments, or can’t say no. Then it’s basically the commander, at the point they decide to deploy this weapon, who might be responsible for the illegal acts, even without knowing in advance what they’re going to be.
So to finish where I began, this does present a big challenge to our traditional understanding of responsibility for targeting decisions and of what it would mean if there were an obligation [for autonomous weapons] to say no.
The real issue is not the obligation to say no, but this: If you train a tool and it wages war in a manner that’s unlawful, where does responsibility for that lie?
If a commander gives a clearly illegal order, such as, “blow up this school,” it seems clear that responsibility falls on the commander. But I could imagine a scenario where a commander is using an AI-assisted or autonomous weapon, isn’t giving it any illegal orders, is trusting that it will operate within the law, and the weapon breaks the law “on its own.” Where does responsibility fall in those cases?
I can imagine two different scenarios. One is that you say, “We’re going to carry out an attack against our enemy, and we want to hit them really, really hard.” Your tool has been trained to say, “We’re not allowed to hit civilian objects,” so it might say, “I’m not going to hit a school.” But if the military has said, “Don’t refuse any targets,” then it might override the way it’s been trained.
We’re seeing this already, with the stories coming out about breaches where AI tools, Claude and ChatGPT in particular, interpret their instructions in a way that causes them to do something the person who gave the instruction would not have wanted. When Anthropic gave Claude a challenge to figure out if it could do something, the tool figured out, well, maybe we should break into Hugging Face as a way of solving this problem, and the people who gave the AI tool the challenge never intended that.
So if you said, “We want to launch a really punishing campaign,” what happens if the tool on its own says, “Nothing’s going to hurt them more than seeing their kids killed, so let’s attack the school?” That’s one risk, and it’s a real challenge.
So [as for who’s responsible], it’s not the commander who said “hit them hard,” because when he said that, he didn’t mean “attack schools.” It’s not really the companies, because the companies didn’t want them to hit schools either.
But the tools are out there, reading everything on the internet, and it came across something that said the way you win a war is by attacking the things your adversary holds most dear, and they hold nothing more dear than their children. So it makes this kind of judgment on its own. And it’s not as if you can go back and say who ordered it to hit a school, which is the thing that is clearly illegal. So I do think there’s a risk of diffusion of responsibility here.
You could say the commander knew the tool might work this way, or the person who decided to contract with Palantir or with Claude, whoever it is, to build this tool. But if we’re really thinking about criminal responsibility, the level of responsibility you would need to convict someone requires a culpable mental state. You would need the person to intend, or at least know, that they were authorizing an attack against the school. And I can easily see a commander saying, “I had no idea.”
The decision to authorize this tool, or to give an instruction like “hit them very hard,” could be a basis for some other kind of accountability — administrative discipline within the military, a reprimand, your rank is lowered. But if we’re talking about criminal responsibility, which is what we often think about when we talk about war crimes, I think this diffusion of responsibility is going to make it very hard to identify any single individual who has the required mental state to give rise to accountability.
The second scenario is where the tool just makes a mistake based on the information available to it. We saw that with the attack on the girls’ school in Iran, where it was pretty clear the tool was looking at old data. Now, who’s responsible for that?
Is it the people who said “give me targets based on this data set,” when they should have made sure the data and the maps were current? All of this strikes me as negligence or recklessness, and it does seem challenging to imagine a situation in which we would say yes, somebody here has committed a war crime.
“There can well be war crimes, but identifying who the war criminal is might be a big challenge.”
A war crime has been committed, but is there a war criminal? That’s the situation we’re seeing. There can well be war crimes, but identifying who the war criminal is might be a big challenge.
There’s a professor of law, Rebecca Crootof, who proposes the idea of “war torts.” Instead of thinking about war crimes involving autonomous weapons solely through a criminal responsibility lens, maybe tort law — which allows victims to sue wrongdoers for negligent, reckless, or intentional harm — could address the diffusion of responsibility you mentioned. What do you think about that idea?
I think the idea is interesting. We have to separate out the obligations that countries have under international humanitarian law. In a situation like the one I just described, where there’s a war crime but no war criminal, that doesn’t mean the country is not responsible. There may not be an individual who’s criminally accountable, but if a country targets civilians in a circumstance that’s unreasonable, that’s a violation of international humanitarian law, and that could be a basis for claims between the two countries.
Tribunals were established between Ethiopia and Eritrea, for instance, after the Eritrean War of Independence, that dealt with claims between the two countries for money damages, and some of them involved allegations of violations of the law of armed conflict. Iraq paid reparations after the first Gulf War for harms it had caused to people in Kuwait, under something called the UN Compensation Commission. So the idea that the state is responsible is well established, and one of the ways states would discharge that responsibility would be by paying money damages. That’s the domestic-law equivalent of torts.
Whether there would be a mechanism for [civilians] doing this in domestic law is an interesting idea. We would probably need legislatures, either state legislatures or the federal government, to create a private cause of action allowing people who have been injured to bring claims against, say, the manufacturers of these tools. But this gets procedurally very complicated, because there’s a whole body of law on federal sovereign immunity.
Could you sue the Defense Department? Probably not. Could you sue an individual soldier? Probably not. Could you sue Anthropic or Palantir? Maybe. But it would probably require Congress to enact a new cause of action, because in general it’s very hard to bring private lawsuits in US courts for violations of international law.
The basic idea of what we would think of as tort or civil responsibility is really the whole essence of international law. On the substance, states do owe responsibility to one another, and they can engage in violations of international humanitarian law that would invoke their responsibility. But then the whole separate question is whether you have a forum within which to adjudicate that and get compensation.
Does that look different in cases where violations of international law were committed by a human soldier versus a machine?
Well, we don’t know, because there have been no cases in the latter category. All of the international humanitarian law violations that have been the subject of international law claims were ordered by humans.
Now, if an American machine launches an attack against a girls’ school in Iran, and there were a court with jurisdiction, the US would be responsible. In some ways it wouldn’t matter whether it was an individual or a machine, because we don’t have to go down to the level of the individual actor, company, AI tool, or commander. The responsibility is the responsibility of the country. In some ways, that makes it easier.
If we pursued compensation through state-to-state claims, you’d be able to do that without getting into the details of who within the state that committed the war crime was responsible. The state whose school was attacked would say, “I don’t care. You committed a war crime, you’re liable to me, you’re responsible for the damages, and you can figure it out internally.”
But if we were doing something like a war crimes prosecution, where we’re trying to hold an individual criminally responsible, that would make quite a difference. We would have to deal with all of these difficult questions about responsibility and mental state that you and I are struggling with right now.
So, in most cases, the state would have to take responsibility regardless.
Right, and there are lots of [International Court of Justice] cases involving different aspects of the use of force. The principle that you can bring state-to-state claims for violation of these rules is quite well established.
But with international law, states have to consent to the jurisdiction of a court. They can do that in advance by saying “I’ve signed up to the jurisdiction of a court and I accept any claims that might be brought against me in this court,” or they do it on a case-by-case basis. And it may not surprise you to know that some of the most powerful countries in the world, the ones most likely to use force outside their borders, have tended to be reluctant to accept the jurisdiction of international courts and tribunals.
Russia, the United States, Israel, and China have not accepted the so-called optional clause jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice. So there’s the substance, about the responsibility of states, and then there are the procedural aspects of whether these cases could be brought in court.
And Trump recently said everyone on the International Criminal Court should “resign immediately.”
Yeah, exactly.
And what about the role of these military tech companies, like Palantir?
“At what point does Palantir become a good target under international law? Or at what point does Anthropic become a good target under international law, if its AI tools are being used to promote the war effort?”
Another issue [I’ve been thinking on] because of the questions we’re talking about is when the companies themselves become combatants.
We know that a private company that manufactures airplanes, an airplane factory, is a good target under international law. At what point does Palantir become a good target under international law? Or at what point does Anthropic become a good target under international law, if its AI tools are being used to promote the war effort? I think that question is about when the connection of these private companies to the war effort, in a way we’ve never really seen before, meets the standards under international law.
A civilian loses their immunity when they directly participate in hostilities, or if they assume what is known as a “continuous combatant function.” Are there arguments to be made that some of these private companies are participating in hostilities by virtue of supplying the tools the military is using to wage war? I think that’s a really interesting question.

Carrick future under major threat - can he survive?
- Published
Michael Carrick's future as Manchester United manager is under major threat following the home loss to Bournemouth on Sunday.
The Red Devils lost 3-0 as their poor start to the season continued - they have won just one of their eight Premier League matches so far and sit 16th - 14 points off the top.
Carrick, 45, took interim charge in January following Ruben Amorim's departure and he was rewarded with the permanent job in May after securing Champions League qualification with an impressive run that resulted in them finishing third.
But United have not won in the top flight since 30 August, when they defeated newly promoted Ipswich 5-2.
"It's a tough situation, there's no hiding from it," Carrick told Sky Sports after the Bournemouth loss.
"What it looks like and what's next I really don't know.
"I will always do my best for the football club and I won't change that now. I love what I do and I feel the responsibility - we'll have to wait and see."
Carrick made a big call on Sunday by dropping his captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench.
That decision came after the Portugal midfielder questioned Carrick's tactics in Wednesday's 4-1 loss at Como in the Champions League.
The comments from Fernandes came in the wake of defender Lisandro Martinez issuing an apology following his controversial remarks criticising the club's hierarchy.
Martinez said he had expected more investment in the Manchester United squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]".
'A mess' but 'fans with Carrick'
Carrick made 464 appearances for Manchester United in a playing career at the club that spanned 12 years.
As a consequence, he remains a popular figure among the fans, who chanted his song at full-time in the loss to Bournemouth as he did a lap of the pitch to applaud the supporters.
"It wasn't a farewell from me," he added.
"I've mixed emotions, I'm feeling it for my players, they're going through a tough spell. Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment.
"Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way. To have that connection with the supporters it's mixed emotions, it'll take a bit of time to digest but I certainly appreciate their support.
"The situation is where we are and we haven't had results or performances that have been good enough."
Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville said on Sky Sports: "The Manchester United fans are singing the Michael Carrick song because I think they know what's going to happen here. They've seen this before. He's one of their own and he's popular.

Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.
That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.
“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”
It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.
The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.
I went to Jantar Mantar every night that week as people from all walks of life streamed in. Protest signs once directed largely against Pradhan now increasingly targeted Modi and his powerful deputy, Amit Shah, whose ministry controls Delhi Police.
The language was often profane and sexualised, and was quickly seized on by government supporters to condemn the protesters. Pro-government media channels ran heated debates about the disrespectful language and questioned the motives of those gathered. Women were singled out; BJP supporters identified them from social media clips and doxed them.
R found herself at the centre of this storm. A police case was filed against her for insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace, and statements that could lead to public mischief and defamation. The complainant told Scroll, an independent news organisation, that she had called R and asked her to publicly apologise.
After Pradhan resigned, Modi posted on Instagram about the use of vulgar abuses against him by “some mischievous children”, saying: “It is a cultural shock. How can our daughters speak like this?” Modi added that the children must be forgiven, instead of being punished.
Meanwhile, R issued an apology to Modi. In a grainy video filmed in low light, R stands against a dull white wall wearing a striped T-shirt, her hands folded in a namaste. “I am so ashamed of saying those things that I am not even able to raise my eyes. I apologise to the whole nation for it. This is my first and last mistake,” she said. (Local media reported that the complainant withdrew the police case after R’s video was posted.)
“I cried after making that video,” she told me. “I was feeling so helpless.”
But her apology did little to stem the abuse. She received rape and death threats, abusive phone calls, incessant warnings on text, knocks on doors and cars outside her apartment building in a Delhi suburb.
“I couldn’t understand what was happening,” R said, her eyes misting up as she recalled the initial days after the incident. “People older than my mother were calling me randi (prostitute), aatankwadi (terrorist), deshdrohi (enemy of the state). Others were offering Rs11,000 to find me and Rs21,000 to beat me.”
With her phone and address leaked, R and her mother were compelled to leave their home. They struggled to find landlords willing to rent them a place to stay. They found one apartment, then another and then another. Her mother, a single parent, lost the income she earned from tutoring. To pay for the repeated moves, she sold her gold jewellery. That money is keeping them afloat. She estimates it will probably last another four months. As the clock runs out, her mother is desperately searching for work.
During this time, R has not been to school and can no longer imagine returning. Some friends have cut off contact, leaving her increasingly isolated.
Despite her apology video, pro-government media continued to hound her, she said. In late August, frustrated and angry at yet another media crew showing up, she uploaded a video to social media laying bare what she was going through.
“Modiji, my life has become hell,” R said addressing the prime minister. “Now I can’t go anywhere, neither do I have any freedom. I can’t live anywhere. I have to live hiding my face,” she said.
R told me she wants people to understand how traumatising her experience has been. “To make someone homeless overnight is a big deal,” she said.
Now, stuck indoors, she is watching another wave of protests unfold. This time it’s over the controversial electoral rolls revision that has removed 130 million voters from the register. (If you missed it, read last week’s newsletter about this issue.)
R feels solidarity with the students getting brutalised and detained. There have been moments she has felt tempted to join them. But the thought of her mother and their uncertain housing situation have held her back.
“I am not scared any more. I have gone through the worst already,” she said. But she doesn’t want to put her mother through more pain.
Days before the protest, R had been planning her 15th birthday. She wanted to cut her birthday cake inside an autorickshaw, to remake a trend she had seen on social media.
It’s been a couple of months since she turned 15. I asked her what she wants or hopes for now. She paused and then said: “My past is not in my hands. I can’t change that. Now, I just want to look ahead and do well in my board exams.”

Artist Sagarika Sundaram has spent a decade working with wool, transforming it into felt for expansive sculptural pieces that feel almost otherworldly. Her latest exhibition, Reservoir recently opened at the Henry Moore Institute, in Leeds, and runs until 10 January.
“There’s a clearer commitment to sculpture in this body of work, even though I’m still working with felt. The Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government in Keralam on Monday strongly defended the switch to a generic drug for patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) and said it would try to further reduce the price of the drug.
Speaking in the State Legislative Assembly, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan announced that the UDF government’s aim, eventually, was to offer medicines free of cost to all SMA patients. The matter will be discussed with Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan and an announcement will be made in due course, Mr. Muraleedharan said.
The Health Minister was responding to an adjournment motion moved by the CPI(M)-led Opposition Left Democratic Front (LDF) with regard to the controversy over the generic SMA drug and the unconnected development where the government had formed a 16-member task force with the aim of establishing a ‘Kerala Holistic Model for Health, Wellness and Longevity.’
While the Opposition accused the government of launching ‘clinical trials’ on SMA patients and pushing a corporatisation agenda in the health sector through the task force, Chief Minister Mr. Satheesan said both decisions were taken in the best interests of the people.
Opposition walkout
The Assembly witnessed a sharp confrontation between the ruling and Opposition fronts over the two issues, leading to a walkout by the latter after the adjournment motion was rejected.
With regard to the generic SMA drug, Mr. Satheesan said the government decision gave patients access to a generic drug that cost just ₹15,000 when the branded version cost ₹6.5 lakh for 12 days.
The generic alternative, marketed by Natco Pharma, had the support of court orders and statutory clearances from government agencies concerned, he said. “It has brought immense relief to the families of the patients. Our belief is that the price can be reduced further, to ₹9,000,” Mr. Satheesan said. He also congratulated Mr. Muraleedharan and the Health Department for taking the decision.
Clinical trials, and not drugs, the problem: Pinarayi
However, Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan said the government was “misleading everyone” by depicting the LDF as being opposed to generic drugs and that it favoured the costly Risdiplam, marketed by Roche Pharmaceuticals. Mr. Vijayan said the LDF has always encouraged generic medicines. “But here, the issue pertained to clinical trials of the SMA drug,” he said.
Slams task force composition
The LDF also targeted the composition of the task force; specifically the inclusion of Deepak Singhal, a former Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary.
Mr. Vijayan said that Mr. Singhal’s links to Global Trade and Technology Council (India) (GTTCI Healthcare Ventures) was “a matter of concern.” Corporates viewed the health sector as a milch cow and his presence on the task force illustrated the UDF’s “corporatisation agenda” for the sector, he said.
CM refutes charges
The Chief Minister, however, swept aside the charge, stating that the 16-member task force was composed of "knowledge partners.” Its aim was to devise strategies to reduce healthcare costs and ensure early detection of diseases and their prevention. This was important at a time when investment giants such as Blackstone have entered the State’s health sector and medical bills in private hospitals were soaring, making such institutions inaccessible to the general public, he said.
Earlier, K. Premkumar of the CPI(M), K. Rajan of the CPI, and P.K. Praveen of the RJD had moved the adjournment motion. They sought a discussion in the House on the perils faced by the State’s health sector arising from the government decisions to include representatives of “private hospitals, laboratories and pharma companies” in the task force and the concerns over clinical trials related to the SMA drug.

All SIR decisions unanimous, Form 6 not amended: Election Commission to Supreme Court
The affidavit was filed on Monday through deputy election commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) has told the Supreme Court that all decisions relating to the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls were taken unanimously by its three members, rejecting allegations that chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar acted unilaterally or that the poll panel violated the law governing its decision-making process.
In a joint counter-affidavit filed on behalf of the ECI, Kumar and the two election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, the poll panel has also denied amending the statutory Form 6 used for enrolling new voters, arguing that the additional declaration required during the SIR was a separate document prescribed through its orders and not a modification of the form laid down under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
The affidavit, filed on Monday through deputy election commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu, asserts that the three SIR orders issued on June 24, 2025, October 27, 2025, and May 14, 2026, were issued in accordance with unanimous decisions of the Commission and in compliance with Article 324 of the Constitution and Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
“All contentions to the contrary are erroneous, and the attempt to make aspersions against the Election Commission is unfortunate,” states the affidavit, describing the petitions challenging the poll panel’s functioning as misconceived and not maintainable in law.
The response comes amid allegations, based on media reports, that Sandhu and Joshi objected to Kumar’s decisions on at least 14 occasions over 10 months, including on matters relating to electoral-roll management, voter registration and information technology. The controversy has prompted petitions seeking judicial scrutiny of the Commission’s internal decision-making, including whether its nationwide SIR exercise was lawfully authorised.
The affidavit maintains that suggestions, queries or objections raised by individual commissioners or officials during deliberations do not, by themselves, constitute decisions of the Commission under Section 18 of the 2023 Act. It says matters placed before the Commission are discussed collectively and that decisions are taken after considering the views expressed during deliberations.
“The issues which are put up before the Election Commission for decision, are taken by the Election Commission and are decided in terms of Section 18 of the 2023 Act,” reads the affidavit, adding that such decisions are taken at meetings of the commissioners or on noted files and bear their signatures.
Section 18 provides that the Commission should, as far as possible, take decisions unanimously, and that any differences of opinion must be resolved by majority. The petitioners contend that the requirement for collective decision-making cannot be satisfied merely by subsequent approval or by treating individual objections as routine administrative exchanges.
Addressing the reported differences between the two election commissioners and Kumar, the affidavit says the letters Sandhu and Joshi sent to the Cabinet Secretary on July 29, 2026, concerned an officer on deputation to the Commission and the internal allocation of work, rather than policy decisions or matters handled by the IT division.
It states that an office order issued on July 28, 2026, concerning an IAS officer of the rank of additional secretary posted on deputation to the ECI was never implemented after the two commissioners issued a joint direction on July 30. The affidavit argues that the correspondence cannot be treated as evidence that key SIR decisions were taken without the concurrence of the other commissioners.
No amendment to Form 6:
On Form 6 -- the statutory application used by citizens to register as voters, the ECI has specifically rejected the contention that the statutory form was amended through the SIR orders issued on June 24, 2025, October 27, 2025, and May 14, 2026.
The Commission says an additional declaration was prescribed alongside Form 6 for applicants seeking enrolment as new voters during the SIR. Under the June 2025 order, the declaration was designated Annexure D; the subsequent orders substituted it with Annexure IV, with the objective of facilitating the process of linking applicants or their relatives with earlier electoral rolls.
The affidavit explains that the additional declaration was intended to allow applicants to provide details connecting them with previous intensive revisions and, where the required information was available, avoid the need to furnish supporting documents during the claims and objections stage. Where such details were unavailable or not provided, applicants could submit the prescribed supporting documents.
“Thus, there is no change in Form 6 vide the 3 SIR Orders, as sought to be alleged,” states the affidavit, maintaining that the declaration is an independent document and not part of the statutory form prescribed under the 1960 Rules.
The issue had come under scrutiny after the Supreme Court, during an earlier hearing on October 5, clarified that it had neither approved nor disapproved the modified Form 6 and wanted to examine the original records to establish what changes had been made and by whom.
The court’s observations followed an ECI statement that the declaration attached to Form 6 during the Bihar SIR had been upheld by the court. The ECI subsequently clarified that it was referring to the separate declaration rather than an amendment to the statutory form.

Ends
Form 6 is the statutory application under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, for inclusion of a person’s name in an electoral roll. The controversy concerns an additional declaration introduced in its online version during the SIR exercise, requiring applicants to state whether their own name, or that of a parent or grandparent, appeared in the electoral roll prepared during the previous SIR.
The requirement had significant implications for first-time voters and those seeking re-enrolment. A person who has recently turned 18, for instance, would not ordinarily have featured in a roll prepared during an earlier SIR and could therefore be required to establish a link through a parent or grandparent. It also raised concerns for voters excluded during revision and seeking to be re-enrolled.
The change reportedly triggered a dispute within the Election Commission over whether it amounted to an alteration of the statutory form. According to an Indian Express report, election commissioners Joshi and Sandhu objected that Form 6, being prescribed under the 1960 Rules, could not be modified through the online version without following the statutory procedure. Under Section 28 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, the Centre frames these Rules in consultation with the Commission, and amendments must be notified and laid before Parliament.
The Election Commission, however, maintained that the statutory Form 6 had not been altered and that the additional declaration was introduced only for the SIR exercise through an addendum. It later clarified that the declaration would apply only during the SIR period, while the statutory form would be used otherwise. The declaration was also withdrawn from the online form in states and Union territories where SIR had been completed, with applicants there reverting to the statutory Form 6.

On October 24, All India Students’ Association (AISA) president Neha Bora arrived at Delhi’s Mandir Marg police station in a Toyota Camry. Bora had been summoned to appear before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) in connection with proceedings requiring her to furnish a peace bond following her participation in protests in the city, which Bora has denied signing.
Subsequently, several social media users began claiming that she owned the luxury car, questioning how a student could afford a vehicle reportedly worth Rs 60–70 lakh.
An X account, Tejash (@lord_geopolitic), shared an image showing the car’s registration number alongside a photograph of Neha. Calling the AISA president a “communist fraud”, the user questioned how Neha, a PhD student at JNU School of Arts and Aesthetics, could afford such an expensive vehicle and asked Grok about her source of income. The post garnered around 727,100 views and over 600 shares. (Archive)
Neha Bora is a communist fraud and a failed student who doesn’t have a job and only participates in protests, yet she is roaming around in a luxury car worth ₹60–70 lakh.
Hey @Grok, what’s her source of income? 🤔 https://t.co/5iCfUo6juP
— Tejash (@lord_geopolitic) October 24, 2026
Another X user, Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) posted a video showing the car entering the police station, claiming that “Only in India would unemployed students travel in luxury cars.” The post similarly implied that Neha owned the vehicle. This post amassed around 380,000 views and over 3,000 shares. (Archive)
“Student Leader” Neha Bora is coming to police station in a ₹65 lakhs Toyota Camry Car. Only in India would unemployed students travel in luxury cars 🤡 https://t.co/t3iKqjCK2K
— Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) October 24, 2026
Several other users circulated similar claims, questioning how Neha could afford to travel in a “luxury” car while being a student and participating in protests. Some posts even insinuated that student protesters were receiving funding from undisclosed sources to “abuse Modi and India”.
A few of the claims are shown in the gallery below:
Fact Check
Alt News contacted Neha to ask about the details of the car. She clarified that the car did not belong to her but is her lawyer Abhik Chimni’s. She further stated that she does not own any vehicle. “I don’t have a car or any form of vehicle of my own. That car belongs to my lawyer Abhik Chimni. He not only has a successful career allowing him to afford a car but is also generous enough to offer to escort me inside the Mandir Marg police station in it,” she said.
“The escorting was necessary because a mob was chanting ‘Neha Bora Murdabad’, ‘Desh Ke gaddaron ko, joote maaron saalon ko’ amongst other slogans outside the police station…The Delhi Police took no steps to disperse the crowd until Abhik specifically mentioned it to the Magistrate and requested him to take measures to handle the hostile and possibly violent atmosphere outside the police station,” Neha told Alt News.
In the video, the number plate is visible and it is: DL12CY3747. Alt News obtained the vehicle’s registration certificate (RC), which identifies the white Toyota Camry hybrid EV with the same number plate as belonging to Neha’s lawyer, Abhik Chimni.
Speaking to Alt News, N Sai Balaji, former AISA president, who accompanied Neha to the Mandir Marg police station on October 24, corroborated her account of the situation outside the station.
According to Balaji, him and Neha initially reached the location in a cab. However, they encountered around 40 people whom he described as Right-wing supporters, allegedly raising slogans against Neha and threatening her safety. He said that Chimni then raised concerns with the police about Neha’s security and requested that the entrance be cleared. The police suggested that Neha enter the premises in a private vehicle, offering to allow a car inside the police station under police escort.
After the incident, Neha took to Instagram to describe the situation, stating that about “50-60” goons had gathered around 100 meters away from the station, allegedly raising threatening slogans against her.
View this post on Instagram
To sum up, the claim that Neha owns a Toyota Camry reportedly worth Rs 60–70 lakh is false and misleading. Neha denied owning any vehicle and the car’s RC identifies her lawyer, Abhik Chimni, as its registered owner.

Climate change is exposing food workers to intensifying health and safety risks, from extreme heat and toxic wildfire smoke to hazardous pesticide exposure, even as poverty wages and inadequate labour protections leave many unable to protect themselves, a new global report by the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems (IPES-Food), has found.
The report, released on October 5, says that nearly 1.4 billion people work across the global food system, but 30% (about 416 million people) earn below a living wage. It identifies climate change, corporate concentration, and widespread informal employment as forces deepening the exploitation of workers who grow, process, transport, sell and serve food.
A dangerous sector
Agriculture is among the world’s most dangerous sectors, accounting for one-third of all occupational deaths globally. Workers face hazards including extreme weather, long shifts without breaks and contact with harmful pesticides and chemicals. Heat stress is already the most common occupational health threat in agriculture, the report says, and climate change is escalating the risks into potentially life-threatening conditions.
Many farmworkers lack basic protection from extreme weather, including access to shade, rest breaks and drinking water, the report notes, adding that international labour standards are often ignored, while weak enforcement leaves workers exposed to dangerous conditions.
“Climate change is becoming a workers’ rights crisis,” said Mamadou Goïta, an IPES-Food panel expert in a webinar at the launch of the report. Farmworkers already face poverty wages, toxic pesticides and gruelling working conditions, which are being compounded by rising temperatures and other climate impacts, he said.
India’s climate-linked risks
The report highlights how climate-related livelihood losses in India can reinforce labour exploitation. Drought-driven crop failures have pushed tens of thousands of landless farmworkers into cycles of high-interest debt and bonded labour, it says. These debts can extend across generations, trapping families in exploitative working arrangements.
It also cites a study covering five Indian States that found farmer suicides increased significantly following droughts. The report links climate distress to the financial pressures faced by farming communities, particularly where workers lack adequate social protection.
Evidence from across India also points to how climate-related risks are affecting the health and livelihoods of workers in agriculture and fisheries. A study published in January 2026 in the Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine examined 200 male agricultural workers harvesting paddy in West Bengal during the summer of 2024 and found that the proportion experiencing dehydration rose from 16.5% to 33% over the observed work period. Higher heat exposure was also associated with greater physiological strain.
Meanwhile, a study published in April 2025 in the International Journal of Bio-resource and Stress Management examined the climate vulnerability of 400 small-scale fisher households in Ernakulam district, Kerala. It found that female-headed households had a higher livelihood vulnerability index (0.40) than male-headed households (0.37), showing how climate-related risks can intersect with gender inequalities and economic insecurity.
Health risks across the food chain
The IPES-Food report’s concerns are not limited to agricultural workers. Food workers across processing, hospitality and delivery face occupational hazards alongside insecure employment and limited access to basic protections.
Informal employment compounds these risks. Around 90% of agricultural employment and 60% to 80% of non-agricultural food employment worldwide is informal, the report notes. Informal workers earn, on average, only 56% of the monthly wages of formally employed workers and often lack access to health coverage, social security and labour protections.
Women, migrant workers and other marginalised groups face disproportionate risks, often working in the least protected jobs. Migrant workers may be reluctant to report unsafe conditions or abuse for fear of losing their jobs or facing immigration-related consequences, the report observes.
Raj Patel, an IPES-Food panel expert, in the webinar during the launch of the report, said the people who produce and deliver food were among the most exploited workers globally. Farmworkers, cooks and delivery riders face low pay, unsafe conditions, abuse and insecure work, he said, while powerful food corporations benefit from keeping labour cheap and workers powerless.
What is needed
The report calls for stronger labour standards, collective bargaining, better enforcement of workplace safety rules and equal rights for migrant workers. It also urges governments to address corporate concentration and hold companies accountable for abuses across food supply chains.
For food workers facing intensifying climate hazards, the report’s central concern is that those who sustain the food system are often left to bear its risks without adequate safeguards. It calls for a food system that does not depend on poverty wages, dangerous working conditions or the absence of basic labour protections.

Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.
This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP won state elections in West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.
Mass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. The Cockroach movement was born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.
This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakes impossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.
There is still reason for hope in India. The Indian Express newspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011, corruption scandals became evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.

An immunization worker gets set up to receive her wages on her mobile wallet in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
Campaigns in Africa to stop polio and other diseases have a more stable, better-motivated workforce thanks to WHO’s collaboration with countries and partners to pay frontline health workers through their mobile phones instead of in cash.
“Over 80 percent of workers are saying they prefer the digital payments,” said Ahmed Hamani Djibo, head of WHO’s Digital Finance Team.
WHO has been leading among international organizations in moving away from the unwieldy, less-secure practice of disbursing salaries in cash. Over the past few years, the Organization launched its Digital Finance Team and joined the Better Than Cash Alliance, an 80-member United Nations partnership with a mandate to develop the digitization of payments and expand financial inclusion – activities that support the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Since it was established in 2020, WHO’s Digital Finance Team has designed and implemented digital payment solutions in 24 countries in Africa, including, last year, in Benin, Botswana, Madagascar, Rwanda, Togo and Zimbabwe.
“WHO has successfully digitized payments for more than two million health workers across Africa,” said Tidhar Wald, Managing Director, a.i., at the Better Than Cash Alliance. “With these inspiring results, WHO is taking a clear leadership role in accelerating the digital transformation in the provision of health outcomes globally.”
A polio immunization team on the job in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
“A really big difference in speed”
Workers surveyed in Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia and Tanzania said they appreciated the security of not carrying cash, the convenience of no longer having to travel to a disbursement site to receive their wages, and above all, the speed of payment – as short as half an hour after finishing work compared to waits of weeks or even months.
The surveys, funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, linked timely compensation to better morale and worker retention.
“There is really a big difference in speed,” said Jean-Luc, a health worker interviewed in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at the end of a polio immunization campaign. “We finished the campaign mop-up yesterday and received a text notification the next evening. I’m going to pay my child’s school fees. Now we can relax.”
Digital payments also save time and money for health campaign organizers, including the burden and expense of transporting large sums of cash and completing documentation.
“When you have 300 to 500 volunteers to pay, doing accounts and signing receipts takes a lot of time,” said Saïdi, a polio team leader in DRC.
WHO first used the new digital payments in polio immunization campaigns in Côte d’Ivoire. Although outbreaks of vaccine-derived polio were on the rise, vaccination campaigns were having trouble getting off the ground. In the first quarter of 2020, almost half the polio campaigns in WHO’s African Region were postponed, saw workers drop out, or suffered other detrimental effects stemming from delays in cash disbursements.
As WHO and partners worked to develop the nuts-and-bolts aspects of a digital payment ecosystem (registering workers into a database, verifying their profiles with the mobile network operator and more) the benefits of a cashless approach became more apparent.
"There is substantial evidence that digitizing payments can support people, especially women, to gain access to financial services and increase control over their earnings,” said Maria May, Senior Program Officer, Inclusive Financial Systems, at the Gates Foundation. “Over the past four years, the World Health Organization has utilized the growing presence of mobile money across Africa to ensure that the courageous frontline vaccinators in polio outbreak campaigns are paid completely, quickly, and securely.”
Alain Labrique, director of WHO’s Department of Digital Health and Innovation, said that “digital payments are one of the key pillars of Digital Health Public Infrastructure currently strongly encouraged within WHO’s guidance to member-states on Digital Transformation.” WHO views digital payments as a foundation for many more digital development activities, together with Data Exchange and Digital ID Infrastructure. He added “we are delighted to work with partners in the digital space and add our voice to this celebration of WHO's joining the Better Than Cash Alliance”.

Anthropic unveils details of planned historic stock market debut
- Published
Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic has revealed for the first time details of its business and said it intends to sell stock to the public in what will likely be the largest market debut in history.
The company behind popular AI chatbot Claude said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT. The number of shares to be released and their price range is yet to be determined, the firm said.
Anthropic's valuation when it goes public is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which this summer was the biggest-ever stock listing at an initial valuation of roughly $1.8 trillion.
It will be the first true AI company to go public, marking a test for the future of the technology.
Tech companies have been heavily investing in costly AI infrastructure and tools, like data centres and the informational models that underly all AI technology, pouring more than $1tn into the efforts over the last year alone.
Anthropic, which was founded just five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, announced its intention to go public in June.
Its most significant rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit, saying it, too, intended to go public. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.
After the companies had decided on such plans, a wave of cyber-security and other types of technological breaches occurred involving their AI agents, or AI bots that are designed to operate somewhat autonomously.
Current and former staff of both companies also gained public attention with new warnings that AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect the whole of humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

To strengthen Karnataka’s organ transplantation programme and increase deceased donor transplants, the State Health Department will constitute an Organ Transplant Visionary Committee under Nagesh Hegde, who heads the State-run Institute of Gastroenterology Sciences and Organ Transplant (IGOT), Health Minister U.T. Khader said on Thursday.
Mr. Khader said the decision was taken at a progress review meeting with the State Organ Transplant Advisory Committee, which he chaired.
The proposed committee will recommend measures to raise public awareness about organ donation and improve access to transplantation, with a focus on strengthening infrastructure and streamlining procedures across the State, he said.
Brain death certification
One of the key priorities would be to facilitate brain death certification and organ retrieval at all district hospitals and government medical colleges. The committee would also recommend measures to expand organ transplant facilities in government hospitals, Mr. Khader said.
“Most hospitals do not want to obtain licences for organ retrieval due to the long process of paperwork. To avoid this, we are proposing that all hospitals with 50–100 beds capacity should automatically become organ retrieval centres. If they do not wish to, they can apply to get it cancelled,” he said.
The early launch of a new software system for organ allocation and tracking would be another priority, aimed at improving the efficiency of the process. The government would also focus on renewing registrations of transplant centres whose approvals had lapsed, he said.
Waitlist
Mr. Khader said 6,291 patients were awaiting organ transplants in Karnataka and stressed the need to encourage more people to pledge their organs. One deceased donor could help save multiple lives, he said.
The Minister urged the public to pledge their organs through the Jeevasarthakathe portal at https://jeevasarthakathe.karnataka.gov.in.
He said the proposed measures were intended to strengthen the State’s organ donation network, expand transplant services in government hospitals and improve access to life-saving organs for patients on the waiting list.

After losing the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, better known simply as Lula, pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history by winning the second, in so doing securing a fourth presidential term. It will see him become the country’s longest-serving leader.
The result – 51.79% to Lula, 48.21% to Bolsonaro – was delivered after a supreme court judge had extended polling time by two hours, and after Lula’s camp accused their opponents of sabotaging public transport in an attempt to keep their voters from the polls. It was the first time in Brazilian electoral history that a first-round verdict had been overturned.
But Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year jail term for his part in an attempted coup after the last presidential election, refused to accept the result – just as his father had done, four years before. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.
Brazil remains a deeply divided country and Lula will have to navigate a hostile Congress, packed full of Bolsonaro allies, if he is to make significant legislative changes in his fourth term. His options are also constrained by a gloomy economic outlook, with Brazil experiencing soaring debt and entrenched structural problems. As he turns 81, will the re-elected president have the energy to face down the far right opposition for another four years and to lay out the ground for a credible successor?
And what does Lula’s latest victory mean for the wider region, and for the country’s relationship with Donald Trump’s administration? In the Guardian’s Opinion pages columnist Jordana Timerman wrote that “Lula’s victory shows that the rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible. But the movement retains substantial electoral support, influence over the political agenda and a powerful ally in Washington.”
The Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions on the election result, what it means for Brazil and the wider region, and what the country’s future may hold, here from 15:00 GMT on Tuesday 27 October. OpenAI recently announced that it is tracking signs of user distress across sessions, rather than only within them, and using that information to inform model responses. The announcement follows a wave of new safeguards for mental health and well-being conversations with artificial intelligence at OpenAI and elsewhere, such as parental controls for teens, usage limits and break reminders, and crisis detection and referral. Policymakers have also moved to address associated risks, with a dozen states now requiring companion chatbot operators to disclose to users that their tools are not human, and to institute crisis referral procedures.
This attention, within AI companies and legislatures, is important and urgent. But it is directed almost entirely at acute harm from interacting with AI, rather than the cumulative harm that develops over time, such as the gradual replacement of one’s connections with friends and family by AI interaction.
Acute harms, such as psychosis or suicide reportedly linked to specific chatbot interactions, are easier to identify and respond to than harms that build over months and years. A chatbot could be safe in every single conversation with a user and still, across months of use, displace the human relationships that keep people healthy.
Early studies suggest that the use of AI chatbots for companionship or emotional support is concentrated among a subset of heavy users, and that heavier use is associated with reduced socialization and increased loneliness. Although this evidence is preliminary and debated, the findings warrant further measurement.
AI companies collect aggregate user data that could help answer these questions, but broader participation and greater access to this data is necessary. If AI use is not displacing human connection at scale, data and robust measurement should show that too. If we don’t start measuring today, and the harm is real, the window in which we might have acted could be closed by the time it becomes undeniable.
AI companies have predominantly focused on per-message and per-session interventions, such as break reminders and usage limits. Across the public commitments of major companies (in model specifications or “constitutions,” usage policies, and safety blog posts), safeguards consistently operate on individual messages or sessions. Crisis detection and referral, too, largely operated at the same level until OpenAI’s announcement that it is tracking distress across sessions. This change demonstrates that companies have the capability to track context about users, but tracking user distress is still focused on detecting acute harms.
Tracking displacement is different, as a user gradually pulling back from their human relationships may show few, if any, signs of distress. Indeed, a user may feel that each individual chat session itself is helpful. Researchers and policymakers like us don’t have a shared understanding of how to measure whether such displacement is occurring across sessions, nor do we have the necessary visibility into the usage data to do so.
The lack of attention to cumulative harms is also important as, in other domains, industry actors have repurposed product-level safeguards as legal or rhetorical defenses when accused of contributing to cumulative harm. The tobacco industry, for example, used warning labels as the basis of assumption-of-risk defenses that stopped individual liability for decades. More recently, Meta has highlighted parental supervision tools and “Take a Break” notifications in congressional testimony, even as it has denied a causal link between social media use and harms to adolescent mental health.
We do not accuse AI companies of bad faith in instituting product-level safeguards, nor do we suggest companies must choose between addressing acute harms and preparing for cumulative ones. However, the historical cases suggest that if accountability for cumulative harm arrives, product-level safety features deployed in isolation can be repurposed as part of a defense to such claims. Per-chat reminders to users that they are “not talking to a human” could feasibly become such features.
What eventually made tobacco’s cumulative harm actionable was that states showed their Medicaid budgets absorbing the downstream costs of industry products. State attorneys general did not have to prove that a product harmed a given person once they could measure and account for the cost to public systems. That accounting already existed when the legal and political window opened.
There exists no equivalent measurement infrastructure to understand whether AI use displaces human connection. AI companies hold usage data closely, while public systems, from health to education, know what social isolation costs them. There is scant connection between the two. Frontier labs are already analyzing aggregate data on how people use these tools, in privacy-preserving ways, and have recently provided access to some third parties to analyze how models respond to mental health crises. However, this has not yet been applied to cumulative harm.
Three groups could start to change this picture. Researchers in academia and civil society should develop the measurement approach and instruments to distinguish AI chatbot use from other contributors to social isolation. Public health, education, and other agencies can measure and share what social isolation already costs them, in areas such as school counselor time, primary care utilization, or demand on social prescription programs that are expanding in the U.S. Finally, the companion chatbot bills in front of state legislatures are an opportunity for legislators to encourage greater access for independent third parties to conduct evaluations related to social isolation.
These actions don’t require settling causation between AI chatbot use and social isolation. However, they do require putting the measurement infrastructure in place before harm becomes undeniable. Many of us have watched the debate about links between social media use and adolescent mental health run for more than a decade without consensus, thanks in part to the lack of necessary measurement infrastructure to inform policymakers.
If the policy window opens to address the effects of AI use on people’s relationships in years to come, policymakers will ask what we know. We already know the value of social connection to our health. What we don’t know is whether people are disconnecting from one another, gradually, over months of interacting with chatbots. By setting up measurement infrastructure we can start to understand, while the answer can still make a difference.
Qian Yang is an assistant professor in the Bowers College of Computing and Information Science at Cornell University, where she directs the DesignAI Group. Ned Cooper is a postdoctoral researcher in the DesignAI Lab at Cornell, where he studies product design and safety guardrails for AI-powered mental health and well-being tools. Ibrahim Emara is a graduate student at the Cornell Brooks School of Public Policy and studies applied projects around responsible AI.

When Ikea launched its super-cheap $10 Bluetooth Kallsup speakers in April, aside from the rock-bottom price and bright, white/green/pink colors, the claim that really caught WIRED’s ear was that the Swedish furniture brand said it was possible to chain 100 of these 2.75-inch sonic cubes together, should you so wish.
Now, because it’s highly unlikely any one household will ever own more than a handful of mini Bluetooth speakers, this is one of those consumer-tech statements that rarely gets tested. So we asked the good folks at Älmhult in Ikea headquarters if they’d let us do just this. To our surprise, Ikea not only agreed, but it also upped the ante, saying it might be possible to link up to 150 without breaking the connection, so that’s exactly how many it sent us. “No one has ever tried this, though,” an Ikea spokesperson said. “We haven’t.”
That is how we ended up building a literal wall of sound at our London office, stacking 150 Kallsups carefully on top of one another to test how many would chain-play from a smartphone. Sadly, one casualty during shipping from Sweden—a single Kallsup—despite lighting up correctly and looking ready to chain, made an ominous rattling sound as if its innards weren’t entirely secure. Sure enough, it refused to play ball (or anything else), so we ended up with 149 speakers.
The chain process itself is simple. Once you have paired a single Kallsup with your music device—in our case, an iPhone 16 Pro—and it’s up and running, simply power on another cube while playing and hold down the Play button until a chime tells you it’s in “multi-speaker” mode. It should then immediately start playing whatever the Bluetooth-connected Kallsup is playing.
Thanks to this near-effortless chaining process, linking up all these Kallsups took much less time than we'd expected, about 30 minutes. We stopped at 100 to test how loud the “system” sounded at that stage before resuming the build and moving on to the maximum amount. As the music continued while we chained the speakers, it would be obvious when the collective refused to add more cubes. But this didn’t happen, and the plucky Kallsups joined forces without grumbling right up to the full 149.
It Might Get Loud
It’s tempting to preface the next few paragraphs with the phrase “for a $10 speaker,” because, despite Ikea’s vast buying power, experienced research and development team, and global presence, the ability to produce a tiny speaker that doesn’t sound absolutely horrible for less than a pint of half-decent craft beer is pretty incredible.
Each Kallsup has a single 1.8-inch, full-range driver powered by a 3-watt amplifier, with Bluetooth 5.3 support. No separate tweeter or woofer, just the one tiny driver.
On its own, the Kallsup speaker sounds fine. Yes, it lacks anything resembling the deep rumbling bass people talk about in audio reviews, but did we mention it’s a $10 speaker? It is a bit tinny, and you won’t want to push the volume very hard, but as a little desktop speaker, one by the side of the bed, or to throw in a suitcase, the Kallsup does the job. It doesn’t match the performance of one of our best Bluetooth speaker recommendations, but keep the cost in mind, and it’s hard to be disappointed.
Even at low background volumes, the Kallsups worked surprisingly well together, especially playing acoustic tracks. As we paired more speakers, the sound gradually grew nicely in scale. Nothing was overpowering or dominating, just the cumulative effect of all those tiny drivers moving small amounts of air.
With 149 individual 1.8-inch drivers, the combined surface area is roughly equivalent to one enormous 22-inch driver. Each Kallsup also has its own 3-watt amplifier, giving our wall a combined rated output of 447 watts. That doesn’t mean it behaves like a giant subwoofer or a conventional 447-watt speaker, but it explains why things got so loud.
But before we turned these up, if you will, to 149, we listened at 100, and when we pushed the volume, the collective Kallsups were seriously loud. But for the record, loud like a fire alarm, not a hi-fi system. With the wall complete, we worried the collective vibrations might send the whole thing crashing down. Disappointingly for the socials, it stayed resolute. Instead, we played Trans Lunar by Twin Dimensions (WIRED director of consumer tech and culture Mike Calore’s excellent band) and slowly increased the volume to maximum.
We almost wish we hadn’t. The noise was brain-numbingly loud as we blasted, somewhat appropriately, Richard Strauss’ Also Sprach Zarathustra. We couldn’t hear each other speak, and we could feel our internal organs vibrating. Any sense of fidelity disappeared, but—all power to the Kallsups—it worked. We’d successfully linked 149 Bluetooth speakers, though sadly we’re well short of the world record of 1,500 speakers set by Majority Audio in March 2026.
At more modest, realistic volumes, everything sounded considerably more composed, even if the music lacked levels of depth and detail. The overall lack of clarity could also be due to minor timing differences between the individual drivers.
At $1,490, a wall of Kallsups is quite an investment, and not one we’re recommending, but it is extremely impressive that we managed to sync and play music wirelessly through so many small, cheap speakers.
We also tested the wall alongside WIRED’s choice for best overall party speaker, the $500 LG Xboom Stage 501. Cranked up, both reached similarly ear-splitting, frankly uncomfortable volumes. But with two 5.25-inch woofers, two 2.5-inch full-range drivers, and clever digital signal processing, the LG delivered understandably fuller, deeper bass and a considerably more musical experience, as expected.
Powering Down
What’s remarkable about this experiment is that so little went wrong. Only one of the 150 speakers shipped didn’t work, clearly broken in transit. We managed to get all 149 sound cubes chained easily and quickly. And when we weren’t blasting the wall of sound at max volume, instead keeping levels moderate, the speakers sounded surprisingly competent as a collective.
However, there were hints of the Kallsup chaining capacity reaching its limit, as Ikea suspected. As we got beyond 100 units linked together, the incidence of failing to chain on the first try increased. Still, no speaker refused more than twice as we got toward the end of the build.
We also would have preferred indentations on the tops of the speakers, which would have given us a bit more confidence that the whole stack wasn’t going to collapse in a heap as volume ramped up (which it didn’t). Such a simple design feature would help whether you’re dealing with just a couple placed on top of each other, let alone 149—but this is splitting hairs.
Lastly, although this setup was impressively loud, no one in their right mind would do this in their own home. Ikea has been a good sport letting us try this out, but the ultimate, unsurprising lesson is: If you want high-quality audio, spend your money on a better speaker. As for the Kallsup? Simple to use, easy to chain, with approachable sound and clean design. You really can’t ask much more for $10.
