How Aldi is pushing down grocery prices
In the summer of 2020, I lived briefly in Ithaca, New York. It's the only time I've lived near Aldi, the grocery store known for low prices. I went twice, and I thought it was fine, but underwhelming. I appreciated the low prices, but it didn't have everything I needed. The store was small and a bit shabby.
I didn't know it yet, but those are the exact ingredients that have made Aldi the fastest-growing grocery chain in America. Per Bloomberg, Aldi plans to have more than 3,000 American locations by the end of 2028, which would be more than any other chain but Walmart. In 2024, Aldi generated some $29 billion in U.S. sales, which is more than Trader Joe's.
Aldi is a German company known for having low, low prices, and it deserves that reputation. Food reporter Deena Shanker told me that her experience comparison shopping over many months was that Aldi either matched Walmart on price or was a bit cheaper. Grocers like Wegmans and Kroger have announced defensive price reductions, and an analysis published in late 2023 of Lidl, another German grocer with a very similar model to Aldi's but fewer U.S. stores, found that grocery chains reduced their markups ~7 percent in areas where Lidl stores opened.
All to say: Aldi is disrupting the grocery business and actually lowering prices even as the cost of food—at restaurants and other grocery stores—goes up and up.
Maybe this sounds a bit humdrum. But I found it totally intriguing and perplexing, because…
- Walmart and Costco's business models depend on low prices, too, and they can offer low prices by having huge stores, giant warehouses, and incredible economies of scale that allow them to pay less for Oreo's, baby carrots, and Jif peanut butter than other grocers. So how the heck is Aldi matching or beating them on price?
- When a company disrupts a longstanding industry, it's typically a startup enabled by new technology—like Netflix using online streaming to disrupt Blockbuster and video rental. But Aldi is not staffed by futuristic robots. Its stores just look like grocery stores, and Aldi was founded 80 years ago, in post-war Germany. So what's going on?
- One of the proudest achievements of America's capitalistic market economy is providing its citizens an abundance of increasingly affordable food. Somewhat famously, Soviet leader Boris Yeltsin toured a grocery store in Houston during the Cold War and was amazed that the average American enjoyed more variety than top Soviet politicians. From 1960 to 2019, Americans spent less and less of their incomeon food each year, even as they enjoyed more frequent restaurant meals, more sushi, and far better beer. But since the pandemic, food has become less affordable. Can American markets no longer provide cheap groceries? Did something break?
One necessary but not sufficient explanation for Aldi's low prices is that management is obsessed with efficiency and cutting unnecessary costs. There's no music in stores, because speakers (and licensing fees for muzak) cost money. The staff places products on shelves still in the cardboard boxes they were trucked in on, because artfully unpacking fruits, bread, and jerky sticks would mean higher labor costs. The shabbiness is intentional — it's the cost of cheaper groceries.
But other grocery chains are similarly obsessed with efficiency. Here's one of my favorite examples about Costco, courtesy of Zachary Crockett and The Hustle: "In another instance, reengineering a container of cashews from a circle to a square shape allowed Costco to stack more items in a single truck, reducing the number of shipments by 24,000 pallets per year. For shoppers, this meant cheaper nuts."
Instead, Aldi's disruptively low prices rely on two primary tactics:
- Private label products: On Aldi shelves, you can find cookies that look a heck of a lot like Oreos and boxes of what sure seem like Ritz crackers. But they are "Benton's Chocolate Sandwich Cookies with Vanilla Filling" and "Savoritz Golden Round crackers." Both are made by Aldi, and therefore cost less, since Aldi doesn't have to pay Nabisco's markup and then add their own. More than 80 percent of Aldi products are these store-brand versions—aka private-label products or, in the case of look-alike Oreos,dupes.
- Limited selection: When the Albrecht brothers took over their family's grocery store in 1946, they had a small store and limited funds for stocking the shelves. But this became their secret sauce: Stocking a very limited selection of items — just essentials like rice and eggs, and just one of each rather than a variety of brands, sizes, and versions — allowed them to keep prices low. They could buy in bulk, which is cheaper, and by not stocking niche products that sit on shelves for weeks or days, they saved even more by avoiding spoilage and limiting shelf space, storage areas, and rent or real-estate costs. Even as the brothers grew rich, they kept stores small and selection limited. This is less convenient— shoppers often have to visit another grocery store to grab things like white pepper that Aldi doesn't stock. But what Aldi does stock is cheaper.
Aldi's low prices made their stores very attractive during periods like the Great Recession and today's inflationary era. The Great Recession, especially, enabled their current growth. But if all Aldi offered was bargain prices in shabby stores, customers might flee to Costco, Kroger, or Whole Foods when the economy recovered.
So another key to Aldi's success is that it's fun. Aldi has a famously chaotic-good middle aisle with rotating buys like fun toys, German spätzle, and advent calendars that contain 24 festive cheeses. And its U.S. stores have expanded their offerings (a bit) to attract higher-income customers: Aldi doesn't just have the cheapest apples, but the cheapest honey crisp apples. Not just super-duper cheap wine but well-priced "premium" wine.
Instead of being a sad place to shop when you're low on cash, Aldi has more flea-market energy: a place anyone might go to hunt for good deals and fun finds. Aldi is beloved; many customers arecult-like in their devotion. In some cases, customers line up for new store openings like early iPhone releases.
My main takeaway from researching and analyzing Aldi for several weeks (foran episode of Gastronomics!) is that there's always something new under the sun. American grocery stores are a mature market. They seem pretty stable equilibrium-y. But they are dynamic and always changing. Aldi didn't need futuristic tech to disrupt the industry; just a strategy developed 80 years ago, then tweaked for the American market. In healthy markets, there's always a way in for new competitors.
My other takeaway is greater appreciation for the famous business idiom: "There are only two ways to make money in business: One is to bundle; the other is to unbundle."
The clearest example of bundling and unbundling is probably television. Cable companies bundled hundreds of TV channels together and charged one high fee for all of them. Then streaming services like Netflix made money by unbundling television — by allowing people to pay for just Netflix. Which felt liberating! For a few years. But now customers are annoyed about subscribing to so many streaming services. So streamers are teaming up to form bundles, like getting Disney, Hulu, and HBO Max all for one reduced price. Now, to make money, you gotta bundle.
Even the person who coined the phrase about bundling and unbundling didn't think it's literally the only way to make money. Still, I often failed to see (un)bundling as a powerful framework outside of the media industry. Until I realized that Aldi is unbundling the grocery store.
For a long time, grocery stores got more bundled. People once went to the baker, the butcher, and the greengrocer. Then the super market put all those things under one roof. And then Walmart, Target, and Costco created superstores where you could buy groceries and clothes and big-screen TVs.
Now Aldi is reversing this process by unbundling the grocery store. Not only does Aldi not have the big-screen TVs and dupes of Lululemon hoodies and pants, it doesn't even have everything on your grocery list. Aldi unbundled the part of the grocery business it can do super cheaply, and it intentionally locates Aldi stores near competitor grocery stores so shoppers can easily go grab the last few things on their list (the rest of the bundle).
With this in mind, I've started seeing bundling and unbundling at work in more and more industries. If you look closely at your own, I suspect you will, too.
My third takeaway is that I just didn't live in Ithaca long enough to grok Aldi. If I'd been there longer, I bet I would have made Aldi part of a multi-store strategy. I get it now! Aldi, please come to Colorado (where I live)!
At the start of this post, I asked three questions inspired by Aldi's expansion. The first two, which are about how Aldi achieved a comparative advantage, I feel like I've answered.
The third was whether the American economy can still deliver a bounty of affordable food. I think the way Aldi's growth pressured competitors to keep prices low shows that grocers are not the right target of our ire over food prices. But grocery stores are just one slice of the food world.

In August 2024, Poland's then-President Andrzej Duda signed amendments to legislation expanding when border security guards could use firearms during attacks on the state border. The bill also introduced a limited exclusion from criminal liability in certain situations. Border officers could already use firearms in self-defense before the amendment became law.
The legislation was introduced in 2024, not recently, as posts suggest. It does not allow the indiscriminate use of firearms, although human rights organizations have warned it could lead to excessive force against migrants and weaken accountability for border officers. The law also does not specifically mention migrants.
In mid-2026, social media users claimed that Poland had passed legislation allowing its border patrol guards to shoot at migrants.
The story spread on X and Facebook, with several people sharing a screenshot of a news article featuring the headline, "Poland passes bill allowing border guards to fire at illegal migrants."
Neither the social media posts nor the screenshot mention the date the article was published, nor when Poland allegedly passed such a law. Therefore, some commenters appeared to believe the legislation is new.
(Facebook user "David J. Harris Jr.")
In short, Al Mayadeen, a Lebanese TV news media outlet, published the article in August 2024, not recently, as the posts imply. That year, Poland passed amendments to an existing law, allowing border security to use firearms in specific situations. The amendments do not state that border officers can attack migrants, though human rights groups argue the language gives undue license to border security forces. As such, we rate this claim as a mixture of true and false information.
On Aug. 14, 2024, Poland's then-President Andrzej Duda signed a bill into law that widened the range of circumstances in which border security guards could use firearms against people at the border. The legislation limits criminal liability for border guard officers who break rules on using force or firearms in certain circumstances. Translated to English, the law states (Page 3, Article 6, Section 2) (emphasis ours):
A police officer, a Border Guard officer, or a Military Gendarmerie soldier does not commit a crime if, in connection with the performance of official duties or tasks, they use or employ measures of direct coercion or firearms in violation of the rules governing their use or employment, in the event of a direct and unlawful attack on the inviolability of the state border.
That exclusion applies only in specified urgent circumstances, including when an officer is defending someone's life, health or liberty or confronting certain armed or otherwise dangerous individuals, and when the circumstances require immediate action (bottom of Page 3 to top of Page 4).
Under the previous law (Page 15, Article 45, Section 1, Subsection D), officers could already use firearms against someone forcing a border crossing with a vehicle, firearm or other dangerous object. The 2024 amendment expanded those circumstances. The bold section shows what the amendment added. It states (Page 4, Section 7) that firearms may be used when necessary to repel a direct and unlawful attack on:
… the inviolability of the state border by a person who forces the crossing of the state border using a vehicle, firearm or other dangerous object, or who acts in another manner directly threatening the life, health or freedom of the authorized person or another person, or who acts with another person who uses such a weapon, object or method …
The law does not, however, state that firearms may be used just because someone is a migrant or attempts to cross the border without authorization.
Human rights nonprofit organization Amnesty International criticized the then-proposed changes in July 2024, warning that the rules were too broad, vaguely worded and could lead to abuses.
Separately, in June 2024, the Polish government imposed a "temporary border exclusion zone" which required journalists and non-governmental organizations to request passes to enter the area, thus restricting oversight of border security forces. The zone has been repeatedly extended and remains in force as of October 2026.
The government proposed the in-question legislation as tensions grew at the Belarusian border, shortly after a migrant fatally stabbed Polish soldier Mateusz Sitek and authorities detained soldiers who fired warning shots at the border. Poland's parliament then overwhelmingly approved the amendments. 
For further reading, Snopes has previously reported on claims involving migrants in Europe and along the U.S.-Mexico border.
Snopes reporting fellow Aleksandra Wrona contributed to the translations in this report.

Scratch that. Brazilian supreme court justice Cristiano Zanin has just ordered voting in the country’s presidential runoff on Sunday to be extended by two hours, granting a request from Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s campaign.
Polls were initially set to close at 5pm Brasília time. Lula’s campaign alleged that authorities in several cities were restricting voter access to public transportation.
The decision follows allegations of attempted voter suppression in at least 10 states, where public transport appears to have been severely limited in what some suspect was a deliberate ploy to stop Lula voters reaching polling stations.
Earlier, Lula told reporters he had never before complained about elections he had been involved in, irrespective of whether he had won or lost. “But this time something abominable is happening.”
However, some polling stations may have already closed since the decision came so shortly after they were due to close. People should now be able to vote until 7pm.
Meanwhile, hundreds of Lula supporters have camped out on Paulista Avenue to watch the vote count, which started at 7pm local time.
Among them is Camilo Buarque, 35, who came with a bright red banner reading: “Lula: My President”.
“I feel so very happy being here and being here fighting for Lula,” Buarque says, predicting his leader will beat Bolsonaro.
“My confidence comes from the energy and the happiness and the love of these people [around me]. This is democracy,” Buarque says as the first results come in, giving Lula the lead. Fireworks exploded in the air above him as the crowd celebrated the early lead.
João Felipe, a 27-year-old logistics worker, is also there waiting for what he hopes will be a huge Lula party.
“I’ve always been poor and Lula was a very important person when it came to helping people improve their lives,” he says.
“Lula is going to turn this election around. Long live democracy,” Felipe predicts.
“My heart is beating a thousand beats a second but I’m confident,” said his partner, Ester Almeida, 28.
Flávio Bolsonaro is following the count from the mansion of one of his campaign coordinators in a wealthy area of the capital, Brasília. The dozens of journalists present are being kept separate from Bolsonaro and allied politicians, but from time to time they can hear bursts of celebration – like after a goal – whenever the count is updated and Bolsonaro narrows the gap with Lula.
When, with 13.65% of the vote counted, Flávio moved just slightly ahead with 50.01%, an AI-generated funk track began playing loudly and the senator’s guests started chanting a line commonly heard in Brazilian football stadiums: “Go at him, Flávio.”
And just like that, the race is already tightening further. Bolsonaro now has 50.01% of the vote, while Lula has 49.99% of the vote with just over 13.5% of ballots counted.
With five per cent of votes counted Lula has taken an early lead with 51% of votes to Bolsonaro’s 48.87%. This is going to be a tight race and a very long night.
One of the most popular figures in Flávio Bolsonaro’s party, congressman Nikolas Ferreira, indicated that the far right could use the extension of voting hours as grounds to challenge the election result in the event of a victory by president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Speaking to journalists outside the mansion in Brasília where Bolsonaro was due to follow the count, Ferreira said that “the only person harmed” by the extension was the senator – without, however, mentioning the voters who, as reports throughout the day showed, had been unable to vote because they had no transport.
“The extension only helps whoever is losing,” said the 30-year-old politician who, in the first round, became the most-voted federal congressman in Brazilian history, with 3.1 million votes. He added that justice Cristiano Zanin “wanted to disrupt the election” by issuing the ruling.
Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, echoed that line and called the justice’s ruling an “intervention”.
“I sincerely hope common sense prevails and that any judicial coup or administrative manoeuvre does not succeed, for the sake of democracy,” he posted on social media.
Now two hours after the initial extension, polls have officially closed in Brazil (save for another surprise extension). Ballot count has begun.
Although voting time was extended across the country, some polling stations had already closed by the time that decision was announced. As Brazil uses electronic voting machines, once they are closed, they cannot be re-opened.
It’s not clear if certain polling stations had restrictions on if people who arrived after the initial deadline were allowed to vote, as rules usually stipulate that only people in line can still vote after the polls close.
The fact that ballot counting was already underway when the polls were suddenly ordered to remain open has led to some confusion and concerns about the integrity of the election results.
Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensified before presidential runoff
Tiago Rogero
Five days after his defeat in the first round of the Brazilian presidential election, leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent almost 24 hours unable to boost his Instagram posts, while his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, could.
Lula’s lawyers included the episode in a list of incidents that they submitted to the electoral court and international observers as “evidence” that Meta, Instagram’s owner, was actively trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.
Reports from Lula supporters saying their content had been removed or its reach restricted flooded social media in Brazil, while about a dozen watchdogs and research groups published reports describing what they called “indications” that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign.
Meta called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”, saying there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”.
The controversy fuelled the electoral battle between Lula and Bolsonaro and gained further traction after the electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”.
Lula supporters are starting to gather on Paulista Avenue, at the heart of São Paulo, in anticipation of a Lula victory.
The mood is upbeat but tense, amid suspicions that there has been a deliberate pro-Bolsonaro campaign to sabotage public transport systems to stop Lula voters reaching polling stations across the country.
Many people on Paulista Avenue outside the iconic São Paulo Museum of Art suspect foul play from Bolsonaro-supporting politicians and business people.
“I think it’s another coup attempt that the extreme right is trying in Brazil. But we need to really fight so we can win,” said Lucas Lopes, a 32-year-old from São Paulo who works with public relations.
“I’m really worried but I’m optimistic,” Lopes added as dozens of Lula supporters blocked the roads and danced with banners and flags.
“It’s a coup,” agreed Caio Marques, a 40-year-old photographer from Franca, a city in the interior of São Paulo state. “Their arrogance is such that they think they have already won and can do whatever they please and won’t be punished.”
Marques’ partner, Gabriela Leôncio, said: “They are [stopping] public transport in strategic places where Lula has historically had more votes. Where Lula has an advantage, people haven’t managed to get to their polling stations ... They are trying several different types of coup.”

A scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power
Tiago Rogero
Thundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in the presidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all.
“Whoever votes for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice once described as “Voldemort” by Elon Musk.
Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup.
Just days before the election runoff, Moraes was once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaro overtake him to emerge as the frontrunner. The justice once hailed as democracy’s “saviour” for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power.
The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contract worth about £20m with Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’s largest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting a close relationship between Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic.
Investigations subsequently revealed that at least four other justices had links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal.
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva v Flávio Bolsonaro: Brazil presidential runoff to decide direction of nation
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the Brazilian presidential runoff.
Leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and senator Flávio Bolsonaro faced a second round of voting after neither secured more than 50% of the vote in the first round.
Bolsonaro, the eldest son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, pulled off a surprise first-round victory, signaling a resurgence of the far-right in Brazil. But polls appeared to have narrowed a few days before Sunday’s vote, with a Quaest poll reported by Reuters showing Bolsonaro on 45% of the vote, with Lula on 44%. A week earlier, Bolsonaro had 46% of the vote, compared with Lula’s 44%.
In the first-round election earlier this month, Bolsonaro secured 47% of the vote, compared with Lula’s 45%.
Sunday’s election is a test for incumbent president Lula: can he can rally enough support to overturn Bolsonaro’s lead?

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

Following reports of iPhone Duos with cracked and broken inside screens, often showing a bright line running from the center to the right side, Apple says in a statement to Bloomberg and 9to5Mac that it’s aware of “an issue impacting the inner display” on a “small number of iPhone Duo units.” If your iPhone Duo is affected, Apple says to contact AppleCare for a replacement.
Apple acknowledges iPhone Duo display ‘issue’ after reports of cracked screens
Apple says a ‘small number’ of iPhone Duos have shown the cracked inner screen problem and that owners should contact AppleCare.
Here is the full statement, which Apple’s Alex Kirschner shared with The Verge:
The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor. We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement.
Kirshner says most units aren’t susceptible and that the issues appear quickly on units with the defect.
Shortly after launch, iPhone Duo users started reporting similar issues where the hinge would tighten, and opening the device caused a crack and the distinctive bright lines on the display. One user in Australia said that an Apple Store replaced their unit “on the spot.”
This weekend, iFixit published its teardown of the phone and gave its perspective on why some phones might be cracking. Where the damage has been happening, iFixit shows how the foldable screen might be pushing against a center bar.
The Verge has contacted Apple about the reports, but has not received an on-the-record response about the issues with these new phones. They’re some of the first devices to launch after new CEO John Ternus took over from Tim Cook.

The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”
Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”
Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.
The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.
Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.
“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.
When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.
Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”
US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.
Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.
US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.
Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.
Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.
His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.
Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.
Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.
Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.
Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”
Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.
Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”
The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.
Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.
Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.
Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.
For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.
Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

Forty Iranian sailors rescued off Sri Lanka coast after medical emergencies
- Published
Sri Lanka's foreign ministry says it has coordinated efforts to treat and repatriate 40 Iranian sailors suffering from unspecified medical emergencies in international waters off the island's southeastern coast.
Ministry spokesperson Thushara Rodrigo told BBC Sinhala they received a distress call on Saturday from Iranian ships "regarding an urgent medical need".
The rescue operation was planned by the Iranian Embassy in Colombo, he said.
Iranian ships have been stranded at sea due to a US naval blockade. Sri Lanka stresses it is neutral in the conflict, but has at times offered help to Iranian sailors in what it says is an obligation to international law.
A BBC Sinhala report last month found that there were 21 Iranian vessels located in international waters near Sri Lanka.
The 40 rescued sailors served on different ships - though Sri Lankan authorities do not have information on how many ships they belonged to, Rodrigo said.
The sailors were brought ashore and taken to Colombo for medical treatment before being sent back to Iran by plane on Saturday night, he added.
He said that several agencies were involved in the operation, including local shipping companies.
According to Rodrigo, Sri Lanka was obliged under international law and humanitarian grounds to provide the necessary facilities for medical emergencies.
"This does not mean that we will provide assistance to those ships," he said. "It is generally an internationally accepted tradition to respond to a distress call after receiving it."
"We have dealt with such cases before. This is a normal process that continues to be implemented."
The ongoing conflict in Iran started when the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on the country in February. Iran responded by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.
Attacks by both sides have persisted as negotiations stalled.
Sri Lanka has sought to remain neutral in the conflict, having rejected military access requests from both the US and Iran and urged both parties to prioritise dialogue.
It has also offered assistance to Iranian ships caught in the conflict on what it argues are humanitarian grounds.
In March, Sri Lankan authorities said they responded to a distress call from the Iranian ship the Iris Dena, which had sunk off its coast after a US torpedo attack.
More than 80 crew members were killed in the attack, and injured survivors were taken to a hospital in the Galle Harbour.
The following day, Sri Lankan authorities allowed another Iranian naval vessel to dock at one of its ports, with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake saying that they would "never hesitate to protect humanity".
Sri Lankan authorities said earlier this month they had no immediate plans to send aid to 19 Iranian ships near its coasts which had reported shortages of food, water and fuel. The authorities said they had to prioritise national interests, the Associated Press reported.

Step 1: To create a portfolio website using Google Gemini AI Studio, go to aistudio.google.com and sign in with your Google account. Next, in the sidebar, under the Build section, tap on New app.
Step 2: Now Google AI Studio directly shows the preview on the right side. Since Google offers free rate limits, you can re-enter the prompt and make the changes you want. To proceed, click the code icon at the top of the preview.
Step 3: Now find the index.html option. Google AI Studio creates several project files, but index.html holds your entire website. In the file list, hover over index.html, click the three-dot menu next to it, then click Download.
Step 4: Once downloaded, open the file from your downloads folder and check that everything works properly without breaking anything. However, I highly recommend skipping the Export and Publish options here. Export lets you download the whole project, while Publish hosts the app within Google; both steps are unnecessary if you want to publish a simple portfolio site.
How to Create a Free Portfolio Website Using Perplexity
Next, you can also build a website using Perplexity. The free version allows you to create a simple portfolio site.
Step 1: To do that, go to Perplexity.ai, sign in with your free account, and click on the Ask Anything box.
Step 2: Paste the prompt and tap Send.
Step 3: Wait for Phubloxity to create a portfolio website. Once done, it will show you the portfolio.html file. Click on it to preview.
Step 4: After you check the preview, click the download option, download it as an HTML file, and save it locally on your device.
How to Publish Your Portfolio Website for Free
To publish your portfolio site, there are plenty of options, but in this guide, I will show you two free, reliable options: Netlify Drop and GitHub Pages.
Method 1: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using Netlify Drop
Step 1: Create a free Netlify account. First, go to netlify.com and sign up with your email. You can also sign up using Google or GitHub.
Step 2: Go to app.netlify.com/drop and drop the index.html you created using Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google AI Studio from your downloads folder, or click the file and select it.
Step 3: Next, it automatically creates a free address. After a few minutes, your project shows as published with a random address such as sunny-tulip-tf52.netlify.app in my case. You can also click on that link to see the live site.
Step 4: However, if you think it can have a better name, open the project settings and change the project name to something short, such as meera-ai. Your address becomes meera-iyer.netlify.app. Make sure your site name is unique, since there will be hundreds of free Netlify sites out there.
Step 5: Once you have hosted the site successfully, you can share your link. Your portfolio is now live for anyone on any device to access it.
Method 2: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using GitHub Pages
Now let’s look at how to publish it for free using GitHub Pages.
GitHub also lets you host a simple website for free, and you can do everything on the GitHub website without installing anything. However, it takes a few more clicks than the Netlify Drop process.
Step 1: First, create a GitHub account. To do that, sign in to your free account at github.com, then go to github.com/new and create a new repository. For example, you can create ramesh.portfolio and set it to public. Remember that free accounts need a public repository for Pages to work. Turn on “Add a README” and finally tap on Create repository options.
Step 2: Once done, you can upload a file to the repository. Click Choose your files or drag and drop the index.html file, and at the bottom type a short message such as “Add portfolio website” and click on the Commit changes button.
Step 3: Once done, open the repository and go to Settings. Then click Pages in the left sidebar. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch, pick main and / (root), and click Save.
Step 4: Now wait until GitHub says the changes can take up to 10 minutes. Wait for your site to go public, refresh the page, and wait for it to update. Once it’s done, click Visit site.
That’s it. GitHub will create your page under your name using a GitHub subdomain.
Final Thoughts
This is how you can use free AI tools to create free portfolio websites. Whether you are a beginner and have never written code before, you can follow this simple step-by-step process to create your first portfolio website.
If you have never built one and don’t even have an idea of creating profile sites, you can simply upload your resume into the AI tool and ask it to convert it into a portfolio website and generate an index.html page. If you have any issues while deploying the site, let me know in the comments, and I am happy to guide you.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

The number of registered medical practitioners (RMP) in Keralam has crossed one-lakh mark, and 32.75% of them got their registrations between 2021 and 2025, data collected from the Kerala State Medical Councils (KSMC) till October 8, 2026, show.
According to RTI data collected from the KSMC, there are 1,13,023 RMPs in the State. As many as 31,446 doctors were registered between 2021 and 2025. A total of 5,981 doctors got registered in 2021, 5,734 in 2022, 5,283 in 2023, 7,065 in 2024, and 7,383 in 2025. As many as 2,695 doctors registered with the KSMC till October 8 this year.
K.V. Babu, Kannur-based ophthalmologist and public health activist, who gathered the information, says that 95,993 doctors were added to the list in the last 27 years. “Keralam’s population is around 3.62 crore. Among the above-mentioned doctors, at least some may have migrated to other States or abroad seeking better opportunities. However, if at least 80,000 of them are here, there is one MBBS doctor for a population of 450 people already,” he says. Dr. Babu claims that the consequences of this trend could be unemployment among medical graduates and commercialisation of health care.
Seats fall vacant
“According to reports, hundreds of MBBS seats have fallen vacant in [deemed-to-be universities] in Tamil Nadu this year [after the final round of counselling for the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test for undergraduate medical courses]. A similar phenomenon could happen in Keralam as well. The government should study this issue before giving permission for new medical colleges,” he says.
M.N. Menon, president, Indian Medical Association (IMA), Kerala State branch, says around 5,000 graduates are coming out of medical colleges in the State every year. “Another 2,000 are passing out from other States and countries. Unemployment among new medical graduates is already high. Instead of granting sanction for new medical colleges, the government should improve the infrastructure in the existing ones and deploy qualified faculty members. Also, we are seeing shortage of doctors and faculty members in government hospitals and government medical colleges. The focus should also be on appointing necessary staff there,” Dr. Menon adds.

"I would absolutely do it again."
Ten years on from making the gesture that catapulted him to iconic status, but which he believes led to his exile from the sport he loved, Colin Kaepernick insists he has no regrets.
It was September 2016 when NFL star Kaepernick knelt during the US national anthem before a match as a peaceful protest against racial injustice and police brutality.
It proved both inspirational and divisive.
In his first interview with BBC Sport since then, Kaepernick reflects on his journey; his pride at seeing England footballers take the knee, athlete activism, the relationship between sport and politics, and the price he paid for being a figurehead for the civil rights movement.
"I knew the protest could potentially cost me my career," he says. "History shows us…that is a reality for athletes.
"We also see this in broader movements, going well beyond costing someone their career, and costing people their lives. We see Malcolm X assassinated, we see MLK [Martin Luther King] assassinated, so the consequences are real."
Having initially sat to protest against the plight of black people in the US, Kaepernick first knelt during the Star-Spangled Banner before his San Francisco 49ers team played a pre-season game. It was an act he would repeat before 11 regular-season contests that year.
At the time, he said he could not stand up for - and show pride in - a flag "for a country that oppresses black people and people of colour", adding: "This is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way."
His stance against racial inequality was seen as heroic by many, inspiring other NFL players to follow suit. But there was also condemnation from those who said it was disrespectful to the military.
Those dissenting voices included Donald Trump - then a presidential candidate.
Trump described the act as "a terrible thing" and unpatriotic. He even suggested Kaepernick should find another country to live in, adding players who refused to stand for the national anthem should be fired.
The NFL said it would fine teams whose players did not stand.
Kaepernick opted out of his contract with the 49ers in March 2017, though the club's management later said he would have been released regardless.
Despite leading the 49ers to the 2013 Super Bowl, and throwing 16 touchdowns in his final season, one of the most talented quarterbacks in the sport never found a new team.
Speaking from New York, Kaepernick says he anticipated the reaction to taking the knee. "What I couldn't have predicted was the people who would show up for me in significant ways, and also the people who worked against me and against the movement," he adds.
Kaepernick eventually filed a grievance against NFL team owners, who he believed had conspired not to hire him because of his protests, reaching a financial settlement in 2019.
That year, the NFL arranged a private workout for Kaepernick, but he chose not to attend, instead holding his own session elsewhere to allow media to be present.
The NFL later admitted it was "wrong for not listening to players earlier", and encouraged "all to speak out and peacefully protest".
'Humbling to see England players take knee'
Following the murder of George Floyd while in police custody in Minneapolis in 2020, taking the knee became a feature of Black Lives Matter protests, and widespread across sport.
England's men's and women's football teams were among those to follow suit.
"That was a surprising moment for me," says Kaepernick.
"I did think about the protest going beyond the US and how that may show up in other countries. To be able to see the national teams going out and protesting, it was humbling. I was happy that they were doing it.
"I also know there's still a lot of work to be done within racism in the UK and more broadly. And this is a global challenge that we are collectively fighting against.
"I was very excited to be able to see players actively calling that out, and willing to begin taking action towards addressing it."
Despite keeping a relatively low profile for most of the past decade, Kaepernick remains a standard-bearer for the civil rights movement.
But while surveys suggest the vast majority of professional athletes intend to use their social media channels to raise awareness about racial injustice, external, he accepts the momentum behind athlete activism seems to have slowed in recent years.
It was notable that several players across five clubs chose to remain standing when Premier League players took the knee as part of October's No Room for Racism campaign.
Anti-discrimination campaign group Kick It Out told BBC Sport the gesture "still has value in raising awareness of the structural inequalities that exist in football and society", but added it could "understand the reasons players might become frustrated with the pace of change".
Reports of discrimination received by the charity more than doubled in the past five years, reaching record levels last season.
"I think we're in a moment that demands protests more than ever," says Kaepernick.
"Why I think protests are not as loud right now [is] because of the concerted efforts that have been taken by organisations like the NFL, like the Trump administration, and corporate entities following along and capitulating in that process.
"While those things are happening, I think the reality of the state of the US, and more broadly the world, demands that we show up in a more significant way."
'Politics inherently part of sports'
Kaepernick is all too familiar with how polarising it can be to take a political stand in sport.
Opponents of taking the knee have claimed it is a political and divisive statement, and that rather than demonstrating backing for the Black Lives Matter movement, it has shown support for the organisation of the same name.
In 2018, critics encouraged people to destroy Nike goods after the sportswear giant used Kaepernick as the face of an advertising campaign featuring the caption 'Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything.'
So what does he say to those who argue that sport and politics should be kept apart?
"They ring hollow and feel very hypocritical, because politics is inherently part of sports," he says.
"We see within [American] football, we see taxpayers funding NFL stadiums. We see our NFL owners going out and supporting political candidates... so to try to position this as if sports aren't political, in many ways feels just laughable to me, and disconnected.
"Now, where the question comes in for people is: 'We don't want the athletes to be political. Everything around them can be political, but the athletes themselves, we don't want them to have a voice in the politics, because that interrupts our entertainment and our ability to disconnect.' For me, that's where society has a challenge with it."
Having encountered significant opposition from high-profile athletes during his first term, Trump seems to have encountered less challenge from the world of sport during his second, notably becoming the first sitting US president to attend the Super Bowl.
He has also appeared at golf's Ryder Cup, and the finals of football's Club World Cup and World Cup, though he was also booed when attending the NBA Finals in New York in June.
"It ties into the conversation of 'are sports political?' when he is going out and actively trying to use them to gain favour and popularity", says Kaepernick, adding that Fifa's controversial decision to award the US President its inaugural 'Peace Prize' last year was "regrettable".
"The part that I think is great to see is when he's showing up to these events and getting booed by the crowd, which speaks to the political environment that he's created, that the majority of the country does not agree with…when it comes to sports, people need to continue to respond accordingly."
'We have a lot of work to do'
Now 38, Kaepernick has published a memoir titled The Perilous Fight, detailing his childhood in California having been adopted by a white family, encountering racism, and his education and evolution. "People saw the moment. But they didn't see the years that made it possible", he says. "The questions about who I was; the injustices I could no longer ignore; the voices of those who came before me that I carried into that stadium...When I took a knee, it wasn't a sudden act. It was the result of years of becoming."
So how did he find the process of reliving his journey?
"Are there moments that are challenging going back to? Yes. But I hope that insight helps other people navigate situations...that helps them move forward or helps them to go accomplish things."
Kaepernick also supports community organisations via his Know Your Rights education campaign, is a philanthropist, and has written a number of children's books.
Even now, he maintains the fitness regime he had during his time at the 49ers, just in case an unlikely opportunity to resume his NFL career arises.
Kaepernick may not have thrown a ball in anger for almost a decade, but he is widely regarded as one of the most significant athletes in modern history.
The way he used his platform to promote change has been compared to legendary boxer Muhammad Ali's support of the anti-war movement, and US athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos giving the Black Power Salute at the 1968 Olympics.
"To even be in the same conversation with the likes of [them], is extremely humbling," he says. "But more importantly, I just try to stay focused on the work.
"What can we do to help people? And how do we collectively move forward as a society? And, ultimately, how we build a society that works for everybody. That feels like a very simple principle that has been lost.
"I know in the US specifically, we have a lot of work to do there. I hope we begin taking the steps to get back to a place where we are actually addressing people's needs. And create a society that is equitable for everyone."
Additional reporting: Pat Nathanson

Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin and extremely long cloud emerges, only to disappear again. The wispy formation appears near the volcano Arsia Mons and gradually elongates until it reaches over 1,000 miles—about the distance from New York to Kansas City as the crow flies—before dissipating. This cycle then repeats for several months.
Since it was first recorded by a probe in 2018, scientists have been unable to find a plausible explanation for the existence of this cloud, often referred to as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until now. Recently, researchers successfully modeled the cloud’s formation for the first time, their results suggesting that it may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in any planet’s atmosphere.
“We found that we needed to include some exotic physics… physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before,” Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Paris’ Sorbonne Université and lead author of the study, said in a press release. “Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.”

Angry players urge ATP rethink over doubles cuts
- Published
More than 150 men's doubles players - including British world number one Henry Patten and the legendary Bryan brothers - have urged the ATP Tour to rethink "drastic" changes which they believe could kill the format.
In a show of collective action, the players have written an open letter to the men's governing body as they fight proposals which would cut draw sizes and reduce prize money from 2028.
"We're at risk of losing a discipline of tennis which is historic - but has a big future," Dutch player Sem Verbeek, one of the architects of the letter, told BBC Sport.
"These proposals would destroy careers, livelihoods and dreams."
The ATP proposed halving the doubles draws at its flagship Masters 1000 events to 16 teams, with smaller tournaments reduced to eight teams.
The percentage of prize money devoted to doubles could fall from 20% to 10% - with the difference redistributed to singles players.
On Monday, a group of 137 current players, 28 legends and 20 national federations signed a letter which they hope will pressure the ATP into rethinking the proposals.
The tour's board - comprised of chairman Andrea Gaudenzi, four tournament representatives and four player representatives - will vote on the plans at next month's ATP Finals in Turin.
The doubles reform is part of a wider review by the ATP, which it says is designed to "strengthen" the tour from 2028.
The ATP aims to create "a more sustainable long-term model", insisting it wants to "maintain the important role" of doubles.
"Commercial success matters. Fairness, player welfare and the long-term health of tennis matter just as much," the players' letter says.
"Let us grow tennis together, without leaving doubles players behind."
Why is doubles under threat?
The proposals provoked an angry response from the men's doubles cohort when they were revealed in July.
British pair Lloyd Glasspool and Julian Cash, who won Wimbledon in 2025 and became world number ones, accused the ATP of trying to "kill part of the sport".
Others within tennis believe reform is needed. They suggest a 20% share of the prize money for doubles is disproportionate to the interest shown by fans.
The doubles players argue the ATP should do more to promote their discipline and attract greater audiences, pointing out it is the format played by most club members and therefore more relatable.
The ATP says the proposals are based on data-led analysis centred on costs, revenue and viewership.
With fewer singles players now competing in doubles, it believes the current size of the standalone doubles events puts severe strain on tournaments.
"We support progress. We also understand the need to grow the sport, strengthen tournaments and increase commercial value," the players' letter says.
"Still, the proposed reforms go much too far."
Might the dispute lead to legal action?
Reigning Wimbledon champion Patten recently told BBC Sport the players were facing "an uphill battle", but remained "optimistic" the tour would consider counter-proposals. Since Wimbledon there have been several meetings between both sides, including recently at the Shanghai Masters.
Many players still believe there is little appetite for negotiation from the ATP. But ATP sources insist a compromise is likely to be found.
Mike and Bob Bryan - the identical twins considered the greatest doubles pair of all-time - said they would support the group considering legal action to protect their discipline.
In 2005, the American brothers led players in a lawsuit against the ATP, when it planned radical changes to doubles.
"The tour's in the healthiest financial state it's ever been - in our opinion it should be creating more opportunities," Bob Bryan told BBC Sport in an interview at Wimbledon in July.
Mike Bryan added: "These proposed changes are anti-competitive. That's the stance we had to take in 2005. We still believe in doubles and we believe in the players fighting for this."

In 2018, anatomists at the Toho University Graduate School of Medicine, Tokyo, Japan, performed a sleep deprivation experiment on lab mice. Mice usually sleep for 12 hours a day. In this experiment, researchers induced sleep deprivation using the ‘gentle handling method’ during sleep hours so that the mice could sleep only for six hours daily.
They discovered that liver fat content in sleep-deprived mice increased without total weight gain compared to another group who were allowed to sleep normally. The liver cells were stressed, and the activity of certain genes that escalate insulin resistance and fat content within liver cells also increased with sleep deprivation.
Experiment on rats
Three years later, a group of Chinese researchers at the Xinjiang Medical University went one step ahead. In this experiment, rats were severely sleep-deprived, turning into insomniacs. Liver enzymes, blood, and liver fat increased substantially. None of these changes were notable among rats who were allowed to sleep without distractions.
They also found the reason for increased liver fat in insomniac mice — the sympathetic nerves that supplied the liver, best known for their role in responding to stress and danger, were hyperactive. When insomnia was treated with a sleeping pill in these stressed rats, the liver fat was reduced with adequate sleep.
There are lessons here, of mice and men. Sleep is an underrated activity among humans. Sometimes, the intentional and forced lack of sleep ‘to increase productivity’ is advertised by men in power to showcase their self-proclaimed metahuman nature. During an interview in 2011, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he had become a workaholic and hardly slept for 3.5 hours in a day, and that yoga and pranayama routine kept him energised and awake.
But medical science has a different story to tell. A study of nearly 55,500 people from Europe showed that those who slept 7-8.5 hours daily had higher life expectancy than those who slept less than seven hours. In those between ages 50 and 75 without sleep disturbances, the expectation of living longer without chronic disease development was significantly higher.
And yoga interventions improved overall sleep quality, efficiency, latency, and duration, contrary to all claims.
Healthy sleep
Sleep is a vital function of human life and accounts for up to one-third of the lifespan. Contrary to normal belief, during sleep, the brain is not ‘resting’ but is engaged in various activities necessary to improve well-being, increase life, and especially impact the liver. The minimum required duration for ‘healthy’ sleep is seven hours.
When 10,000 persons with sleep disorders were followed up for one year, incident fatty liver disease was noted in 14, while in those without sleep disorders, it was only six. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease association was significantly higher among persons with shorter sleep duration (less than six hours per night) and excessive daytime sleepiness. A high-quality study showed that inadequate sleep duration was strongly associated with an elevated risk of developing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and adequate sleep helped prevent it. With every one-hour decrease in sleep time from the recommended seven-eight hours, the risk of fat deposition in the liver increased by 24% compared with those who slept adequately.
However, when people who lost sleep during the weekdays caught up on the debt during weekends (known as weekend catch-up sleep), the development of fatty liver disease reduced significantly. Compared with non-nappers, long daytime nappers (more than 60 minutes) had a higher risk of developing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
Identification
Correlation may not be causation, but with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which is associated with other conditions such as obesity, high blood pressure, increased waist-hip ratio, low functioning thyroid, and high blood cholesterol, studying and identifying independent associations make realistic sense.
In people who sleep less than six hours at night, have a persistently poor sleep quality, or nap more than one hour during the day, independent of other disease conditions, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease development was a strong association. The next time someone brags that sacrificing time and quality of sleep is an achievement associated with success, know that success comes with fatty liver disease. And it is not worth it.
(Cyriac Abby Philips is a senior consultant and physician-scientist at the Liver Institute, Rajagiri Hospital, Kochi)
