Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Q2 FY27 marked a major milestone for Ather Energy as the listed electric vehicle (EV) major turned profitable for the first time. The Tarun Mehta-led company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹1.3 Cr during the quarter under review compared to a net loss of ₹154.1 Cr in q2 FY26 and a net loss of ₹51.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. This was also the first EBITDA-positive quarter for Ather as margins improved to 4.9% from -9.6% in Q2 FY26. Excluding other income, the EV maker’s EBITDA margins stood at roughly 0.8-1%, while adjusted gross margins further improved to 24%. With this, the EV maker has achieved a milestone that most of its new-age rivals, including listed Ola Electric, is yet to crack. Such is the contrast that Goldman Sachs recently downgraded its outlook on Ola Electric to “sell”, citing the Bhavish Aggarwal-led company’s challenging path towards turning positive cash flow. However, Ather is not yet “out of the woods,” insisted CEO Mehta during the company’s earnings call. Rather than prioritising profit after tax (PAT), he said that the company is focused on capacity addition to ramp up its sales volumes and bolster its top line. Hence, it is planning to invest ₹122 Cr to expand the combined capacity of its existing factory in Karnataka’s Hosur and its upcoming unit at Maharashtra’s AURIC by another 2.25 Lakh units per year. This would bolster its total installed capacity to 11.4 Lakh units by Q2 FY28 – a core part of its medium-term strategy. With its maiden profitability quarter out of the way, how is Ather planning to continue the momentum going forward? Fixing The Capacity Gap Ather believes that capacity addition is its crucial bottleneck as supply, and not demand, is the overhang on its performance. “Pre-orders are up 108%, registrations are up 60% and production is up 45%, all year on year,” noted Mehta. He added that while the company sold 33,000 units a month in the previous quarter, their internal estimates indicated unrealised sales of 20,000 units a month. Hence, the Hosur capacity addition could have an immediate impact. Given the factory is already up and running, Ather plans to scale the installed capacity of 35,000 units per month at the unit by another 6,000 in Q3 FY27 itself. That said, the expansion at its AURIC plant could take longer as it will only go live by Q4 FY27. On the margin front, Mehta explained that elevated commodity prices of raw materials like aluminium, copper, and plastics hurt gross margins by 9.4% during the quarter. He, however, added that temporary interventions like price hikes temporarily managed to counter these elevated costs. “We believe roughly 5.3% of the (overall) margin improvement we have driven over the last two quarters is broadly structural in nature. This is largely because price hikes seem to have landed well in the market… More temporary levers include SKU management and pulling back incentives or other support mechanisms,” added Mehta. However, he noted that the company will only be able to utilise the aforementioned internal ‘temporary levers’ (which brought 2.7% in margin improvement between Q4 FY26 and Q2 FY27) for a finite period if supply constraints and commodity prices remain elevated. “If either situation eases, we may open up these levers (incentives and more SKUs) again,” added Ather CEO. Why Konarc Is The Key To Ather’s Future Ather’s recently launched mass-market model Konarc appears to be one of the critical pieces that has unlocked its profitability. The company plans to focus on this segment to foster growth going forward. “Konarc focuses on the fundamentals, targeting more petrol-scooter buyers to buy electric,” Mehta said. He cited features that cater to the mainstream audience’s practical needs, such as 14-inch front wheels, longer rear suspension, a metal body, a centre stand and a 10-year battery warranty. Konarc also offers a potential margin advantage compared to other products like Ather’s Rizta. The model is already a few thousand Rupees lower than Rizta on a like-for-like basis, and the management expects Konarc’s margins to further improve by around 6-7 percentage points against Rizta going forward. “We could reduce the average ex-showroom price customers experience without affecting gross margins … Konarc is a useful lever that could allow us to improve margins without pushing prices up further, or perhaps reduce the average ex-showroom price a little while maintaining margins, assuming commodities do not ease,” noted Mehta. That said, the company is not planning to hike prices barring further cost pressure from commodity inflation. The CEO also shed light on how Ather had strategically rolled out Konarc to thread the needle between increasing sales and protecting margins. While the company had initially planned to launch Konarc’s entry-level variants first, the management saw that the demand for their existing 450 and Rizta scooters was outstripping the supply. This led to a decision to introduce the mid-level Konarc variants into the market to avoid lower-margin products from cannibalising their demand. Ather now plans to launch Konarc’s entry-level SR1 variant only once their additional capacity in AURIC is online, enabling them to drive volumes without bringing down margins. It seems Ather might finally have figured out the key to profitability lies in pricing, cost management, and product mix. Expanding the market through Konarc is another win for the company as well. But it still has to overcome the hurdles of commodity costs, effective capacity expansion, and converting demand into deliveries.

Caribbean seeks reparations and questions role of monarchy before King Charles visits
The royals are coming, and the Caribbean wants to be heard
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- The royals are coming, and the Caribbean wants to be heard.
Islanders are seeking slavery reparations from Britain, a formal apology for its role in the slave trade and greater independence from the former colonial power.
The Bahamas National Reparations Committee said it already knows what awaits the Caribbean as King Charles III and Queen Camilla prepare for this week's trip: “Schools emptied of children who will stand in the sun and wave for the Crown that has taken everything from their ancestors and comes back smiling.”
Charles is expected to visit the Bahamas on Tuesday to begin the nine-day trip to the Caribbean. His last official visit to the archipelago was in July 1973 as a prince who granted the Bahamas independence, ending 300 years of British rule. But the Bahamas remains a Commonwealth realm, along with six other Caribbean nations that recognize Charles as their king and head of state.
While in the Bahamas, Charles is scheduled to visit Clifford Park, where the archipelago’s black, turquoise and yellow flag was raised for the first time more than half a century ago.
His visit will raise important questions, said Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.
“Why do we still have a king? What does this person really represent to us? Why is he coming and how will that benefit us?” she said.
A psychology professor at the University of the Bahamas, Campbell-Dean said she recently mentioned Charles’ upcoming visit to her students, and they were not excited. She responded: “I know y’all might not care about this man who is coming, but here’s why this is of importance.”
Leaders across the Caribbean have long been pushing for an apology and reparations from Britain.
In early September, Jamaica took its case for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. It was an unprecedented legal maneuver, even though the British government has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.
After three days in the Bahamas, Charles is scheduled to fly to the South American country of Guyana. The former British colony was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the region during the colonial era, with thousands of slaves uprising during the 1823 Demerara rebellion on the plantation owned by the father of former British Prime Minister William Gladstone.
More than 200 slaves were killed as a result; several were decapitated and their heads placed on poles.
In a recent interview with ITV News, Guyanese President Irfaan Ali said Charles has “rightfully recognized slavery as the darkest days in human history.”
“Moving to the apology is the next step,” he added. “You exploited the region. You destroyed lives. You created underdevelopment.”
While in Guyana, Charles is expected to meet with Ali and elected leaders of Amerindian villages known as “toshaos.”
Nikita Miller, toshao of Chinese Landing, a rural Amerindian community in northern Guyana, said she was not invited.
She noted that her community has been mired in a decades-long land fight with miners seeking to extract gold from the area, and she would have liked the opportunity to talk about an issue that affects other toshaos as well.
“We have been suffering,” she said. “We want the government to respect Indigenous rights. … We have long-standing issues with our land.”
Miller said she believes the king’s visit might help improve things for Guyana overall, but not for Amerindian villages.
After two days in Guyana, Charles is scheduled to fly to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and meet with leaders of 56 member states. Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders have said slavery reparations should dominate conversations.
The British royals have long visited Jamaica, but it’s not on Charles' itinerary this time.
It’s just as well, said 51-year-old Rastafarian Steven Bennett.
“We don’t need any royal wave or photo-taking while the wounds of our ancestors are still being ignored. He still refuses to formally apologize for chattel slavery,” Bennett said. “Until the British monarchy is ready to stand on Jamaican soil, look us in the eye, apologize, and talk about actual repair and restitution, he has no business here. We want justice, not a parade.”
Jamaica in recent years has been pushing to oust Charles as head of state and become a republic like Barbados did in 2021.
Antonio Williams, a 25-year-old university student, said young Jamaicans have zero connection to the Crown.
“I think Buckingham Palace has read the room after the absolute PR disaster of William and Kate’s Caribbean tour a few years back,” he said, referring to the 2022 visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales to the region, where they faced protests and calls for reparations.
“We are actively moving toward becoming a republic and breaking these colonial ties,” Williams said. “Having the king visit now would just be incredibly awkward. Skipping us is a sign that they know their influence here is expiring.”
But 68-year-old retired civil servant Hermine Reid recalled with fondness how Charles’ mother, Queen Elizabeth II, used to visit Jamaica.
“It was always such a grand, respectful occasion, and people would line the streets in their Sunday best,” she said. “Things are very different now. It’s a little sad for my generation to see how much the relationship has fractured, but I suppose this is simply the modern era. Jamaica is growing up and charting its own course, and the king clearly recognizes that.”
___
Myers Jr. reported from Kingston, Jamaica.

New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know
- Published
New Zealanders will head to the polls on 7 November to elect a new government.
The rising cost of living, unemployment and healthcare are among the main concerns of voters, who will choose members of parliament.
There is no clear frontrunner, based on pre-election polls. The incumbent centre-right prime minister, Christopher Luxon, won the last election in 2023 with a promise to "build the economy".
Here is everything you need to know about New Zealand's 2026 general election.
How does the voting system work?
New Zealand holds a general election every three years and uses a Mixed-Member Proportional system or MMP.
Each voter makes two choices - the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.
The candidate in a constituency with the most votes wins and becomes an MP.
Political parties on the other hand must win at least 5% of the total party votes to secure a seat in parliament. The seats are also allocated proportionately - if a party wins 40% of the total party votes, it will get 40% of the seats alloted for parties.
The New Zealand parliament typically has 120 seats - 71 are allocated to constituencies and the remaining 49 are distributed to parties proportionately.
New Zealand elections rarely result in an outright majority and parties forge coalitions to form a government.
New Zealand adopted the MMP in 1996 to address concerns that small parties were being left out of the vote.
Who are the candidates?
The current government is led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, whose centre-right National party came to power in 2023. It governs in coalition with the ACT and New Zealand First parties.
His party emphasised economic management, restoring a budget surplus, and expanding KiwiSaver, New Zealand's retirement savings scheme.
The main opposition is the centre-left Labour party, led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins.
Labour has focused on reducing living costs, improving healthcare and transport, and investing in housing, jobs and public services.
National's coalition partners also have their own priorities. ACT, led by David Seymour, has advocated stricter immigration policies, while New Zealand First, led by Winston Peters, has proposed changes to voting eligibility, with the party proposing that voting in New Zealand should be restricted to citizens only.
The Green Party, co-led by Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson, is another player. It has campaigned on issues including wealth taxes, renewable energy and public services.
Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, is also competing for parliamentary seats, with housing, healthcare, education and constitutional reform among its priorities.
What are the main issues?
Cost of living is a major concern for New Zealanders.
A September 2026 Ipsos survey found that 63% of respondents identified inflation and the cost of living as one of the country's most important issues. Healthcare and hospitals came second at 44%, followed by the economy at 34%.
Unemployment is also a growing concern, with 21% of respondents identifying it as a major issue in the same survey. It overtook housing to become New Zealand's fourth most important issue.
When will the results be known?
Polling places open from 09:00 local time on 7 November (20:00 GMT 6 November). Voting ends at 19:00. Advance voting started on 26 October while overseas voting began earlier on 21 October.
Preliminary results will be released progressively from 19:00 on election night through New Zealand's official election results website. These initial results will not be the official final count.
The Electoral Commission is scheduled to declare official results on 27 November, after the counting and verification process has been completed.
A clear result on election night could provide an early indication of which parties are best placed to form a government. However, a tight race could delay negotiations if no party wins an outright majority.
New Zealanders may therefore have to wait beyond election night to find out which parties will form the next government and who will lead the country for the next three years.

Young adults in China looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having children or pets have found an answer: raising bricks.
Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.
Raising “brick babies” is easier than caring for house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day then waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article described the bricks as being “practically immortal”. “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”
A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on the Chinese social media platform Weibo.
Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick “parent” told Chinese media the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.
One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.
Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.
“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”
Young people in China are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society, such as having children and working long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the unemployment rate much higher.
China’s birthrate is in decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of intensely competitive studying, many young people are choosing to shun the rat race and opt instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low-effort, low-stress lifestyle; one well-suited to raising bricks.
The trend has become so popular that Chinese media have started to warn about the health risks.
Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of itchy eyes and runny noses. Xuedong Li, a retired professor of moss from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged people to keep their bricks in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.

‘Role confined to re-posting’: Bombay HC quashes FIR against student linked to controversial Op Sindoor post
The Bombay High Court said that the student's role was limited to re-posting and noted that she has already suffered custody.
The Bombay High Court on Tuesday quashed a FIR against a 20-year-old engineering student who was arrested in May last year for re-posting controversial posts on Operation Sindoor, India's military action in response to the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack.
A single-judge bench of Justice Milind Jadhav observed that she is “a young engineering student”, while allowing her plea. The court also said that the student's role was limited to re-posting and noted that she has already suffered custody.
"The post is undoubtedly contentious, arousing passion and hatred. However, the applicant's (student) role is confined to re-posting the said post which was already available on the social media platform," the court said, as per news agency PTI.
She had re-posted social media messages that purportedly ended with the phrase “Pakistan Zindabad” at a time when India and the border nation were in the middle of a military conflict.
The court reportedly took note of the post pertaining to religious sentiments and advised sensitivity and responsibility. "At first glance, it is seen that the contents of the post may have had the potential to create apprehension of disturbance between religious communities, however, the mere possibility that a publication may cause displeasure or resentment cannot, by itself, constitute sufficient ground for criminal prosecution," the order said.
The court also observed that the post was deleted within two hours and that the student had apologised.
Student claims ‘public humiliation, casteist abuse’ over reposting
The student, represented by advocate Farhana Shah, had challenged the college’s May 9, 2025 decision to rusticate her, calling it “arbitrary and unlawful”.
She was subsequently arrested, remanded to judicial custody, and denied bail by a Pune magistrate. The Bombay High Court had later granted her bail on May 25, 2025.
The student argued that she re-posted a message on Instagram from a user, and claimed she faced public outrage and abuse both on and off campus due to the outrage.
Though she deleted the post and issued an apology, the college proceeded with her expulsion, alleging that her actions were “anti-national” and posed a threat to campus harmony, her petition alleged.
The petition stated that, despite her re-posting the message without any ill intent, she had to face "public humiliation, casteist abuse, and was branded with derogatory and communal terms" both within and outside the college campus.
“Although she deleted the post following the controversy, she was rusticated from the college, which claimed she had anti-national sentiments and posed a risk to the campus community and society,” it added.

The Cerberus quadruped robot sold by Radeco is a modified version of the Boston Dynamics robot Spot upgraded with military-grade equipment and designed to detect dangerous substances.
Credit:
Radeco
Hundreds of employees at the US robotics firm Boston Dynamics signed a petition calling for executives to halt a sale of the company’s robot dogs to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement—but executives stood by the deal, while saying the robots would not be weaponized.
On September 25, the Department of Homeland Security contract awarded $1.3 million to a Connecticut company called Radeco to provide ICE with modified versions of Boston Dynamics’ quadruped robots. But Boston Dynamics workers sent the petition letter with more than 300 signatures—half of them anonymous—to the company’s executives in early September and shared copies with The Boston Globe and WBUR public radio station.
“Many of us have gotten messages from friends and family, asking us in disbelief and horror if this news is true, and how we can live with ourselves if it is,” according to the petition. “The risk for Boston Dynamics is simply too great to continue with this deal.”
The petition described the signatories as employees who normally “love showing off what we do to our friends, family and the world” and who “love challenging ourselves to innovate and change the perception of what robots can do.” The 300 signatures come out of a total Boston Dynamics workforce of approximately 1,400 people.
Spot’s Cerberus upgrade
The ICE contract covers the purchase of four Boston Dynamics Spot robots that were modified by Radeco to be marketed as a robot platform named Cerberus. The contract describes these Cerberus robots as being intended to “detect radiation, toxic gas leaks and explosive threats in urban environments or disaster zones,” along with enabling other remote observation and inspection missions.
A centerpiece of the upgraded robot is an oxygen sensor that is intended to “ensure the air quality is breathable when personnel are placed in confined spaces such as tunnels.” The Cerberus robot dog also has a camera equipped with 30-times zoom capability, 360-degree cameras, and infrared thermal imaging.
The Cerberus robot dog would come with an optional Spot robotic arm that enables it to manipulate objects and open doors, along with providing additional camera views when extended. The ICE contract describes the robot as being generally capable of navigating complex industrial environments on its own and executing “repeatable autonomous missions with minimal human intervention.”
Such a purchase was justified in the ICE contract as supporting the Homeland Security Task Forces’ mission to carry out “counter-illicit cross-border tunnel operations” and dismantling “cross-border human smuggling and trafficking networks” being conducted by “criminal cartels, foreign gangs and transnational criminal organizations throughout the United States.”
“Spot robots are tools that help keep people out of harm’s way,” a Boston Dynamics spokesperson told Ars in a statement. “Regardless of any political implications or personal feelings about the organizations involved, if our robot can help keep people safe, we believe it should.”
From fighting transnational crime to deportations
Boston Dynamics has also emphasized that the robots would primarily be used by ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations unit that is focused on combating transnational criminal organizations, according to WBUR.
However, the Brennan Center for Justice has documented the Homeland Security Investigations unit as frequently being involved in deporting undocumented workers and conducting workplace raids during the first administration of President Donald Trump. These operations occurred between 2018 and 2021, before being halted by US Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas early in the term of President Joe Biden.
During Trump’s second term that began in January 2025, the Homeland Security Investigations unit once again diverted thousands of agents to immigration enforcement and deportations after one of Trump’s executive orders redefined the unit’s primary mission, according to the Immigration Policy Tracking Project.
The Boston Dynamics employee petition specifically referenced an ICE and Homeland Security Investigations workplace raid that detained 475 primarily South Korean workers at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America facility in Georgia on September 4, 2025. Hyundai Motor Group became the parent company of Boston Dynamics after acquiring the US robotics company in June 2021.
“We cannot be proud of working at Boston Dynamics when that work is being used by a government agency that brutalizes civilians, including some of our own colleagues at Hyundai,” according to the employee petition. “All elements of the ICE organization, not just Enforcement & Removal Operations, have worked to sow fear among all people living in this country.”
That single largest immigration enforcement operation of its kind sparked public outrage in South Korea and led to South Korean leaders questioning the country’s business investments in the United States. However, Hyundai has maintained its operations at the US electric vehicle production at the Metaplant America factory and still plans to deploy thousands of Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robots starting at its US facilities.
Boston Dynamics says Spot won’t be weaponized
The Boston Dynamics leadership team has stood by the ICE contract with Radeco, which would mainly involve Boston Dynamics providing technical support for the modified robots, according to The Boston Globe.
The company also responded to the employee petition via an email from Amanda McMaster, former interim CEO for Boston Dynamics. That email was obtained and quoted in part by both The Boston Globe and WBUR.
“We believe this decision is in line with our purpose of ethically advancing intelligent machines in service of humanity,” McMaster wrote in her email. She urged workers to “respect and accept this decision, even if you do not agree with it.”
McMaster also pointed to the company’s terms and conditions for sale of the Spot robots that prohibit “intentional use of the Product to harm or intimidate any person or animal, as a weapon, or to enable any weapon.” The company previously signed an open letter opposing the weaponization of “advanced-mobility general-purpose robots.”
The Boston Dynamics spokesperson told Ars that the company has “worked productively” with the Department of Homeland Security and Homeland Security Investigations unit for years, and said the latter have abided by the company’s terms and conditions of sale.
The robotics company said it would also “take immediate action” if any customer misused Spot, although it said “there have been no cases of a customer violating those terms and conditions” while working with the Department of Homeland Security and other “public safety agencies.”
“That would include specific steps like voiding the warranty, refusing all future software updates, terminating their license, taking any appropriate legal action available to us, and likely never selling to that customer again,” said the Boston Dynamics spokesperson.
Future workforce concerns
The Boston Dynamics employee backlash to the ICE contract comes as the company is developing a new advanced robotics and AI facility in Waltham, Massachusetts, near its headquarters. The $100 million project includes creating 1,250 new jobs by 2033, according to a company press release.
The ICE contract represents “a complicated and emotionally charged topic for many people, including some of our own employees,” said the Boston Dynamics spokesperson. “As our company continues to grow at a rapid pace, we will continue welcoming a highly diverse group of employees with views on every side of the social and political spectrum.”
But as Boston Dynamics ramps up its production capabilities and deployment of robots such as Spot and Atlas, the employees who signed the petition expressed concerns that the company’s association with the ICE contract will threaten both workforce hiring and retention.
“We fear we will lose teammates over this decision, and worry about the risk it creates to achieve our shared company goals,” according to the petition. “This decision makes Boston Dynamics a less attractive employer—it will make it more challenging to build the team we need as we scale.”

Trump administration illegally fired James Comey's daughter, judge rules
- Published
The US justice department illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey, a federal judge has ruled.
Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father, a critic of US President Donald Trump, and because of her perceived political affiliations.
Judge Jesse Furman ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.
A spokesperson for the justice department said in a statement that it disagreed with the decision and "will appeal in due course".
In his ruling, Judge Furman said Comey's dismissal violated the US Constitution as well as her right to a fair legal process.
He said the US attorney general can fire federal prosecutors but only "in a particular manner and only for certain reasons".
Furman noted that in Comey's role, "she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases and consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike".
Comey has worked on cases against the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs, who was convicted on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends last year.
Furman ordered that Comey be given back pay from July until December 2025, when she accepted a new job.
In a statement, Comey's lawyers said: "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
Comey had previously said the only reason she was told about her firing was that it "came from Washington".
A complaint filed by her lawyers in September 2025 stated that they believed Comey had been fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both".
The justice department said in court filings that the decision was made by former Attorney General Pam Bondi.
The Trump administration has twice brought charges against James Comey, including for allegedly lying to Congress, but that case was dismissed by a judge who said the prosecutor who brought the case was unlawfully appointed.
Earlier this year, the justice department charged Comey with knowingly and wilfully making a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm, on the president. He has denied any wrongdoing.
The case stems from a 2025 Instagram post shared by Comey that contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump.

U.S. measles cases more than double what they were last year as outbreak spreads
The U.S. is grappling with its worst resurgence of measles in decades, with cases particularly high in the state of Pennsylvania.
New data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows there have been more than 4,580 measles cases across the U.S. since Oct. 22, which is more than double the number for the whole of 2025.
The vaccination status of 96% of those who contracted measles in 2026 was "Unvaccinated or Unknown," according to data from the CDC.
A measles outbreak across Pennsylvania has grown as officials urge residents to get fully vaccinated against the disease.
At least 1,338 cases of measles have been confirmed in 44 counties across the state so far this year, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health on Friday. There were 21 new measles cases as of Oct. 21. More than 250 people have been hospitalized and 5 people have died, the department also said.
In Lancaster and Mifflin counties, two of the counties with the highest number of cases, local Amish communities, which have low vaccination rates, are being impacted the most. Of the five who have died, three lived in Lancaster County
On Thursday, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen held a roundtable with Mifflin County healthcare providers to assess their needs in combatting the disease.
"Our state metrics and data tell part of the story of the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania, but listening to the people on the ground caring for people in affected communities like Mifflin County is essential to refining our public health response," Bogen said in a statement.
One of the best ways to protect oneself from getting the measles is vaccination, according to health officials. Two doses of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine known as MMR, is nearly 97% effective against measles, according to the CDC. One dose is about 93% effective.
In Pennsylvania, the health department said healthcare providers have seen more residents interested in getting vaccinated for measles. Across the state, more than 39,000 measles vaccines were administered during the first three weeks of October – higher than an average of 25,000 vaccines administered across the state in one month, the health department said.
Earlier this month, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a disaster emergency after rising measles cases. There have been over 160 confirmed measles across the state, according to Oct. 20 data from the New York State Department of Health.
Utah has also experienced a high number of measles cases. More than 700 people in Utah have been diagnosed with measles this year, according to Oct. 20 data from the Utah Department of Health and Human Services. There have not been any measles diagnoses in the state in 3 weeks, according to the department.
In South Carolina, which was dealing with an outbreak earlier this year, there have been at least 997 measles cases in 2026, according to the South Carolina Department of Public Health. The outbreak ended in April.

One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

Manchester United: Players to return to training on Tuesday but uncertain if Michael Carrick will be in charge
Man Utd beaten 3-0 by Bournemouth at Old Trafford to heap the pressure on head coach Michael Carrick; captain Bruno Fernandes was dropped and United are eight games without a win; players set to return to training on Tuesday after Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox met for talks on Monday
Monday 26 October 2026 20:13, UK
Manchester United's players are set to return to training at Carrington on Tuesday - but it is still uncertain whether Michael Carrick will be in charge.
United head coach Carrick was at Carrington on Monday to watch the club's U21s take on Hull in a behind-closed-doors game.
The first-team players had a scheduled day off but Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and Jason Wilcox, director of football, also met at the training base, with their talks focused on next steps following Sunday's 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth.
It remains to be seen what the United hierarchy, which includes Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the part-owner, will decide.
United's defeat to Bournemouth saw Carrick drop captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench after he questioned his tactics following the 4-1 Champions League loss to Como. It extended United's winless run to eight games across all competitions.
Carrick has overseen United's worst start to a Premier League season. They are 16th in the table, with seven points from their seven games, and just one point adrift of the relegation zone.
Carrick was initially appointed as United boss in January 2026 on a contract until the end of the season, following Ruben Amorim's sacking earlier in that campaign. He delivered a brilliant run of results, winning 12 of 17 matches to earn a third-place finish in the Premier League and a return to the Champions League.
Carrick was nominated for Premier League Manager of the Season and, in May, signed a new contract running to 2028.
How a 'strange day' at Carrington unfolded
Sky Sports News' Danyal Khan:
"It's been quite a bizarre, strange day at Carrington. This morning, we saw director of football Jason Wilcox and CEO Omar Berrada arrive quite early. A few players were in receiving treatment on injuries. Captain Bruno Fernandes, Patrick Dorgu, Manuel Ugarte and Benjamin Sesko were all in.
"Michael Carrick arrived just before 2pm. From what we understand, he was here to watch the U21s take on Hull City.
"It paints quite an awkward picture. On one end of the car park at Carrington you have the academy building, where Carrick would have been watching the U21s' game, while on the other side you would have had Wilcox and Berrada discussing his future as well as what is the future of Man Utd, what are the next steps potentially in the head coach position.
"As far as we know, no talks between Carrick and Wilcox happened. It's quite tough when you look at the timeline because the game will have finished around 4pm.
"We saw Wilcox leave Carrington around 4.30pm. We understand Carrick left around 4.45pm. Would they have had talks today? It remains to be seen.
"Carrick's future remains in huge doubt and there's no further clarity on whether he will continue or not."
Why there hasn't been swift action on Carrick's future
Sky Sports News' Rob Dorsett:
"I thought this would happen pretty quickly. The fact it hasn't happened makes me think one of two things are going on.
"Probably the most likely is Man Utd's bosses are taking their time to consider who they want as a replacement. The worst-case scenario for Man Utd would be if they sacked Michael Carrick and the person they went for didn't want the job, or they couldn't agree a deal with them and they were left in limbo for days, possibly weeks.
"We know it happens in football all the time - clubs try to set up a replacement before they get rid of the incumbent.
"The second thing is they are very conscious - and it was made clear to them at Old Trafford - just how popular Michael Carrick is among the Man Utd support.
"The same thing happened with Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2021 - he gave the most incredible departure video, despite being sacked by Man Utd.
"The club wanted to make sure it ended amicably. I think Man Utd bosses are thinking the same thing here. There might not be an exit video from Carrick but they want this done humanely and respectfully.
"If they don't, the backlash from supporters could be even stronger."

Harry Kane becomes first Englishman in 25 years to win Ballon d'Or
LONDON — Harry Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d'Or on Monday thanks to his prolific scoring last season.
Kane scored 73 goals for club and country last campaign — he was Europe's top scorer — and smashed scoring records in Germany for Bayern Munich and at the World Cup, where he captained England to a third-place finish.
The 33-year-old Kane says winning the prestigious individual award was built on so much more.
"Anything is possible with hard work, when no one else is watching, to go through the ups and downs, to learn through resilience, determination and self-belief," an emotional Kane said in a message to young players, after reflecting on his early career struggles.
"My journey wasn't straightforward. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs," he added. "I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration as well."
Kane was followed in the voting by Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal — voted best young talent for a third straight year — 2024 winner Rodri and record eight-time winner Lionel Messi.
Kane thanked his teammates, coaches, parents, children — "It's past your bedtime" — and wife Kate, " my best friend. We've been through ups and downs for sure. You're my biggest supporter. You always want the best for me."
Kane led Bayern to the Bundesliga and German Cup double, scoring a hat trick against Stuttgart in the cup final. Bayern also reached the Champions League semifinals.
At the World Cup, he scored six times to pass Gary Lineker as England's all-time leading World Cup scorer and placed himself among the all-time top five in tournament history. His lineup lost to Argentina in the semifinals but beat Mbappé's France for third place, England's best World Cup placing in 60 years.
An Englishman hadn't won the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001.
"It's massive for England, for our country. (The ceremony) being here in London was a good omen for me," Kane said. "It's been too long. Certainly (there have been) incredible English players... To put us back on the map, to put us here with this trophy I'm extremely proud. Playing for England is my biggest honor, the thing I love to do the most."
England coach Thomas Tuchel told Kane the Three Lions are "lucky to have you as our leader."
"I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I'm delighted to see that you have now been formally recognized by the football world," Tuchel said.
Fans packed the streets and climbed light poles near the London Palladium, where the event was held, for a glimpse of the arriving athletes. Kane stopped to sign autographs on his way in.
They stayed through the ceremony and chanted Kane's name as he left the theater near Oxford Circus after midnight.
Kane planned to celebrate with family and friends, but just a little.
"We have a cup game on Wednesday so it can't get too messy," Kane said, noting he has an early Tuesday flight back to Munich in time for team training.
Monday's ceremony was held in London for the first time in recognition of the inaugural winner 70 years ago, England's Stanley Matthews in 1956.
Putellas hat trick of awards
Earlier, Spain star Alexia Putellas won her record-equaling third women's Ballon d'Or after leading her former club Barcelona to multiple trophies last season including the Women's Champions League.
Putellas, who joined London City Lionesses in the offseason, also helped Spain win the Women's Nations League last December.
The 32-year-old midfielder ended Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati's three-year reign.
Putellas won the prestigious award in 2021 and 2022, tore her ACL and saw Bonmati rise to stardom. Bonmati, who completed her women's Ballon d'Or three-peat in 2025, was not on this year's shortlist after breaking her leg in December.
There wasn't a women's Ballon d'Or until 2018, when Ada Hegerberg won it.
Putellas urged young players to approach the sport with "love and passion."
"Believe in yourself, that's the most important thing," she said. "If you have a dream, go for it, even if at some point you have to start from zero."
Putellas had joined Barcelona in 2012 and called her time at the Catalan club "something special."
"I'm really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player (at Barcelona)," she said. "What I experienced last year was like a perfect story."

Every morning, Michelle Seo receives a morning briefing from Chattiana, her Muse artificial intelligence agent.
Chattiana’s briefing lists Seo’s agenda and to-do list, and plucks water-cooler topics from the headlines in her various newsletters along with links to the sources.
“I'm kind of challenging myself as an introvert to start more conversations,” Seo, a San Diego-based public relations consultant, tells WIRED. The newsletter, she says, gives her a sense of the daily news and options for filling an awkward silence on a Zoom call.
Seo is far from the first person to consume her news with an AI assist. In fact, the trend has become so common that some news outlets are starting to produce content that treats AI agents—not human readers—as the intended audience. This can look like anything from feeds optimized for AI to pieces structured to allow agents to create personalized articles.
“We believe that the media ecosystem is changing,” says Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron. ”We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging, that LLMs are becoming more important in the way that people are consuming” their news.
Major publishers have responded to that change in a variety of ways. Many, including WIRED’s parent company Condé Nast, have signed deals to allow AI platforms to surface their content. Outlets are grappling with “generative engine optimization,” or GEO, strategies to ensure articles appear in responses to AI prompts. Last year, AIOSEO, a SEO plug-in for WordPress sites, launched a feature that provides websites with LLM.txt files, which help AI discover and interpret sites’ content.
Others have taken a more defensive posture: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally trained models on reporting. That case is still ongoing.
What Axios and a handful of others are trying, though, represents a more foundational shift in how the media operates—and who its stories are for.
“We have always said,” Cameron says, “that we want to be where the audience is.”
At the Digiday Publishing Summit in September, Axios announced the upcoming launch of Axios Direct: feeds designed for AI agents.
“We do believe that a significant portion of news consumption will move into AI systems, LLMs, and devices,” Cameron says. She describes the feeds as a more efficient way for agents to access Axios content, cutting back on narrative to prioritize structured data—more similar to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.
The two initial Direct feeds are aimed at corporate clients. The first, which launched this fall, gives the AI agents of Axios Pro Deals subscribers access to merger-and-acquisition content. The second feed will act as a source to train in-house large language models, and will launch next year.
Starting with feeds aimed at businesses makes sense. Corporate budgets tend to have more tolerance than individual subscribers for experiments, especially if these unproven concepts could offer even a slight business advantage. But the third Axios Direct feed, which the company plans to develop next year, will be consumer-facing—a way for individual subscribers to have Axios’s reporting sent directly to their agent. All three feeds will look similar to RSS feeds—not aesthetically pleasing, as they aren’t intended for the human eye, but instead taking the form of standardized lines of text.
While Axios is trimming its (already brief) content to satisfy AI, Every is taking a different approach. The six-year-old tech media and software company, which announced a $2 million funding round from investors including LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman last year, expects its subscribers to treat AI as almost an extension of themselves.
Every’s founder Dan Shipper says the most common way Every’s content differs from a typical article is that its writers include prompts in pieces whenever possible, allowing readers to test concepts themselves. An article about a new model, for example, includes a series of prompts the reader can copy-paste into AI, demonstrating how the model answers questions and evaluates input.
Certain types of articles—such as guides—also include buttons that readers can press to “Read With Claude” or “Read With ChatGPT.” Clicking pulls up a prompt, instructing AI to “Start with a tight summary: one paragraph, bulleted. Then offer to go deeper.” Writers pack stories with details without worrying about losing readers’ attention, knowing agents will pick out the most relevant bits.
Two years ago, the outlet launched its first “extendable” article: a long-form feature accompanied by a database of reporting, from interview recordings to news articles to YouTube videos. Readers could query a chatbot, which would fetch additional details from the database.
Recently, Every published a 8,000-word article about Codex that subscribers can consume in even more forms. Drawing from the database, subscribers’ agents can tailor a new piece—be it an article, podcast, or video—to suit their interests. One reader might want a bulleted summary, while another could request a short film of interview bits.
“As a writer, you have to make choices about what goes into the story you're telling,” Shipper says. “And there's always a question about, are those the right choices? Or, are those the right choices for a particular reader?” With AI, journalists no longer choose.
“People are gonna do crazy, crazy stuff with this,” Shipper adds.
As outlets eye AI agents as a new audience, another question looms: Can publishers actually make money off of this?
Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, a professor of communication at the University of Copenhagen, says that while the market of publishing for agents is “emerging,” it remains immature and “extremely uneven.” Major questions remain, he says, about price points and how AI agents will interact with content in the future.
Cameron and Allison Murphy, Axios’s chief operating officer, are optimistic about AI as an audience proxy. According to the executives, Axios’s short-form, highly structured style has already made the publisher a favorite for AI to pull from, when responding to prompts. “Time is money for crawlers,” Murphy says. “They don't want to have to go three quarters down the page to find the main point. So, that's something that's already benefiting us.”
But does AI crawling its content actually benefit Axios’ bottom line? Even if readers don’t actually visit the Axios homepage, the brand visibility in and of itself can be positive, Nielsen says. It’s not unlike publishers making content for social platforms like TikTok and Instagram that rarely bring viewers back to their websites.
Publications in general are grappling with how difficult it has become to monetize certain types of content when a chatbot can offer up answers on a silver platter. People only want to pay for information that other publications—and LLMs—don’t have. At Every, that means in-the-weeds guidance on AI and how to use it; at Axios Pro Deals, it’s speedy access to information that could move the market. An all-access Axios Pro Deals subscription costs $2,499 a year, while an annual Every subscription costs $288.
Shipper sees that $288 as a subscription for a human reader, along with their agents. “I may not want to read all of your stuff every month,” Shipper says. But if his subscription can include his agent, “I may want my agent to know it so that it can tell me, ‘Hey, this thing is important.’”
Murphy says that Axios’s starting point is one of acceptance: People are already using AI to absorb information, and that more people will be doing so in the near future.
“I also try to make it a little less existentially terrifying by thinking, this isn't the first time this has happened in media,” Murphy says. People get their news via social media, via short-form video, via podcasts. “It isn't really AI as the audience,” Murphy adds. “It's AI as a tool that helps us reach our audience.”

TL;DR: India received 759.4 mm of rainfall during the June–September 2026 monsoon, 12.6% below its long-period average. East and Northeast India recorded their lowest seasonal rainfall since 1901, while the South Peninsula received 24% less rain than normal. Although extremely heavy rainfall events rebounded to 388, southern reservoirs held 24.76 BCM against a ten-year average of 43.33 BCM. Historical records show repeated drought declarations in districts such as Ananthapuramu in Andhra Pradesh, while post-monsoon soil moisture remains below average in several states. Together, these indicators reveal an uneven monsoon impact and highlight areas requiring closer monitoring.
Context
India’s monsoon tells two stories this year. The country received 12.6% less rainfall than normal between June and September 2026, but the shortfall was far from uniform. Eastern and northeastern India received 26% less rain than average, while the southern peninsula recorded a 24% deficit.
The season began on a difficult note, with June rainfall nearly 40% below normal. July brought a brief recovery, with rainfall slightly above average, but the deficit returned in August and September. The rebound, in other words, did not erase the shortfall.
What does this mean for the land and the people who depend on the rain? The IMD had warned of a below-normal monsoon in May, when El Niño conditions were expected to develop. But the national rainfall deficit is only the starting point. To understand where drought risks are emerging, it is necessary to look beyond how much rain fell to where it fell, how long the dry spells lasted, and how much moisture remained in the soil.
Who compiles this data?
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) publishes rainfall data and monsoon forecasts, while the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (NCFC) monitors agricultural conditions using rainfall, soil moisture and satellite indicators. The India Drought Monitor, developed by IIT Gandhinagar’s Water and Climate Lab, tracks drought conditions using meteorological and satellite data.
Where can I download clean & structured data related to this?
Clean, structured datasets related to Indian rainfall, drought conditions, agriculture and water resources are available on Dataful.
Key Insights
India’s 2026 monsoon ranks among the weakest in decades, with sharp regional deficits
India received 759.4 mm of rainfall during the June–September 2026 southwest monsoon, just 87% of its long-period average (LPA). According to the IMD, this was the country’s fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall since 2001 and 13th-lowest since 1901. The national shortfall, however, conceals sharper regional deficits.
East and Northeast India received 1,016.3 mm, or 74% of its regional LPA, making it the lowest seasonal rainfall for the region since 1901. The South Peninsula received 542 mm, or 76% of its LPA, ranking fourth-lowest since 1901 and second-lowest since 2001. Northwest India received 94.1% of its LPA, while Central India recorded 97%, within the normal range.
The shortfall also affected the monsoon core zone, which includes much of India’s rain-fed agricultural area. It received 779.9 mm, which is below the lower limit of the normal category (782.8 to 881.2). Across India’s 36 meteorological subdivisions, 17 (42% of the area) recorded deficient rainfall, 18 (53%) received normal rainfall, and one, in Odisha (5%), recorded excess rainfall. At the district level, 282 of 741 meteorological districts (38% of total area) recorded below-normal rainfall, while 34 (5% of total area) received significantly below-normal rainfall. Another 312 districts (42% of total area) recorded normal rainfall, 90 (12% of total area) received excess rainfall, and 16 (2% of total area) recorded substantially above-normal rainfall.
Extremely heavy rainfall events rebound in 2026, driven by a July spike
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) classifies rainfall of 115.6–204.4 mm in 24 hours as very heavy and rainfall exceeding 204.4 mm as extremely heavy. During the June–September 2026 monsoon, India recorded 1,765 very heavy rainfall events and 388 extremely heavy events. Extremely heavy events rose from 296 in 2022 to 426 in 2023 and peaked at 473 in 2024, before declining to 303 in 2025 and increasing again in 2026. Very heavy rainfall events followed a different trend, rising from 1,875 in 2022 to a peak of 2,632 in 2024, before falling to 2,109 in 2025 and 1,765 in 2026. July 2026 alone recorded 269 extremely heavy events, the highest July count in since 2022, compared with 84 in 2025. These figures show that although the overall frequency of very heavy rainfall has declined since 2024, extremely heavy events rebounded in 2026.
Historical El Niño years show a recurring concern, but widely varying rainfall outcomes
Historical data in the IMD’s El Niño table show why the phenomenon matters when assessing India’s 2026 monsoon, but also why it cannot explain the season’s outcome on its own. Of the 17 El Niño years listed between 1951 and 2023, 12 recorded below-normal June–September rainfall, including seven with deficits exceeding 10%. Yet outcomes varied considerably: rainfall was 22.3% below normal in 1972 and 20.9% below normal in 2002, while 1994 recorded a 13.9% surplus and 1997 ended almost exactly at normal, despite being the only Strong El Niño among all.
Monthly figures reveal another important distinction. In 2002, July rainfall was 50.6% below normal, contributing to a seasonal deficit of 20.9%. In 2023, above-normal rainfall in July and September partly offset August’s 36.1% shortfall, leaving the season 5.3% below normal. A seasonal total can therefore conceal sharp monthly swings, just as a national average can mask regional rainfall deficits.
That distinction is relevant to the 2026 monsoon. India received 759.4 mm of rainfall, or 87% of its long-period average, with particularly large deficits in East and Northeast India and the South Peninsula. IMD reported that El Niño strengthened during the season, but the historical comparisons do not establish how much it contributed to this year’s shortfall. Nor does deficient seasonal rainfall alone establish the severity of agricultural drought.
Southern reservoirs fall to less than half their year-ago levels
The clearest concentration of pressure appears in the reservoir data. On 15 October, CWC’s 178 monitored reservoirs nationally held 68.58% of their live-storage capacity. Their storage was 16.44% below the corresponding ten-year average. Of the 178 reservoirs monitored by the Central Water Commission, on 15 October 2026, 105 held more than 80% of their ten-year average storage, while 73 were at or below that level. Of the latter, 31 had storage at or below 50% of normal.
The shortfall was concentrated in the South. Its 50 monitored reservoirs held 24.76 BCM, against a ten-year normal of 43.33 BCM, a deficit of 18.57 BCM. This accounts for approximately 74.5% of the net national storage shortfall of 24.93 BCM, including the effect of a small surplus in Central India.
State-level departures varied considerably. Storage was 61.50% below normal in Tamil Nadu, 59.33% in Andhra Pradesh and 51.63% in Telangana. Karnataka was 32.28% below normal, while Kerala was 17.67% below. These figures indicate a weaker reservoir position, but do not translate directly into equivalent reductions in water available to every user. Actual supply depends on the reservoirs serving an area, existing commitments, alternative sources and distribution systems.
The timing is also important. Tamil Nadu receives a substantial share of its rainfall during the October–December northeast monsoon, making subsequent rainfall and reservoir inflows important to watch. The 15 October 2026 figures are therefore a snapshot, not a final assessment of water availability for the coming months. Even so, the regional imbalance is clear: the national storage figure masks the depth of the shortfall in southern India.
District data show where rainfall deficiency meets underlying drought vulnerability
It is also important to look at districts apart from broad regions. IMD’s seasonal rainfall distribution records 282 districts with deficient rainfall and 34 with large-deficient rainfall. Together, that is 316 districts, or approximately 42.6% of the 741 districts listed. Further, 312 districts are recorded in the normal category, 90 with excess rainfall and 16 with large-excess rainfall. The distribution confirms that the deficient season was far from uniform. It also needs to be interpreted precisely: a rainfall-deficient district is not automatically a district officially declared drought-hit.
The agriculture ministry’s Crisis Management Plan (CMP) for drought provides a list of districts where state governments declared drought from 2011-12 to 2025-26. It has 472 districts declared drought over the years, and such declarations peaked in 2015-16 with 294 districts declared drought-affected, and in recent years, it declined: 71 in 2023-24 (Karnataka 31, Maharashtra 15, Rajasthan 12, Andhra Pradesh 13), and only 5 in 2024-25 and 4 in 2025-26, all in Andhra Pradesh. Ananthapuramu was declared drought-affected in 11 years, followed by Barmer, Jaisalmer, Bellari and 14 other districts with declarations in 10 years each.
A separate 2024 district risk assessment by the Department of Science and Technology identifies underlying vulnerability. It places 91 districts in the very high drought-risk category and 188 in the high category, 279 districts in total. More than 90% of districts in the Very High category (83 out of 91) are located in Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, and Maharashtra. These classifications combine hazard, exposure and vulnerability. They identify relative structural risk, rather than establishing that all these districts experience drought. The left image provides the Drought exposure Map, while the right image shows the current drought conditions as on 21st October, 2026, according to the India Drought Monitor.
Root-Zone Soil Moisture overlaps with low reservoir storage levels in Southern India
The NCFC’s report dated 19 October 2026 provides a more recent indicator of agricultural conditions. It compares root-zone soil moisture for 8–14 October with the average for the previous ten years.
The report finds that root-zone soil moisture was similar to or better than the ten-year average in parts of Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh, eastern and northern Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. In contrast, soil moisture was below the ten-year average in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and the Northeast region.
The comparison suggests that the effects of the monsoon deficit were not uniform across the country and that some areas entered the post-monsoon period with less soil moisture than their historical average. For agriculture, root-zone moisture is particularly relevant because it reflects water availability in the soil where plant roots draw moisture.
The overlap between below-average soil moisture and low reservoir storage in parts of southern India warrants particular attention. At the same time, soil moisture at or above the historical average in parts of eastern and central India shows why a national rainfall deficit cannot be used as a proxy for conditions in every district.
The coming weeks will bring further evidence about how these conditions develop. In Tamil Nadu, the northeast monsoon and associated reservoir inflows will be especially relevant. Elsewhere, changes in soil moisture and water storage will help clarify whether the seasonal rainfall deficit translates into continuing agricultural or water-supply pressure.
Why does it matter?
A national rainfall deficit reveals little about whether a farmer’s soil holds enough moisture or a household can count on its water supply. In 2026, 316 of 741 meteorological districts recorded deficient or large-deficient rainfall, while southern reservoirs held substantially less water than their ten-year average. The NCFC also reported below-average root-zone soil moisture across several states in October 2026. Together, these indicators point to pressure on water availability, although local supplies depend on reservoir storage, existing commitments, alternative sources and distribution systems. Subsequent rainfall and reservoir replenishment will be particularly important for Tamil Nadu during its northeast monsoon season. Historical drought declarations and district-level risk assessments add another layer, helping distinguish the current rainfall shortfall from recurring drought exposure.
Key Numbers
- 13% below average: India received 759.4 mm of southwest monsoon rainfall in 2026, against a long-period average of 868.6 mm.
- 388 extremely heavy rainfall events: Up from 303 in 2025, an increase of approximately 28%, despite the deficient season.
- 316 of 741 districts: Recorded deficient or large-deficient seasonal rainfall, accounting for approximately 42.6% of the districts listed.
- 42.85% below average: Southern India’s monitored reservoirs held 24.760 BCM on 15 October, against a corresponding ten-year average of 43.327 BCM.

If you really want to get serious about AI performance, you'll want to upgrade to the 64-GB or 128-GB configurations—though third-party retailers like Amazon don't sell them. You'll have to buy directly from Apple for that, and the prices are exorbitant. But the 36-GB model that's on sale has plenty of juice for dipping your toe in the world of on-device AI, and it's a home run for video editors, designers, musicians, and engineers.
Beyond performance, it goes without saying that all MacBook Pros have the best speakers, displays, build quality, trackpads, and keyboards of just about any laptop. I test dozens of new laptops every year, and while some have come close (such as the Surface Laptop Ultra I just finished testing), none have taken the crown.
You might be wondering if waiting to see these new MacBooks next week is worth it. Maybe. I can't guarantee that this deal will stick around, and I don't know what these new MacBooks will be like. Rumors say that they will sport the same chip options as the current MacBook Pros, meaning we'd get an M5 Pro and M5 Max once again.
