FIAPF’s decision to make A-list status official, with Tokyo among the 17 festivals named, is unlikely to change much about the event, according to the filmmaker leading its competition jury.
Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer, the director of “Bad Boy Bubby” and “Ten Canoes,” was asked at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival’s jury press conference on Tuesday whether the classification mattered or was a redundant system.
“I think Tokyo has always been considered one of those festivals by most people who attend festivals. Tokyo was effectively an A festival. And so in that sense, I don’t think it makes a lot of difference,” de Heer said.
He allowed that the classification seems to be carrying more weight in determining the quality of films a festival can secure. “And so in that sense, it may help that it is officially now again A, but I don’t think it changes the festival so much,” de Heer said.
In March, FIAPF, the international federation of film producers’ associations, replaced its four-category accreditation system with a single list and designated 17 festivals as A-list, a term the industry had long used informally. They include Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Toronto, Busan, Shanghai, Cairo and Tokyo. Busan and Toronto made the list for the first time.
Korean producer Oh Jungwan, founder of Bom Film Productions (“The Foul King,” “A Tale of Two Sisters,” “A Bittersweet Life”), said de Heer’s answer covered it and that she was “not a film festival person.”
“So I don’t know what is A-list or not. So maybe probably A-list means good, so but as an audience, we’re not going to the festival because of their A-list or not. We just go to watch film and enjoy the feeling, the festival feeling,” Oh said.
Pressed by the journalist, who had hoped someone would call out a system that ranks some festivals above others, de Heer offered a final word: “It matters a great deal to some people, and not at all to others. And that is as it should be.”
The rest of the jury, Japanese actor Watanabe Makiko (“M/Other,” “Love Exposure,” “Tokyo Vice”), New York- and Tokyo-based producer Alex Lo of Cinema Inutile, whose credits include Jim Jarmusch’s Venice Golden Lion winner “Father Mother Sister Brother,” and Tokyo-based colorist Yov Moor (“The Taste of Things,” “Grand Tour”), did not weigh in on the question. The five-member panel will choose the Tokyo Grand Prix from 15 competition titles. The festival runs through Nov. 4.
De Heer was also asked about prospects for Australia-Japan co-productions. “It makes no sense for a Japanese film to shoot in Australia, it makes no sense for an Australian film to shoot in Japan. Europe is very good at doing co-productions only on a financial basis, really. Australia is not so good at that,” he said. Co-productions built on “a natural story where some things need to be shot in Japan, some things need to be shot in Australia” will always be possible, he added, “if the scripts come and if they are right.”
Lo, whose “Heads or Tails?” won best director at Tokyo last year, said producers in Europe, the U.S. and elsewhere “are increasingly seeking co-production opportunities,” largely because local government support is lacking.
On how a divided jury would settle on a winner, de Heer said the answer would depend on the situation. “I’m with four other very reasonable people, and I’m sure we can find a way through that we don’t end up with some sort of lesser compromised film, but a really interesting film that maybe some of us don’t like,” he said.
Oh, a Tokyo juror for the second time, recalled once arguing for seven hours on behalf of a film. “Every other jury [member] hated me,” Oh said, adding that she hoped she would not have to fight de Heer for seven hours this time.

Neha asserts that her message was “directed at the organisation’s struggles for democratic rights, student rights, accessible education and communal harmony”. Despite significant economic progress and sustained public health efforts, anaemia — driven significantly by iron deficiency — continues to be one of India’s most pressing public health challenges. Affecting over half of Indian women and almost three-fourths of children, anaemia contributes to maternal mortality, an intergenerational cycle of malnutrition, impaired cognitive development, reduced productivity and substantial economic losses. The Government of India’s 7X7X7 Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, which was launched recently, rightly recognises the multifactorial nature of anaemia through a comprehensive approach spanning prevention, screening, treatment, dietary diversification and behaviour change. Yet, one proven preventive intervention remains significantly underutilised.
The promise of fortification
That intervention is Double Fortified Salt (DFS) — salt fortified with both iodine and iron. Salt offers an unparalleled opportunity to address iron deficiency. Consumed daily by virtually every household across India, in predictable quantities regardless of income or geography, it is uniquely suited to deliver a preventive nutrition intervention at population scale. DFS also addresses one of the fundamental challenges of anaemia control — sustained compliance.
Delivering iron through an everyday food complements interventions such as iron supplementation and dietary diversification, whose effectiveness depends on regular adherence. India already has one of the world’s most successful public health platforms in Universal Salt Iodisation, with around 95% of households consuming iodised salt. Building on this existing infrastructure, DFS is already distributed to an estimated 76 million people across four States through government safety-net programmes. Global and Indian evidence strongly support DFS. A global review has shown that DFS can reduce anaemia by up to 21%. Randomised controlled trials in Bengaluru, Darjeeling, and Punjab, along with large-scale implementation in Uttar Pradesh, have shown improvements in iron status and confirmed that, when manufactured to validated specifications, DFS is acceptable to consumers, reduces iron deficiency, and is highly cost-effective. A DFS standard has been issued by the Government of India’s Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI), and the Government of India actually mandates DFS’ inclusion in the national school feeding programme (PM POSHAN and the national early childhood development programme- Integrated Child Development Scheme, or ICDS).
At an estimated cost of ₹14-₹20 per person annually, DFS represents one of the most affordable population-level nutrition interventions available, with a benefit-cost ratio of 4.2:1 for national DFS introduction, primarily driven by improved health outcomes and subsequent increases in labour productivity. India also possesses the manufacturing capacity to produce high-quality DFS at scale. Established fortification technologies, centralised salt production and existing laboratory infrastructure make quality assurance and regulatory monitoring simpler than for many other fortified foods.
What the barriers are
What has limited DFS from wider adoption? The barriers are now primarily institutional rather than technical. The next imperative is to accelerate its nationwide adoption and ensure last-mile access, particularly the Public Distribution System apart from social safety-net programmes, across all States through a central flagship scheme. Although DFS is recommended under PM POSHAN and ICDS, its integration into the largest safety net programme i.e., the Public Distribution System (PDS) — which reaches around 800 million beneficiaries — remains uneven because implementation depends largely on State governments. Greater policy commitment, dedicated financing, stronger quality assurance, wider commercial availability and consumer awareness are now needed to accelerate nationwide scale-up. These are implementation challenges — not technological ones — and are well within India’s capacity to address.
Like all public health nutrition interventions, DFS should be implemented within a robust regulatory framework. It should complement existing strategies under Anaemia Mukt Bharat, align with India’s sodium reduction goals, and continue to be accompanied by screening for haemoglobinopathies such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease. These safeguards are well recognised through experience of rice fortification programme and can be readily integrated into implementation and monitoring systems.
The launch of the revised AMB strategy provides renewed momentum to strengthen the preventive pillar of India’s anaemia response and advance the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
Potential to be a global model
India has already shown the world how science, policy, public systems, and public awareness can transform nutrition through Universal Salt Iodisation. By scaling DFS nationally, India can not only accelerate progress towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat but also contribute to global efforts to reduce iron deficiency by demonstrating an affordable, scalable model for other low- and middle-income countries.

South Africa meet Australia in third Test series-decider at Cape Town with careers on the line for tourists
Australia's Marnus Labuschagne may have one innings to save his skin as poor run continues in South Africa; Steve Smith faces late fitness test; series locked at 1-1 after South Africa's innings victory in Gqeberha; watch live on Sky Sports Cricket from 7.30am, Tuesday
Monday 26 October 2026 13:17, UK
Australia are about to play a Test match in Cape Town for the first time since the ball-tampering scandal back in 2018 that paused a number of their cricketers' careers.
Should they lose to South Africa this week in the series decider, live on Sky Sports Cricket, a number of careers could be ended.
Having been humbled by an innings and 31 runs in Gqeberha last time out, a game in which they were torpedoed for 99 in the first innings, the Baggy Greens need a response.

If that does not come, the reaction from the Australian media could be more abrasive than the piece of sandpaper Cameron Bancroft aimed to conceal down his trousers eight years ago.
The batting has been creaking for a while.
In the 4-1 Ashes thrashing of England last winter, it was held together by Travis Head, Steve Smith and Alex Carey as others toiled, while in South Africa so far the tourists have managed only three individual fifty-plus scores - one for Head and two for Matt Renshaw.
Without Head in Durban, things would have been even grislier. His second-innings 121 was 81 more runs than the next highest score by an Aussie in the game.
Even the great Smith - who received a ban for the role he played as skipper in 'Sandpapergate' in 2018, along with Bancroft and David Warner - has stuttered: three innings' in the 20s and a knock of three.
He was hampered by a neck problem in Gqeberha and faces a late fitness Test ahead of the winner-takes-all Cape Town finale.
If he fails that, it could aid Marnus Labuschagne's hopes of staying in the side.
Labuschagne and selector Bailey under big pressure?
Former Australia captain Ricky Ponting had branded Labuschagne's spot as "untenable" after a lean return at home to Bangladesh left him without a Test century in 43 innings, stretching back to the 2023 Ashes in England. That has now extended to 47 innings.
Labuschagne has had no trouble starting in South Africa, the country of his birth - reaching the 30s in three of his four outings. But he has not kicked on.
Pinned lbw. Sliced loosely to cover. Brilliantly caught by Simon Harmer at gully. And then a criminal dismissal as he inexplicably holed out to long-on in the second innings of the second Test, a game Australia were trying to save.
If he misses out this week, it could be curtains. If he plays and fails, it could be a similar story. If Australia fail as a team, perhaps pressure will mount on head selector George Bailey?
Former skipper Steve Waugh said before the Ashes that Bailey has previously shown a lack of "appetite" to make the big calls, while the selection of the now-jettisoned Nic Maddinson for the South Africa tour was panned at the time by Matthew Hayden.
Maddinson ditching after recall highlights Australia's issues
Maddinson, 34, had not played a first-class game since March 2025 due to a testicular cancer diagnosis and averaged 6.75 from his first three Tests back in 2016.
Hayden accused selectors of "disrespecting first-class cricket" and "promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we've seen in a generation of cricket."
Maddinson has not been as good as mediocre in this series, with his average a paltry 14 after amassing only 56 runs from four knocks - 48 of which came in one innings to punctuate a 33-ball duck, a four-ball duck and a 10-ball eight.
He has since been released from the squad, with Renshaw poised to open alongside Head in Cape Town.
Considering what he went through health-wise, people were rooting for Maddinson to perform but he hasn't. It raises the question over whether a younger player should have been given a go instead.
Ollie Davies, Sam Konstas and Campbell Kellaway were options. Nathan McSweeney, too.
The problem Australia have is that unlike in previous eras when they had players averaging north of 40 and banging out domestic runs - often in English county cricket as well as at home - waiting in the wings, they don't now.
All of the prospects mentioned above average mid-30s or lower in first-class cricket.
Will Bavuma extend excellent record as captain?
South Africa, by contrast, have a pretty much guaranteed source of runs in captain Temba Bavuma, whose brilliant 179 from 334 balls in Gqeberha means he is averaging 49.95 across his last 28 Tests.
His nuggety ton last time out was scored after he came in at 12-2.
He was at the other end as the Proteas slumped to 110-6 before pushing them to 425-9 and was ultimately left to celebrate a 12th win in 14 Tests as skipper.
This feels like a great chance to make that 13 from 15 unless Australia are able to pull something out of the bag in Cape Town.
Unlike in 2018, something within the rules this time.

Las Vegas, Oct 27: A United Airlines flight was diverted back to Las Vegas shortly after takeoff over the weekend due to what police said was a report of a passenger making a terroristic threat.

Anthony Albanese has admitted he got it wrong after telling parliament a $6m grant to a golf club in his electorate was to stop “raw sewage” going into the nearby river.
The grant given to Marrickville golf club in Sydney’s inner-west is under scrutiny as part of a larger $560m invitation-only grants scheme, which transparency advocates say largely funded projects promised at the 2025 election in Labor-held seats.
Infrastructure department officials told a Senate estimates hearing on Monday afternoon the $6m grant given to the club in Albanese’s electorate did not fund works to prevent raw sewage from flowing into the nearby river, contrary to the prime minister’s claims.
“I can confirm that sewerage is not a component of this grant,” the department’s assistant secretary, Jacinta McDonald, said.
The assistant education minister, Anthony Chisholm, defended the prime minister’s response, saying the scope had changed since the local council’s original proposal.
“I think that was part of the original plan. But as often happens, as the scope of these sorts of announcements happen, the scope can change, and the New South Wales government, is my understanding, stepped in in support of the sewerage work,” Chisholm said.
First reported by the ABC, Albanese, who holds honorary social membership at the club, has swatted away any criticism that he influenced, or benefitted from, the decision, which was signed off by another minister.
In question time in early September, the prime minister told the house the money would go toward “an environmental project stopping raw sewage going into the Cooks River during flooding”.
“[The golf club] has existed for a long time, almost a 100 years, and they have a septic tank because it is on the floodplain, when it floods in Marrickville raw sewage flows into the Cooks River – that is what the funding is for,” Albanese said in another response to questions about his involvement in the decision-making process.
The prime minister was grilled repeatedly by the opposition about the grant in question time on Tuesday afternoon and the shadow energy minister, Dan Tehan, accused the prime minister of misleading the parliament, and urged him to correct the record.
In response, Albanese conceded “it was not correct” to say the funding was for sewerage works but said it was a matter for the infrastructure department, and noted the council was finalising the design of the project – including improvements to the clubhouse, stormwater harvesting, a new toilet and landscaping.
The NSW government committed in September 2025 to address sewerage infrastructure at the club, he said.
“I’m advised that the club, of course, has a long history. And indeed, in the media release announcing the project, it spoke about the venue’s last major remodel being in 1947. So this is a local club, owned by the council,” Albanese said.
“The [federal] funding was going to be for sewerage. The New South Wales government have stepped in, which is appropriate given that New South Wales run water and sewerage.”

A recent review of international clinical practice guidelines published in The Lancet Rheumatology highlights a shift in the management of non-specific low back pain towards clinical assessment, patient education, physical activity, and exercise, while discouraging routine imaging when there is no suspicion of serious disease.
Examining guidelines issued between 1994 and 2026, the review underscores the importance of assessing symptoms and identifying warning signs before deciding on investigations or treatment. Bengaluru-based specialists said the approach reflected a growing emphasis on restoring function and avoiding unnecessary investigations and interventions.
Ravikumar Mukartihal, senior consultant orthopaedic and robotic joint replacement surgeon at SPARSH Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the approach had moved from investigation-driven care to one focused on clinical assessment and restoring function.
“Most cases of non-specific low back pain do not indicate a serious structural problem and can be managed without extensive investigations or invasive procedures,” he said.
Treatment should focus on understanding symptoms, reassuring patients, maintaining normal activities, prescribing appropriate exercises and physiotherapy, and using medication judiciously, he said.
Treat the patient, not the scan
Karuna Kabadi, neurosurgeon at Apollo Speciality Hospital, Jayanagar, said a disc bulge or prolapse described in an MRI report was an observation about the disc, not necessarily a diagnosis explaining the pain. “Many of us may be having disc bulges but do not have symptoms and feel perfectly fit,” she said.
Back pain can arise from muscles, ligaments, and joints, and may also be associated with systemic diseases. A disc bulge may cause symptoms when it irritates or compresses a nerve, resulting in shooting pain in the buttock or leg, commonly known as sciatica. A detailed history and clinical examination help doctors assess the likely cause, with imaging supporting the diagnosis where necessary, she said.
Ravikumar T., Head and Consultant of the Department of Orthopaedics at Ramaiah Memorial Hospital, said incidental findings on scans could cause unnecessary anxiety if patients interpreted them as proof that their spine was damaged.
“Treat the patient and not the scan,” he said, noting that disc bulges and mild degenerative changes were also seen in people without back pain.
Non-specific back pain can involve several factors, including muscle strain, weak core muscles, poor movement patterns, sedentary habits, stress and inadequate sleep. Clinical examination helps assess pain, movement limitations and neurological signs before treatment is decided, he said.
Movement over prolonged rest
The review found that most guidelines recommended taking a patient’s history, conducting a physical examination and assessing psychological factors, including risk-stratification tools where appropriate. Routine imaging was generally discouraged without indications of serious pathology.
For acute low back pain, recommendations commonly included self-management, heat therapy, spinal manipulation and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). For chronic pain, they included exercise therapy, psychological interventions and multidisciplinary care, with acupuncture and spinal manipulation recommended in some guidelines as part of broader treatment programmes.
Dr. Ravikumar T. said treatment had moved away from prolonged bed rest and early reliance on strong painkillers towards reassurance, education, continued activity and structured physical therapy.
“Movement is medicine,” he said, warning that avoiding activity out of fear of scan findings could cause muscle deconditioning and prolonged disability.
Dr. Kabadi said sitting for long hours and reduced daily movement contributed to mechanical back pain. Staying active, avoiding prolonged sitting and following guided physiotherapy and muscle-strengthening exercises could help, although consistency was essential.
When is a scan necessary?
Doctors stressed that discouraging routine imaging did not mean scans were unnecessary. Imaging remains important when there are warning signs of serious disease, progressive neurological deficits or persistent symptoms for which the findings could change treatment.
Surgery also has a role in selected patients, but decisions should be based on clear clinical indications rather than an MRI finding alone, Dr. Mukartihal said.
The specialists said the focus should be on appropriate clinical assessment and treatment tailored to each patient, with the aim of restoring movement and function while avoiding unnecessary investigations and procedures without overlooking serious underlying conditions.

Amgen's Imdelltra used in combination with AstraZeneca's immunotherapy Imfinzi reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to the Astra drug alone in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, according to data from a study presented at a major medical meeting on Saturday.
Imfinzi is currently the standard of care following chemotherapy for patients with this very aggressive and hard-to-treat disease whose cancer does not worsen after initial chemotherapy.
The study found that those given both drugs lived for a median of 21.1 months, compared with 12.7 months for those treated only with Imfinzi.
"If you give Imdelltra earlier and earlier, you get bigger clinical benefit," said Paul Burton, chief medical officer at California-based Amgen. He called the results "unprecedented in advancing the treatment of extensive-stage small cell lung cancer."
Imdelltra's U.S. list price is about $30,000 per cycle, or over $390,000 a year. Wall Street analysts have estimated annual sales reaching more than $2.5 billion by 2030, according to LSEG data.
The Amgen drug is currently approved for adults in the advanced stages of small cell lung cancer that has worsened despite chemotherapy, based on data showing that Imdelltra reduced the risk of death by 40%.
Full results of the 563-patient trial were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Amgen had previously announced that the Phase 3 study was successful.
Imdelltra belongs to a dual-target class of drugs called bispecific antibodies designed to pull immune system T cells into contact with cancer cells to destroy them. Imfinzi is an older type of immunotherapy that essentially blocks the mechanism tumors use to hide from immune-system assault.
Most lung cancer cases are non-small cell, while up to 15% are the small cell variety targeted by Imdelltra. About 250,000 new cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
Very few people diagnosed with small cell lung cancer are candidates for surgery, and most are initially given radiotherapy and chemotherapy, Burton said.
Survival rates depend on when the cancer is diagnosed, but the overall 5-year rate is only around 9%, according to the American Cancer Society.
Amgen said that nearly 80% of trial patients treated with the combination were alive after one year, compared with 53% of those on Imfinzi alone, as patient follow-up continues.
Serious side effects, including low white blood cell counts, occurred in 20.9% of patients on the dual therapy and 10.8% with the single therapy. A potentially dangerous condition known as cytokine release syndrome, an aggressive inflammatory response, was reported in 49.6% of patients who received Imdelltra. But only one case was serious and there were no CRS-related deaths.
Adverse events led to discontinuation of the combination therapy in 5.7% of trial patients and 5.8% of patients given only Imfinzi.

The wonderful counter to rising prices at the very top end of the watch world is that, frankly, things have never looked better for those seeking proper mechanical watches on a budget. Entry-level timepieces keep getting better and cheaper—and this isn't just from newly established microbrands hoping to make a name for themselves, but from the major players, too.
Recently, I was asked to pick a couple of wallet-friendly watches for WIRED's Gear newsletter, and it sent me down a glorious rabbit hole where I was genuinely surprised by superb timepieces well below what WIRED has previously set for affordable watches (the sub-$1,000 bracket). Far from dropping three figures on a decent automatic, you can now get almost anything you desire from a watch for far less than $500.
To check my math and make sure I wasn't going slightly crazy, I reached out to WIRED's wider circle of watch experts with a devilishly tricky, unenviable challenge: Pick their favorite mechanical watch for less than $400, the sort of price where quartz watches dominate. It was a hard ask, but they delivered. Here's the list—all are exceptional value, and watches we'd be delighted to sport on our wrists.
Caravelle Sea Hunter
Caravelle has no right to make a mechanical dive watch this attractive and capable for a mere $300, but here it is. The secret to its timeless look is that Bulova's budget brand sensibly fashioned this modern Sea Hunter heavily on the diver's design from the late 1960s, while bumping the size up to a more modern 39 mm. Elegant and stylish, it's practically a GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watch. But with 200 meters of waterproofing, a 120-click unidirectional bezel, and a 42-hour power reserve, the Sea Hunter is a compelling sports watch. Throw on a rubber strap for diving, a nato for casual (our pick is Artem), or stick with the three-link steel bracelet for a more classic look.
Orient Bambino Version 7 38 mm
Unquestionably one of the best-value automatic dress watches you can buy today, the $295 Orient Bambino’s timeless 38-mm design with white dial and leather strap has been carefully shrunken down from the original 40.5-mm casing, making this piece incredibly wearable (both in these smaller watch times and when case sizes inevitably get larger again.) You can view the automatic Japanese movement through the exhibition case back, and there's even 30 meters of water resistance—not that you should be swimming with such a watch. Want something less traditional? Go for the pink dial with a stainless steel bracelet.
Brew Metric Lite Retro
This new smaller take on Brew's original Metric Retro is the choice of Mike Christensen, British GQ's lifestyle director and watch editor. Cashing in on the current trend for very small watches, Mike loves that this 30-mm piece is wearable for both men and women. “This li'l Brew number is so retro they decided to call it exactly that,” he says. At just $375, the stainless steel Metric Lite Retro, complete with a matching bracelet, uses an automatic movement visible through the open caseback. It has 50 meters of water resistance, and even sapphire crystal atop the striking dial. Proper retro charm that's forgiving on the bank balance.
Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound
Chris Hall, a watch expert who writes for WIRED, The New York Times, Financial Times, and others, as well as his excellent The Fourth Wheel Substack, recommends the Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound at $259. “It was the model that marked Timex’s return to mechanical watches about a decade ago, and unlike so many watches at this level, it isn’t a rip-off of something else: It’s a tribute to one of Timex’s own designs,” Hall says. “It’s small, quirky, and very much its own thing. Never mind the mechanics, getting real personality and credibility at this price is what’s really impressive.” At 34 mm on a leather strap, the design feels pure, and the 30-meter water resistance is a bonus.
Sea-Gull 1963 “International Edition”
Looking a little further afield can often pay off in the watch world. A prime example is the Sea-Gull 1963, a hand-wound mechanical chronograph based on a vintage pilot's timepiece originally built for the Chinese Air Force back in 1961. Many call this watch the gateway drug to watch collecting, but there are a few different versions. Here we've gone for the “International Edition,” which seems to be a budget model of the 1963 Sea-Gull, as it sells alternative iterations for more on its own website. The design is faithful (including the ST1901 movement), the 38-mm size is perfect, and you can't argue with the unfathomably low $269 price.
Baltic HMS
Founded in 2016 by Etienne Malec and debuting on Kickstarter in 2017, this French micro-brand was inspired by the watch collection Malec inherited from his late father, whose family hailed from northern Poland near the Baltic Sea. The brand has quickly become a darling of watch reviewers, so it's no surprise that two of WIRED's watch experts have chosen the 1940s-inspired three-hand HMS (cheating ever so slightly as the HMS clocks in at $430).
Robin Swithinbank, who writes on watches for The New York Times, Financial Times, and Business of Fashion, and hosts the Luxury Society Podcast, has been won over by the 38-mm HMS 002 Silver (above right). “At any price, I like my watches simple, legible, and hardwired with the kind of style that never dies. Baltic absolutely nailed it with this,” he says. Powered by an automatic Miyota 8315 movement with a 60-hour power reserve, it also has 50 meters of water resistance.
Tim Vaux, who writes for both Hodinkee and British GQ about watches, prefers the HMS 003 Salmon (above left). It's smaller than the 002 at 36.5 mm, but still uses the Miyota 8315 movement. “In 2026, there’s no need to look at the household names anymore. The HMS 003 has one of the most classically configured dials you’ll find at any price,” Vaux says. “Walk into a room wearing this and nods of approval will come from all angles. With the Salmon dial, you can’t go wrong.”
Bulova A-11 Hack Watch
As Caravelle's big brother, Bulova has appeared in our bargain watch roundups before. Still, this time, Felix Scholz, editor-in-chief of Revolution Australia and cohost of OT: The Podcast, chose the A-11 Hack Watch, on sale for just $357. “Military watches hold a special place in the hearts of watch enthusiasts,” Scholz says. “And while they might not be rare or intrinsically valuable, the hacking watches produced by numerous American makers during the Second World War are among the greatest.”
Legible and functional, Scholz says such pieces are a true slice of history, and that Bulova is one of the historic manufacturers of this type. “The A-11 Hack captures the spirit, but the less martial blue dial feels contemporary, and doesn't make you look like you're LARPing as a reenactor.”
Citizen Tsuyosa
Pickings are admittedly slim for genuine automatic GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watches under $400, but take a look at the $396 Citizen Tsuyosa with its classic black dial and integrated stainless steel bracelet. It features a 40-mm case, 50 meters of water resistance, sapphire crystal, 42-hour power reserve, and a 3 o’clock date window that will see you from beach to boardroom. If black is too serious, Citizen offers several dial hues (gold and green is a nice combo).
WIRED's top pick, however, is the new, more wearable 37-mm range conveniently on sale right now at just under our $400 target. If you venture above $600, park Citizen and go for the Lorier Falcon or Traska Commuter 36 instead.
Vostok Amphibia
WIRED watch expert Laura McCreddie-Doak has seen our Chinese chrono option and upped the ante with this Russian dive watch. Vostok traces back to the Soviet Union's Chistopol Watch Factory, a supplier to the USSR Ministry of Defense during World War II. This Amphibia 420269 (there are many, many other models) has a 2416B automatic movement that offers a 31-hour power reserve. Bafflingly just $151 on a steel bracelet, it's rated for 200 meters of water resistance, thanks to its unique, pressure-tightening case design. “This watch needs no other justification for inclusion on this list other than it was worn by Bill Murray as Jacques Cousteau-alike Steve Zissou in Wes Anderson’s The Life Aquatic,” says McCreddie-Doak.
Seiko 5 Sports
Finally, we come to the almost inevitable inclusion of the Seiko 5 Sports automatic. The familiar and affordable Seiko 5 Sports line began in 1968 as a tougher, sportier evolution of the 1963 Seiko Sportsmatic 5. The lineup is still going strong with dozens of variants plus a back catalog of thousands. That explains why, for the second time on this list, two of our experts chose the 5 Sports.
WIRED watch writer and author Josh Sims says the Seiko 5 Sports “is the MPV of watches: dependable, rugged, adaptable, as happy in the city as out of it. For my money—and this really is a lot of watch for, relatively, not a lot of money—it also has the cool of not being Swiss. Seiko isn’t just a giant of Japanese watchmaking; it’s a giant of watchmaking that deserves more r-e-s-p-e-c-t, and remains as relevant as ever.” Sims has gone for the SNSX Series that starts at $385.
Holly Ross, as executive editor of Vanity Fair’s On Time watch supplement, has gone for the Seiko 5 SRPE71 (pictured above), a model that's not new but still available if you look. “What is not to love about this chic, timeless, durable, and mechanical Seiko 5? And for a neat $320, it makes it even more desirable.”

In a couple of hours, a decade of the company’s research — boosted by a partnership with Merck — was going to culminate in the presentation of the first Phase 3 study to successfully demonstrate that a customized mRNA-based therapy called intismeran could improve outcomes for patients with melanoma.

Srinagar, Oct 27: Leader of Opposition Sunil Sharma on Tuesday criticised the Jammu and Kashmir cabinet expansion, alleging that the government had failed to maintain regional and cultural balance.
Speaking to reporters after the induction of four new ministers into the Omar Abdullah-led government, Sharma congratulated the newly inducted ministers but said governments must represent all regions and sections of society.
“Governments are formed not just to win elections. Governments have to take every section along. Every region, every area has to be taken along. Religious, regional and cultural balance has to be maintained. Today, that was not seen,” Sharma said.
Asked about the removal of the portfolio held by cabinet minister Satish Sharma, the BJP leader said it was too early to comment.
“Right now, it would not be appropriate to say anything,” he said, adding that he would first congratulate the new ministers.
On questions about discontent within the National Conference over the cabinet expansion, Sharma said the matter concerned the party internally and had nothing to do with him.
“Who is upset and who is happy with them is none of our concern. This is their organisation’s internal matter,” he said.
When reminded of his earlier remark that the National Conference would split on the day of the cabinet expansion, Sharma urged patience, saying only a few minutes had passed since the ceremony.
“Have some patience. Please be patient; you will get to know everything,” he said.

There are some days when there’s so much that needs to get done, I daydream about having a clone of myself. Between paying bills, life admin like renewing my driver’s license, keeping up with doctor’s appointments, and planning meals, it’s a lot. And that doesn’t even begin to touch the work that goes into making a podcast or managing my social life.
When AI agents run your life
Muse, organize my life. Make no mistakes.
This feeling of overwhelm resonates with Sari Azout. She’s a mom of three who works in tech. “There is just so much doing,” she told Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. “I wake up, and I have to do meal coordination and get my kids up for breakfast, coordinate carpools. Then a lot of work during the day, but there’s the email from the teacher, there’s the 20 group chats asking if you want to participate in this group gift. They don’t call it ‘the invisible load’ for no reason.’”
Silicon Valley says it has a fix for this kind of mental overload. They don’t want to clone us — at least not yet. But they do think they have the next best thing: AI agents.
Azuot was skeptical when she first got an invite to try an agent, but she says she eventually came around on the technology after back-to-school shopping snuck up on her. She used her agent to get it done. “It blew me away,” she said. “I remember that night coming home just feeling so calm and reading my son a book and feeling present. And I was like, ‘Wow, I actually was very cynical about something that is giving me more time for living.’”
Azout’s experience is, more or less, the sales pitch for AI agents: They’ll help you save time with everyday tasks, so you have more of it for what you want to do. But what are agents, exactly? Are they really all that? And what do we gain — and give up — when we use the technology?
On this week’s episode of Explain It to Me, I spoke with Reece Rogers, a senior software reporter at Wired, to find out. Rogers says to think of agents as the next evolution of AI chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT.
“I’d create this mental model of a tiny digital assistant that’s constantly searching the web, going through your email, and checking your calendar, trying to find ways it could proactively be helpful for you,” he explains. “Agents are more proactive. It’s scanning your email 24/7 and sending you a message, maybe highlighting a potential calendar conflict.”
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Rogers, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
What agents are out there right now?
At the start of this year, there was a tool called OpenClaw that really sparked this with early adopters in San Francisco, but now there are much more consumer-friendly versions, with one of the most notable being Meta’s Muse.
There’s also a tool from OpenAI called Dots. But where Meta’s Muse is free to download, OpenAI’s Dots is still behind a $100/month paywall.
You tried an AI agent for a recent story you wrote. How was that experience?
One personal example, to share something that I’ve actually been using agents for, is our couch. It’s broken, and finding a new couch has been a pain. We want a sleeper bed, but we want these specific colors. We have this specific budget. I’ve been using Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots to try to find a few different options for us.
One interesting thing is that Meta’s Muse is connected to Facebook Marketplace. There are these really good integrations where I can give it all these details, and it found a few good couches that are only maybe a couple blocks from me.
I really enjoyed OpenAI’s Dots experience as well. I spent about an hour talking to it on the phone, and the AI agent made a packet of all these different options I could find. Just this morning, it flagged that one of them is now 40 percent off.
Is that how this tech is typically used?
Most people are using this as part of a workflow. I attach it to my email, I attach it to my calendar, and I’m using it as a personal assistant to organize my life. But people have been quite creative.
One of the breakout uses for Meta’s Muse is people have been connecting their bank account statements and then using it to scan for subscriptions they might want to cancel. So it can be used in many different ways, though I will say I do not connect it to my own bank account for a myriad of reasons.
I’m not going to lie, the idea of giving any third party access to my bank information does not thrill me. I don’t love that concept.
That’s one of my biggest concerns about these AI agents: how much personal information we’re handing over to these large companies.
When I tested Meta’s Muse, it wanted access to my email, my bank account, even my passport expiration details. The pitch is convenience, but Muse users are automatically opted in to having all of their interactions with Muse used to train Meta’s AI models.
I would definitely recommend, if you’re sharing personal details, go into the settings and turn that off because you might be handing over even more information about yourself than you initially realize.
What is the privacy situation with all of this? We all have various apps where we don’t read and still click “I agree,” but this feels like it could be more invasive.
Yes, especially because it’s all about automation. If you’re automating things and it has access to all of your data, it could make mistakes and embarrass you in ways you might not even be thinking about.
There was this one really interesting story of someone who had connected an AI agent to their work Slack in addition to their bank account. And their agent just automatically posted how much money was in their checking account for all of their coworkers to see.
Oh no.
I would be mortified. So there are these kinds of mistakes that these AI tools can still make. If you’re interested in experimenting with them, I would be really thoughtful with how you’re setting up these tools as well as what kind of information you feel comfortable sharing.
“You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users.”
How are these AI agents being marketed? AI is not popular right now. Just ask any politician who has a data center coming to their state. People are not loving it. How are they trying to sell this to the average person?
The AI backlash really is at a fever pitch right now. You could almost see that in the way that AI companies are trying to market these tools. They’ve really, really leaned into cuteness and into adorable mascots.
Muse, if you haven’t seen its agent, looks like a mix between a Labubu and an Ewok. It’s very furry, very cuddly, very cute. OpenAI’s tools also have similar kinds of blobs with large eyes that might be a little endearing.
I feel like companies are hearing this kind of feedback that people aren’t trusting AI right now, or maybe they have moral or ethical reasons they don’t want to use these tools. You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users.
Do you think AI agents are ultimately going to worm their way into our lives despite how unpopular AI companies are?
I do think so. I think in a couple months, maybe when I go home from Christmas, I would not be surprised if my mom had an agent on her phone because it does feel like it’s breaking through to average people in the way that ChatGPT had a moment a few years ago.
Even though there’s a lot of distrust for large companies like Meta, I think there are some appealing parts of this that will bring in millions of people. I do see this as the future of the internet.
When I think of the dream of the average person working in AI in Silicon Valley, it’s “We’re going to use AI. It’s going to free up the free time of so many people. Work is going to get done faster. You’re going to have more leisure time.”
Has that been the case for the people you’ve spoken with who are using this? Has it given them more free time to enjoy themselves or has it done something else?
You would think so, right? You would think that if people are automating these boring aspects of their life, that they would have more time to go touch grass, go see a movie, have some fun. But it does feel like that time just gets filled with other work, other productivity measures.
While agents may be able to take some more annoying or tedious things off of your plate, I am not as optimistic that it’s going to give us this utopia or freedom where I’m always at the beach.

The row over the distribution of “experimental drug” meant for “clinical trials” to spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) patients assumed political dimensions in the State, with the Opposition quick to latch on to the issue, demanding that the government assuage the concerns of the parents.
All hell broke loose on Tuesday, with parents of SMA children claiming that the SMA drug given free of cost at the SMA clinic in SAT Hospital was an “experimental drug” as the marking on the carton said “physicians’ samples/ for clinical trials only.”
Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan expressed concern whether “the sick children were being treated like mere guinea pigs” as well as shock at the Health Minister’s “criminal negligence.” On Wednesday, senior CPI(M) leader K.K. Shailaja too said the government cannot “change the drug just like that merely because it is cheaper.”
However, the fact remains that the decision to shift to the generic version of SMA drug had been taken during the previous government so that uninterrupted supply of the drug can be ensured. The purchase processes were initiated in February 2026 itself.
SAT Hospital authorities had clarified on Tuesday itself that no “experimental drug” was being given to children and that only the generic version of the original molecule, approved by the Central Drugs Standards Control Organisation (CDSCO) was given to the patients.
“We had a shortfall in the supply of the drug. On Monday, rather than send SMA patients away, we procured some samples of the generic version from Natco and distributed it. There is no change in the drug and the scaremongering about “experimental drugs” is unnecessary,” sources at SAT Hospital said.
“No experimental drug was given to SMA children. What was given was the generic version of Risdiplam, the patented original formula by Roche, now manufactured by the Indian firm Natco Pharma and which has been approved by drug regulatory bodies in the country. The drug is priced at 97% less cost than its patented version and makes it possible for the government to give the drug free of cost to more patients,” a hospital statement said.
On Wednesday, SAT Hospital authorities said they too back the physician samples. “We received the government supply on Tuesday evening and, hence, we opted to replace the drug,” Superintendent of SAT I. Riaz said.
SAT Hospital has been running an SMA clinic since 2022. At the time, Roche Pharma was the only firm licensed to produce and market the drug Risdiplam for SMA. The cost of one 60 ml bottle was ₹6.3 lakh.
Keralam is the only State to utilise public funds for providing free SMA treatment to children. With more children being identified with the disease and getting registered for free treatment, sustaining the free drug supply was becoming a problem.
It was in 2025, after the patent period of Risdiplam expired, Natco obtained the licence of the Drugs Control General of India to manufacture the generic version of Risdiplam. The generic drug is priced at ₹15,900 a bottle.
According to the National Policy for Rare Diseases (2021), manufacturing and licensing of drugs for rare diseases by Indian pharma firms is an important objective so that the precious medication can be accessible to more patients at a lower cost.
“The generic version has all regulatory approvals and is being used by all premier medical institutions in the country to treat SMA patients. Keralam cannot continue to procure the original molecule at high prices when an approved generic formulation is available at a fraction of the price. The government’s decision to embrace generics is a patient-centric move and it is highly commendable because it prioritises equitable access to life-saving drugs over vested commercial interests,” public health expert B. Ekbal said.
IMA representative N. Sulphi, too, pointed out that the controversy was nothing but a fallout of the rivalries between two pharma firms.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan said the generic version of Risdiplam had been approved by an expert committee and that any concerns about the quality or efficacy of the drug were misplaced. The government’s only intention was to make the drug accessible to more patients, he said.

With a tactile dongle for on-the-fly customization and a metal chassis, the Wallhack M-001 is the most fun I've had reviewing a gaming mouse in a long time.
Magnesium shell. Hot-swappable, rechargeable batteries. 52-gram weight. Functional and innovative dongle. Satisfying tactile experience. Great styling and design language.
TIRED
High price point. Slightly outdated sensor. Only 2.4G wireless connectivity with dongle; no Bluetooth or USB-C connectivity on mouse.
Batteries. They're not typically thought of as a significant source of innovation. Most companies have spent the last few years removing mice in favor of more lightweight designs.
That's what's made the return of the replaceable and rechargeable battery surprising—something I once thought to be a lost technology from a bygone era. A few companies have recently realized that the ability to pop out and replace your battery in seconds is a great way to extend mouse life without needing to increase battery size or efficiency.
From the handful of mice I’ve tested with hot-swappable batteries so far, Wallhack does it best. The mouse is designed around the function’s ease-of-use, and everything else comes together to make a mouse that feels not only competitive for gaming, but also well thought-out and satisfying to use in everyday life.
Effective Shape
The M-001’s shape is a standard right-handed, symmetrical design. This means the mouse’s left and right sides are shaped identically, but only the left side has thumb buttons. There are two main buttons, two side buttons, a standard ratcheting scroll wheel, and a power switch on the underside.
With a length of 120 mm, the M-001 is slightly shorter than contemporaries like the Razer Viper V4 Pro (125 mm) and Logitech Pro Superstrike X2 (127 mm). The overall width and height are comparable, at 63.5-mm tall and a 39-mm wide. The largest difference is the profile of the mouse: The front end sits significantly lower than other mice, and the rear has a more significant hump, which creates a more angled shape overall. When using a palm grip, this puts your hand at a slightly more aggressive forwards angle, with your palm sitting higher and your fingers pointing more downwards. It’s a slight difference, but I found this angle to be better for quick movements compared to a more “flat” design. However, like most shape-related choices, this is ultimately down to individual preference. (To compare mouse sizes, I typically use a website like eloshapes)
The two main buttons are lightly sculpted, with subtle concavity for fingers to comfortably rest in. Similarly, there is a subtle taper at the bottom center of the mouse which makes lifting and moving easier. The side buttons use a simple, rounded shape placed just above the taper, making it easy to rock your thumb upwards to press them without getting in the way. They’re just elevated enough that the buttons don’t recess into the shell when pressed. The only shape-related issue I had was the scroll wheel, which is a good bit more elevated than other mice. This isn’t a huge issue, and I adapted to it after a few hours of use, but it’s something I could see being off-putting for users accustomed to a lower-profile scroll wheel.
(Not) Heavy Metal
The most important part of this mouse’s construction is the magnesium shell, which provides significantly more rigidity than the plastic shells used on most mice. Because of this, the mouse feels incredibly sturdy and solid. The metal shell also gives the mouse a cool, slick feeling underneath your fingertips, which I prefer to the matte plastic feeling that most mice have.
Despite using metal, it only weighs 53.6 grams, making the M-001 quite light by most standards, It still falls slightly behind the Viper V4 Pro’s 50.3 grams and lags way behind Corsair’s superlight, 36-gram Sabre V2 Pro Ultralight. But the M-001 is incredibly solid, with none of the flexibility or flimsiness that most plastic mice have. When compared to other magnesium mice like the AngryMiao Infinity .97 or Corsair’s magnesium-shelled Sabre, the M-001 has an entirely solid upper shell without any cutouts or holes, which feels much better for regular use with a multitude of grip styles (plus, it’s much less likely to have dust, dead skin, or anything else build up inside of it). While the full magnesium shell increases weight, it’s a worthwhile trade-off for a smooth and rigid shape.
It’s also worth noting that some of Wallhack’s promotional material depicts the mouse as being a solid black color, but this isn’t quite the case. The unit I received is much closer to a gunmetal color, with a significant amount of metallic flake across the finish. The color looks fantastic in person, but it's difficult to properly capture in images.
Flipping over this mouse reveals one of the more atypical design decisions being made: the lack of a bottom shell. Instead of an entire underside, there is a thin frame around the circumference of the mouse that holds six feet in place. Between them is a chasm that reveals the entire PCB and battery.
Of particular note is the PCB’s function inside the mouse: Instead of simply sitting inside of the shell, the PCB works as a primary structural component. Similar techniques have been used in designing supercars and sport bikes, with the Ferrari F50 using the engine block as a stressed member that provides rigidity to the entire car, a technology borrowed from Ferrari’s F1 team. This provides some obvious benefits to rigidity and weight-savings, but it’s also just undeniably cool to be able to flip over your mouse and see the entire circuit board.
Right behind the PCB is the star of the show, a hot-swappable battery. While I’ve tested quite a few mice with this technology, none of them have managed to make the battery-swapping so satisfying. Instead of being attached with magnets or a rotating locking mechanism, the batteries use a custom-made -spring-loaded ejector similar to an SD card or a Nintendo Switch cartridge. To insert the battery, simply press until you feel a click, and it will lock into place. To remove it, do the same: press until you feel a click, and it will pop out slightly. Of all the mice I’ve tested with removable batteries, this is by far my favorite mechanism to use: It’s intuitive, fun, and feels sturdy.
This battery system does come with a trade-off. Because hot-swappable batteries means an effectively-infinite battery life (as long as you remember to plug the old one into the dongle when you swap), Wallhack has decided to entirely remove the USB-C port on the mouse. This means it only functions as a 2.4G wireless mouse and cannot be plugged or charged in directly. This isn’t a huge issue (it never inconvenienced me, since there was always a fully charged battery ready to swap in), and it theoretically means the connection quality will be better, since there’s fewer components between the antenna and the receiver. But it is worth noting that, if a battery dies or your dongle craps out, there’s no other way to use this mouse.
The Perfect Dongle
In every high-polling mouse I’ve reviewed, the dongle has been a bit of a pain point. A high polling rate necessitates proximity, which in turn requires in a small thing sitting on your desk. In most cases, these things have only one or two functions: They connect to the mouse, and they maybe have a small number of LED indicators (between 1 and 3) that can display battery life, connection quality, or some other setting. Almost every time, they’re small and light enough to slide around on your desk and will inevitably end up falling behind it once or twice due to the weight of the cable pulling it back.
With the M-001, nearly all of these issues are resolved: The dongle is given purpose, function, and I’d even argue dignity. Instead of the small, existing-by-necessity designs that most manufacturers ship with their mice, Wallhack has managed to make a beautiful piece of industrial design. The dongle is a medium-sized metal wedge sporting a gunmetal gray finish identical to the mouse. It has two camera-like dials up front, a button, and a slot for a rechargeable battery. The DPI dial features numbering from 400 to 25,600, and the polling dial goes from 125 Hz to 8,000 Hz.
The dials both have LED indicators next to them, which illuminate alongside the mouse to indicate a setting being changed. When rotated, they both have a satisfying ratcheting mechanism that’s stiff enough to avoid accidental inputs, without being difficult to turn using a single finger.
While I loved these dials from the moment I saw them, I really didn’t expect to use them much. I’ve always been more of a set-and-forget type of person. But after testing this mouse for a while, I regularly found myself using both of the dials: On-the-fly DPI adjustments were great for games like Marvel Rivals. I tended to prefer, for example, a higher DPI for Thing and a lower for Thor. Polling adjustments, too, were useful in situations where older games (like Destiny 2) got grumpy when I was using a mouse above 1,000 Hz.
Performance and Software
Like many mice today, the M-001 uses an in-browser customization client. Wallhack’s web client, Wallhack Terminal, takes a unique stylistic approach, relying on a black-and-white, text-based system that resembles Command Prompt more than a typical gaming software. This is both a breath of fresh air stylistically, and much more straightforward than some of the software I’ve used in the past.
The configurator has an extensive feature set, including adjustments for mouse rotation, acceleration, and lift-off distance, which is adjustable by millimeters instead of the vague Low/Medium/High that some softwares use. The sensor can also be pushed to scan faster than the mouse’s 8,000 Hz polling rate, which can potentially improve the accuracy of the sensor, but limits battery life.
Along with adjusting DPI and polling with the dials on the dongle, switching them to the red “DPI” And “Hz” text allows for more granular adjustments within the configurator.
The sensor inside the mouse is a Pixart PAW3950. For anyone who doesn’t have an exhaustive list of mouse sensors floating around their head, this is the same type of sensor used in the 2022 Razer Viper V2 Pro (branded as the Razer Focus Pro 30k). That's four years old at this point. It’s not quite a cutting-edge sensor anymore. But unless you're in the top-tier of competitive play, the sensor will feel consistent and reliable enough, being able to easily track and manage direction changes during fast-paced shootouts. My personal daily driver is a Viper V2 Pro with the exact same sensor (I prefer the shape to the V3 and V4), and it’s still perfectly serviceable after four years of use.
The main buttons inside this mouse use Omron Optical switches, while the side buttons opt for low-profile Omron blue-dot mechanical switches. The scroll wheel’s encoder is a mechanical unit as well, which means it doesn’t have quite the same longevity as the optical units some mice are beginning to use. However, they are easier to replace or fix if something does go wrong.
The internal design of this mouse is impressively simple: There are six feet on the underside, and the outer four all have screws underneath. When you remove these four screws, the bottom half of the shell comes off cleanly (no flimsy plastic clips!), and a few more screws separate the internals from the top shell.
Mice Should Be Fun
I’ve said many times that, when it comes to peripherals, technical specs are only one part of the story. More than that, it’s important to have a device you enjoy using. Of all the mice I’ve tested, the M-001 is by far one of the most enjoyable. The shape is comfortable and natural for multiple grip styles, and the material ensures that the mouse feels rigid and stable despite its light weight. The dongle is a brilliant design that elevates itself from a sad desk tchotchke to a practical and functional device. And the battery mechanism is one of the most clever and fun designs I’ve seen in ages.
Everything about this mouse is deeply satisfying, and I found myself excited to use it every time I sat down. Of course, this mouse isn’t at the cutting edge of sensors or switches, and because of this, I can’t exactly recommend this mouse to someone looking for an ultra-cost-effective option with min-maxed specs. But in using the mouse on the daily, I didn't find that it mattered as much as you might think. 8,000 Hz polling and a 25,600 DPI sensor are enough for all but the pros. Instead, it uses tried-and-true internals that function perfectly well and, more importantly, have crisp and precise tactile responses.

The recent protests called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and helmed by Opposition parties, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar have exposed a chink in journalists’ armour. The crackdown on journalists, especially freelancers and independent journalists, during the October 10 protests, has rekindled the debate on who has the right to be recognised as a journalist and about who decides who is a journalist.
One has seen how during the CJP protests, both in July over the NEET paper leak and in October over the demand for the CEC’s removal, freelancers and independent journalists, and content creators descended in hordes at the protest venue already bulging at the seams with reporters from registered media houses. However, during the second round of protests on October 10, phalanxes of riot police removed them from the protest site and sent them to detention centres. Only journalists with the Press Information Bureau (PIB) or Directorate of Information and Publicity (DIP) accreditation were allowed to cover the protests.
A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi, while hearing a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) which seeks the protection of the right to freedom of expression by freelance journalists and content creators, wondered whether the right to freedom of expression empowered every citizen of this country to be a journalist. “If everyone starts becoming a journalist, it will create problems for every other person,” the CJI said. During the hearing, senior advocate Indira Jaisingh said that there must be a national protocol for police not to obstruct the professional work of any journalist who has an identity card from the employer. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said that in the present era, any person with a mobile phone could claim to be an independent or freelance journalist when he/she would, in fact, be making reels only to garner popularity on social media to earn money by either presenting one-sided stories or sensationalising events.
Recognising journalists
These developments have put the focus back on the question of who recognises journalists. As per the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, a working journalist is a person whose principal avocation is journalism and who is employed in a newspaper, electronic media or digital media. This definition excludes people employed in a managerial or administrative capacity. Further, Central and State governments provide accreditation to working journalists, freelance journalists, camerapersons and technicians. Accreditation recognises working journalists and others and gives them access to designated official sources of information. For journalists in Delhi-NCR, accreditation is provided by the PIB for covering the Central government while the DIP accreditation gives them the right to cover the Delhi State government. Media accreditation guidelines of the PIB and DIP define the eligibility criteria for all those seeking accreditation. However, one of the major issues with government accreditation is that it has a quota depending upon circulation (for newspapers, periodicals and magazines), subscribers (for news agencies), licence under uplinking and downlinking guidelines (for private satellite TV channels), and unique visitors (for digital news publishers). Therefore, all journalists in recognised media organisations don’t get accreditation. This leads us to the question on how all working journalists can be recognised.
One solution could be a national media council or commission. Just like there is the Bar Council of India for lawyers and an Institute of Chartered Accountants of India for chartered accountants, the media council can recognise all working journalists, freelance journalists, camerapersons and technicians. Just like you need a law degree to practise law, a medical degree to become a doctor, the media council may mandate a degree or diploma in journalism and mass communication while applying for a licence.
A few years ago, the Press Club of India drafted a Media Transparency (and Accountability) Bill, which mandated the formation of a national media council, among other things. Recently, some other journalists’ bodies have also submitted a memorandum to the government with the same demand. As more and more people with a camera claim to be freelance journalists, it may be high time for the government to give some serious thought to the idea of such a council.
Rakesh Goswami is Professor of Journalism at Indian Institute of Mass Communication, New Delhi
