Olivia Chow romps to victory as head of progressive new Toronto council
Ex-Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith and Chow's stepson Mike Layton also elected
Olivia Chow is preparing to lead Toronto for another four years, after an emphatic victory over former councillor Brad Bradford Monday night.
Chow will oversee a progressive, new-look council with several of her key allies elected, putting her in a strong position to pursue her agenda.
The returning mayor started the year looking comfortably ahead, before it appeared Bradford could surge into the mayor's chair.
In the end, she won a massive victory — netting roughly 530,000 votes, according to the unofficial results (official results will come once they've been certified by the city clerk).
A close race and new messaging
While Bradford received just one per cent of the vote in the 2023 mayoral byelection, he gained on Chow through 2026.
As the race heated up after Labour Day, the gap between challenger and incumbent appeared to narrow significantly.
The timing of the surge seemed like it would be good for Bradford, coming toward the end of the race, when advance voting appeared to be more than 70 per cent higher than the 2023 mayoral byelection.
But as polling suggested the wind was in Bradford's sails, the Chow campaign settled on a clear message about the challenger and his platform, particularly his pledge to create a public utility company to handle the city's water and wastewater.
Bradford said the plan would help raise funds for city hall and cut costs for residents, but Chow said it would mean the city losing control of an asset that is working well and opens the door to privatization.
That message may have struck a nerve with Torontonians, said political strategist Blue Knox, who served as former mayor John Tory's director of communications.
"Canadians like for their public institutions to stay public," she said.
"Her campaign was able — whether you agree with it or not — to very clearly distill their attack on one of Brad Bradford's promises."
Olivia Chow, left, and Brad Bradford were the two front-runners to be Toronto's mayor in a race polls suggested was close at the end. (CBC)
Erin Morrison, vice president of Texture Communications and a Chow supporter, said she thought the policy was a "serious mistake" from the Bradford campaign.
"That really started to play a role in the campaign with about 10 days to go," she said.
"Chow, to her credit, really knew that that was problematic to her voters … and made an issue out of it."
Strong get-out-the-vote operation
The Chow campaign was able to rely on a formidable team to help spread her campaign message and her criticism of her opponent.
She ran a "disciplined campaign," Knox said.
Even the Bradford campaign acknowledged on election night the combination of Progress Toronto, Ontario NDP supporters and unions backing Chow was a formidable force to reckon with.
"It's tough organizationally," Bradford's head of communications Laryssa Waler said shortly before polls closed.
"They know how to get them out to vote. They have union support, they're very, very organized."
Mandate to stay on the same path
While Bradford's camp had offered a slew of new ideas, particularly around the city's finances, Chow's camp stayed close to her record: renters, transit fares and a school nutrition program.
Knox said the Chow campaign's decision to stick to a few key promises building on the work of her first term in office will make for a smoother transition.
It means Chow's "hands aren't tied" to a series of rigid campaign pledges and she will get to "be flexible to different circumstances that come up."
Bradford conceded to Chow on election night. (Prasanjeet Chaudhary/CBC)
Chow pledged a 10-ride fare cap for riders on the TTC, enhanced protections for renters, a school lunch program and tax cuts for independent grocers. She also said she would continue work to build more affordable housing.
Delivering those promises will be made easier by a council still relatively aligned with Chow's core goals.
A number of high-profile progressive allies, including Nate Erskine-Smith and Mike Layton, Chow's own stepson, will join her at city hall.
Morrison said the 2026-2030 council should be one Chow can lead on most issues — getting her agenda through without needing to resort to strong mayor powers, which she has said she will not use.
"I think that tonight is good news for Chow in the sense that she's got even more progressive allies on council," she said.
"I think she's going to find it an easy council to work with."

Excellent controllers tailored for VR or “regular” gaming. Solid performance on supported VR games. Virtual Imax-scale 2D gaming. Doesn’t pretend to be for work or productivity.
TIRED
Pricey. Blink-and-miss-it battery life. Unpredictable performance for installed games. Problematic pairing for streaming games.
Valve has had a complicated relationship with virtual reality gaming. Its Steam client—the number one distribution platform for PC games—has long supported VR titles and works with headsets from other manufacturers. But the company's flagship VR headset, 2019’s Valve Index, never quite escaped its niche. It saw a huge sales spike in the run-up to the release of headline title Half-Life: Alyx, but by February 2025, it accounted for only 13.2 percent of VR headsets used on Steam.
Enter the Steam Frame, Valve’s second attempt at snatching the VR gaming crown. More than a hardware refresh, it promises to reimagine PC VR gaming, operating as a stand-alone headset like the Meta Quest 3, the current reigning champion, while letting users seamlessly stream games from a more powerful remote machine. It mostly succeeds—but a few issues hold it back.
All in Your Head
Specs-wise, the Steam Frame is one of the better VR headsets, though far from a powerhouse. It packs a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip—a slightly dated offering, having debuted in 2023—with 16 GB of RAM, and either 256 GB (at the $1,059 price) or 1 TB ($1,299) of storage, plus a microSD slot for expansion, allowing it to install and run games locally.
It’s aesthetically pleasing, with a sleek black shell and glossy front that have given it a futuristic look. More importantly, it’s comfortable to wear, weighing 440 grams—75 grams lighter than the Quest 3. Valve smartly moved the 21.6-watt-hour Lithium-ion battery to the rear of the head strap for better balance, and thanks to cozy padding, it doesn’t feel hot against your head, even when running demanding games. The cable linking the battery to the headset makes adjusting the elastic straps a little fiddly, though.
The only real comfort drawback is if you wear glasses. While the Steam Frame comes with a spacer to add more depth (which easily clips on magnetically between the inner headset and the padded face gasket), the internal dimensions were still too narrow for me to wear with any of my spectacles. Custom Zenni prescription lenses are available if contact lenses aren’t an option, but it’s a pricey add-on.
Once it’s on your head, dual speakers push audio down the arms directly to your ears, with physical volume controls easily accessible on the left side of the headset. The audio lacks bass but has good directionality, bringing those immersive VR experiences to life. Dual microphones let you use voice controls, while outward-facing cameras enable positional tracking and provide a pass-through view—albeit monochrome with everything looking bluish. A dial at the top lets you adjust lens spacing to your required interpupillary distance, and an inner switch locks it in place.
The lenses themselves are decent, but again not spectacular. Valve uses two LCD pancake lenses (though rumors already hint at a revised OLED model), with a per-eye resolution of 2160 x 2160. That means sharp visuals and legible text—I could easily read fine details on notepads in Half-Life: Alyx, for instance—but you can discern pixels if you peer closely. The real win comes with a 110-degree field of view, enabling wide spans of virtual real estate, and refresh rates ranging from 72 to 120 Hz, with an experimental mode boosting it up to 144 Hz. As a result, games can look incredibly smooth when running on the Steam Frame.
The controllers might be the best part of the package. The dual grips mimic the Quest 3 controllers but outdo them with a full controller layout spread across the pair. They boast the same highly precise Tunneling Magnetoresistance thumbsticks as the regular Steam Controller, along with a full D-pad on the left, four ABXY face buttons on the right, two shoulder triggers and an underside button on each—squeeze that in, and the grip switches from controller mode to laser pointer to make selections in VR.
Position detection is great, with full six-degrees-of-freedom tracking, while excellent haptics deliver solid rumble and per-finger capacitive sensing for nuanced, precise interactions with virtual objects. You can also pair a regular controller to the Frame via Bluetooth, but the included ones are so good you likely won’t ever feel the need to—these are now the pinnacle of multipurpose VR controllers.
What Will Play?
After setup—a now-familiar routine for VR gamers that includes running necessary updates and drawing safe boundaries so you don't knock into furniture—you’ll sign in to your Steam account directly on the Steam Frame. It runs SteamOS 3 just like the Steam Deck or Steam Machine, the familiar home screen now floating in a VR void. Navigate to your library, and you can install whatever you like directly onto the Frame.
Unfortunately, while there’s a filter for games officially categorized as compatible, it’s unclear what rubrics Valve uses, or how many games have even been tested. Of my 1,300-plus-strong Steam library, only a meager 18 were marked “Great on Frame.” The strangest absence from that list is the totemic Half-Life: Alyx (which comes free with every Steam Frame purchase), especially odd given it runs without issue. Other dedicated VR games are hit and miss when installed directly on the Frame—I tried Obduction (opened and crashed, repeatedly), Doctor Who: The Edge of Time (ran with juddery performance and could only move by clicking in on the thumbsticks), Dungeons of Eternity (fine, bar some aiming and tracking issues), and Surgeon Simulator VR (totally fine).
You’re not limited to VR games on Frame. You can install and play anything in your library as 2D on a vast virtual cinema screen. Don’t bother with demanding AAA games—the hardware isn’t up to running them—but indies and AA-tier games can look phenomenal like this. Playing Hades II blown up to Imax-scale was a fantastic experience. Again, performance is unreliable—gorgeously animated Metroidvania MIO: Memories in Orbit launched when installed locally, but couldn’t load its assets, leaving me standing on invisible platforms and with no way to navigate the world.
The Frame also seems to default 2D games to 720p resolution. You can override this, but it may drop performance. Frame rates for all of the above games hopped all over the place, though mostly hovering around the 72 or 90 fps benchmarks. It feels like Valve has a lot of updating work to do to ensure Steam Frame can reliably function as a gaming platform for VR or non-VR titles. Right now, running anything is a gamble.
Wi-Fi Woes
The most annoying thing is that the Steam Frame isn't designed solely as a stand-alone headset—pairing it with a more powerful desktop (or laptop) should, in theory, let the PC do the grunt work and stream the output to the Frame. The package includes a dedicated 6-GHz wireless adapter—plug it into any device with a USB-A 3.0 port running Steam, and it should provide a dedicated network for the Frame. The headset connects to both the adapter and your home network, creating a mesh that reduces latency by using whichever has the least network traffic.
In practice, I could barely get it working. I tested it on a Windows 11 PC, a Windows 10 PC, and a Steam Machine—in every case, the Frame could connect to the remote device through the home network, but the adapter appeared as connected but unpaired. When it detected and created that mesh network (on rare occasions), streaming was flawless, but when connected only through the home network, performance was laggy enough to irritate.
Whether playing natively or through streaming, battery life is poor—expect two hours at the high end for locally run games, and maybe three if you’re purely streaming. Such short playing time makes the inability to physically connect Steam Frame to a PC with a cable all the worse, which would also overcome the streaming issues.
Better Days to Come
The biggest hurdle for most VR gamers is likely price. Like all of Valve’s recent tech, the Steam Frame is a casualty of RAM and storage shortages across the electronics industry. Like the Steam Machine, it feels almost compromised, especially that three-year-old processor. It doesn’t feel like $1,000-plus worth of headset, especially when its overall performance only just about beats the significantly cheaper Quest 3.
Yet despite its many early hiccups, the Steam Frame is incredible fun. The VR titles that work without issue are brilliant to play here, and the cinema mode for 2D games is the best implementation of that feature I’ve experienced on a VR headset. Streaming shows potential if Valve can work the networking kinks. If it gets that polish over the coming months as Valve pushes out inevitable updates, it could really shine.
I especially love how it’s unapologetically a gaming platform. It’s not trying to claim VR is useful for productivity, or office tasks—that ship sank along with Apple’s Vision Pro—and mercifully, there’s not even a hint of a blighted “Metaverse” here. The Steam Frame is for gaming, end of story. If Valve can iron out its software issues and make sure more games run on it properly, it’ll be a great way to play.

Mourinho keeps Clasico midas touch 13 years on as La Liga heats up
- Published
Jose Mourinho has done it again.
The Real Madrid manager celebrated Kylian Mbappe's late winner at Barcelona on Sunday with a trademark knee slide, as he maintained his midas touch over their bitter rivals.
Mourinho has become just the third Real boss to go six El Clasicos in a row without defeat - 13 years after he last led Los Blancos in this fixture.
Four wins and two draws in his past six matches in charge of Real Madrid against Barcelona put him up there with Miguel Munoz (1962 to 1965) and Vicente del Bosque (2001 to 2003) as Real managers who have gone six in a row without defeat against the old enemy.
It was also just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona for Real, with the return of Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions
And more importantly for Mourinho, Mbappe's double in Real's 2-1 win ended Barcelona's nine-game unbeaten domestic run with a crucial Clasico victory at the Camp Nou.
A Real defeat would have allowed Barcelona to establish a commanding nine-point advantage but the result has transformed the top of La Liga, bringing Mourinho's side to within three points of their rivals.
"In my view, Real Madrid do not play to win at the Camp Nou, Real Madrid play to win La Liga," he said.
"We could win with luck, but we won with calmness and with all merit," he said. "It's a very strong group. Everyone works very hard. Everyone was ready to win.
"The credit goes to the players. When you win, the credit goes to the players. But when you lose, the blame falls on you. And that's why we see coaches being sacked from their positions every week."
The Portuguese, who returned to Real 13 years after his first stint in charge this summer, has now won six and lost six El Clasicos.
He said: "I've learned that I have an extraordinary group, with the quality and mindset to play.
"In midfield, having a mix of talents gives us more than just having two players with similar characteristics. This mix of talents gives us balance when defending and quality when we go on the attack.
"We've beaten several teams by four or more goals, but this is Barca, and the players put on a great performance. We need to continue like this and don't go over the moon after this win."
Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said he didn't want to give excuses for the defeat but admitted his team lacked fresh legs after a demanding few weeks.
"We missed the freshness," he said. "It's not easy for our players. We have to recover well, train well and we have to respond from this defeat.
"In big games, small things are important and they decide the games and today, it wasn't on our side.
"I can see that today we were not fresh and this is what we have to change."

Pandemic preparedness, support for Ukraine, and the fight against superbugs topped the agenda Tuesday as WHO and UK health leaders met in London to discuss their shared global health priorities.
In their first one-on-one meeting, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and UK Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Steve Barclay MP spoke at length about their shared commitment to delivering a pandemic instrument – a new international agreement being negotiated by WHO Member States – to strengthen global collaboration to help protect the world from another pandemic.
Mr Barclay outlined the UK government’s priorities for a pandemic instrument, which include faster and more efficient data sharing between WHO Member States; quicker, more equitable access to affordable vaccines, tests and treatments; and stronger collaboration on scientific research and development.
“The World Health Organization has reached a significant milestone this year in the marking of its 75th anniversary, and I’m proud of the UK’s longstanding relationship with WHO to improve public health,” Mr Barclay said. “The UK is playing a leading role in tackling some of the world’s greatest health threats, including antimicrobial resistance for which we recently announced £39 million for research into new drugs to combat infections.”
In 2022 and in the previous biennium, the UK was the largest contributor to WHO’s Core Voluntary Contributions Account. The account provides flexible funds that WHO can use and allocate as needed within its approved programme budgets. 
Earlier in the day, Dr Tedros joined International Development Minister Andrew Mitchell and Health Minister Will Quince for the annual UK-WHO Strategic Dialogue to discuss how to tackle global health challenges together and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. 
They spoke about effectively responding to health emergencies, preventing the next pandemic and confronting threats to health posed by climate change.
Ministers Mitchell and Quince emphasized the importance of building strong health systems in countries and protecting the health and rights of women and girls. Ministers also cited the importance of reform to strengthen WHO as an organization, expressing support for WHO’s extensive efforts to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.  
“WHO highly values its strong and impactful collaboration with the UK Government to promote and protect the health of people worldwide,” Dr Tedros said as the meetings concluded. “Today’s strategic dialogue with Ministers Mitchell and Quince, and my productive discussions with Secretary of State Barclay, demonstrated the UK’s commitment to global public health, its support of the World Health Organization, and the great potential and impact of our partnership. I look forward to continuing our joint work to make the world healthier and safer on many fronts, from combatting antimicrobial resistance to supporting the UK and countries around the world to develop a generational accord to prevent and respond to future pandemics.”

Earlier this week, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine for violating consumer protection laws dating back to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. $25 billion is a massive fine, the largest Meta has ever faced, but it still had us folks at WIRED wondering: Would Meta even feel the pain?
A quick recap of the case: Filed in 2021, the suit alleged that the company violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act by lying to Meta users about the way it handled their data. (Later, New Mexico’s attorney general also made claims against Meta’s content moderation policies.) In September, a jury ruled in favor of the state. Then came the multibillion-dollar penalty.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
Meta’s legal troubles have proliferated so much this year that it’s hard to keep track of them. Earlier this year in New Mexico, a jury ruled that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state’s Unfair Practices Act. That trial was related to child safety. A second phase of the case resulted in Meta being ordered to pay $567 million.
Meanwhile, a Los Angeles County superior court found Meta—and Google-owned YouTube—liable for harming a user’s mental health with the addictive design features of their apps. The plaintiff, a young woman, was awarded $6 million; Meta is on the hook for the bulk of that payment. Then in August, Meta settled a landmark federal case brought against the company by the majority of US states. This suit, once again, centered on addictive features in its apps that were alleged to be harmful to kids. As part of that settlement, Meta will pay the states between $17 and $18 billion over 10 years.
Added up, that’s a lot of billions. And yet: It’s still just the cost of doing business for Meta. Reuters reports that in the most recent New Mexico trial, the state’s attorneys originally asked Judge Francis Mathew to award the state between $35 and $45 billion. That would’ve been significant for the state, but would that extra $20 billion have kneecapped Meta? Nope.
Even if Meta was forced to pay the total maximum fine of the New Mexico ruling—a whopping $219 billion, or $5,000 across 43 million violations, reduced by the judge to $25 billion—the company would have felt only a mild sting. As of writing, Meta is worth around $1.7 trillion. Its stock took a hit on Thursday, but that was due to a confluence of factors, like Meta’s earnings report on Wednesday, the company’s massive capital expenditures on AI, and AI stocks dragging overall.
At this point, with no immediate monetary damage to Meta, it would take an accumulation of events to force some kind of change, legal experts tell me. For one, Meta has a clear perception problem: Juries are ruling against it, protesters have railed against it, even its own employees have been more vocal about the company’s internal policies.
Every time Meta doesn’t settle a case, the evidence presented during trial can be scrutinized by the public and used in future cases against Meta, says Corban Rhodes, partner at DiCello Levitt, the outside law firm representing New Mexico in this case. “This trial included more than 100 exhibits that we were able to put into public record, things that had been kept secret for more than a decade since Cambridge Analytica,” Rhodes told WIRED.
One such item is a 2018 email that then COO Sheryl Sandberg sent to a few colleagues days after the Cambridge Analytica scandal broke. Sandberg wrote, “The single biggest issue we face—and I really need everyone to know this—is that there were a MILLION developers with access to the data. We are going to have many, many, many more moments like this in the next month and year.”
There are early signals that private insurers may start balking at having to cover the cost of a tech company’s legal defenses. Some experts are suggesting that insurance companies could even end up being de facto governance for AI, as they “inject responsibility into how AI is designed, developed, and deployed as a condition for obtaining insurance.” Meta learned this firsthand in March, when a Delaware judge ruled that insurers do not have a duty to defend Meta against the literal thousands of lawsuits being brought against it.
There’s no well-defined number at which Meta suddenly becomes vulnerable—the company is unlikely to ever fold from legal penalties alone. But problems could crop up if shareholders or board members stop seeing the company as some inanimate entity and start to focus on the individual directors or officers who have been making bad decisions, says Brian Quinn, a law professor at Boston College Law School who studies corporate law, M&A, and transaction law. Like, say, the people who keep appearing in lawsuits.
“The way that indemnification law is written right now, the fact that a person in a company was found to have violated a law doesn’t necessarily make them liable. It can be believed that they were acting in good faith, or in the best interest of their company,” Quinn says. “But problems start to arise if shareholders say, wait a minute, there’s not only evidence that this director or operator is violating the law, but it has appeared in the same set of facts seven times now.”
After a huge accumulation of these kinds of results, Quinn says, some angry shareholders might stand up and say the corporation should no longer be able to indemnify those directors. That’s when you might see change, because Meta’s executives would no longer be as protected.
Finally, since litigation is often behind the curve on society-disrupting technology, Meta’s legal woes are likely far from over—especially as it wades deeper into AI. “Regulators and courts have for a long time been focused on the impact of social media 1.0 and 2.0, and I think we’re moving on from that era,” says Rhodes. “I expect the next wave of litigation will be focused on AI.”

SERUA ISLAND, FIJI – As the sun sets over Fiji’s tiny Serua Island, its climate-threatened inhabitants soak in one of the reasons they have rejected attempts to relocate their village — the “$100 million views.”
The island looks like a utopia from the mainland, two steep palm-covered knolls sandwiching its low-lying center, flanked by coral reefs and rich fishing grounds.
But it is on the island itself that the risk from rising seas becomes clearer, with a concrete sea wall providing the only defense against waves that are already swamping homes.
“The stronger the air pressure, the higher the waves. So the waves wash through inside the village,” Serua Island resident Avenai Ranuku.
Dozens of homes are in harm’s way when cyclones hit Fiji, as are vegetable crops and graves.
Water laps at the feet of concrete piles where homes and a hospital once stood on the island’s eastern end, and two homes were also moved from the western side where land has been washed away.
Despite the risks, most residents say they would rather strengthen the island’s defenses than abandon their ancestral home.
Ranuku remembers when Category 5 Cyclone Winston hit as a child and the island’s population moved up one of the island’s peaks to take shelter.
“Terrifying,” Ranuku said of that night.
“All of the villagers, when the chief mention it, we go up. No one left behind. We help everyone, carry everything from the house, food. This is our evacuation plan.”
Safe on higher ground, Ranuku could hear “waves going around, and the roof of the houses being washed away.”
From that same haven on the hill, Ranuku explained why the threat of cyclones and sea level rise doesn’t deter people from living on the island.
“We love this island, you know. Fresh air, go out fishing every day, that’s why they don’t want to leave.
“Many people used to say, they go to that house on the hill to see the sunset, it’s a $100 million view.”
Serua Village worked with Habitat for Humanity in 2025 to write a detailed disaster risk reduction plan, as most of the population rejected calls for it to relocate.
Instead, residents wanted to protect their ancestral home and the culture linked to it.
The report found nearly 20% of homes on the island were in critical condition, and just three houses were strong enough to withstand a cyclone.
“Serua Island experiences more frequent seawall overtopping during high tides and king tides, saline intrusion affecting soil fertility, and standing water after rainfall, elevating health risks,” the report said.
“The assessment shows there is a lack of natural form of wave breakers on Serua Island, and it is constantly threatened by sea level rise and cyclones.
“More than 50% of houses have a combination of unstable foundations and roofs, and weak joints, walls, and bracing, making these homes most vulnerable to cyclones and severe weather events.”
On receiving the report, the village wasted no time in working to strengthen its resilience.
During a visit in October, dozens of workers were renovating homes along the northern coastline.
Flimsy walls and corrugated iron roofing were being removed and taken by boat to the mainland.
Some homes had already been raised to mitigate flood risk, and others would soon follow.
The report also recommended improving access to the island by building a more robust path.
During low tide, it is possible to walk the 750 meters to the island, guided by a string of power lines protruding from the sea floor.
But at high tide, the only access is by boat, and even then the report said work is needed to make docking on the island safer and easier.
It is work Ranuku said his village is committed to.
“Why would we want to leave?” he said, looking across the water to Fiji’s Coral Coast.
“We have $100 million views.”

SA chief pledges review over 'disappointing' Test crowds

A senior South African cricket official has pledged to order a review into the low crowd which attended the first Test against Australia in Durban.
Despite South Africa being the reigning world Test champions and Australia the number one-ranked side in the world, fewer than 20,000 fans attended across the five days.
Australia, who are touring South Africa for the first time since the 2018 sandpaper scandal, won by 214 runs and can wrap up the three-match series when the second Test gets under way in Gqeberha on Sunday.
"It is impossible to overlook our disappointment that just under 20,000 fans attended across the five days," said KwaZulu-Natal Cricket Union chief executive Heinrich Strydom.
"A Test match of this quality deserved greater support in the stands. This is something we will reflect on through a thorough internal review.
"We need to listen to our supporters, reconnect with our communities and continue to find ways to make Test cricket more accessible, engaging and appealing.
"Test cricket is part of our sporting heritage and its future depends on all of us."
Attendances for Test cricket have been declining in many places around the world, most notably in South Africa and the West Indies.
However, live sport does remain a big draw in South Africa.
While the Test against Australia was ongoing, a football cup final between Orlando Pirates and Mamelodi Sundowns was being held across town in Durban which attracted more than 50,000 fans.
"While we recognise supporters face competing demands on their time and finances, we must also understand better what influences their decisions to attend and what more we can do to make live cricket an attractive and worthwhile experience," added Strydom.

Tamil literature is replete with references to Siddha practitioners, traditional healers, and the faith, or lack of it, that people have in them. A segment of Tamil literature that has focused on class and caste hierarchies has also looked sharply and sensitively at the socio-economic determinants for access to health care. Among the pioneers of drawing technology and science into his writings in Tamil was the legendary, prescient novelist and screenwriter Sujatha. But in modern Tamil fiction, the employment of medicine and medical issues as the central theme and plot has been rather minimal.
While there might be only a few texts in popular, modern Tamil fiction that weave the story around a medical condition, these form a significant contribution to the genre. Muthumeenal’s Mul focuses on leprosy, and Sivakami’s Pazhayana Kazhithalum offers a health perspective couched in caste discrimination.
Among the Tamil writers who have formed a strong bond between their stories and health issues, Imayam stands tall, not merely through sheer numbers, but through depth of content. Many of his short stories and novels couch the essential human experience he portrays in medical conditions, each wrapped in the other, not distinct, but influencing and impacting each other.
Health in Tamil fiction
But before we dip into Imayam’s work, a full-length novel of note on a core health issue is Mul (thorn) by Muthumeenal, a deep and personalised account of living with leprosy. The narrator is a young girl whose life has been upended when she finds suspicious patches on her body. She moves into an institution where medical care is provided, around which the story is built, and the multiple angles, including stigma, politics, loneliness, and internal struggle, are woven into this autobiography. The public-health message is stigma-busting: that leprosy is treatable, and early therapy can cure it.
In retired IAS officer Sivakami’s work, a Dalit feminist treatise, Pazhayana Kazhithalum (The Grip of Change), the text deals strongly with the social determinants of health — caste violence, gender-based violence, bodily autonomy, and the mental and physical toll of bigotry.
In Imayam’s Ippothu Uyirodirukkiren (I’m Alive… For Now), the author artfully folds in the themes of both the above novels — crafting a social commentary within the nephrology ward of a government hospital where a teenager with end-stage kidney disease has been admitted. It follows his rapid decline, his transition onto dialysis, and organ donation. Reviewers have praised its ‘authentic’ portrayal of nephrology, the disease, and the treatment.
But this is an achievement across various novels that Imayam, a school teacher and politician, has penned. While known for his sharp critique of caste and gender hegemonies, Imayam has also built a strong subgenre of medical literature. Unlike authors who use disease as a generic plot device or a melodramatic tool to lead up to a crisis, he treats medical conditions with gripping sociological depth and clinical accuracy.
A Sahitya Akademi winner, Imayam attempts to explain the human condition through pain, suffering and debility, and as his longtime collaborator-translator Justice Prabha Sridevan says, “an astonishingly astute understanding of the feminine condition.” His recent novel, Noiputtru (disease), also talks of life derailed by leprous patches.
Set in a Tamil Nadu leprosarium in the 1960s, the novel documents the lived experiences of patients ostracised from their families and confined to State-run institutions, including detailed descriptions of the diagnostic and treatment processes. The descriptions of the impact of leprosy are merciless — thickening ears, flattened noses, and physical disfigurement — there’s no way to conceal this in the deliberate, yet sparse prose of the author.
Imayam’s world of illness
Very few novels in Tamil come with the searing commentary that he delivers in Sellatha Panam (A Woman Burnt). Unlike in the case of the protagonist of the above-mentioned novels, here, Revathi, an upper-caste woman who is forced to take the extreme move after her inter-caste marriage, is trapped in a liminal world and confined to bed. Around her, in the waiting corridors of the burns ward, social realities are exposed, the niceties ripped off, though his most effective literary tool is conversations between people. It is said Imayam spent time observing the JIPMER burns ward while researching the book.
Just launched, the English translation of Uppu Vandikaran (The Salt Vendor) harks back to the dark, panic-driven emergency of the pandemic lockdown. It’s not just about falling ill with COVID-19; instead, it exposes the lacunae and inadequacies in the medical system, as Chellamuthu goes from one hospital to the other, being rejected by each one of them since he cannot produce a certificate confirming his infection- a situation the world was familiar with during the first couple of years of the 2020s. Similarly, his short story Government Pinam (The Government Corpse) is situated in the pandemic, focusing on a boy quarantined with his sick father in a house sealed shut by government officials.
In Imayam’s debut novel Koveru Kazhudaigal (Mules), over three decades ago, a significant segment is about how the women of the Vannar community deliver through traditional midwifery practices, outside of medical institutions. He also broaches the subject of patient attendants, a subject gaining currency in a nation growing increasingly grey, and the care of the elderly comes into the spotlight. In Pinathuku Sondhakkari (Owner of the Corpse): Meenakshi, a live-in attendant, is left alone to handle her elderly employer Ramanan’s sudden death, his children away and slow to return.
Manamurivu (Divorce) deals with the gendered nature of infertility, dragging the reader through IVF clinics, menstrual cycles, hormone injections, and the inordinate stress to bear children on the woman in the relationship.
Since the COVID-19 pandemic drew science and medicine into drawing rooms and headlines, willy-nilly, it remains to be seen whether Tamil literature will now make room for more health-related content.

Apple has just released iOS 27.2, bringing Apple Pencil support to the iPhone Duo. The software update also includes an “Edge Light” feature for the iPhone Duo that’s intended to illuminate your face during video calls.

The latest iOS update also adds dual-camera use in group FaceTime calls.
Apple previously said the iPhone Duo would add support for the Apple Pencil “later this year.” The company’s first foldable comes with revamped iOS 27 controls designed to work across the device’s 7.6-inch inner display and 5.4-inch outer screen. Polymarket has investigated 'dozens' of election-related cases
Polymarket has investigated "dozens" of bets on its prediction markets related to the midterm election, according to the company's head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista.
At least two of these Polymarket investigations have been referred to its regulator, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, according to a person who is familiar with the probes, but not authorized to speak publicly about them.
These investigations into election insider trading and manipulation come as prediction market Polymarket — and its chief competitor Kalshi — have exploded in popularity over the past year. But the fast-growing industry also faces significant legal challenges from states and political pushback from lawmakers who argue betting on the outcome of elections poses serious risks to the democratic process.
In April, Kalshi banned and fined a handful of political candidates from betting on themselves. A month later, NPR reported that campaign staffers had made "thousands" using insider polling information to bet on their own candidates on platforms like Polymarket and PredictIt.
Polymarket's Bautista — a former FBI official and cryptocurrency analyst — told NPR her team of 16 and a new election surveillance system are actively policing election bets ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.
"If you have information that you have a duty to protect, don't trade on it," Bautista said. "It's explicitly against our terms of use on both platforms, but also is against the law. If you decide that you are smarter and can do it, we will find you."
Bautista joined Polymarket in June. She oversees information gathered from both the U.S.-regulated version of Polymarket, which requires users to provide their real identities, and its bigger brother, Polymarket International, which is essentially unregulated and where trading can be done anonymously and with cryptocurrency. Despite this, Bautista said crypto trades are rarely completely anonymous.
"There's never been a case that we work where we haven't been able to identify, potentially, who these people are," Bautista said.
She said her election surveillance system pulls in "gigabytes" of data on each user from social media, Federal Election Commission data, cryptocurrency companies, banking partners, statistical models and other public information sources. If a user hits a certain number of internally-defined red flags, Bautista gets an alert on her phone.
"We're getting hundreds of alerts a day," Bautista said.
When asked about the specific detection criteria and thresholds, Bautista did not comment citing system security. But she said insider trading and market manipulation all look the same regardless of the financial market.
"We're looking at threat vectors and risk areas that have existed for decades in traditional markets," Bautista said. "But we recognize, too, that when it comes to prediction markets, we're seeing some of the old tried and known tactics, but being applied to a new vector through prediction markets."
Back in May, Kalshi, Polymarket's top rival, announced its own election surveillance system that also uses FEC data. Their system purportedly blocks any campaign staffer listed by the FEC from betting on an election. In July, Kalshi said it had blocked "dozens" of staffers from trading on elections, though at least one staffer told NPR they got around this. The staffer shared records of their recent trades and spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of consequences for their future employment.
Prediction markets for elections are uniquely vulnerable to market manipulation and insider trading, said Rajiv Sethi, an economics professor at Barnard College at Columbia University, who has studied prediction markets for decades.
"[Election prediction markets] have the possibility of being a self-fulfilling prophecy," Sethi said. "Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging."
Bautista said her Polymarket team and surveillance system is learning from past cases and putting their feet in the shoes of would-be insider traders and market manipulators.
"If I was worried about somebody trying to materially move an election market to make it look like one option was more likely to happen than the other and I identify a pattern where they're opening several different accounts and they're doing that in short bursts and I see device IDs consistent across different trades placed in short succession with new wallets across five or four different accounts," Bautista said. "If I were to work that case and then action that, the findings of that tactic go back into the process to create the detections."
As prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the last two years, the industry's federal regulator, the CFTC, has done little to police these new financial markets, largely leaving that work to the companies themselves.

The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
- Published
Mohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru.
But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work.
The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out.
"The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working."
He wears the camera for five or six hours a day.
"It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim.
He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities.
Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work.
That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world.
Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data.
"Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig.
His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work.
"For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says.
Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says.
"We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off."
But his customers are getting more demanding.
"Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands.
"Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people."
And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year.
Why is such data so important?
If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data.
Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact.
"Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application. For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says.
And until recently, that data was not available.
"There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco.
At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia.
Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content. It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients.
"You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that. Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US."
But are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs?
At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai.
For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says.
The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about.
"By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says.
Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI.
"AI cannot be viewed merely as a technical system. We need to develop a socio-technical system in which ethics is upheld through human agency, ensuring that AI delivers beneficence rather than maleficence."
'This is survival'
Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development.
Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day.
Mohammed Arman has been working in the textiles industry in Bangalore for 10 years.
"Garments stitching and cutting. I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed. Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even tells them," he says.
He has recently started wearing a head-mounted camera that records his work.
"For me, it's simple. This is survival. I have a family back home in Bihar, and every rupee I send back matters. If someone offers me extra money to wear a camera while I do the exact same work I've been doing for 10 years, I'm not going to say no.
"It doesn't cost me anything. I'm already doing the stitching, already doing the cutting. Now I just get paid a little more for it," he says.
While there is demand for such footage it will be collected somewhere.
"India's current role in this industry is largely as a supplier of raw material - people strap on cameras, record themselves doing ordinary tasks, and that footage gets shipped off to labs abroad," Agarwal says.
But he argues the value of that kind of work will quickly become eroded, as more companies compete for collection contracts.
"India can't afford to stay a footage supplier. It needs to move up the value chain: from recording raw video to owning the pipeline that turns that video into something usable - cleaning it, structuring it, validating it, and ultimately setting the standards for what counts as high-quality training data," he says.
For some people collecting data is attractive part time work.
Science teacher Jolly Arifur was looking for work she could do from home that would fit around her young son.
"For the past seven months, I strapped a rig-mounted camera on my head while doing my routine domestic work scrubbing, cooking, sweeping tile floors, and folding laundry."
Arifur, who lives in Guntakal, Anantapur, fits the recording work around her teaching.
"I get paid two to three dollars per hour. If I record three to five hours a day, that's a good amount in hand it's become an extra source of income for me, on top of teaching. I'm managing both honestly, fantastically."

BENGALURU: The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in Karnataka concluded on October 27, with the state losing about 99.76 lakh voters from its original electorate of 5.5 crore, bringing the total electorate to 4,54,55,689 (or 4.54 crore).
About 86.56 lakh of these voters are in the 20-29 age group, while the number of new voters stands at 6.83 lakh.
As of June 16, when the rolls were frozen for the SIR process, the state had about 5.5 crore voters. However, during the subsequent enumeration phase, which resulted in the August 24 draft list, about 19.48% or 1.08 crore voters were removed after being categorised as ASDDO (Absent, shifted, dead, duplicate and others).
The largest chunk of voters removed from the draft list were those classified as 'permanently shifted'. This category accounted for 65.45 lakh voters, or 11.8% of the ASDDO list.
The total number of people who made it to the final list after the notices phase was 43.2 lakh out of 43.82 lakh, with 61,867 voters excluded from the final list following the notices.
The state has the largest number of voters between the age of 30 to 39 years of age, accounting for 1.02 cr of the 4.5 cr voters at present. 
At 2.29 voters, there are four lakh more female voters to their male counterparts in Karnataka.
The two-month claims, notices and objections phase, which began on August 24, saw about 43.8 lakh of the 4.4 crore voters on the draft list (4,46,35,975) being issued notices. Officials said about 60,000 of them were excluded from the final list. Claims and objections could be filed only during the first month of this phase, until September 23.
Between June 16 and September 23, 7.87 lakh citizens sought inclusion in the final voter list through Form 6 applications, while 4,530 NRIs sought inclusion through Form 6A. Objections to existing voters and requests for deletion, filed either by voters themselves or their families, amounted to 58,475.
Meanwhile, 10.99 lakh voters from the draft list sought modifications to their details, ranging from spelling corrections to changes in polling booth locations.
The SIR exercise in the state began on June 20, with the deployment of 59,050 booth-level officers (BLOs), 332 Assistant Electoral Registration Officers (AEROs) and 224 Electoral Registration Officers (EROs). There were 5,905 BLO supervisors, each overseeing 10 BLOs. The district commissioners were designated as District Election Officers (DEOs), with 34 such officers across the state.
The number of BLOs and AEROs increased over time to 60,932 and 4,258, respectively.
Recognised political parties appointed 1.33 lakh booth-level agents (BLAs) during the enumeration phase to ensure the forms reached voters. These BLAs were also instrumental in filing objections against voters on the list during the subsequent claims and objections period.
The enumeration phase began on June 30 and was granted two extensions. While it was originally scheduled to end on July 29, the CEO's office announced a 10-day extension to August 8 on July 15, owing to the large number of voters requiring ASDDO classification. The deadline was subsequently extended by another 10 days.

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.
Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.
The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.
Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.
At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”
Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.
When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.
“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.
The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.
In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

How much of Antonelli's success is down to his ability? - F1 Q&A
- Published
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is one step closer to becoming the new F1 world champion after winning the United States Grand Prix from pole position.
The 20-year-old Italian, who leads team-mate George Russell by 123 points in the standings, will secure the title in Mexico City on Sunday by finishing ninth or higher.
BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race in Austin.
- Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet' 
  - Published1 day ago
This weekend, both Mercedes drivers had the new upgrades but Kimi Antonelli dominated qualifying and the race while George Russell didn't quite achieve the same success. There is a theme throughout the season. How much of that is down to driver ability, driving style etc and how much is down to car set-up and strategy. Is George better than this or has he reached his limit? - Julian
The dominant theme of the 2026 season has been the degree to which Kimi Antonelli has stepped up his game after a mixed rookie season that contained some definite highs, but also quite a few difficulties.
In doing so, he has overwhelmed George Russell, who has accepted and is more than willing to say that Antonelli has simply done a better job than him this season.
Antonelli's performances this year have lived up to the billing with which he came to F1 - that he could be the sport's next generational talent.
He has had some luck, and some of his wins have turned on fortune - safety cars in Japan and Madrid, for example.
But he has also performed at a level of consistent excellence, and produced some absolutely standout performances, most obviously Monaco, Monza and Austin.
The Mercedes has on average been the best car, but Antonelli is the only one of the team's two drivers who has always been a factor. He fully deserves the world title that he is almost certain to clinch this weekend in Mexico City.
As for Russell, he has fundamentally used driving style as an explanation for his relative struggles, saying the previous cars suited his, and the new ones Antonelli's. He has won only three races compared with Antonelli's nine.
On Sunday, team principal Toto Wolff said Russell had struggled in Austin to get the right set-up on the Mercedes with the new upgrade package, which has been problematic since it was introduced in Malaysia.
Wolff said: "George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category and merits to be put in the group of the very best ones. And we've seen that last year.
"This year, we see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fine. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles and he struggles more than maybe Kimi. And that is on us.
"We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.
"So what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all about the intelligence, the ability, the determination."
Driving style and set-up are genuine reasons for a driver to struggle in certain circumstances.
However, it's also a case that the absolute elite, the all-time greats - drivers such as Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton and Fernando Alonso - tend to find a way to be at the top of their game regardless of the car's behaviour.
The worry for Russell right now is that if Antonelli is at that level - and it looks as though he has the potential to be, given his performances in only his second season - he will have his work cut out to beat him consistently in the future.
So he needs to regroup over the winter, come back next year and prove he can get back on to Antonelli's level.
With Lewis Hamilton's intentions clear of staying in F1 until there is an African Grand Prix, which I think will most likely be with Ferrari, what does that mean for the young talents who desire to drive for Ferrari? Will it be at least another four to five years before we see new drivers replacing either or both Lewis and Charles Leclerc? - Liam
Lewis Hamilton repeated in Austin last weekend that, ideally, he would like to still be racing when Formula 1 returns to Africa.
"I'm now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that's been my dream, to be able to race in Africa," he said.
"So, yes, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."
Whether he can manage to stay that long is another question.
Formula 1 has said the African Grand Prix in Rwanda will be held in the "early 2030s".
The aim is for that to be in 2030 but it's not clear whether the new track will be ready by then.
Even if they make that deadline, will Hamilton still be racing? He will be 45 at the start of 2030. That's the same age as Fernando Alonso is now, and he is still going strong.
Hamilton's answer alludes to his current contract, which it is believed lasts until the end of 2027. So he would need to do another one of three years to make it to 2030.
As he says, if he is still performing at the level he is now by the middle of next year, why not? But as yet it's not clear what Ferrari will think about that.
Hamilton's presence - and the long-term contract held by team-mate Charles Leclerc - does raise questions about Ferrari's driver academy.
First and foremost, those questions surround Oliver Bearman, who is yet to finalise his new contract with Haas for next season.
Bearman has had a strong season and a new deal is believed to be pretty much a formality - driver and team have expressed their desire to stay together, and the Briton was talking in a BBC 5 live interview at the weekend very much as if he would still be a Haas driver next year.
But Bearman has higher ambitions than staying at Haas for the rest of his career.
If Hamilton and Leclerc are going to be at Ferrari for the next four years, Bearman would have every right to be asking the team what that means for him.
If he isn't going to get into the senior team, what can they do to further his career? Do they let him go, so he can pursue his ambitions elsewhere, or do they allow him to do that while still maintaining links?
These questions become even more pressing for Bearman now Brazilian Rafael Camara - also a Ferrari young driver - is joining Haas for 2027.
Bearman needs to beat the Brazilian if he is not to face an existential threat to his future as a potential driver for a top team.
What's been happening with Alex Albon this season? Williams team-mate Carlos Sainz seems to have the better of him, and the car doesn't look to be in a good place. - David
Of the two Williams drivers, in a team that is struggling, Carlos Sainz has had the better season.
But it's not as stark as it perhaps appears just looking on the surface.
Sainz leads Albon by two points in the championship, and while the qualifying comparison is skewed heavily towards Sainz on a head-to-head basis at 13-5, the time gap between them is 0.115 seconds.
As if Albon was not already having a rough season, to top it he incurred the wrath of Fernando Alonso in Austin after the two collided on the first lap, leaving both with damaged cars.
Alonso said: "The quality of the drivers in the lower third of the grid is very low, as we saw today with Alex."
Williams are in such a state this year that comparing the drivers should be treated with a degree of qualification.
The car has been slow, and the team have struggled with consistency between parts, as well as quality and degradation.
In other words, two parts that should perform the same have not always done so, and some of them wear out and lose performance quicker than others.
Of course that works across both drivers but it does make comparisons difficult.
Albon was asked about the comparison with Sainz in qualifying in Monza last month.
He pointed out that the crash he had in Canada when he hit a groundhog had been costly because there was a new engine in the car that weekend, which was written off. That meant he had to run an old engine longer than ideal.
And he alluded to Williams suffering from the same issues with varying engine performance that happened in the early days of the new engine rules at Mercedes and McLaren.
"There's a few things," Albon said. "In the beginning of the year, it was very battery-dominated.
"If you think even just the George and Kimi situation, that's the manufacturer side of it having issues. So you can imagine it's not just them two that have had problems.
"There's been a few qualifying sessions where the corners have been good, but you don't see it in the lap time. It's on the stopwatch.
"And then we're also going through our own issues as a team. And that's not just on my side. There's also a side where to say that both cars are performing in the same way would not be true. We've been fighting some inconsistencies in the cars that's been there since the beginning of the year.
"We're much better now at getting on top of them. If you look at the last four or five weekends, we're actually very close in terms of performance. But it's taken a while to get there."
Do you foresee a world in which live F1 coverage ever returns to free-to-air telly in the UK or is it now stuck behind a paywall for eternity? I've now taken a different career path but becoming an engineer in F1 was my ultimate ambition when I was applying for university in the early 2010s, inspired by BBC's live coverage. - Ian
In the UK, the current situation is that Sky has exclusive rights to broadcast F1 behind a paywall, while Channel 4 has highlights on free-to-air television, with live coverage of the British Grand Prix.
Sky has the rights until the end of 2034, after it struck a new deal for a larger fee earlier this year.
That came in the wake of Apple buying the US rights starting from this season.
At the same time, the television market is in flux as streaming becomes increasingly prevalent as a means of consuming content.
In that context, as well as the wider sports broadcast situation, it's hard to imagine a situation where F1 could return fully to free-to-air television.
The wider picture is it is still on free-to-air in some countries - Brazil as an example.
But F1 would also argue free-to-air does not always mean more people getting sight of the sport, depending on how it's promoted in various ways, and viewing habits are not the same in all countries.
Social media output is also an important consideration. At the same time, F1 is a business that exists to make money.

The rift between the Vice-Chancellor and Syndicate members of Mahatma Gandhi University (MGU) in Keralam has escalated, with all 12 government-nominated Syndicate members resigning from the governing bodies of private and aided colleges in protest against the Vice-Chancellor’s decision to override the Syndicate’s nominations.
The dispute centres on the appointment of university representatives to the statutory governing bodies and management councils of private and aided colleges. Syndicate members said the varsity had traditionally nominated only Syndicate members to the governing bodies of individual colleges.
Accordingly, the Syndicate submitted its list of nominees to the Vice-Chancellor on October 5. However, the Vice-Chancellor allegedly invoked his special powers to replace several nominees with new members, overriding the Syndicate’s decision. Three Syndicate members were not assigned any responsibility, prompting the government nominees to resign from the governing bodies.
The Syndicate has accused the Vice-Chancellor of inducting Sangh Parivar nominees into the committees. “We will be meeting the Minister for Higher Education to apprise him of the situation and seek legal action in consultation with Mathew Kuzhalnadan, MLA, also a member of the Syndicate,” said Jobin Jose Chamakkala, a syndicate member.
Stance of V-C’s office
The Vice-Chancellor’s office, however, offered a different version of events. It said the Vice-Chancellor decided to prepare his own list of nominees after the Syndicate rejected his request to include representatives of the Senate and the Academic Council.
“While the Syndicate members insisted on making nominations only from among themselves, the Vice-Chancellor demanded that the Academic Council and the Senate should also be represented in these governing bodies. Meanwhile, the delay in finalising the nominations began causing difficulties for several colleges affiliated with the university. It was under these circumstances that the Vice-Chancellor decided to make the nominations on his own. Even this list included 70% of the Syndicate members, while the remaining 30% were drawn from the Academic Council and the Senate,” the office said.
Official sources, meanwhile, added that the resignations would not automatically invalidate the list of nominees. “If the Syndicate does not initiate steps to cancel the nominations in their entirety, it could leave the Vice-Chancellor with more vacancies to fill with people of his choice,” they pointed out.
Left-leaning teachers quit IQAC
In a parallel development, Left-leaning teachers have resigned from the university’s Internal Quality Assurance Cell (IQAC) committee, widening the fallout from the dispute. Their protest followed the Vice-Chancellor’s decision to defer an agenda item on electing an Academic Council representative to the university’s Statutory Finance Committee.
The election had been listed as the first item on the agenda of the Academic Council meeting. However, the Vice-Chancellor deferred it without taking it up for consideration, prompting the teachers to resign, sources said.
