Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.
“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”
After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”
Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.
The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.
Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.
Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.
“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”
Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.
Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.
Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.
He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.
“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”
The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.
Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.
“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

Anthropic filed key paperwork on Monday ahead of a high-anticipated initial public offering, providing new details about its finances and the risks facing its business.
According to the filing, the artificial intelligence company plans to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. The IPO could come later in November, The Wall Street Journal reported. The S-1 prospectus does not include details on how much the company plans to raise or its targeted valuation; The New York Times reported in August that it was looking to raise more than $100 billion with a valuation around $2 trillion.
“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic wrote in the filing. “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.”
The paperwork offers a window into the company’s finances through the first half of 2026. Its revenue grew to more than $16 billion, up from about $4.5 billion in 2025. The Claude maker emphasized its growing enterprise business, noting that more than 11,900 customers spent at least $100,000 in the past twelve months; more than 1,900 spent $1 million or more; and roughly 250 customers spent $10 million or more.
Despite its growing revenue, Anthropic has yet to turn a profit. It posted a net loss of $80.7 million in the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion in the same period last year.
While it’s expected that a company accurately reports its risk factors, the prospectus also features a particularly thorough list of potential business quagmires, noting that investing in the stock carries “a high degree of risk.”
Those risks range from the ability to secure adequate compute to intense competition from rival labs to advanced AI systems’ potential to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
The filing warns about the possibility that sophisticated AI could be abused by threat actors to launch cyberattacks and develop novel biological weapons, or by authoritarian governments to surveil their citizens. Anthropic also pointed to the risk that it could lose control of the AI models it develops.
It also highlighted the volatility of government action, specifically noting the Trump Administration’s decision to designate the company as a supply-chain risk.
“While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the U.S. government, and in turn adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations,” the filing concluded.
In September, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI—which filed confidentially for IPO in the summer—announced that it no longer intended to go public this year, citing concerns over the risks posed to humanity by AI.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of OpenAI, who had reportedly lost faith in the lab’s ability to develop advanced AI models safely. Anthropic markets itself as highly safety-conscious; its CEO, Dario Amodei, has repeatedly commented on the risk that AI could eliminate scores of jobs, and act against human interests.
The filings also outline Anthropic’s ambition to develop sophisticated AI models capable of accelerating scientific discovery, curing disease, and spurring economic growth.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” the company wrote.
The company did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.
On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

Gaming major Nazara Technologies swung back to the black in Q2 FY27 and reported a profit of ₹35.4 Cr against a net loss of ₹33.9 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, the bottom line improved from a loss of ₹82.5 Cr in Q1 FY27. It is pertinent to note that the year-ago loss figures were skewed as the listed gaming company had lodged ₹914.7 Cr in impairment and other losses during the quarter ended September 2025. Meanwhile, the profits came on the back of improving margins and operating revenue zooming nearly 52% to ₹803.2 Cr during the quarter under review from ₹526.5 Cr in Q2 FY26. On a QoQ basis, the top line rose 87.3% from ₹428.8 Cr in Q1 FY27. The company attributed the surge in revenue to BlueTile and BestPlay adding ₹329 Cr to its top line from August 2026 and healthy organic growth across its verticals. Including other income of ₹13.7 Cr, Nazara’s total income stood at ₹816.9 Cr in the quarter under review. Meanwhile, total expenses (including the ₹6.7 Cr in impairment expenses) also rose 43.7% to ₹767.6 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹534.3 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. In a filing with the exchanges, Nazara said that its EBITDA improved 93% YoY to ₹120 Cr in Q1 FY27, while its EBITDA margin jumped 311 bps YoY to 14.9% in the quarter under review. “This quarter demonstrates the company we are building: a portfolio of high-quality games on a single, shared platform. Bluetile and BestPlay grew EBITDA 64% in their first two months as part of Nazara, while sustained investment in content delivered organic growth of 11% in revenue and 17% in EBITDA across our existing gaming studios…,” said Nazara CEO Raymond Stauffer. Others Tested

It also has the expected pet camera-on-wheels features, like two-way audio and video, night vision, and 4K imaging. During initial testing, the camera didn't charge properly on the dock and often froze or stopped charging. I got a second model to test, and it worked better—it handled tasks on command, returned to the charging station, and recognized my cats. However, I still don't think its AI-powered companion features are cool enough to justify that price tag. If price is no issue for you and you want a moving camera on wheels, it's worth checking out.
SwitchBot Pan/Tilt Cam Plus 3K for $50: I generally liked this pan/tilt camera, which offers a 360-degree horizontal field of view and a 115-degree vertical field of view, and can be mounted with the provided tools. It also has two-way audio, voice commands, and smart-home support like Amazon Alexa or Google Home. It has eight infrared LEDs that support enhanced night vision, with a range of up to 32 feet. Through the app, you can adjust camera settings for motion detection or tracking and switch to privacy mode when you want the camera to stop recording. However, it only works with 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi and, like many other cams on this list, requires a paid subscription plan to access enhanced features like AI recognition, smart event summaries, unlimited cloud storage, and access to historical recordings. It also required several firmware updates throughout testing and would freeze during updates. It also lagged when moving through the app and often froze for a prolonged period when first opening the app.
Amazon Blink Mini 2K+ for $40: This small, budget-friendly camera supports 2K video, 4X hybrid zoom, and color night vision. In his testing, reviewer Simon Hill found its motion detection reliable, but only with a subscription: $3 per month or $30 per year for one camera, or $10 per month or $100 per year for unlimited cameras. You can record locally by purchasing a Sync Module 2 ($50) and inserting a USB flash drive. Luckily, you don't need a subscription to record the motion-triggered footage from the camera to the Sync Module 2. You just need to insert an approved USB flash drive (up to 256 GB) into the Sync Module 2 to enable subscription-free local storage. Without a subscription, however, live viewing is limited to five minutes, recording is unavailable, videos load much more slowly, people/animal detection isn’t included, and you can’t share clips.
Enabot Ebo Air 2 for $199: The new model from Enabot is an improved interactive robot toy and camera on wheels from the brand’s lineup. It’s got a 2K HD camera, two-way audio, and a built-in laser toy, and you control the robot’s movements from your phone’s app. It’s lightweight and compact, and it can easily maneuver around objects. While acting as a pet camera, the robot also entertains (or scares or confuses) your pet by making animal noises, doing tricks like spinning and zigzagging, and displaying “emotions” via its front screen. It also has a built-in laser toy that my cats actually played with, along with key features like 24/7 video recording with smart playback, motion detection, and activity alerts.
Petcube Play 2 for $75: This Petcube camera attempts to combine popular laser toys that cats love with a pet security cam, with mixed results. Like many other cameras in the brand’s lineup, the Play 2 has excellent color and night vision, an extra-wide view, and two-way audio. The laser toy is supposed to auto-engage when motion is detected, but this often didn’t happen during my tests. When the laser did work and caught my cats’ attention, the feature turned off quickly. Plus, because the camera needed to sit high on a shelf to see the area, the laser was often too high for the cats to attempt to catch. You can manually play with the cat using the laser through the app, although it’s often laggy, and my cats ended up more perplexed than playful when the laser was on. It’s a solid camera, but the toy aspect falls a bit flat.
Furbo Mini for $25: I love this super-affordable, 360-degree-rotating basic pet camera. Furbo’s app is easy to use, the 1080 HD feed is clear, it can be mounted on a wall, and it has two-way audio. It’s powered via USB, but it works only with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, so beware. As with most other pet cameras, to access the full features—like smart detection, alerts, and access to historical video footage—you’ll need Furbo Nanny, the paid subscription service. Luckily, Furbo offers a 14-day free trial to see if the service is a good fit.
Petcube Bites 2 Lite for $80: With HD 1080p live video, night vision up to 30 feet, 8x zoom, two-way audio so you can talk to and hear your pets, and food-dispensing abilities, this pet camera has all of the bells and whistles. It also includes an easily detachable plastic treat dispenser that holds up to 1.5 pounds of kibble. You can toss treats remotely from the app, and you can also control the amount and distance. With the subscription service, the app alerts you when the device detects motion or sound and logs it with playback video. I like the customization options and clear video feed, but—like other Petcube devices—you need the extra Care plan to unlock all the best features.
Enabot Rola PetPal Robot Pet Companion for $200 (treat dispensing): A pet camera on wheels, this rolling model has the best of intentions, but the sometimes glitchy app makes the combo pet camera/toy/feeder a little unpredictable. Through the app, you can watch your pets on the security camera and drive the robot around, pressing buttons to do tricks and dispense treats. You can watch the camera feed live in the app, and you can also schedule recordings, which are viewable via cloud playback. It also assembles a 30-second “day in the life” compilation. The robot is also supposed to detect abnormal movement or sounds, like barking or broken glass, and send a smart alert to the owner with a timestamp while away from home. Through AI-powered pet recognition, the bot can also snap a picture of your pet, but the AI features were unreliable when I tested them.
Petcube Cam for $32: It's simple, compact, and doesn't have all the bells and whistles like more advanced models do, but it’s a great price for a reliable, basic pet camera. Like others in Petcube's lineup, it has a 1080p HD camera, night vision, and two-way audio. It sits on hinges and can angle up and down, with the option to flip the video feed in-app if you want to lay it horizontally. You'll need the brand's subscription Care plan to access any features beyond the live feed. You can set a “motion zone” to receive notifications only in a specific area, and you can connect your phone’s location to the app so you’re alerted more often when you’re away. You can also share the camera feed with others so they can watch remotely, and specify the footage you want to share. This camera is basic, but it delivers a high-quality camera feed and advanced extras that make it a steal at this price.
Catit Pixi Smart Mouse Camera for $51: This cutie looks like a miniature mouse with oversized, magnetic feet that attach to a metal stand. The mouse legs hinge so you can adjust the camera’s height and angle. While adorable, it’s expensive for what it is: The lens doesn't move, and it requires a microSD card to capture video beyond a live feed. With the SD card, you can scroll through recorded video to see activity from past days, record live footage, and save photos and videos to your smartphone’s camera roll. Even with the SD card, though, it was hard to pinpoint the exact time when reviewing footage. The live video feed can be laggy, and there were connectivity issues a few times. It’s a tad expensive at this price point for its (lack of) capabilities.
Closer Pets TreatView with Pet Camera for $100: With an HD camera, two-way communication, motion detection, a built-in memory card, and a one-cup storage for kibble or treats, which you can schedule or dispense at random—on paper, this pet camera has all of the bells and whistles. The video feed was always clear, though the audio was a bit laggy and hard to hear. The treat portions were huge, dispensing a heaping handful of kibble even at the lowest setting. The dispensing alert was super jarring, and my pets were frightened by it—there was no way to silence it. Because of the kibble-dispensing hole's placement, the camera is angled low, making it hard to see the area I wanted. This is an okay pet camera, but its additional features become a burden rather than an asset.
How I Tested
To find the best pet cameras to test, I first looked for security cameras with extra pet-specific features. I set up each camera individually, noting any difficulties with initial setup, Wi-Fi configuration, and the camera feed's speed and reliability. I tested each camera for at least a week (most for much longer) in various spots around my house, and I rigorously tested the extra features available on most of the cameras, like scheduled feedings, food-dispensing, playtime, and scheduled recordings, noting any issues I experienced. Over the months of testing, I went out of town several times and completely relied on these cams to keep an eye on my two children—I mean, cats.
So, Is There Really a Difference Between Security Cameras and Pet Cameras? Sort Of
Security cameras let you keep an eye on your house (and pet) while you’re away, but pet cameras often include additional pet-specific features, such as the ability to dispense treats and interact with your furry friend via a two-way speaker. These cameras with special features can help ease common pet issues like separation anxiety or boredom. The Enabot Rola PetPal Robot Pet Companion, for example, has attachments that let you remotely give your pet a treat or engage in “playtime.”
That's not to say you can’t use a security camera as a pet cam, but like any other smart home device that connects to Wi-Fi, it could be hacked and compromise your privacy. Make sure your Wi-Fi password is strong, and set up two-factor authentication in your camera’s app. It’s also a good idea to keep it turned off when you’re home, as an extra precaution.

The maker of miracles may no longer be God, but it does rhyme with him.
Anthropic, creator of Claude, filed its S-1 paperwork on Monday in preparation for a gargantuan initial public offering. The document runs over 300 pages and spans more than 240,000 words, some 50,000 more than the New Testament. It asks potential investors to prioritize mission over money: "Mission" appears 79 times, while "money" — the thing an S-1 is filed to generate, in this case, a bajillion dollars worth — a mere 17.
The company professes it could "bend the arc of geopolitical history toward freedom"; it could grow economies everywhere, including "the poorer parts of the world"; it could cure "diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia." Page 4 of the S-1 is not dissimilar from Jesus in Matthew 11: "The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them."
Anthropic aims to "bring forth an age of miracles," it writes, and the investors who buy in should be true believers. Because in the wrong hands, as you'll see if you turn your missals to page 46, AI can be built in ways that pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."
While S-1s are definitionally visions of the future and full of hype, most are drab financial documents, eye-popping for their prospective profits more than their prose. But Anthropic didn't just open up its book; it wrote its own Good Book, a Bible-like statement of good and evil that joins a growing canon of the company's sacred texts. If you were to stumble onto any random page of this S-1, you'd be forgiven for thinking you were reading not a perfunctory government filing but the scripture of a doomsday religion.
Anthropic has long dodged allegations of fomenting a new, questionable faith. Headlines and takes on Anthropic's cultishness abound: "The Cult of Anthropic" (The Information), "Anthropic is a Cult and Claude is rapidly becoming its God" (The New York Post), "Has a cult ever started a company as successful as Anthropic?" (Peter "Beware the Antichrist" Thiel). Critics point to the employees' extinction predictions — p(doom) is not too far from p(rapture) — and ties to the effective altruism movement. It doesn't help that Dario Amodei was reportedly a Y2K prepper in high school. Anthropic has welcomed the reputation in other ways, inviting religious leaders to oversee the construction of Claude's rules.
In its S-1, Anthropic asks investors to take an actual leap of faith.
Let's play: Is that an Anthropic core value or one of God's 10 commandments?
Anthropic asks its employees to act for the "global good," be "helpful, honest, and harmless," and "hold light and shade." They shall have no other gods — as in, "put the mission first." And, just as followers must sublimate themselves to praise God, Anthropic employees must be "low-ego." The S-1 says it at least nine times.
To understand Anthropic, you'll need to understand 42 ornate terms. The S-1's glossary is sprawling, including neologisms for virtuous acts ("closing the loop") and evil deeds ("prompt injection"). Then there's "Constitutional AI," a type of large language model that is trained with goodness in mind. The SEC's "Plain English Handbook" implores companies to use "concrete, everyday words" and to avoid "relying on glossaries and defined terms." But can you truly be AGI-pilled if you don't speak of "interleaved thinking," "mechanistic interpretability," or "multi-agent orchestration"?
You use language like this because we need to be — and I say we as in society — true believers that this is going to work.James Bort
It's exceedingly hard to get a job at Anthropic, and not just because of the massive pool of cash-eyed engineers seeking IPO windfalls. The company has an intensive interview process, one it name-checks in the S-1. It looks for honesty, trust, and (you guessed it) a low ego. "We are willing to turn down candidates who don't demonstrate them, even if they are extremely strong technically," the S-1 reads. They must, in other words, be devotees through and through.
Accepted engineers become "Ants." Most tech companies have a name for their employees: Googlers, Metamates, Amazonians, Nvidians, Palantirians. Anthropic's moniker evokes the image of a collective, company as colony. In Proverbs 6:6, ants are considered diligent and prepared. Staffers may yell its teachings at their OpenAI foes: "Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise!"
CEO Dario Amodei — Amodeity — leads the ants' march, along with his six apostles. These cofounders pull equal cash salaries and are "distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission," the S-1 says. And, while the company opens itself to a broader group of believers through its forthcoming IPO, the divine cofounders will retain majority decision-making power.
Anthropic has its own form of tithing: The cofounders all made voluntary pledges of 80% of their personal equity to philanthropy. They incentivize their employees to do the same, promising to match donations.
Cult is an overused word, and many parts of Anthropic are far from cultish. Where cults are led by a liturgical leviathan that squashes the speech of their participants, Anthropic touts its culture of open dialogue. "Our teams operate in a truth-seeking environment where the best argument wins, not the loudest voice or the most senior title," the S-1 reads.
Americans' faith in the presidency, Congress, the Supreme Court, the military, the police, higher education, public education, news media, the medical system, and traditional organized religion are each at record- or near-record lows — and just as AI has brought on tremendous economic and social uncertainty. In that cauldron of doubt, tech founders — with their world-historic money, power, and ubiquity, and in their pursuit of it — sense an opportunity, to offer promise and purpose. As Sam Altman once said, "The most successful founders do not set out to create companies. They are on a mission to create something closer to a religion." They may also be trying to build devotion out of necessity, as the economy and stock market increasingly relies on AI gains.
"If these companies fail, what happens?" asked James Bort, an assistant professor of entrepreneurship at DePaul University, and coauthor of a recent research paper on "cultic startups." "You use language like this because we need to be — and I say we as in society — true believers that this is going to work."
Anthropic didn't respond to my request to know more about how it wrote the S-1. So, we asked Claude: If the S-1 is a confession of faith, what are you? I am its product, Claude said. "The word made flesh, or at least made weights."

My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed.
Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD.
While there he became involved with Operation Omega, a group that smuggled humanitarian aid across the border from India to Bangladesh during its war with Pakistan in 1971. This led him to cut short his studies so that he could begin work as a consultant economist and project planner. Over the years he worked on many projects, including for the University of New South Wales from 1984 to 1986 in the Solomon Islands on a smallholder project and a post-cyclone survey.
In 1989 his work took him back to Bangladesh, where he was employed by the World Bank to develop a flood action plan. Fourteen years of his life, from 1992 to 2006, were then spent with the Department for International Development, working on ways to help tackle the social and economic problems related to rural poverty in India.
He was also particularly proud of a cyclone recovery and reconstruction project he worked on in 2007 for the World Bank, which led to the building of cyclone shelters in Bangladesh.
In 2006 he became a trustee and then chair of trustees of the Humanitarian Centre in Cambridge, which later became the Centre for Global Equality. Two years later he had to leave work after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, but eventually he was lucky enough to receive a lung transplant that prolonged his life considerably.
That allowed him to focus on being a trustee, chair and patient president of the charity Action for Pulmonary Fibrosis, giving over the last decade of his life to fighting on behalf of people with the disease so that they can be provided with better diagnosis, care and treatment. He was also president of the European Pulmonary Fibrosis Federation.
In 1976 he met Hilary Gretton, a nurse, and they married five years later. She survives him, along with their children, Rosie, David and Euan, and seven grandchildren.

Quick Answer
To stop Google from using your Gmail, Drive, and Photos data for personalized ads, visit google.com/search-personalization, open Connected Content Apps, and disconnect Google Workspace and Photos. Then turn off personalized ads at myadcenter.google.com. You can also delete past activity at activity.google.com.
It’s not hyperbole to say AI agents are genuinely helpful. The big tech companies aren’t stupid to be investing billions of dollars to build these AI agents, but they need more than your money to help you – your data. Google is best placed to play this smart answers game considering it owns some of the most widely used services in the world – Search, Gmail, Chrome, Photos, and Android.
If you’ve let Google’s AI look at your Gmail or Google Photos for smarter answers, there’s a catch. As of October 16, 2026, Google’s privacy policy says data from those apps can also help personalize ads. Google is also testing ads in AI Mode for people who have connected their apps.
Here’s what changed, what it does and doesn’t mean, and how to turn it off.
Table of Contents
What changed
Since 2021, Google’s privacy policy has said that it doesn’t use your Gmail, Drive, or Photos content for personalized ads. According to Ars Technica and Google’s own archive, the old line read: “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos.”
The current policy, effective October 16, 2026, adds a condition:
We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos, unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.
A new passage in the same section spells out how this happens:
You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive… For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.
You “choose” this through Personal Intelligence, the opt-in feature that lets AI Mode and other Search tools draw on your Gmail, Calendar, and Photos. Calendar is US and English only for now, Photos isn’t available in every region, and Drive, though named in the policy, isn’t currently one of the apps you can connect to Search.
The ads side is already live as a test.
What it means for you
It’s easy to overstate this, so here’s what Google actually says.
What Google says won’t happen:
- In its Search help page, Google says: “Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or your Google Photos library.“
- Advertisers don’t get access to your connected apps, and Google doesn’t share your name or email with them.
- Google says it won’t personalize ads on sensitive categories such as race, religion, sexual orientation or health.
What can happen:
The same help page says Search “may reference summaries, excerpts and inferences” from your connected apps, and “that same info may be used to show you ads.” The policy gives an example of personalizing answers: ask Search about a recent hotel booking, and it may use booking details from an email. The ads link comes from the help page: that same kind of info may now be used to show you ads.
Search vs. Gemini:
The ad test is in AI Mode in Search. Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub says “Your Gemini Apps chats are not being used to show you ads.” The policy still lists “Gemini Apps” among services you can connect your data to.
Beyond AI Mode:
When you connect your apps, Google says all Search services can access them, including Search, Discover, Maps, Shopping, Flights, Hotels, Translate, and News. The same page says human reviewers may see some of that data.
Where this applies:
Connecting content apps to Search is available to adults in a long list of countries, including the US and India. The UK and EU countries don’t appear on that list. Personal Intelligence in Gemini is not available in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, Nigeria, or the UK. Google hasn’t said where the ads test is running, and the policy wording is global. What we think is, since Google doesn’t offer either feature in the UK yet, UK readers look largely unaffected for now.
How to opt out of Search Personalization
Disconnect Gmail and Photos from Search (web, Android, iPhone)
As per Google’s help pages, the steps are the same on the web, Android, and iPhone:
- Open your Google Account and go to Data & privacy > Personalization settings > Personalized Recommendations in Search services. Or you can click this if you are already signed in: google.com/search-personalization.
- Under Additional Personal Intelligence, open Connected Content Apps.
- Disconnect Google Workspace and Google Photos.
To go further, turn off Personalized Recommendations on the same page. Google says it’s updating these settings, so labels may differ.
Disconnect apps in Gemini
- Gemini mobile app (Android/iPhone): tap Menu > your profile picture > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps.
- Web (gemini.google.com): select Menu > Settings & help > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps.
Turn off Google Workspace and Google Photos, plus any other apps you don’t want connected.
Turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center
Go to My Ad Center, select On or Off next to Personalized ads, choose Off, and confirm.
Google says it will then stop using your saved account info and activity for ads, and will show ads based on general factors like the topic you’re viewing. You’ll still see ads; they just won’t be tailored to you. This doesn’t stop connected-app data from being used for AI answers.
Clean up what’s already saved
Disconnecting doesn’t delete your Search Services History, which can still be used for product improvement. Review and delete it at activity.google.com. In Gemini, disconnecting doesn’t delete your Gemini Apps Activity either.
Should you disconnect?
Personal Intelligence is genuinely useful: asking about your trip without pasting in your booking is the whole point, and Google says advertisers don’t get access to your connected apps.
But helping you and choosing your ads are different uses, and the ads part was added after Personal Intelligence launched. If that bothers you, disconnect. A middle path is to keep Personal Intelligence on and turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center. Your data still feeds Google’s AI answers, and Search Services History can be used for product improvement, including AI model training.
The bottom line
While you’d see a lot of noise around these changes on social media, know that this change doesn’t touch everyone’s inbox, because it’s opt-in. But if you connected Gmail or Photos to its AI, what that AI learns can now help pick your ads, starting with a test in AI Mode. If that trade isn’t for you, the switches above take minutes.
FAQs about Search Personalization
1. Is Google reading my emails to target ads?
Not directly, according to Google. It says ads aren’t based “directly” on your inbox, but summaries, excerpts, and inferences Search draws from connected apps can be used for ads.
2. I never turned on Personal Intelligence. Am I affected?
As per the policy, Gmail, Drive, and Photos content isn’t used for ads unless you make it available to other services. It’s opt-in, but worth checking the settings above in case you connected and forgot.
3. Does this apply to Gemini chats?
Google says Gemini chats aren’t used to show you ads right now. The ad test is in AI Mode in Search.
4. Does disconnecting erase what Google already has?
No. Delete your Search Services History at activity.google.com and your Gemini Apps Activity separately, as we described earlier in this article.

SAT Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam, the premier tertiary-level child health institution in the State’s public sector and one of the chosen Centres of Excellence for Rare Diseases in the country, has found itself in the eye of the storm following allegations about “clinical trial drugs” being given to spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)-afflicted children.
With Opposition political parties intent on carrying forth with the campaign that “experimental drugs” were used on SMA patients, the Superintendent of SAT Hospital, I. Riaz, appealed to all and sundry not to undermine the government’s efforts to make the drug for SMA available to a larger number of patients.
According to him, the decision to provide SMA patients with a less expensive, generic version of the original molecule against SMA, in place of the imported original drug costing several lakhs of rupees for a single vial, had been taken by a technical committee comprising experts in the field.
The purchase procedures initiated during the previous government’s time were completed by the present government. The drug meets all regulatory requirements and quality norms, Dr. Riaz added.
‘Unfounded rumours’
Dr. Riaz appealed to all to stop spreading unfounded rumours about the generic SMA medicine and push patients and their families into an anxious state. He pointed out that the medicine had been available in the open market for nearly a year and was already being used by several SMA patients. To raise the argument that it was an experimental drug, just when the government begins to distribute it free of cost, was preposterous.
Several health experts pointed out that quality generics were the only way to make expensive medicines accessible and affordable to a large number of people. If people can willingly accept generic oncology drugs, then to find fault with the generic version of SMA drug alone was just hypocrisy.
Financial assistance
The superintendent also condemned attempts by vested interests to link the financial assistance extended by Natco Pharma under their corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiative to renovate one of the wards in SAT Hospital, to the distribution of generic SMA drug.
SAT Hospital Health Education Society (SATHHES) regularly receives corporate social responsibility funds from various agencies, public and private-sector institutions, and individuals to undertake development projects related to patient care at the hospital
On March 25, 2026, the then Superintendent of SAT Hospital had written to Natco, seeking their assistance to renovate the isolation ward in the hospital
Following a site visit and assessment by company representatives, Natco Pharma transferred ₹25 lakh as the first instalment to the SATHHES account. The company representatives subsequently visited the hospital in the first week of August to meet the Health Minister and hand over a certificate related to the contribution.
The attempts being made to portray this in relation to the generic SMA drug of Natco given at SAT Hospital is malicious and ill-intended, Dr. Riaz said.
It was common for agencies, companies and public-sector institutions providing CSR funds to hand them over and take photographs in the presence of the Health Minister or the Chief Minister, he added.
Instead of spreading baseless allegations, the efforts of the government and SAT Hospital to safeguard the welfare of patients with SMA should be given more support, Dr. Riaz said.

Did you know that an Indian woman scientist had a notable role to play in the development of anti-epileptic drugs and anti-malarial drugs? That the same woman also told us most of what we needed to know about the medicinal plants in the subcontinent?
By the standards of her time, unlike other women scientists, Asima Chatterjee did get recognition for her research while she was alive, but it cannot be said that she received the adulation and celebration that her male peers did. That doesn’t make Asima Chatterjee any less tall a figure in the history of Indian science, and the nation must be grateful for her pioneering work in organic chemistry and the sub category of phytomedicine – using plant extracts to treat various conditions, even prevent them.
109 years ago, Asima Chatterjee was born, on September 23. Her love affair with chemistry began at a young age and she went on to pursue this, with a Bacherlor’s degree and a masters in the subject. At a time when few women were able to take up higher education, she went on to complete her Doctor of Science degree in pre-independent India, specialising in phytochemistry. History records her as the first Indian woman to be awarded a Doctor of Science by any Indian university. She went on to gain expertise in research methodology at the University of Wisconsin, Madison and the California Institute of Technology, working with international experts in the field before returning to India.
She took a great interest in a sector that sought to harness the natural plant biodiversty of India and phytochemistry skills to develop newer compounds and drugs that could be used to treat people. Today plant-based extracts form key elements of critical drugs. Plant-derived drugs range from pure compounds extracted from herbs to complex botanical extracts approved as prescription medications. Chatterjee sank herself into the development of clinically useful drugs from indigenous plants – striking success with isolating the chemical constituents of Marsdenia tinctoria – which led to the formulation of the anti-epileptic drug later marketed as Ayush- 56.
Chatterjee also made huge breakthroughs in developing anti-malarial drugs derived from plant extracts. But the greatest achievement that she is credited with is her extensive research on the chemistry of alkaloids found in Caranthus roseus, or the Madagascar periwinkle, which contributed leaps to the understanding of compounds with anti-cancer properties. No less important is the foundation she laid for modern pharmaceutical chemistry, utilising physical and chemical methods to to determine the complex molecular structures of numerous organic compounds, and recording her methodology meticulously.
Beyond her pioneering work in the lab, Chatterjee was also an ace institution builder and educationist. During her academic career, she served as a professor of chemistry at the University of Calcutta at a time of intense gender barriers in academia, and was later appointed as the Khaira Professor of Chemistry, a prestigious chair in the varsity.
Her work in science was recognised with a Padma Bhushan in 1975, Chatterjee creating a record here too, being the first woman scientist to achieve this honour. She was the first female scientist to be elected as the General President of the Indian Science Congress Association and was also a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy. No wonder then that she was the first female recipient of the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Chemical Sciences (1961), India’s top science award, introduced in 1958. She was also awarded the prestigious CV Raman Award and PC Ray Award.
Today, as the debate rages about bringing scientific vigour and scientifically validating traditional systems of medicine in the country, Chatterjee was a beacon even in this area, her work bridged the gap between traditional Ayurvedic knowledge and modern rigorous chemical analysis, to benefit humanity. Legacy
But Asima Chatterjee’s achievements cannot be confined to just the scientific arena, her immense achievement must also be counted at a time when formidable gender barriers stood in the way of female achievements, breaking the glass ceiling and making it possible, even inspiring, generations of women scientists to make their bold foray into the sciences. Being that rare Indian women scientist who got substantial recognition during their lifetime, in the scientific world, and yet she was largely missing from mainstream narratives, and global histories of science.
But today, we say her name, properly celebrate her legacy. Asima Chatterjee, exceptional chemist, phytochemist and extraordinary pioneering scientist who opened the portals the world of science for generations of women. Say her name, say Asima Chatterjee.

New Delhi, Oct 27: The two-day conclave of the BRICS Parliamentary Forum on Tuesday adopted a joint declaration strongly condemning the 2025 Pahalgam attack and all acts of terrorism as it pledged to combat the menace in all its forms and manifestations and also stressed on non-intervention in the internal affairs of any country.
The joint declaration, announced by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, also condemned the imposition of unilateral economic and secondary sanctions saying such coercive measures have far reaching negative implications on human rights, including the right to development, health and food security of people.
The BRICS Parliamentary Forum supported a comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including its Security Council, saying this reform should make it more just, equitable, democratic, representative, effective, and efficient, better reflecting contemporary realities and the needs of the international community.
"We express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed. We condemn in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir (in Pahalgam) on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured.
"We reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens," the declaration read.
The Forum said terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and that all those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law.
"We urge to ensure zero tolerance for terrorism and reject double standards in countering terrorism. We emphasise the primary responsibility of States in combating terrorism and that global efforts to prevent and counter terrorist threats must fully comply with their obligations under international law, including the Charter of the UN...," it read.
The Forum said it looks forward to further deepening counter-terrorism cooperation and calls for an expeditious finalisation and adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism in the UN framework and concerted actions against all UN-designated terrorists and terrorist entities.
"We reaffirm our adherence to the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, non-intervention in internal affairs, and the peaceful settlement of international disputes, as enshrined in the United Nations Charter, as essential foundations for global stability, peace and development," it said.
The Forum reaffirmed its unwavering support for the peaceful resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict based on the two-state solution, with the two States living side by side, in peace and security, in accordance with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions.
It asserted the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination, freedom, and an independent, sovereign State.
The Forum expressed deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in West Asia and, recalling the respective national positions, called for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation.
It strongly condemned all violations of international humanitarian law, including deliberate attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure, including in BRICS member states, as well as the denial or obstruction of humanitarian access and the targeting of humanitarian personnel.
Iran and United Arab Emirates, which are directly involved with the West Asia conflict, are members of the BRICS. Apart from India, other member nations of the BRICS are: Brazil, Russia, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia and South Africa.
The Forum underlined the need to address accountability for all violations of international humanitarian law.
"We recognise international efforts undertaken by BRICS members to promote respect for, adherence to, and effective implementation of international humanitarian law," it said.
Recognising the urgency of addressing climate change, the BRICS parliamentary body calls for intensifying efforts, through dialogue and international cooperation, to implement nationally determined contributions, strengthen mitigation and adaptation efforts, with a view to achieving the objectives of the UNFCCC and the goals of its Paris Agreement as applicable.
The Forum acknowledge the transformative potential of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI) and information and communication technologies (ICTs).
"We emphasise the necessity of ensuring the open, safe, secure, stable, equitably accessible, peaceful and interoperable use and development of ICTs environment while respecting sovereignty and national security of each country.
"In addition, promoting energy efficiency of AI systems, fostering AI science and innovation, leveraging AI for economic growth and social good and mitigating potential risks would be essential for promoting a just, fair, equitable and prosperous future of all countries, especially those of Global South," it said.

Anthony Albanese has promised a “swift government response” to safety threats to MPs and floated the provision of duress alarms for electorate offices, saying politicians and their staff have put up with threats for too long.
The prime minister’s pledge to the Labor partyroom came hours after senator Fatima Payman again slammed her former government colleagues over the lack of staffing given to her office, controversially asking: “Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office?”
MPs across the political divide have spoken forcefully of the need for more protection for their offices after the alleged attack on the Indi MP last week, raising alarm about threats and violence directed to their staff. Politicians are also revealing the scale of abuse, online and offline, directed toward them, including death and rape threats.
In the first Labor partyroom meeting since the alleged attack, Albanese gave a long address saying this week “must be a turning point” for civil discourse and how threats are responded to. He also conceded there needed to be more investment in security and safety for politicians.
Albanese said MPs have had to “put up with the threat environment for too long”, that the government “need to do more”, and “more can and should be done”.
“You’ve all dedicated so much to the safety of others in the workplace. I’m determined to make sure we do everything for your safety and the safety of your staff as well,” he said.
Albanese did not give specifics, but promised a “swift government response” on safety, and noted numerous MPs had raised the prospect of receiving duress alarms, or panic buttons, to alert authorities of a safety incident. This was among a “series of options” under consideration.
Home affairs minister Tony Burke also told the meeting that the government was looking at safety at polling booths around election time.
Government sources said numerous changes were being considered, with a fulsome response and proposal likely to be revealed in coming days. MPs have raised a wide range of concerns, including greater security and hardening of their electoral offices, better communication with federal police, and resources for security at their private homes like CCTV and lighting – all options understood to be under consideration.
An ongoing review into Commonwealth workplaces will also be expedited by Labor, with recommendations specifically about safety and security to be delivered soon.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor told his MPs in a Coalition partyroom meeting of ongoing conversations with the government about personal safety and the importance of getting it right, but did not raise any specific proposals.
Payman speaks out
Payman, who quit Labor in 2024 to sit on the crossbench, on Monday night lashed out at the prime minister for not responding to a request for additional staff in line with other independent political offices.
The prime minister has discretion over the allocation of personal staff, which are typically more senior advisers. All politicians receive electoral office staff, but Payman has zero advisers while 16 other crossbench MPs and senators shared 30 advisers, according to an internal document tabled in the hearing.
In a Senate estimates hearing, Payman questioned minister Don Farrell whether the staff allocation shortfall was due to Albanese having a personal gripe with her, claiming her staff were severely overworked.
“If [Albanese] cares so much about the welfare and wellbeing of people who work in this building, then I implore you [Farrell] and the prime minister to please look into the fact that my staff are burning out,” she said.
“Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office? To me? For him to take our request seriously?”
Farrell and other Labor senators in the hearing strongly rejected the insinuation, but Payman refused to withdraw the comments when asked until her staffing request was dealt with.
Payman told Guardian Australia last week there had been a massive increase in the number of death threats and hate comments since 2024 when she defected from Labor. Payman said her office manager had opened mail last year containing human faeces, resulting in a biohazard team having to respond.
“We had all these people in hazmat suits come through [the office],” she said. “The trauma that that inflicts on my staff members is horrible. No office or no worker should ever have to deal with that kind of crap.”

Shares of Ather Energy jumped as much as 8.1% to an intraday high of ₹1,702 on the BSE after HSBC and Nomura raised their price targets following the electric two-wheeler maker’s Q2 FY27 results. At 11:28 IST, the stock was trading 6.8% higher at ₹1,680.60, giving the company a market capitalisation of ₹66,672.4 Cr (about $6.9 Bn). The gains extended yesterday’s rally, when Ather shares closed 13.7% higher at ₹1,574 on the BSE after the company announced its Q2 FY27 results during market hours. Adding to the positive sentiment, HSBC and Nomura retained their ‘Buy’ ratings and raised their price targets, citing better-than-expected margins and stronger growth prospects following the launch of Ather’s Konarc scooter range. HSBC raised its price target to ₹1,800 from ₹1,600. The brokerage said Ather delivered a strong second quarter, with EBITDA breaking even ahead of expectations despite commodity cost pressures. Nomura increased its price target to ₹2,070 from ₹1,926. It said Ather’s EBITDA margin, excluding other income, stood at 0.8%, beating its estimate of negative 2.6% and the consensus estimate of negative 2.7%. Stronger bookings and improved growth visibility following the Konarc launch were other positives. Ather’s Maiden Profitable Quarter Ather reported a consolidated net profit of ₹1.3 Cr in Q2 FY27 as against a loss of ₹154.1 Cr a year earlier, supported by stronger revenue growth, improving margins, and other income. It had posted a net loss of ₹51.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue rose 62.9% YoY and 20.3% QoQ to ₹1,464.2 Cr. Including other income, EBITDA stood at ₹74.2 Cr, with a margin of 4.9% as against -9.6% a year earlier and 0.8% in Q1 FY27. Total income rose to ₹1,527 Cr from ₹940.7 Cr a year earlier. However, operating revenue remained ₹61.5 Cr below total expenses of ₹1,525.7 Cr, underscoring other income’s contribution to net profitability. CEO Tarun Mehta said during the earnings call that Ather would prioritise capacity expansion and sales growth over near-term net profitability. He cautioned that some margin gains came from temporary measures, including changes to its product mix and reduced incentives, which offered limited scope for further support if commodity prices remained elevated. Ather To Expand Manufacturing Capacity Ather plans to invest ₹122 Cr to expand manufacturing capacity at its Hosur plant in Tamil Nadu and its upcoming Factory 3.0 in Maharashtra’s Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. The expansion is expected to add 2.25 Lakh units of annual capacity. At Hosur, the company plans to invest up to ₹58 Cr, including taxes, to add capacity for 75,000 units annually by December 2026. Ather has also earmarked ₹53 Cr for a new battery line, which is expected to be completed by Q3 FY28. At Factory 3.0, the company plans to invest ₹64 Cr to add 1.5 Lakh units of annual capacity to the planned 5 Lakh units. The expansion is expected to be completed by Q2 FY28. Ather will finance the investments through a combination of debt and internal accruals. During Q2 FY27, it also raised ₹1,300 Cr through a qualified institutions placement and ₹200 Cr through a preferential equity allotment. The expansion follows a sharp increase in customer interest. Enquiries rose 109% YoY to around 10 Lakh in Q2 FY27, while pre-orders more than doubled to 1.8 Lakh. Vehicle sales increased 42% to 93,211 units. Ather launched its sub-₹1 Lakh Konarc electric scooter range during the quarter, taking its portfolio to 15 variants across three product lines.

Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer, president of the competition jury at this year’s Tokyo International Film Festival, talked about the significance of ‘A-list’ ratings for film festivals at the jury press conference today.
Tokyo has recently had its status as an A-list festival reaffirmed by the Fédération Internationale des Associations des Producteurs de Films (FIAPF), a Brussels-based global organization that rates film festivals. But the practice of rating festivals, and the process and criteria for rating them, has proved controversial over the years.
In March this year, FIAPF overhauled its festival accreditation system for the first time since 2007, with a new framework that classifies 17 festivals as “A-list” and expanding the overall number of accredited festivals around the world. Five of these festivals are based in the Asia Pacific region, including Tokyo, Busan, IFFI Goa, Cairo and Shanghai.
When asked about the ratings system, De Heer said: “Tokyo has always been considered an A-list festival by most people who attend festivals, so in that sense I don’t think it makes a lot of difference. This sort of categorization seems to be becoming more important in terms of the quality of films that are available to a festival, so in that sense it may help that Tokyo now officially has that rating again, but I don’t think it changes the festival so much.”
Watch on Deadline
FIAPF’s old system classified festivals in four groups: competitive, specialized, non-competitive and documentary and short film festivals. The 2026 reform collapsed the four categories into one group of 49 accredited festivals across 29 countries on five continents.
When pushed on the subject with another question, De Heer said: “It matters a great deal to some people and not at all to others, and that is at it should be.”
De Heer is heading the main competition jury at this year’s Tokyo film festival, along with Korean producer Oh Jungwan, New York and Tokyo-based producer Alex C. Lo, French colorist Yov Moor and Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe. The jury also talked about international co-productions, as several films in this year’s line-up of 15 competition titles have been structured this way.
Lo agreed with a question from the audience about the growing trend: “I didn’t notice there’s an increasing number of co-productions in the festival line-up, but it’s true that a lot of producers in Europe, US and the rest of the world are increasingly seeking co-production opportunities, mainly due to the link to their local government production support.”
When asked about the potential for co-productions between Japan and Australia, De Heer noted that the Australian film industry does not approach co-production in the same way as European producers: “It makes no sense for a Japanese film to shoot in Australia, and it makes no sense for an Australian film to shoot in Japan. Europe is very good at doing co-productions only on a financial basis. Australia is not so good at that.
“The sort of co-productions that work out of Australia have a natural story where some things need to be shot in Japan, some things in Australia. Those will always be possible if the scripts come and if they’re right.”
The jury also talked about their criteria for judging the 15 films in competition, which includes titles from across Europe and the Asia Pacific region. Oh Jungwan said: “For me as a jury member, I’m looking at whether I’m convinced by the story the director is telling and the way he’s telling it.” She later said she’s also prepared to fight for the films she loves and once had a seven-hour discussion about a film when serving on another jury.
Yov Moor said: “When watching each film, I’m looking at what is interesting and sincere in the film, but also really trying to imagine what the next film of this director could be.”
Makiko Watanabe added: “I try to see films without any preconceived notions and don’t try to look for answers while watching. As jury, there are other things we need to look at, but mostly I’ll look for what touches me and later digest what I took from the film.”
Tokyo International Film Festival opened last night and runs for ten days in the Hibiya-Ginza district of Tokyo. It closes on November 4 with the awards ceremony and a screening of Korean filmmaker Yeon Sang-ho’s Colony.

The Edge brings Fitbit’s screen-equipped offerings up to speed with better health tracking, a brighter display, and improved durability. After testing it, I’m still not ready to give up my Fitbit Air.
Google’s first repairable tracker. A bigger screen with adjustable brightness. More advanced health metrics and workout tracking.
TIRED
Band fastening can be finicky. Auto-pause can be overly sensitive. No Google Wallet.
Earlier this year, the Google Fitbit Air won me over and made me wonder why I ever wanted a display on my fitness tracker in the first place. Of course, not everyone is ready to quit the screen cold turkey, especially if your wearable doubles as your everyday smartwatch. Google Fitbit hasn’t introduced a new tracker with a screen since 2023, and the older models are starting to fall behind on health features and hardware. That deters both newcomers who want a screen and longtime users who have to choose among aging models.
At $180, the new Google Fitbit Edge costs $20 more than Fitbit's Charge 6 ($160) and $80 more than the screenless Air ($100), but far less than Google's Pixel Watch 5 ($400). After 12 days of testing, I’d recommend it to Fitbit owners looking to upgrade. Personally, though, the Edge hasn’t given me enough reasons to give up my Fitbit Air.
A Screen Has Its Perks
The Edge is comfortable enough to wear throughout the day and overnight. Its dimensions are slightly larger than the Charge 6’s (39.2 x 25.5 x 11.5 mm versus 36.73 x 23.09 x 11.20 mm), but I found the capsule shape sat more naturally on my wrist than its predecessor’s rectangular build. It feels like a better option for people with slimmer wrists and those who might find the Pixel Watch or Apple Watch too bulky to sleep with.
As with any smartwatch, comfort also depends on the band. The Edge comes with Google’s Active Band, which is fine for workouts but isn’t my favorite of the available options. Google also offers the HNBR (high-performance synthetic elastomer) Active Sport, the breathable Performance Loop, the silicone Magnet band, and the Metal Links band.
I found myself alternating between the Metal Links and Performance Loop. I love the look of the former for a night out or a more formal setting, and the latter is best for everyday wear. The Performance Loop’s micro-adjustable fit makes it easy to get a precise fit, but it's just as easy to pull it a little too tight. I also noticed that the band occasionally popped loose while I was adjusting it. The tracker was still attached from one side, so I wasn’t worried about losing it, but the fastening mechanism didn’t feel as secure as it should. I eventually noticed that the locking button was stuck and had to fiddle with the mechanism to fix the issue.
The 1.34-inch display is the Edge’s obvious advantage over the screenless Air. I noticed the difference most during workouts. On outdoor runs, I could check my metrics and control my music without slowing down. The display also reaches roughly twice the Charge’s maximum brightness, making it easier to read in direct sunlight. With Google Maps integration, I could follow turn-by-turn directions from my wrist while running or cycling, without having to pull out my phone.
I do prefer Wear OS’s more colorful interface; Fitbit’s watch faces also feel a little elementary by comparison. But Fitbit’s software offers up to seven days of battery life, which is a feature the Pixel Watch can’t match. The Edge is also compatible with both iOS and Android, unlike the Pixel Watch. Plus, in a first for Fitbit, the Edge is Google’s first repairable fitness tracker, with modular construction including a replaceable battery, matching the Pixel Watch. This is likely due to battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union, which will require removable and replaceable batteries in smartphones, smartwatches, and similar devices starting February 18, 2027.
Two Steps Forward, One Step Back
The Edge is a significant upgrade over the Charge 6 when it comes to health and fitness capabilities. Google has added more detailed workout metrics and a few hardware upgrades that make the Edge a more capable fitness tracker.
Some of the additions are aimed at long-term health tracking. Like the Pixel Watch 5 and the Air, the Edge offers monthly blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Its SpO2 readings now include nightly averages, ranges, and changes over time. There’s also 24/7 heart rate tracking, cardio load metrics, and an updated ECG app with atrial fibrillation (AFib) detection. Alongside nutrition logging, if you use a continuous glucose monitor (CGM), you can view glucose insights.
Like any Google wearable, most features are locked behind Google Health Premium, which costs $10 per month or $100 annually. Without the subscription, you still get the core metrics and scores, but the deeper analysis and AI coaching are inaccessible. In other words, the Google Health Premium membership is essential to the experience. (Buying any new device gets you a three-month trial.)
The hardware has also caught up to Google’s latest models. A barometric altimeter measures elevation changes and floors climbed. The Edge also finally gets an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. Its display brings more of these metrics to your watch face, including live workout data and visual guidance.
Google adds a gyroscope that improves automatic activity recognition, but it may have overcorrected a little. During outdoor runs, the Edge auto-paused when I stopped and resumed when I started moving again. At times, it was too sensitive; even taking a single step forward while catching my breath sometimes restarted my workout. It’s not a major downside, but worth noting that I sometimes had to correct the Edge’s decisions.
The Charge 6 supports contactless payments, but the Edge doesn’t, which feels like a regression for a newer model. If you want to use the Edge as a smartwatch, the lack of NFC technology is disappointing. I didn’t miss it much myself because I rarely leave home without my phone, but it’s a beloved feature that shouldn’t have disappeared without good reason.
The Fitbit Edge is a robust smartwatch, and Charge 6 owners will be happy with the improvements. I’m less convinced it’ll win over newcomers. The Fitbit Air remains the most appealing value in Google’s lineup, and the Edge doesn’t offer much more to change that. Without NFC for contactless payment, it feels like a smartwatch with one too many compromises.
