iPhone Lockdown Mode: The pros and cons of enabling Apple's security feature
Lockdown Mode makes your iPhone much more secure against spyware, but most people don't need to use it.
The iPhone's Lockdown Mode has been around since 2022, but you might not have heard about it, let alone used it. It's one of those features that's well-hidden in the Settings app, plus it's not really meant for the average person. Apple itself calls the tool an "extreme" layer of security for the few people who may be targeted by commercial spyware such as NSO's Pegasus. Journalists, activists and politicians are among the potential targets of such spyware.
Anyone with an iPhone running iOS 16 or newer can try out Lockdown Mode. It's also available on iPadOS 16 and later, watchOS 10 and newer, and macOS 13 Ventura and later. To turn it on, open Settings and go to Privacy & Security. Scroll down until you find Lockdown Mode, then tap Turn On & Restart and confirm with your passcode. It's simple as that, and you'll find the option to disable it in the same place.
What Lockdown Mode disables on your iPhone
What makes Lockdown Mode strong is how it blocks many of the iPhone's features when enabled. However, many of those features are ones you likely use every day. In Messages, most kinds of attachments are blocked. Even link previews stop working, since they can serve as a backdoor for spyware. Lockdown Mode also restricts how JavaScript works in browsers, which may cause some websites to load slowly or not work at all. FaceTime calls are also blocked; only people you've called recently can reach you.
Your iPhone's connectivity is also limited when Lockdown Mode is on. For instance, wired connections are disabled when the device is locked — meaning it cannot communicate with a computer or accessory without your passcode. For wireless connectivity, your iPhone will no longer automatically connect to unsecured networks, and support for 2G and 3G networks is completely disabled (though these networks were discontinued in the US years ago).
You also can't install configuration profiles, which isn't ideal if your school or employer requires one. If you have an Apple Watch, phone call notifications from your iPhone won't show up on it. You'll see reduced functionality across other Apple services too: Home invitations and Game Center are not available, and photo sharing is restricted.
Who should leave Lockdown Mode on?
If Lockdown Mode sounds aggressive, it's because that's exactly what it was designed for. Back in 2023, an exploit known as "Blastpass" used iMessage to install the Pegasus spyware on Apple devices. However, researchers found that devices in Lockdown Mode were completely immune to the spyware. Apple offers a 100 percent bonus on top of the regular reward through its Security Bounty program to anyone who finds a way to bypass the feature, which shows how much the company trusts it. By restricting your iPhone to avoid potential attack vectors, you're given maximum security in exchange for reduced functionality and convenience.
The feature offers some flexibility: you can exclude certain contacts from messaging restrictions so your family can still send you videos or documents. You also have the option to exclude certain websites and apps from the feature. However, loosening these restrictions makes your device a little more vulnerable to attacks. If you think you're a target, it's best to keep all the default protections turned on.
For most people, there's no need to use Lockdown Mode. Apple devices already have many security and privacy features built in. Spyware like Pegasus usually targets public figures and is often deployed by governments that want to spy on opponents or protesters. If that's the case for you, it's definitely worth turning on Lockdown Mode — Apple may even send you a notification if it believes you've been targeted by spyware. If you're curious, try using Lockdown Mode for a few days to see what it's like. Chances are that the inconveniences it creates are not worth the extreme level of protection that few people need.

Britain's posh schools are heading to India for students and profits
- Published
On the outskirts of Chandigarh city in India's north-western Punjab state, a 473-year-old legacy British public school opened its first all-girls international campus earlier this year.
In contrast to the prominent Gothic-style central building on the school grounds in Bedfordshire, England, the Indian premises are more modern, with purpose-built academic blocks. But a conspicuous red-brick clock tower bears the imprint of the school's British heritage.
The Bedford School, Mohali, is the newest in at least half a dozen British public schools (elite, fee-paying private schools with a long history), including three of the country's oldest, that have set up shop across the length and breadth of India. Their expansion comes amid tighter market conditions in China and the introduction of VAT on private school fees in Britain from 1 January 2025.
Since 2023, Bengaluru - India's Silicon Valley and a hub of software and start-up companies - has been home to the prestigious Harrow School, alma mater of India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Shrewsbury School has a campus in Bhopal in central India, while Wellington College has chosen to set up base in Pune, a western city that calls itself the "Oxford of the East" for its well-regarded universities and colleges.
Millfield, Queen Elizabeth's School and a few others are reportedly on their way with satellite campuses in the coming years.
For decades, India has been home to well-established local boarding schools modelled on the colonial British public-school system, serving elite, aristocratic families. But this market has rapidly expanded with newly wealthy Indian families increasingly aspiring to give their children more global exposure.
"Our international curriculum is quite a driver for many of them," Caroline Pascoe, head of school at Harrow in Bengaluru, told the BBC.
Harrow and Bedford are among the few schools in India that follow an all-through Cambridge curriculum - a global education framework recognised at 10,000 schools worldwide - from primary through to A-levels.
Harsimran Singh Kocchar, whose own extended family runs a chain of schools across India, says he decided to send his five-year old daughter Parineet to Bedford Mohali because of the "holistic focus of the school on character development, confidence and not merely academics".
He said he was also drawn to the fact the school did not have a "VIP culture" unlike many Indian equivalents.
"All kids are treated the same. Children of ministers and bureaucrats don't get greater privileges," said Singh.
Beyond the growing ranks of well-heeled local families, non-resident Indians who have either returned home after long stints abroad, or those still in the UK or Middle East wanting their children to connect to their roots, are also a significant market for these schools, says Pascoe.
Sixty per cent of Harrow's staff in Bengaluru are international and, like the others, it has imported its unique traditions to its Bengaluru campus: teachers are called Beaks, and students wear the traditional Harrow hats and uniform and take part in The Long Ducker - a cross-country race that happens across its schools globally. There is also a house system - a hallmark of traditional British education.
These quintessentially parochial quirks are blended with local customs such as singing the Indian national anthem every morning or celebrating Ganesh Chaturthi, a major Hindu festival.
While India's growing economic credentials and burgeoning population of newly minted millionaires are a natural tailwind for expansion, this growth is partly being driven by a slowdown in China.
Much of the expansion of British public schools abroad in the past decade was driven by China and Hong Kong - half of the 151 satellite campuses operated by 50 UK schools are situated in these countries.
But that growth has slowed following changes in regulation, and "increased scrutiny, and even resistance, from national governments", according to a 2025 study by the UK-based Private Education Policy Forum (PEPF, external) think tank.
A new 2024 Chinese law that required schools to integrate patriotic education into all subjects further challenged expansion and even led to planned campuses being cancelled, prompting these schools to consider other locations like India and Vietnam, according to PEPF.
Moreover, in the 2024 Autumn Budget, Britain introduced a 20% VAT on private school fees. Naomi Atkins, founding principal at Bedford School Mohali, says this has forced many private schools to look overseas.
"They are in a desperate situation. Even those that hadn't previously looked for international expansion are now suddenly active in India," she told the BBC.
But India has not been an easy market, she admits.
Most of these schools are set up in partnership with local investors or operators.
While in the past schools in other countries might have been able to do deals at 10% of revenue - the fee that they would charge the local partner-investor - margins in India may have shrunk to as low as 1% in some cases, says Atikins.
There has also been some over-estimation of the size of the market, she says.
Even though India has nearly 250 million children enrolled in schools, English education is deeply entrenched in the country and competition from local players is much more intense compared with other non-English speaking countries like China, Korea or Vietnam.
India's per capita income is also far lower and the high price-points of the British schools - which can charge up to £15,000 or more for full boarding - can limit growth.
"I've worked in Indonesia, Malaysia and China but Indians are much more price-sensitive - they like a bargain," says Atkins.
That is why Bedford Mohali has set its fees at roughly half those charged by other British schools.
Between 2011-12 and 2022-23, the satellite campuses of British schools generated £152.4m in profit, according to PEPF, and this profit has grown substantially over the years.
But in India, it appears growth is likely to be slow and steady rather than explosive.
The country's old colonial roots and new money afford the legacy institutions a significant business opportunity, but it is unlikely to be big enough to offset the loss of the Chinese market, at least immediately.

Swiss Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria has been medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husband
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria was medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husband Monday, officials said, as Nigerian authorities continued monitoring 52 people who had been in contact with her.
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Pate said the woman, the country’s first case in the current outbreak, left the capital, Abuja, early Monday with his approval. Her condition had improved significantly, and she was stable, conscious and able to communicate, he said.
“This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place,” Pate wrote on X. Her husband, a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria, has shown no symptoms.
The World Health Organization’s regional director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, said the evacuation was arranged because the couple are Swiss citizens and that Nigerian medical teams had stabilized the woman after treating her through the acute phase of the illness.
Switzerland will take over her care and monitor her husband, while Nigeria will continue following 52 other contacts, Janabi said.
“With the evacuation of the patient and her husband, Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases,” he said, stressing that vigilance remained critical.
Pate said containment measures remained in place and urged Nigerians to remain vigilant.
The woman tested positive after returning to Abuja from Uganda. Nigerian authorities said Friday they had yet to establish how she contracted the virus.
Switzerland’s foreign ministry told The Associated Press that she had not visited Congo and was believed to have been infected while traveling to Uganda with her husband.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had both traveled through Uganda’s Entebbe International Airport on Oct. 3. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but later declared itself free of the virus.
Kenya has recorded nine cases, including two deaths, since confirming its first case earlier this month.
The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus.
The latest figures from Congo’s health ministry show more than 9,900 cases, including more than 4,800 deaths, since the outbreak began in May.
The WHO has said the outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to surpass the death toll of the deadliest: West Africa’s 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed 11,000 people. Nigeria was among the countries affected, recording 20 cases before its outbreak was declared over after three months.
—-
Banchereau reported from Dakar, Senegal.

Aga banned for fake prescription from family member
- Published
Ethiopian marathon runner Ruti Aga has been handed a six-year ban after she attempted to explain a positive test for a banned substance using a prescription from a non-existent clinic, issued by a doctor who turned out to be a family member.
Aga, who won the 2019 Tokyo Marathon, tested positive for methylprednisolone after winning a half marathon in China in March.
She received a two-year ban for testing positive for the prohibited steroid - used to reduce inflammation and classed as performance enhancing by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada).
The 32-year-old was given a further four-year ban for tampering with evidence and misleading investigators during an interview.
"Aga attributed her positive test to treatment for a knee injury, submitting a prescription from a clinic that did not exist, issued by a 'doctor' who turned out to be a family member with no medical registration with the relevant authority," the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Thursday.
"When questioned, the family member claimed to have used an old prescription pad from a former workplace. But that clinic confirmed the individual had never worked there and the prescription was not theirs."
Aga, who has finished second three times at World Marathon Majors, has been provisionally suspended since 10 September and the ban will run from that date.

Ireland’s Ringrose doubtful for Nations Championship
DUBLIN, Oct 27 : Ireland centre Garry Ringrose is a doubt for next month’s Nations Championship campaign due to a hamstring injury, the Irish Rugby Football Union said on Tuesday.
• The 31-year-old missed Leinster’s 24–18 win over Munster last Saturday after suffering the injury in training and, as Ireland’s squad assembled on Monday, was allowed to remain with his club for rehabilitation.
• Flyhalf Sam Prendergast also missed Leinster’s win in the United Rugby Championship because of a wrist injury but will stay with the Ireland squad as he continues to work his way back to fitness.
• Winger Jimmy O'Brien is following return-to-play protocols for a concussion, after failing a head injury assessment in Leinster’s victory in Dublin.
• Ireland have four games in November, starting with Argentina before facing Fiji and South Africa at Aviva Stadium.

Donnie Iris, regarded as Pittsburgh’s biggest hometown rock hero for a six-decade career that included hit singles in the 1960s and ’80s, died Monday at 83. He had been fighting bladder cancer for three years.
Iris’ biggest chart success came as a member of the Jaggerz, who reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1970 with “The Rapper” — a song that dealt with “rapping” with girls, not the genre whose name had not yet been coined.
That group petered out, but he went on to have continued success, especially regionally, as the frontman of Donnie Iris and the Cruisers in the age of power pop and Midwest rock. A decade after “The Rapper” broke through, Iris had a hit again with “Ah! Leah!,” which reached No. 29 on the Hot 100 in 1980. They had two more mid-level chart hits in 1981 with “Love Is Like a Rock” and “My Girl.”
His modest success during that era on the Billboard charts was hardly indicative of just how beloved he was in his native Pennsylvania and the Midwest region, widely seen as being to Pittsburgh what Michael Stanley was to Cleveland.
“For my money, he was the most beloved Pittsburgh musician of all time,” Joe Grushecky told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. Grushecky, as the leader of the Iron City Houserockers, would have been one of the few other viable candidates for that title. But, as he told the newspaper, “I don’t know anyone who was loved more than Donnie. He just had that warmth about him, and it came through in his performance.”
Iris was a trouper to the end, performing his final show less than a month ago, on Sept. 28, at Citizens Live at the Wylie, seated in a chair shortly after having radiation treatment in the afternoon.
“He sang like a bird that night,” his longtime keyboard player and best friend, Mark Avsec, told the Post-Gazette. “It was the first time on a chair, and he didn’t like that. But the poor guy, the cancer was spreading, and he was in pain, and he really wanted to do that show and be with the people.”
Iris began singing in a doo-wop group in high school in the early ’60s, then moved on to rock ‘n’ roll and R&B cover bands before the Jaggerz were formed in 1964. They were eventually signed to Gamble Records, the brainchild of Philly soul greats Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff, and released their first album, “Introducing the Jaggerz,” in 1969.
In the late ’70s, he became a guitarist for Wild Cherry, after that group had already hit the big time with “Play That Funky Music.” It was in the Wild Cherry days that he met Avsec, who continued on with him in Donnie Iris and the Cruisers and continued to perform with him all the way to last month.
They recruited Marty Lee Hoenes, Albritton McClain and Kevin Valentine to complete Donnie and the Cruisers and released their first album, “Back on the Streets,” in 1980, followed by “King Cool” the following year, “The High and the Mighty” in 1982 and “Fortune 410” in 1983 before being dropped by MCA Records in 1984. Even set adrift from major labels, they continued to record into the 2010s.
Iris was championed in 2025 in a well-read blog post by industry pundit Bob Lefsetz, who wrote, “I didn’t buy the solo debut, ‘Back on the Streets,’ but I did buy the follow-up, ‘King Cool.’ The joke, of course, was that Donnie Iris was anything but cool. He was a man whose music was au courant, but whose look was passé, maybe because by time he made it he was in his late thirties, whereas his contemporaries had all made it in their twenties…”
Lefsetz continued, “Donnie specializes in straight-ahead rock, and all his records are very listenable. So I did, listen that is. I know ‘Stagedoor Johnny’ and ‘Never Did I’ by heart, not that you can hear them on streaming services, MCA has only deigned to release the greatest hits. And then Donnie Iris lost his deal with MCA and disappeared. ‘Ah! Leah!’ survived, some people remember seeing him on MTV, but there was no press, no airplay, it’s like he didn’t exist.”
Then, as Lefsetz noted, “Turns out he became a mortgage broker… Sure, Donnie continued to play music, but he needed to pay the rent, put food on the table. You’d be stunned so many of your heroes end up working straight jobs.”
Indeed, per the Post-Gazette, Iris went on to own SimCorp in Aliquippa. He admitted he got some business from customers who wanted to deal with the rock star they’d identified with or grown up with, or whose annual birthday shows they were still going to see. “It got me some business I normally wouldn’t have,” he acknowledged.
Lefsetz was compelled to write about iris by seeing a video of him performing “Love Is Like a Rock” and, like many fans, being impressed he still had his chops, “sans plastic surgery, sans much hair. It’s still him, the essence… What is truly stunning is when he starts picking that Fender. Like it’s a high school in New Castle, Pennsylvania and it’s another night in the sixties. And he’s not only picking, HE’S INTO IT!… Donnie isn’t showing off, he’s just doing what he does, AT 82! It put a smile on my face, made me feel good not only about Donnie Iris, but rock and roll.”
In one of dozens of responses to Lefsetz’s column, his partner Avsec wrote, “We’ve been together for almost 50 years… And one of the joys of my life is watching the crowd watch Donnie. I’ve never seen such JOY on people’s faces. It happens every time we play, and we’re fortunate enough to be playing decent size venues, especially in Western Pa and Northeastern Ohio. Donnie is going through his third course of chemotherapy. If the treatments drag him down, he does not show it. He still sings his butt off. Screams and everything. I don’t think he has ever had so much fun on stage. Donnie always tells me he’s having the time of his life. Same goes for me.”
In another response, former A&M promo executive Richard Pachter wrote, “‘Ah! Leah!’ may be the most rock and roll video ever made. That rug! Those teeth! That skinny guy with the hairy chest! But despite all that, it’s beyond great. It’s the personification of it all. I’m not kidding! THAT is rock and roll!”

Less than a month after its mass release of hundreds of manuscripts that it said contained solutions to long-standing mathematics questions, OpenAI is back with three more “major” discoveries in math, computer science, and physics. What’s different this time is the choice to have external experts that OpenAI describes as “shepherds” guiding the results in computer science and physics, while for the math problem it says that they advised it to release the AI output for researchers to work through their own explanations.
OpenAI announces three big science discoveries and a new way to work with academics
This time OpenAI says it’s taking new advice from scientists on how to release the results.
OpenAI results added to GitHub today:
Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation. The proof uses an auxiliary partial differential equation to establish Sogge’s local smoothing for waves in every spatial dimension at least two. It also yields the Kakeya maximal and dimension conjectures and Stein’s spherical restriction estimates throughout the interior of the conjectured range. We are releasing the model output directly, as we did in our October 6 release.
The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False. The paper gives a deterministic algorithm that exactly counts satisfying assignments of fixed-width CNF formulas in subexponential time and polynomial space. The case of 3-SAT refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis. An independent working group of computer scientists led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi, and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the proof. At the group’s request, we are making the materials public immediately so others can examine them as well.
This approach could have its own issues, the company admits, and the AGMAI panel of math advisers OpenAI put together just said yesterday that “we recommend that AI companies do not adopt” the practices of designating certain people to receive the output first, citing unequal access, borrowed reputation, and biased selection as a few of the issues. Instead, they recommended that in the future, AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with Lean-formalized proofs, info on how the problems were chosen, funding for people working on understanding the results, and other information.
The physics information has not been released in full, but is a “mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics.” According to OpenAI, “David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work.”
The computer science collaboration is said to prove that the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which has been widely believed to be true, is actually false. OpenAI says verification of the result will be guided by a group of three experts that includes UC San Diego’s Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who were part of the group that originally proposed it in 1999, as well as MIT professor Ryan Williams. The group decided to release the AI output write-up and Lean proof on GitHub today.
They also released an open letter to the community asking for input on how to examine the claim, and about setting norms for dealing with AI-generated breakthroughs:
We would welcome discussion of three broader questions:
What expectations should govern early access to AI-generated results, disclosure of conflicts of interest, and the use of unpublished material for subsequent research?
How should credit recognize both new discoveries and the work of checking, fixing, simplifying, explaining, and extending them?
How can we support students and researchers as methods and research directions change, while preserving the understanding and judgment needed to question results and develop new ideas?
There’s similar documentation for the math breakthrough, where its model “produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions.” Just a few months ago, NYU professor Hong Wang was awarded a prestigious Fields Medal by the International Mathematical Union for resolving the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions.

Ukrainian data shows its air defenses largely held up against one of Russia's most prominent new threats despite a 10-day Starshield slowdown.
Though high-speed interceptor drones were hindered by the reported throttling, Kyiv's forces managed to intercept 74% of Russian jet-powered Shaheds from October 14 to 24, compared with a typical rate of 77%, according to analysts at the Washington-based think tank Institute for the Study of War.
The organization bases its analyses on interception data released by Ukraine's air force, which said Russia had launched hundreds of the turbojet attack drones over the 10-day period.
The drop of three percentage points, or roughly 3.8%, translates to a "still relatively high interception rate" but doesn't mean Ukraine can rest easy, the ISW analysts wrote.
Many interceptons were owed to Ukrainian fighter jets countering Russian jet Shaheds with air-to-air missiles or guns.
For months, fighter aircraft have been Ukraine's primary and most successful air defense so far against jet Shaheds — an assessment that Ukrainian air force spokesperson Col. Yuriy Ihnat repeated to local media on Monday after Starshield services returned to normal.
"We are counting on the aviation component," he told RBC Ukraine, referring to helicopters and fighter jets.
One of Ukraine's main aircraft in this fight is the F-16 Fighting Falcon, which Ihnat said in April could shoot down 10 Russian Shaheds each in a single night. The F-16 carries the M61A1 Vulcan, a six-barrel, Gatling-style rotary cannon that fires 20mm rounds.
Kyiv requisitioned more than 50,000 of these rounds from Denmark last week in a scramble to bolster its air defenses while Starshield, the military version of Starlink that its interceptor drones rely on, was limited by a speed cap. That many rounds is enough for roughly 100 sorties.
The F-16 pillar can't last forever
But ISW analysts wrote that the F-16 strategy poses a few complications for Ukraine. Using its gun to shoot down jet Shaheds, for example, "requires a high pilot skill level and increases the risk to the airframe and pilot," the wrote.
The practice also increases maintenance demands for Ukraine's already-strained fighter jets and distracts them from other missions they could be needed for, the analysts added.
"Supplementing the Ukrainian air defense umbrella with interceptor drones is Ukraine's best chance at developing a robust air defense umbrella capable of sustaining high interception rates of Russian jet-powered drones over the long term," the analysts wrote.
Indeed, before Russia began surging launches of jet-powered drones, Ukraine had reported much higher interception rates of over 90% against propeller Shaheds in some months.
These had been largely boosted by Ukraine's mass adoption of interceptor drones, or small drones that cost just a fraction of traditional interceptor missiles.
But Russia's increased use of turbojets on its attack drones, the more advanced of which can fly at speeds of up to 370 mph, meant Ukraine has to radically evolve its designs to keep up. While it now has several types of drones capable of catching and destroying jet-powered Shaheds, the new interceptor effort as a whole is still in early stages.
Many of these new interceptors became ineffective during the 10-day slowdown of Starshield, which Ukraine said stopped working when a drone flew faster than 100 mph.
The reason for the connectivity problems is still unclear. They emerged as President Donald Trump and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk both openly criticized Ukraine for strikes on Russian energy infrastructure as the White House sought to lower gas prices.
Trump and Musk have separately said they were not responsible for the slowdown to Starshield, which is owned and operated by the US government.
Musk, while maintaining that the US controls Starshield, later also accused Ukrainian forces of breaching civilian network Starlink's terms of service by using it for drone strikes.
On Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Starshield services were restored.
Meanwhile, some Ukrainians are already bracing for a new threat from Russia through cheap, mass-producible cruise missiles. One such missile, the Filin, has been listed by Russia as capable of flying as fast as 500 mph.

Gadi Eisenkot is the man who could bring an end to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s grip on power in Israel. He has been neck and neck with Netanyahu in parliamentary polls that kicked off on Tuesday October 27.
Netanyahu has been Israel's PM for 19 years -- his first tenure (1996–1999) lasted 3 years and 18 days; his second tenure (2009–2021) lasted 12 years and 74 days, while his third tenure began in 2022, and he has been the PM since.
Netanyahu is now facing a tough battle in the October 27 Israeli parliamentary election, fighting for survival against ex-Army chief Gadi Eisenkot.
According to reports, opinion polls showed a close race between Netanyahu's Likud party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk with backers on the right and in the centre.
This election in Israel comes in the backdrop of the wars in Gaza and Iran that have put Netanyahu under scrutiny.
Reserved, media-shy, and a relative newcomer to Israeli politics, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot presents a clear contrast to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Military career: Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff, has spent most of his life in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).
He enlisted in the Golani Brigade in 1978 and rose over a 40-year career to become chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, serving under Netanyahu, according to CNN.
He almost always dresses in black, speaks halting English and tends to respond in interviews with bullet-point lists, a reflection of the military culture that shaped him.
His tenure included one of the most contentious episodes in recent Israeli military history. In 2016, Sgt. Elor Azaria shot and killed a wounded Palestinian attacker in Hebron.
Despite pressure from right-wing politicians – including Netanyahu – Eisenkot backed a military investigation and trial, saying he was defending the army’s discipline and ethics.
Political career: Eisenkot is a relative newcomer to politics. He entered politics in 2022 alongside another former chief of staff, Benny Gantz.
After the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, the two joined Netanyahu’s emergency war cabinet. But they left in June 2024, pointing to the absence of a clear post-war strategy, CNN reported.
His image as a straight-talking security hawk from humble roots has resonated in a nation going to the polls on October 27 for the first time since Hamas attacked Israel three years ago.
He would be the first prime minister who is Sephardic, Jews who trace their recent origins to the Middle East and North Africa, AFP reported.
Unlike Netanyahu, who comes from an elite family and whose father was a prominent professor in the United States, Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan Jews, and grew up on Israel's geographic periphery.
Eisenkot is the second of nine children and a father of five.
Eisenkot garnered broad public sympathy after his son Gal and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza. His working-class roots constitute another element of his appeal.
His background came into the spotlight when a senior commentator on the pro-Netanyahu Channel 14 television station described Eisenkot as "a monkey" controlled by "Ashkenazi elitists," AFP reported.
He was referring to Jews of European descent who have historically dominated Israel's political and economic institutions.
Gadi Eisenkot's stance on Iran, Gaza:
Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hawkish security views that have hardened since October 7, 2023.
On Gaza, Gadi Eisenkot has vowed to end Hamas rule within 18 months, according to AFP.
He recently said this could be achieved either through the implementation of US President Donald Trump's ceasefire plan, which envisages Hamas's gradual disarmament and a transfer of power, or through "creative operations" aimed at destroying the movement's military wing.
Eisenkot lambasted Netanyahu over his handling of the Gaza war, accusing the prime minister of prolonging the conflict and endangering the Israeli hostages for political reasons, a charge which eventually led him to leave the war cabinet.
In practice, Netanyahu’s stated aims are broadly similar, but Eisenkot argues that “as long as Netanyahu is in office, Hamas stays in power.”
He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
CNN reported that before entering politics, Eisenkot warned that continued Israeli control over the Palestinians in the occupied West Bank risked creating a bi-national state, which he called “the end of the Zionist vision.”
Since October 7, however, he has rejected the two-state solution, stating in an interview recently that anyone who still advocates for it is “delusional,” without presenting any alternative vision.
He does oppose formal annexation and illegal outposts and has called the Israeli government’s plan to build in the controversial E1 area of the West Bank a “mistake” because of the international cost.
He also vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity and recently beat up an American journalist and a French mayor, decrying the incidents as "Jewish terror" abetted by Netanyahu's government.
On Iran, Eisenkot shares Netanyahu’s central goals of preventing it from acquiring a nuclear weapon and of weakening Tehran’s proxy network, CNN reported.
Eisenkot, however, has criticised the lack of strategy in the latest conflict and argues that military gains need to be accompanied by diplomacy.
Besides, the decision to end the war in Iran is largely believed to be in the hands of the United States, rather than Israel.
Meanwhile, commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called "Dahiya doctrine", named after a Beirut suburb, in which Israel vowed massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas populated by the Lebanese militants.
According to CNN, like nearly all of Netanyahu’s rivals, Eisenkot broadly supported Israeli military operations in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
1. Addressing a key source of resentment among Israelis following three years of war, Eisenkot has promised to curb exemptions from military service for religious students.
2. He promised a "universal national service law" requiring ultra-Orthodox Jews and Arab citizens to perform either military or civil service.
3. Eisenkot also promised to try to restore the international image of Israel, badly strained after three years of war in Gaza and violence in the occupied West Bank.
4. He has sought to appeal to centrist and liberal voters by pledging to "protect judicial independence, the rule of law, minority rights and a free press".
5. He promised to try to restore the international image of Israel, badly strained after three years of war in Gaza and violence in the occupied West Bank
6. He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity and recently beat up an American journalist and a French mayor, decrying the incidents as "Jewish terror" abetted by Netanyahu's government.

- The claim that U.S. President Donald Trump or another White House official ordered the slowdown of Starlink and Starshield services in Ukraine in October is unproven.
- Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, reported on Oct. 14 that SpaceX, the spaceflight and telecommunications company Elon Musk founded, had imposed speed restrictions on its Starlink and Starshield satellite internet services in Ukraine. Beskrestnov warned that the slowdown severely limited the flight speed of Ukraine's drones and "disrupted" a number of its military missions.
- Reuters reported on Oct. 15 that Pentagon officials received an order to limit Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade satellite internet service, "from inside the White House." That same day, British newspaper The Telegraph reported that it was Musk who first approached Trump with the idea to slow down SpaceX services in Ukraine. The paper reported that one anonymous source said Trump "agreed" with Musk's idea. On Oct. 20, The Wall Street Journal also reported that one anonymous source said Trump and Musk spoke about slowing down Starshield speeds before Musk reportedly "ordered" restrictions.
- Snopes could not independently verify Reuters', The Telegraph's or the Wall Street Journal's reports because they relied on anonymous sources. Considering the fact that Trump and members of his cabinet publicly and repeatedly denied having given the order to slow down Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine, we cannot give this claim a rating. The Pentagon and the White House did not provide relevant comment when asked about the above news reports.
- Snopes will update this article if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have contacted SpaceX and an adviser to Zelenskyy for further information about who ordered the slowdown in SpaceX's services in Ukraine. We await replies to our queries.
On Oct. 14, Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Facebook (archived) that SpaceX, the spaceflight and telecommunications company Elon Musk founded, had imposed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield, its commercial and governmental satellite internet services, in Ukraine.
Beskrestnov wrote that the restrictions came without warning and had disrupted a number of the Ukrainian military's missions.
In the days following the disruption, as speculation abounded about who had ordered the slowdown of SpaceX's internet services in Ukraine, some social media users claimed it was U.S. President Donald Trump or another White House official.
For example, following a Reuters report, one Threads user, whose post was quoted (archived) by activist organization The Other 98% on Facebook, wrote (archived):
So it's official: Reuters has confirmed that the White House gave the order to disrupt Starlink so Russia could attack Kyiv with no advanced warning. The US aided and abetted Putin's killing of numerous civilians in Ukraine. Trump's a traitor, a Russian asset who is using US military technology to help our enemy.
Similar iterations of the rumor spread on X and Instagram as Snopes readers contacted us for more information.
It is unclear, as of this writing, who ordered SpaceX to slow down Starlink and/or Starshield services in Ukraine on or around Oct. 14. The slowdown has been widely reported by Ukrainian officials and reputable news organizations citing affected military personnel in Ukraine, plus U.S. officials have commented on the matter. Therefore, there is no reason to doubt that the slowdown did occur.
On Oct. 15, Reuters reported that Pentagon officials received an order to limit Starshield — SpaceX's military-grade satellite internet service — "from inside the White House." The following day, British newspaper The Telegraph reported that it was Musk who first "approached" Trump with the idea to slow down SpaceX services in Ukraine. The paper reported that one anonymous source said Trump "agreed" with Musk's idea. On Oct. 20, The Wall Street Journal reported that one anonymous source said Trump and Musk spoke about slowing down Starshield speeds before Musk reportedly "ordered" restrictions.
Trump told reporters on Oct. 16 that neither he nor Musk were responsible for the decision to slow down SpaceX services in Ukraine. Writing on X, Musk said (archived) the "US military and ultimately POTUS" were responsible for the secure Starshield system and that the commercial Starlink product could not be used for "offensive military action."
Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 14, 2026
Snopes could not independently verify Reuters', The Telegraph's or The Wall Street Journal's stories because they relied on anonymous sources.
When asked about the reports, the White House referred us to Trump's Oct. 16 comments. A Pentagon spokesperson said via email, "There has been no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
Considering the fact that Trump and members of his cabinet publicly and repeatedly denied having given the order to slow down Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine, in direct opposition to Reuters', The Telegraph's and The Wall Street Journal's reports, we cannot give this claim a rating.
On Oct. 24, Zelenskyy said (archived) on X that Starlink and Starshield speeds were "where they need to be."
SpaceX did not return a request for comment on who ordered the slowdown of Starlink and/or Starshield services in Ukraine on or around Oct. 14 or on why this occurred.
Starlink is a satellite internet service. Using SpaceX's rockets, the company has sent more than 11,000 of its own satellites into low-earth orbit. The satellites communicate with each other and Starlink terminals on Earth to connect customers to the internet. Starshield is similar, but is designed for government use.
Ukraine has used Starlink terminals since February 2022. The New York Times reported in July 2023 that artillery teams, drone commanders and pilots could watch drone footage simultaneously using a Starlink connection, which allowed them to find and hit targets faster.
What happened to SpaceX services in Ukraine?
On Oct. 16, Beskrestnov said that SpaceX had "implemented a speed limit for Starlink terminals while in motion" of 100 mph when those terminals were using the military-grade Starshield network that the company supplies to governments. The restrictions meant that if a terminal moved faster than 100 mph, its internet connection would cut out.
The Associated Press, which interviewed Beskrestnov after the speed limitation came into force, said such a restriction posed a problem for Ukrainian drones, which frequently travel at speeds faster than 100 mph.
For example, the Assocated Press reported that Russian Shahed-class drones could fly at more than 250 mph. Being restricted to 100 mph meant Ukrainian drones could not chase down or intercept Shahed-class drones and were in turn more vulnerable to Russian offenses. (Shahed is the name of an Iranian-designed drone that Russia frequently uses for attacks inside Ukraine.)
On Oct. 16, Zelenskyy told reporters (archived) in Brussels that the Ukrainian military uses Starlink to "intercept jet-powered 'shaheds'" as well as for "mid-range strikes against enemy military targets in our temporarily occupied territories." He added that troops also "receive food and water delivered by drones using Starlink."
That same day, Zelenskyy said speed restrictions had not been fully lifted. It is not clear exactly how long the restrictions have been in place.
On Oct. 17, Zelenskyy reportedly told journalists that Ukraine had driven Starlink terminals at speeds higher than 100 mph outside Ukraine and those terminals had continued to receive a connection, suggesting the speed restrictions affecting the country's troops were deliberate and only applied in Ukraine.
Trump, US officials said they had 'nothing to do' with SpaceX service slowdown
Speaking during NBC's "Meet the Press" on Oct. 18, Zelenskyy blamed the Starlink and Starshield speed restriction on the U.S. government and SpaceX. He said (time code 21:25), "It was the message from American government to limit this bit, and, technically, SpaceX did it."
Zelenskyy made this claim despite Trump saying of the decision two days earlier (time code 11:21), "I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," referring to Musk.
Trump did not elaborate on how SpaceX might have suddenly placed limits on Starlink or Starshield speeds in Ukraine without the knowledge of himself, Musk or another decision maker.
Also on Oct. 18, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any United States involvement in slowing down Starlink in Ukraine. He said (time code 00:42), "We had nothing to do with it. I don't, I don't — The United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down."
Rubio also repeated Trump's Oct. 16 suggestion that the slowdown somehow occurred without a major decision maker, saying, "It sort of happened."
The Secretary of State also claimed Ukraine does not have access to Starshield, SpaceX's secure network for government entities. This is at odds with Beskrestnov's Oct. 14 statement that said restrictions applied to Starlink terminals on the Starshield network. On Oct. 19, Rubio told journalists in Uzbekistan that Ukraine had "benefited" from Starshield, though did not elaborate on how.
Snopes asked Beskrestnov to clarify whether Ukraine had access to Starshield. We await replies to our queries. The State Department referred us to Rubio's Oct. 19 remarks.
In response to a request from Ukraine's former Minister of Defence Mykhailo Fedorov to have speed restrictions on Starshield lifted, Musk wrote on X:
Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.
If Beskrestnov is correct that the October speed restrictions applied to the Starshield network, Musk's statement would likely place the responsibility for any changes with Trump or the U.S. government as the owner of the system. Trump and the Pentagon both denied having made changes to capabilities they provided to Ukraine.
On Oct. 24, Musk wrote on X (archived) that Ukraine had "violated" Starlink's terms of service by using it for "offensive drone strikes to kill people." Musk appeared to suggest that SpaceX had restricted service in Ukraine in order to close a "loophole" that had allowed it to use the civilian satellite internet for offensive strikes.
Musk claimed Zelenskyy had admitted in an Oct. 16 X post to using Starlink for offensive strikes. Zelenskyy wrote at the time that Ukraine used Starlink for "for mid-range strikes against enemy military targets in our temporarily occupied territories."
Musk's Oct. 24 post appeared to suggest SpaceX made the decision to restrict Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine. He did not clarify whether he, as the company's CEO, had given the green light for that decision.
In response to Musk's post, Beskrestnov wrote on Facebook (archived) that Ukraine could not use Starlink for strikes within Russia because the service does not work in that country, appearing to suggest that Ukraine had not broken any terms of service.
Starlink troubles come at unsettled time for US-Ukraine relations
The sudden restrictions on SpaceX services came amid tensions between Ukraine and the United States. During an Oct. 15 Newsmax interview, Trump said he found Zelenskyy "more difficult to deal with than Putin" and appeared to repeat an earlier call for elections in Ukraine to replace its president.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy told British broadcast journalist Piers Morgan on Oct. 14 that he felt "betrayed" by Trump after the Starlink speed restrictions. He said he believed this was deliberate act by SpaceX and the U.S. that, he added, resulted in Ukrainian lives being lost.
Additionally, on Oct. 18, Zelenskyy told NBC's "Meet the Press" that intelligence sharing from the United States to Ukraine had been "blocked for some period of time" but that U.S. officials had "de-blocked" it.
The next day, Zelensky posted on X that he had "no early warning from our partners" before Russian strikes on Kyiv and other regions overnight. He added in a separate post that units using Starlink or Starshield services still did not work at speeds above 100 mph "in various sectors of the front."
Rubio said on Oct. 19 that the U.S. has never stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, a claim repeated in the Pentagon spokesperson's statement to Snopes.

Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
- Published
A magnitude seven earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens of others, according to Chinese state media reports.
The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu region as on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau.
The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa.
Authorities have declared an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 32 others have also been injured.
Power has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, local reports said.
Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.
Strong tremors were also felt in the cities of Qamdo and Nyingchi in Tibet.
Videos on social media show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark, although these have not been independently verified.
The region is prone to devastating seismic activity.
In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China.
Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing.
Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China.
With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

Environmentalists celebrate Lula's reelection in Brazil
Environmentalists, Indigenous groups and climate scientists are relieved after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's reelection in Brazil
MANAUS, Brazil -- Environmentalists, Indigenous groups and climate scientists are celebrating the reelection in Brazil of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, which brings the prospect of a continued focus on stopping the illegal cutting of the Amazon, the largest rainforest in the world.
But supporters also warned that a Congress increasingly dominated by the far right and the agribusiness caucus could undermine those efforts to protect the forest and combat climate change.
Lula defeated Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro, in Sunday’s runoff with 51.78% of the vote to 48.21%. After trailing in the first round, Lula staged a comeback to win by 4.4 million votes.
“The Amazon can breathe a sigh of relief!” said David Lapola, a Brazilian scientist and lead author of a chapter on so-called tipping points in an upcoming United Nations climate report. Scientists debate the threshold beyond which the dense, humid Amazon rainforest could shift to a drier ecosystem, with irreversible consequences for biodiversity and the climate. The forest absorbs vast amounts of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that drives global warming. About 60% of the Amazon lies in Brazil.
Lula’s victory reflected shifts in voter support and higher turnout nationwide. In the Amazon, Indigenous communities and advocacy groups mobilized voters and, aided by court rulings last week, helped secure government transportation for those living in remote areas.
The Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil, known as APIB, was among the organizations that went to court to secure Indigenous voters’ access to the polls. Lula’s victory reflected the “strength of grassroots mobilization in defense of democracy, life and Indigenous peoples’ rights,” it said in a statement.
Flávio Bolsonaro refused to concede Monday and said he would ask the electoral court to nullify the results. He faces a high hurdle: presenting evidence of fraud sufficient to overturn Lula’s winning margin and persuading the court before the results are certified Dec. 18. Early signals from Brazil’s institutions and regional leaders, including conservative presidents who oppose Lula, suggest the outcome will be accepted at home and abroad.
Flávio Bolsonaro had pledged to pursue policies aligned with those of his father, who governed from 2019 through 2022. Deforestation surged under Jair Bolsonaro as his administration weakened environmental enforcement agencies and loosened regulations. Lula’s government last week announced the lowest Amazon deforestation rate on record.
Lula is expected to continue efforts to curb deforestation and finance a sustainable economy through international donations as well as public and private funding. While he was the clear favorite for environmentalists, climate scientists and others who want to protect the Amazon, Lula has put forward policies that have drawn criticism. Most recently, he has supported efforts to drill for oil in offshore waters near the Amazon.
Still, Flávio Bolsonaro presented a stark choice that for many environmentalists felt would put the Amazon and Brazil's overall environmental protections at risk. He had denied climate change while casting himself as an environmental defender. However, he offered few details on forest protection or financing, calling for “modernizing” environmental laws and giving Amazon landowners more decision-making power — proposals environmentalists warned could weaken safeguards and accelerate deforestation.
Brazil’s Climate Observatory, a nonprofit coalition of 172 organizations, welcomed Lula’s reelection but said seven in 10 incoming lawmakers oppose the climate and environmental agenda. It cited recent measures weakening pesticide rules, Indigenous land rights and environmental licensing, and urged Lula to broaden his alliances and strengthen ties with Congress.
“The goal of ending deforestation across Brazil’s biomes must be pursued relentlessly,” the group said.
Amazon Watch, a nonprofit focused on environmental protection and Indigenous rights, also welcomed Lula’s victory while warning of legislative obstacles.
“A Congress strengthened by forces seeking to open Indigenous lands to mining and weaken environmental protections remains a serious threat,” said Ana Alfinito, an Amazon Watch legal adviser.
WWF Brazil said the country’s vast biodiversity and share of the Amazon give it a strategic role in addressing climate change. It credited Lula with strengthening Brazil’s leadership through international cooperation.
“Maintaining this leadership is essential to mobilizing other countries, raising the ambition of global commitments and turning agreements into concrete action,” the organization said.
Claudio Angelo, the Climate Observatory’s head of international policy, said Lula’s reelection had already delivered a result: a $500 million pledge Monday from the Netherlands to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a Brazil-backed fund launched at last year’s U.N. climate summit in Brazil.
The initiative pays developing countries to keep forests standing but has struggled to secure an initial $10 billion by year’s end. The Dutch pledge brings commitments to $7.8 billion.
Angelo said prospective donors had put plans on hold pending the election results, calling the Dutch pledge a vote of confidence in Lula’s victory.
“There was justified concern that a Flávio Bolsonaro victory could derail the TFFF, that Brazil would pull out and the fund would miss its $10 billion target,” Angelo said.

One of Japan’s largest labor union groups plans to seek 2027 wage increases for regular employees in line with this year’s target, signaling sustained pressure for higher salaries.
UA Zensen will push for a 6% increase in overall wages for full-time employees — the same as this year — including a 4% rise in base salaries, according to a draft policy framework released Tuesday. The group eventually secured a 4.72% gain for the current year.
The group plans to seek an additional 1% hike for employees at firms where wages lag significantly behind peers, as well as a 7% raise for part-time workers.
The target offers an early sign that Japan’s wage growth may continue, a key factor supporting the Bank of Japan’s case for further interest-rate hikes. In its July outlook, the central bank projected that a cycle of moderate wage and price increases would persist, underpinned by continued labor shortage.
The BOJ is expected to hold rates steady at its meeting ending Friday, while leaving the door open to a December hike, according to people familiar with the matter. Markets are pricing in an 80% chance of a move by December.
UA Zensen represents about 1.97 million workers across the retail, restaurant, materials and service sectors, spanning a broad range of employment arrangements, including part-time and contract workers.
Supported by strong wage gains in pay negotiations earlier this year and easing inflationary pressure, Japanese workers’ real wages have risen for eight straight months through August. Yet, the cost of living remains one of the biggest political headaches facing Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
In talks on next year’s wages, a representative of UA Zensen said it would focus on narrowing the gap between companies that have delivered solid pay increases and those that have fallen behind.
UA Zensen’s proposal follows a target set by its umbrella federation, Rengo, which is also seeking wage increases of around 6% next year, slightly above this year’s level.
“Real wages have started to rise across Japan, but given the outlook for prices and the economy, we don’t think this has become a stable trend yet,” Takeshi Matsui, vice president of UA Zensen, told reporters. “We don’t believe real wages have turned positive yet for workers at small and medium-sized companies,” he added.

A fresh controversy has erupted in Tamil Nadu after Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) leader and Leader of the Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin accused the Chief Minister Vijay-led Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government of polishing rice meant for free distribution under the Public Distribution System (PDS) and selling it as Grade A fine-variety rice at ₹30 per kg. According to news agency PTI, Stalin's remarks came after complaints from consumers across the state. He accused the Vijay-led government of transparency failures and questioned the procurement process. In a social media post, Stalin alleged, “The government announced that fine-quality Ponni rice could be bought for ₹30 at cooperative outlets to counter rising rice prices. But people across the state complain that regular free ration rice is merely being polished and sold under this label.” He further said, “In the Cumbum region, when people confronted a TVK MLA over this polished rice, the MLA fled the spot.” The Tamil Nadu LoP said the distribution was limited to around 250 locations for the state’s 22.8 million family cardholders, with each family allowed to buy only five kg, even as complaints continued to emerge. Seeking a full explanation from the ruling government, Stalin said there should be no “polishing” of the facts. He asked, “When did this government float tenders to procure fine Ponni rice? Which companies won the bids, at what cost did they supply it, and how much subsidy is the TVK government actually passing on to the public?” He also drew a parallel with the previous DMK regime and recalled that former CM M Karunanidhi introduced a special public distribution scheme through open tenders in 2007, when prices of essential commodities were high. Stalin said that, under the scheme, the government provided palm oil, dal and pulses at subsidised rates. Separately, the AIADMK also criticised Chief Minister Vijay, accusing him of prioritising the refurbishment of his office over addressing key governance and public-welfare issues in Tamil Nadu. Udhayakumar accused Vijay of focusing more on office decorations, including nameboards, and providing security escorts for his inner circle than on key governance tasks such as disaster management and controlling inflation. Udhayakumar said, “What is the Chief Minister's job? Is it just decorating the CM's office, installing plaques, and beautifying his residence? Jayalalithaa, polishing and repackaging it as fine-grain rice before selling it for ₹30 per kg. “People who bought this rice are protesting in districts like Ariyalur, Salem, and Namakkal. France has released its Global Health Strategy for 2023-2027, in Lyon today, in the presence of three French Ministers, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Health and Prevention, the Minister of Higher Education and Research, and WHO’s Director-General.
As a lead player for shaping global health policies, France has called on national and international stakeholders to support building a new global health architecture towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and in particular SDG3, focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, at all ages.
The new Health Strategy aims to help reduce health inequalities and strengthen the One Health approach to better prevent and prepare for future global health emergencies. It urges the global community to address the health consequences of climate change and the environmental impact on health systems.
To underscore WHO’s and France strong collaboration and in recognition of France’s pivotal global health role, Dr Tedros travelled to France to join the launch event.
“France was a founding member of WHO in 1948 and has been a strong friend to WHO throughout the 75 years since then,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health, and the new Global Health Strategy will enhance that role. It aligns well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, empower and perform for health.”
France shares key health priorities with WHO, adopting a crosscutting approach and prioritizing universal health coverage (UHC) as part of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. France also provides support for transformative initiatives at WHO such as the WHO Academy and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) which the Ministers visited today.
Dr Tedros addressed the audiences at the Academy and IARC together with Ms Catherine Colonna, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention, and Ms Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research.
"The World Health Organization, whose 74th anniversary we are celebrating today, must continue to play a central and driving role,” said Ms Catherine Colonna, the French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “France will continue to support the WHO and its ambitious governance and financing reforms."
"France is also committed alongside the WHO Academy through several partnership with universities, research institutes, and public health institutions," remarked Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research. "Our goal is to enrich the learners' experience through a diversified training portfolio within the Academy."
"The launch of this Global Health Strategy is the perfect opportunity to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the WHO. The Organization plays a central role in global health, and we must continue to support it," said Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention. "This is why, I am announcing today, France is keen to host, in the first quarter of 2024, in partnership with the WHO, the first international financing conference for the fight against meningitis."
The 2023-2027 French Strategy for Global Health is the fruit of collaboration involving a wide range of French actors: public agencies, civil society organizations, higher education and research organizations, scientific institutions, foundations, organizations of human, animal and environmental health specialists, local government bodies and the private sector. They will all be represented within a monitoring committee to track the Strategy’s implementation and progress.

Ray-Ban heir Leonardo Del Vecchio seeks to buy Italian newspaper critical of him, owners reject offer
The publication’s seven founding shareholders, including editor-in-chief Marco Travaglio, said that they had no intention of selling.
The majority shareholders of Italian newspaper Il Fatto Quotidiano on Monday rejected a takeover proposal from Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio, heir to the founder of Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, amid a long-running public dispute between the billionaire and the publication.
Del Vecchio, 31, had sought permission to conduct due diligence before proceeding with a voluntary offer to take Societa Editoriale Il Fatto (SEIF), the Milan-listed parent company of the newspaper, private, Reuters reported.
The publication’s seven founding shareholders, including editor-in-chief Marco Travaglio, said in a statement on Sunday night that they had no intention of selling. Together, they hold a majority stake in the company.
Del Vecchio says he wants to protect editorial independence
The proposed acquisition comes amid repeated clashes between Del Vecchio and Il Fatto Quotidiano over its reporting. On X on October 22, Del Vecchio accused the newspaper of running a smear campaign against him and used derogatory language to describe its journalists.
On Monday, he said his interest was in improving the publication’s financial position while preserving its reputation for independent journalism and investigative reporting.
He argued that the newspaper’s willingness to publish critical coverage was something he wanted to retain, adding that his proposal was intended to help secure its future rather than influence its editorial stance.
SEIF had a market value of approximately 5.5 million euros ($6.16 million) at Friday’s close. Its shares rose 17.3% by 1216 GMT on Monday.
Ray-Ban heir has existing Italian media interests
Del Vecchio has already established a presence in Italy’s media industry through his holding company, LMDV, which is facing debt pressures.
His interests include a 30% stake in Il Giornale, a newspaper previously owned by the Berlusconi family, and ownership of the QN network of regional newspapers.
The proposed purchase of Il Fatto Quotidiano would have expanded his media portfolio, but the founding shareholders’ refusal to sell has stalled the initiative.
Inheritance battle adds to billionaire’s public profile
Del Vecchio remains embroiled in a dispute over control of Delfin, the family holding company, following an inheritance battle. He has also clashed with EssilorLuxottica chief executive Francesco Milleri.
The businessman has attracted attention beyond corporate affairs. Earlier this month, he appeared on the Pulp podcast, hosted by a rapper and a YouTuber, where he discussed past problems with drug addiction and made claims about his sexual history.

The Indian Institute of Technology Bombay on Friday said its researchers have developed a low-cost device that can screen for anaemia and sickle cell disease using a drop of blood.
A research team from the Department of Chemical Engineering, led by Mahesh Tirumkudulu, has developed a simple, low-cost point-of-care approach that uses the length of a blood smear (the distance that a drop of blood spreads across a glass slide) to detect anaemia, and detect and monitor treatment for sickle cell disease. IIT Bombay said.
Prof Tirumkudulu's team built their own automated device to have a uniform method of creating a smear. Under these controlled conditions, the researchers observed that blood from different people gives different smear lengths, and this difference holds useful information.
Prof. Tirumkudulu explained that more viscous blood spreads less easily and, therefore, produces a shorter and thicker smear under the same conditions.
Once the team confirmed that the method could sense small differences in blood viscosity, they decided to investigate whether those differences could help identify disease. It was found that anaemia lowers red blood cell concentration and haemoglobin, while sickle cell disease makes red blood cells rigid.
The researchers said their patented automated smearing device can be manufactured cost-effectively. Also, the test itself requires only a pipette, glass slides, an inexpensive chemical, vials for the sickling treatment, and a ruler or imaging device to measure smear length, they added.
"This makes our technique particularly useful in places where conventional diagnostic laboratories are difficult to access, and it doesn't require any special expertise to use," said Dr. Mahrukh Mir, a former PhD scholar in Prof Tirumkudulu's lab, and the first author of the study.
The researchers pointed out that blood viscosity cutoffs vary for various groups of people because certain genetic differences affect how blood reacts when oxygen levels drop.
Also, the anaemia test could miss identifying some patients when the usual link between viscosity and anaemia does not hold, such as in a rare condition called hyperviscosity syndrome, where blood plasma is unusually thick.
Currently, the technology is licensed to Rheoheme Private Limited, an IIT Bombay startup, and the team is now working with the National Institute for Research in Tribal Health, Jabalpur, in Madhya Pradesh and All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Nagpur, toward regulatory approval, while exploring extending the device to measure clotting time and glucose levels.
"Our initial aim was to understand the physics of spreading blood drop, and that led to the medical applications," added Prof Tirumkudulu.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

అయితే, అసలు వీడియోలో ఆయన CJP నాయకుల గురించి ఎలాంటి వ్యాఖ్యలు చేయలేదు. ముఖ్యంగా, CJP పార్టీ ఏర్పడకముందు, సౌరవ్ దాస్, ఆశుతోష్ రంకాలను అరెస్టు చేసి కస్టడీలోకి తీసుకోవడం కంటే చాలా ఏళ్ళ  ముందే ఈ వీడియో చిత్రీకరించబడింది. కాబట్టి, ఈ వీడియోలో ఆరోపిస్తున్నట్లుగా ఆయన ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసి ఉండే అవకాశం లేదు.
వీడియోను నిశితంగా పరిశీలించినప్పుడు, అందులో కొన్ని అసమానతలు కనిపించి వైరల్ వీడియోను HIYA, Resemble AI డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్ ద్వారా ఇది డీప్ ఫేక్ ఆడియో అని నిర్ధారించాము.
పైగా, ప్రభుత్వానికి చెందిన PIB ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ కూడా వైరల్ వీడియో నకిలీదని స్పష్టం చేసింది.
