Leaders in the US Space Force would like to have a new spaceport up and running in four years, adding a third heavy-lift launch site to relieve pressure from bases in Florida and California that have shot rockets into orbit for nearly 70 years.
The obvious problem with that ambition is 2030 is four years away, and Pentagon officials have not determined where the new spaceport should go or how to acquire land for it.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink first mentioned the service’s search for a third launch base in May. A congressionally mandated study of the Space Force’s launch infrastructure identified the need for “another site that’s capable of heavy and super heavy launch capability,” Meink said in a House Armed Services Committee hearing.
The Trump administration released a space transportation policy in August that endorsed the construction of more launch and reentry sites for commercial and military missions. This week, the Space Force general responsible for procuring launch services for the military laid out an “aspirational” timeline for a new launch site.
“We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” said Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, head of Space Systems Command. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities, the Americans that live near it. In many ways, it’s much like an airport, but even louder. So there’s a lot of consideration.”

Ranking England's Ballon d'Or winners - how does Kane compare?
- Published
English Ballon d'Or winners have been few and far between. Triumphs to be treasured, names never to be forgotten.
Harry Kane, England's great talisman and captain, is the first to claim football's grandest individual accolade in 25 years after a sensational campaign in Bayern Munich colours - and only the fifth Englishman to ever do so.
Before him Michael Owen, in 2001, was the first Three Lions star to take it since Kevin Keegan's successive triumphs 22 years earlier.
England World Cup winner Bobby Charlton did it in 1966, and that came after Stanley Matthews won the inaugural prize a decade earlier - handed what began life as the European Footballer of the Year award in 1956.
Others have come close - Billy Wright, Bobby Moore, Gary Lineker, David Beckham and Frank Lampard are all among the runners-up. Lucy Bronze, in 2019, and Beth Mead, 2022, also more recently finished second.
Of course, the award has gradually evolved into the global behemoth it is today.
The caveat with those earlier winners is that it was not a worldwide prize - until 1995 it was only open to European players, and only in 2007 did it expand to include all players from all clubs across the world.
However, that does not detract from the award-winning performances these stars produced - each enjoyed prize-worthy campaigns that caught voters' eyes across Europe and the world.
But who among the five to have held the coveted prize is England's greatest Ballon d'Or winner?
5. Michael Owen, Liverpool, 2001
We won't hold it against Michael Owen for suggesting he didn't know what the Ballon d'Or was when Gerard Houllier first rang to announce he'd won it.
And, in fairness, the then 22-year-old swotted up sufficiently by the time he received the award, reeling off a list of previous winners.
Owen in those days, even after his initial hamstring struggles, was explosive, electric - searing pace and acceleration complemented by the most ruthless of finishes. He became a renowned goalscorer in his teenage years and, by 2001, was one of the most sought-after youngsters in world football.
Owen's Ballon d'Or-winning year was one of iconic moments. He helped Liverpool to a treble, clinching the League Cup on penalties before beating Arsenal in the FA Cup final - Owen scored twice late on to turn the game in Liverpool's favour.
The leveller was an acrobatic and clinically taken strike inside the Arsenal box, the winner a devastating break in which the prolific striker darted away from Lee Dixon and Tony Adams before slotting past David Seaman with his left foot.
The forward then set up two of the goals as Houllier's side beat Alaves 5-4 in extra time in the Uefa Cup final, having earlier in the competition scored a famous double against Roma at the Stadio Olimpico that carried the Reds through.
He finished the season as Liverpool's top goalscorer with 24 in all competitions. Owen's most iconic performance that year, however, came for England against Germany, scoring a famous hat-trick in Munich.
Injuries meant Owen never maintained that peak for as long as he would have hoped. Indeed, only Brazilian great Ronaldo claimed a Ballon d'Or at a more tender age.
4. Stanley Matthews, Blackpool, 1956
Sir Stanley Matthews, first and oldest winner of the Ballon d'Or - a prize then decided by voters from 16 countries.
Twelve of the panel put the Blackpool winger on their ballot, with six placing him first - beating Alfredo di Stefano and Raymond Kopa, who competed in the inaugural European Cup final for Real Madrid and Reims, respectively. That alone shows how revered Matthews was.
Matthews, two months shy of his 42nd birthday when he received the award, led Blackpool to second in the English top flight. This was behind Manchester United's Busby Babes that season, though voters were likely influenced by his performance in the FA Cup final three years earlier. Then, the Tangerines beat Bolton 4-3 in a match dubbed the 'Matthews Final' and broadcast in cinemas.
In an era where following the game often came largely via radio and newspaper reports, Matthews' mythical status drew fans to stadiums in huge numbers, with curious onlookers keen for a glimpse of his magic whenever Blackpool came to town. He dazzled for England, too.
Matthews was born during the First World War and would remarkably continue playing for another nine years after his award, retiring aged 50. His longevity no doubt was a factor, but should not take away from his continued brilliance.
Matthews was famous the world over, lauded by fellow stars for his creativity and ingenuity at a time where greatness did not boil down to individual stats. A creator rather than a scorer.
He was innovative, too. Nicknamed 'The Wizard of the Dribble', he would perform stretching and breathing exercises, do extra training and take care of his diet - fasting and not drinking alcohol.
Most poignantly, he was one of football's great entertainers, described by Ballon d'Or founder Gabriel Hanot - who was thought to have preferred Di Stefano - as the sport's Charlie Chaplin.
Matthews was adored by a generation, an outside right who became an icon. He received the award in the modest surroundings of Blackpool Town Hall, a low-key affair but one that cemented his legacy.
3. Harry Kane, Bayern Munich, 2026
Now, Harry Kane has produced one of the most sensational individual campaigns on record. You could argue that should place him higher, but those above him on this list have done some heavy lifting, too.
Looking at his output from the beginning of the 2025-26 season to the end of this summer's World Cup, the evaluation period for this year's award, Kane has delivered the most goals for club and country by any player in Europe's top five leagues since Lionel Messi's astonishing 2011-12 return.
The England skipper netted 61 times in 51 outings across all competitions for Bayern, winning a German league and cup double while also becoming the fastest player to hit a century of Bundesliga goals.
He also scored 12 times for his country, with six of those coming during England's run to the World Cup semi-finals.
The argument, of course, is that Kane is playing for a dominant Bayern side in a league they are heavy favourites to win each year.
The counter is the 33-year-old has redefined the centre-forward role - his incredible passing range and hold-up play making him an all-round playmaker.
Kane has been developing and maturing into one of England's all-time greats ever since those early loan spells at Leyton Orient and Millwall. His Premier League output for Tottenham was phenomenal season upon season, gradually adding assists to a prolific goal output.
In Munich, especially last season, Kane has just taken that to another level.

2. Bobby Charlton, Manchester United, 1966
The question mark hanging over those winners pre-1995, when the award opened beyond European players, or even before 2007, when it became truly global, is whether there was a more worthy recipient sitting outside the current criteria.
Some may argue Igor Belanov was slightly upstaged by Diego Maradona in 1986, for example.
But 20 years earlier, few could dismiss the credentials of a man who pioneered the Three Lions' first and only World Cup triumph, Manchester United's Bobby Charlton.
A survivor of the Munich Air Disaster in 1958, Charlton and United went on to win the FA Cup in 1963 and English top flight two years later. By 1966, at the age of 28, Charlton was in his prime, heading into the World Cup on the back of 16 top-flight goals from midfield for United that season.
Not only was he at the heart of that United side, who reached the European Cup semi-finals, he was the man England boss Alf Ramsey decided to build his team around for a first World Cup on home soil.
After an opening goalless draw with Uruguay, Charlton gave England's campaign lift-off with a scampering run from the halfway line followed by a trademark strike from distance that was still rising when it crashed into the corner of the Wembley net.
Charlton helped carry the hosts to the semi-finals, where he scored twice as England knocked out Euesbio's Portugal, before he and West Germany's Franz Beckenbauer tussled in the final as England won 4-2 in extra time.
Benfica's Eusebio finished second to Charlton in the Ballon d'Or rankings that year and Bayern Munich's Beckenbauer was third, with Charlton's World Cup performances showcasing not only his knack for a goal, passing range and poise, but also his selflessness. A true team player.
It was a fruitful era for individual success at Old Trafford. Scotland's Denis Law won the Ballon d'Or two years earlier and Northern Ireland's George Best scooped the prize in 1968 as United won the European Cup.
Charlton finished second in successive years after his triumph. But his pivotal role in England's World Cup triumph earns him the runner-up spot on this list.

1. Kevin Keegan, Hamburg, 1978 & 1979
It had to be, really.
Kevin Keegan scored 20 times as Liverpool won the European Cup and English First Division in 1977, and were a whisker away from completing the Treble - losing the FA Cup final to Manchester United. He also finished as Ballon d'Or runner-up to Borussia Monchengladbach's Danish star Allan Simonsen.
Keegan followed Simonsen to Germany by the time the award was announced, joining Cup Winners' Cup holders Hamburg on a lucrative deal, though they were hammered by his former side in the European Super Cup - and Keegan endured a slow start to Bundesliga life that was not helped by an eight-week suspension for punching someone in a friendly during the winter break.
Keegan soon settled but his first season was nothing spectacular. Instead 'Mighty Mouse' made a flying start to the new campaign - one in which Hamburg would become Bundesliga champions for the first time.
He also produced some impressive individual displays for England, even though the Three Lions missed out on that summer's World Cup, scoring against Brazil in a friendly and twice against Denmark in September.
Keegan's form was timely. He arguably deserved to win the Ballon d'Or a year earlier, which perhaps lingered in voters' minds, making 22 of the 26 ballot papers and ranking top on nine to finish above Barcelona's Austrian star Hans Krankl.
Keegan continued to flourish after Christmas to finish with 17 top-flight goals, including 11 in 12 games during the run-in. But it was more than just the goals, with Keegan a scampering, relentlessly creative presence.
The fluid, attacking HSV were in the midst of storming their way to a European Cup final when Keegan was named Europe's best player for a second successive year on Christmas Day 1979, this time being named top by 18 of the 26 voters.
The permed Keegan was the continent's biggest star and a cultural icon, too.
Hamburg would lose the European Cup final to Nottingham Forest at the Bernabeu, Keegan's last game before leaving for Southampton.
But he stands alone as the only British player to win two Ballon d'Or awards - at the time, only Johan Cruyff had matched his feat of going back-to-back - and that, of course, makes him England's greatest recipient.

- Pokémon UNITE will shut down globally on March 23, 2027.
- The game's final update arrives on November 12, 2026, and it adds a Library feature, Unite Coin Exchange, missions, and login bonuses.
- Players must download the Library's asset data before shutdown to access it after the game is taken offline.
Pokémon UNITE is shutting down globally on March 23, 2027. This marks the end of the nearly 6-year-old free-to-play multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) game, which launched in 2021. The Pokémon Company announced the end of service (EOS) on October 27, 2026, confirming that players will get new features and a chance to revisit their in-game memories before the shutdown.
Pokémon UNITE’s Last Major Update Arrives in November 2026 Before Shutdown
As part of its farewell plans, Pokémon UNITE will receive its final major update on November 12, 2026. This update will add a Unite Coin Exchange, special missions, login bonuses, and the Library feature, including new Pokémon UNITE codes.
The new Library feature, mentioned in the official Pokémon UNITE End of Service blog post, will allow players to revisit their collections and achievements even after the servers shut down. Meanwhile, the Unite Coin Exchange will give players a new way to obtain previously released items before the game goes offline.
Moreover, the exchange event will let players trade special Unite Coins for previously released items. Players can earn these coins through the new login bonuses and missions, which include winning matches in ranked and other battle modes.
To make sure you don’t get FOMO after the game is offline, the Library will let players view their owned Pokémon licenses, Holowear, Trainer fashion items, Boost Emblems, battle items, and achievements after the game’s service ends. Players will also be able to visit the Practice Area to check Pokémon moves and Holowear effects, and customize their Trainer and Pokémon for commemorative photos.
However, players must complete the Library’s initial asset data download before the shutdown to access the feature afterward. The developers also warned that Library data generally cannot be transferred between devices. This also means that it may not be recoverable if the game or its data is deleted or lost.
Pokémon UNITE will officially end service on March 23, 2027. Until then, players can take part in the farewell activities and make the most of the game’s final months. As for the players who are interested in competitive Pokémon battles, they can check out Pokémon Champions, a traditional turn-based stadium battle game.
What are your favorite memories of Pokémon UNITE? Let us know in the comments.

Ayush Shetty has withdrawn from the Hylo Open 2026, a BWF Super 500 tournament, after retiring hurt at the French Open in Paris last week.

The withdrawals leave Lakshya Sen as the main name in India’s men’s singles line-up. He will be joined by H. S. Prannoy, a World Championships bronze medallist, along with Kiran George and Tharun Mannepalli.
Shetty’s 2026 began with an injury-affected start to the season, but the Badminton Asia Championships in Ningbo in April changed its course. He beat Li Shifeng, Jonatan Christie and defending champion Kunlavut Vitidsarn on his way to the final, where he lost to Shi Yuqi. The silver made him the first Indian man in 61 years to reach the men’s singles final at the continental event. He rose to a career-high world ranking of 18 that month.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

In the winter of 2022, two parents carried their sick, coughing baby boy into an emergency room deep in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains. The small rural hospital had no pediatric specialists, no pediatric nurses, and no children’s intensive care unit. But it was hours closer than any hospital that did.
The doctor at that rural hospital recognized immediately that the baby’s condition was beyond their capacity to treat. They called regional children’s hospitals like ours for help. But the winter of 2022 was the peak of the “tripledemic” — Covid, influenza, and RSV striking children simultaneously — and every children’s hospital in northern California was overwhelmed. None of us had room for one more.
There was no single call the team at that hospital could make to locate a pediatric ICU bed. They worked a phone tree, hospital by hospital, asking for an opening. Meanwhile, the baby’s condition worsened. As the team tried to insert an infant-sized breathing tube, the baby died.
That patient’s death and others like it were galvanizing for those of us in on the other end of those desperate calls for help. Saying no to our colleagues and the patients they’re caring for feels horrible.
But the extraordinary crush of the tripledemic has continued. In 2026, the unprecedented pediatric patient crowding of 2022 has become a normal Tuesday.
In this new normal, community hospitals across the country are transferring children to dedicated pediatric centers not just because a child is critically ill, but increasingly because smaller hospitals have quietly lost the ability to manage even common conditions. A 1-year-old with an allergic reaction, a 6-year-old with an asthma attack, a teenager with gallstones — community hospitals once handled these patients locally. Now, as they degrade or eliminate pediatric care, that local safety net is disappearing. The nation’s relatively few children’s hospitals can’t accommodate every sick child, much as we would like to. We now routinely turn sick children away and hope one of our colleagues somewhere else will have a bed.
There is another story from that same winter of 2022. Two parents brought their sick baby girl to a small rural hospital in Washington state’s Northern Cascades. For 12 hours, doctors there tried to find a hospital that could take her. Again, no children’s hospitals had room.
Finally, the emergency physician called Washington’s Regional Medical Operations Coordination Center, or RMOCC — a kind of air traffic control for patient transfers that can match critically ill patients to available beds across a region. The RMOCC pediatrician who answered later recalled the terror in the calling doctor’s voice: “Don’t you know I feel like I am having a heart attack every moment I am caring for this tiny baby? It has been 12 hours. I am terrified she will die here. Why can’t anyone help?”
The RMOCC found a hospital willing to make an exception to its infection-control policies and accept the baby into a neonatal ICU. Unlike the California baby, she lived.
The Washington RMOCC closed last year after budget cuts. It is seeking renewed funding in this year’s budget.
There are many reasons for the collapse of pediatric capacity. Most are fundamentally financial. Hospital bottom lines require high reimbursement, high volume procedures, and expensive, complex treatments. Children’s care often reimburses below the cost of care, meaning that pediatric admissions for common childhood diseases lose money. Hospitals are incentivized to abandon pediatric care in favor of complex adult surgical programs and cancer treatments.
There are three changes in health care policy that could save and restore regional pediatric capacity.
First, Medicaid payments for pediatric care need to reflect the costs of that care. Hospitals can’t be asked to lose money on pediatric admissions and ED visits. Unfortunately, coming cuts to Medicaid seem likely to make reimbursement for children’s care worse rather than better. The incoming Congress must act to preserve and augment funding for pediatric care.
Second, regional RMOCCs like Washington state’s should be a standard part of regional disaster planning and a state and national funding priority. At least 19 states had regional or statewide MOCCs in 2023, though many were open only during surges, and some, like Washington’s, wound down with the end of the pandemic. When a sick child arrives at a rural emergency department, the hospital shouldn’t have to resort to a phone tree to find an accepting specialty facility. A single phone call to a regional air traffic control system for patient movement saves time and lives.
Finally, children’s hospitals need support to be regional resources to the smaller hospitals that depend on them for advanced pediatric care. Incentives for providing telehealth consultations, training, and quality improvement support for community hospitals are essential, as children’s hospitals face the same fiscal realities as their rural peers and cannot provide infinite unfunded support to their communities. Remote support from pediatric specialists can reduce the need for transfers and make local care safer, which could drive down pediatric care costs in the long term.
In pediatric medicine, we like to say that “children are not little adults.” Unfortunately, they are also not what health care executives call “priority populations.”
But children deserve to have quality care available in their own communities. They shouldn’t have to spend hours in waiting rooms and hallways awaiting transfer to overwhelmed regional centers. As pediatric physicians, we’ve gone from seeing the crisis coming to living the crisis every day. So far that crisis has been mostly hidden within the walls of our hospitals, but it’s time everyone know: Our children are out of room.
Jonathan E. Kohler, M.D., is a pediatric surgeon in Sacramento, Calif. Mary A. King, M.D., M.P.H., is a pediatric intensivist in Seattle.

Thousands of farmers from Maharashtra on Monday began a statewide vehicular long march from Akole in Ahilyanagar district towards Mumbai.
The farmers, who hail from over 20 districts of Maharashtra, are travelling to Mumbai via Nashik district in a large convoy of vehicles. They are slated to arrive at the city’s Azad Maidan on Tuesday night.
On Tuesday morning, the convoy was seen passing through the Kasara Ghat in the Thane district.
About The Long March
The long march is being led by the All India Kisan Sabha, the farmers’ wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist). Before the vehicular convoy began its journey, a foot march was organised in the Akole town, and was led by the AIKS’ national president Ashok Dhawale, national general secretary Viju Krishnan, CPI(M) MLA Vinod Nikole and AIKS Maharashtra State President Yashwant Zhade, The Times of India reported.
Here is a look at the demands of the farmers:
- Enhanced drought relief measures: AIKS national joint secretary Ashok Nawale was quoted as saying by the newspaper that the farmers are demanding adequate compensation and long-term measures to deal with the drought crisis that the state is facing. He described the advance assistance of Rs 5,000 announced by the Maharashtra government earlier this month as too meagre.
- Loan waivers: In July, the Maharashtra government had announced that farmers who were covered under the Mahatma Phule Shetkari loan waiver scheme would get loan waivers of up to Rs 2 lakh. The protesters on the long march to Mumbai are demanding that farmers who paid their loans on time should also get the benefit of the waiver, Loksatta reported.
- Land titles: The protesters are also demanding that land titles be accorded to farmers who carry out agricultural activities on forest land, temple trust land or grazing land.
The Maharashtra government has declared a drought in 305 out of the state’s 358 talukas, in the backdrop of a 19 per cent monsoon deficit and the prospect of El Niño conditions intensifying. The state government has stated that it will implement 12 relief measures in these talukas with the aim of providing assistance to farmers facing the impact of deficient rainfall.
Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis has said that the decision to provide advance assistance was taken as the procedure for obtaining drought assistance from the Centre is not likely to be completed before Diwali.

Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.
A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.
On Saturday, the CJP – a pressure group with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.
The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.
Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained, including the CJP leaders who were kept overnight.
In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar and instead proposed three alternative venues – all much further away from parliament – which provoked outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”
Ranka and Das were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.
In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.
The jailed CJP leaders were also given the backing of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who said the people of India would “reclaim Jantar Mantar”.
“Waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” said Gandhi.
The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.
The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.
The crackdown was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.
Kiran Stacey contributed to this report

By the early 1880s, bacteriology was emerging as a rigorous science. Within the circle of German microbiologist Robert Koch in Berlin, investigators were attempting to isolate specific disease-causing organisms. The logic was to prove that a microbe caused disease, one had to grow it in pure culture, separate it from contaminants, and study its properties systematically. The available solidifying agent was gelatin. It provided a temporary structure to the nutrient broth, allowing colonies to form on the surface. But gelatin was fundamentally flawed: It liquefied at temperatures approaching 37 degrees Celsius, precisely the temperature required to culture many human pathogens. Even worse, several bacteria secreted enzymes that digested gelatin itself. The medium collapsed, colonies merged, and experimental clarity dissolved into formless fluid. For scientists attempting to establish causation of individual species in infectious disease, this was not a minor inconvenience: it was a structural limitation.
Who was Fanny Hesse?
Fanny Angelina Hesse was not formally appointed as a scientist. She assisted her husband, Walther Hesse, who worked in Koch’s laboratory. She prepared materials, maintained cultures, and drew meticulous illustrations of bacterial forms for publication. She was present, not as an investigator, but as a quiet labourer in daily experimental work. It was in that proximity that she repeatedly encountered the gelatin problem. Failed plates, melted surfaces, cultures lost at incubation temperatures. The frustration was practical and persistent. At home, however, she handled another substance entirely. Agar jellies prepared in her kitchen remained firm even in summer warmth. They did not soften as gelatin did. They did not seem to degrade. One evening, in what history records only briefly but imagination can render vividly, the domestic and the scientific converged. The problem of the laboratory and the memory of the kitchen overlapped. She suggested that if agar could withstand heat on the dining table, why would it not withstand incubation in the laboratory?
Before the laboratory
Agar is a complex polysaccharide extracted from the cell walls of certain red algae, mainly species of Gelidium and Gracilaria. Chemically, it consists primarily of two components: agarose and agaropectin. Agarose is a linear polymer made up of repeating units of galactose and 3,6-anhydro-L-galactopyranose, and it is this fraction that gives agar its remarkable gelling property. Agaropectin contains sulfate groups and contributes to viscosity and charge characteristics. The word “agar” is believed to derive from the Malay term agar-agar, meaning jelly.
Long before bacteriologists struggled with melting cultures in Berlin, agar had already lived a quiet life in kitchens. Extracted from red seaweed and known in parts of Asia for nearly two centuries, it was used to set desserts into firm, translucent gels. Unlike gelatin derived from animal tissue, agar did not collapse in warm weather. It held its structure. It was stable. It obeyed heat differently. In the nineteenth century, European cooks encountered agar as an exotic culinary thickener. But in scientific circles, its potential was invisible. The laboratory and the kitchen were separate worlds, divided by sex, habit and hierarchy. No one imagined that a domestic ingredient could resolve a foundational problem in bacteriology.
Thus, Fanny Angelina Hesse’s suggestion to replace gelatin with agar, was out of the box.
Moment of trial
When agar was introduced into nutrient media in Koch’s laboratory, the transformation was immediate and decisive. The medium remained solid at incubation temperatures. It did not liquefy. Most bacteria lacked the enzymatic machinery to degrade it. Colonies appeared as discrete, visible units, each derived from a single organism. For the first time, bacteriologists possessed a surface that was chemically inert, thermally stable, and optically clear. The ability to isolate pure cultures became reliable rather than tentative. Within months, the method was embedded in the experimental practices that led to the identification of the tuberculosis bacillus and other pathogens in the decades to come.
To understand why agar transformed medicine, one must first grasp the idea of culture. A culture medium is an artificial nutrient environment that allows bacteria to grow outside the human body under controlled conditions and at a controlled temperature. Individual bacteria are invisible, but when placed on a suitable medium, such as agar, they form individual visible colonies. This enables laboratories to isolate the exact organism from samples like blood, urine, or sputum. Once identified, the bacteria are tested against different antibiotics to determine which drugs are effective and to detect resistance. Imagine culture is like switching on a floodlight in a dark room. Agar becomes the illuminated stage where hidden microbes step forward, enabling precise diagnosis and rational treatment.
The breakthrough was not dramatic in spectacle. It was a shift merely in material. Yet that shift altered the trajectory of microbiology.
Aftermath and recognition
The scientific practice and literature of the period absorbed agar rapidly, but credit did not travel with equal speed. The technique became standard practice. Petri dishes were designed to accommodate solid media. Textbooks described agar plates as routine apparatus. The name of Koch became synonymous with bacteriological rigour. Fanny Hesse’s contribution receded into footnotes. For decades, the laboratory bench carried her insight without carrying her name. Only later did historians of science begin to recover her role and situate it within the broader narrative of microbiology.
Agar today
More than a century later, agar remains foundational. In every microbiology laboratory, from district hospitals to advanced research institutes, agar plates are prepared daily. Blood agar to detect haemolysis, MacConkey agar to differentiate lactose fermenters, chocolate agar for fastidious organisms. Selective and differential media, all structured upon the same seaweed-derived matrix. Antibiotic susceptibility testing depends on agar diffusion methods. Colony counting for public health surveillance relies on agar surfaces. Molecular biology workflows begin with bacterial colonies grown on agar plates before plasmid extraction or genetic analysis. Even in the era of automated diagnostics and genomic sequencing, agar persists as the primary tool for culturing living microbes.
Today, major production occurs in countries such as Japan, Spain, Chile, China, Indonesia, and Morocco, where seaweed is cultivated or harvested. Beyond microbiology, agar is widely used in the food industry as a vegetarian gelling agent, in confectionery and desserts, in pharmaceuticals as a stabilizer and laxative, and in biotechnology for gel electrophoresis to separate DNA and RNA fragments.
Its properties remain unmatched. It melts at high temperatures but solidifies at lower temperatures, allowing sterile preparation and convenient pouring. It is largely resistant to microbial digestion. It forms a clear, stable gel that supports nutrient supplementation without chemical interference.
Firming up microbiology
Without that transition from gelatin to agar, the systematic isolation of pathogens would have been delayed. The architecture of modern microbiology would have developed more slowly, along a more convoluted path.
Fanny Angelina Hesse recognised continuity between her kitchen and her laboratory. Today, when a microbiologist streaks a plate and waits for colonies to appear, the act is routine. Yet beneath that routine lies the insight of Fanny Hesse. Without her intervention, the discipline might have remained uncertain at its foundation, its cultures unstable, its conclusions tentative.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.
“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.
The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.
While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.
The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.
Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.
As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”
On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”
What else we’re reading about
Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.
Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.
Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
32
At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check
For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”
For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.

Barcelona and Spanish striker Alexia Putellas reclaimed her crown when she won the 2026 Ballon d’Or Féminin at the Palladium Theatre in London, England, on Monday.
It was the third Ballon d’Or for Putellas, having won the trophy in 2021 and 2022. The 32-year-old has had a fantastic year with FC Barcelona, winning the Liga F, Copa de la Reina, Supercopa de España and the UEFA Women’s Champions League.
Spain continued its domination with her in the midfield, winning the UEFA Nations League and finishing runner-up in the UEFA Women’s Championship.
“I want to start by saying thank you teammates. I think anyone here could have fairly won this trophy and be giving this speech here right now. A great pleasure to play alongside each and every single one of you. Incredible experiences as a team, we overcome some difficulties, some injuries, some moments we weren’t expecting as a team and a great pride for me as captain,” Putellas said.
“All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn’t matter if you’re a boy or if you’re a girl. It doesn’t matter where you come from. Don’t listen if someone tells you, you can’t do it. Believe in yourself.”
The award is also more iconic because it was given in London, where Putellas currently plays. Having won 36 trophies at Barcelona, she left the Spanish club as its most decorated women’s player to join Women’s Super League side London City Lionesses this summer.
Putellas became the joint-most successful player to win the women’s Ballon d’Or, tied with her national teammate Aitana Bonmati, who had completed a hat-trick of the titles last year.

UK ‘set to miss’ heavily-reduced aid spending target of 0.3%
The UK needs to allocate additional funding in the upcoming Budget to meet it’s international aid targets, think tank says

The UK will need to allocate additional funding for international aid if it is to meet its target of 0.3 per cent of gross national income, with a current estimated shortfall of £410 million, according to a new report.
Forecasting by the Center for Global Development (CGD), a think tank focused on global development, shows planned spending is likely to undershoot the target and meet only 0.29 per cent of national income.
Its most conservative forecast estimated a £250m shortfall, while a gap of as much as £580m, leaving a spend of 0.28 per cent of national income, was “very plausible”.
It represents material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid, the CGD said in a blog post published on their website, with the extra money enough to halve cuts to Africa that “will cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de-facto exit from the south and east of the continent”.
It could also fund reform of the Green Climate Fund, which helps other countries’ ambitions on cutting emissions.
The UK chancellor, John Healey, is expected to outline new budget proposals on Wednesday amid speculation of potential tax rises or spending cuts to fill a growing black hole in the public finances.
The CGD has urged the new foreign secretary and international development minister to resist any artificial delay to aid spending and insist that the Treasury honors its commitment to 0.3 per cent.
It said the upcoming Budget “is a moment for the new government to put its stamp on how Britain is run”.
“The government made steep and damaging cuts and set a new target of 0.3 per cent for 2027 that would be a 25 year low. The very least it could do is ensure that target is fulfilled,” the CGD said.
The shortfall was attributed to higher forecasts for nominal national income, driven partly by inflation and rising energy prices following the conflict in Iran.
As aid spending is calculated as a proportion of gross national income, the higher forecast means the government must spend more in cash terms to meet its 0.3 per cent target.
The government announced in February 2025 that it would cut aid spending from 0.5 per cent to 0.3 per cent of gross national income by 2027 to fund higher defence spending. The reduction is expected to free up £6.5 billion for defence in 2027-28.
The new target is the lowest proportion of national income spent on aid since 1999.
The cuts come as aid budgets are under pressure internationally, with other major donors including the US, France, Germany and Japan also reducing spending.
A Foriegn, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”
Gideon Rabinowitz, Director of Policy and Advocacy at Bond, a UK network for organisations working in international development, said that the NGO has “repeatedly warned that the UK aid budget is at risk of falling below the targeted 0.3% of GNI”.
“Today's analysis further confirms our fears and risks leaving communities experiencing the impacts of conflict, crisis and climate change worldwide to pay an even higher price,” Rabinowitz said.
“With this injustice in mind, the Chancellor must use the Autumn Budget to honour Labour's manifesto commitments - by ruling out further cuts to the UK aid budget, and ensuring savings by other departments spending the UK aid budget are returned to the FCDO and that credible and transparent spending targets are set and maintained,” he added.

Very severe cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’ to trigger extremely heavy rain across 16 Andhra districts
Widespread rainfall is forecast across Andhra Pradesh on Tuesday and Wednesday, with extremely heavy rainfall likely in several districts.
Very severe cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’ began impacting coastal Andhra Pradesh early Tuesday, bringing gusty winds and heavy rainfall that are expected to intensify across the state’s northern coast over the next few hours, State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA) managing director Prakhar Jain said.
According to the India Meteorological Department, the cyclone, which had moved with a speed of 22kmph during the previous 6 hours, was at 5:30am centered roughly 260 km from Visakhapatnam, 300 km from Kakinada, 390km from Machilipatnam, and 380 km from Gopalpur in Odisha.
It is projected to turn northwestward by Tuesday evening and make landfall between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, near Yanam, by Wednesday morning. Wind speeds along the coast are expected to reach 90–100 kmph on Tuesday, and may increase to 115–125 kmph with gusts up to 140 kmph during landfall.
Deep Dive
Jain appealed to people to remain alert, avoid unnecessary travel and stay indoors in safe locations. He specifically warned people against standing near trees, large hoardings and dilapidated buildings, which could collapse or be uprooted in strong winds.
Widespread rainfall is forecast across Andhra Pradesh on Tuesday and Wednesday, with extremely heavy rainfall likely in several districts. The combination of intense rain and strong winds could cause damage to trees, electricity infrastructure, temporary structures and buildings in vulnerable areas.
He said extremely heavy rainfall was forecast in Kakinada, Konaseema, East Godavari, West Godavari and Eluru districts on Tuesday. Heavy to extremely heavy rainfall is likely at several places in Srikakulam, Manyam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Polavaram, Anakapalli, NTR, Krishna, Guntur and Bapatla districts.
Heavy rainfall is also likely in Palnadu, Prakasam, Markapuram and Nellore districts.
On Wednesday, extremely heavy rainfall is forecast in Visakhapatnam, Anakapalli, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Polavaram, Kakinada, Konaseema, East Godavari, West Godavari, Eluru, NTR and Krishna districts.
Officials said the rainfall intensity and the geographical spread of the impact would depend on the cyclone’s movement and the conditions prevailing during landfall.
Eight State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams and seven National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams have been kept ready in the cyclone-affected districts. An additional three SDRF teams and five NDRF teams are also available for deployment, if needed.
In addition, 115 teams have been prepared to remove fallen trees and rescue teams equipped with 13 boats have been prepped to respond to emergencies, including road blockages, flooding and the need to evacuate people from vulnerable locations.
The arrangements are intended to facilitate rapid response and minimise disruption to essential services during and after the cyclone’s passage.
The Andhra Pradesh government on Monday night released ₹27 crore for cyclone-related preparedness and relief operations.
Each of the seven districts in north coastal Andhra will receive ₹2 crore each, while 13 other districts will be provided ₹1 crore each, to fund precautionary measures and emergency-response activities in the affected areas.
Jain said people in vulnerable coastal and low-lying areas have been urged to take precautionary measures and remain in safe locations.
SDMA also said people could reach out to them through the Mana Mitra WhatsApp number: 9552300009.
Officials said Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) secretary Bhaskar Katamneni and chief executive officer Prakhar Jain were reviewing cyclone preparedness measures and coordinating with officials from various departments.
Chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu is being briefed on the precautionary measures implemented across the state.
Preliminary assessments indicate that 16 districts, spanning 2,460 revenue villages and 92 urban areas, were expected to face significant impact. Authorities have designated 1,763 cyclone shelters, set up 2,907 control rooms at mandal levels, and deployed 3,185 nodal officers.
Beaches have been closed, and traffic on coastal roads will be suspended from Tuesday afternoon.
All fishermen who had ventured into the sea have returned home, and 30,043 fishing boats secured at harbours to minimise the risk of damage.

Almost no one expects Donald Trump to keep his word, but unlike most, Neil Young ain’t taking any crap from the former Apprentice host.
Having repeatedly told Trump to keep his MAGA mitts off his classic Rockin’ in the Free World song, the 80-year-old Grandfather of Grunge took the poll struggling POTUS back to court today with new $10 million copyright infringement suit.
And, as Young always does on the guitar, the two time Rock & Roll Hall of Famer let Trump have it.
“Rockin’ in the Free World is a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten,” the short but sharp complaint says. “The lyrics paint vivid street-level portraits – a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity – while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all. In short, the Song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for.”
Trump first used the 1991 hit back at the very start of his first serious (semi-serious?) White House run in 2015. Young told him to back off then and told Trump to back off again in 2020 with legal action. As Young’s critiques of Trump got louder and louder in song and from the stage, it seemed the 45th and now 47th President, or at least his attorneys, got it — until October 12. in Youngstown, Ohio.
Watch on Deadline
The the five-page filing in federal court in Virginia states: “Just prior to Donald J. Trump taking the stage to speak at the Youngstown Rally, the Committee caused Rockin’ in the Free World to be played. On information and belief, the Committee has caused the Song to be played numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections.”
As today made clear, you don’t mess with old Neil and you don’t break your word to him.
“Donald J. Trump (‘Trump’) is now and at the time of all rallies this year was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies and that Young has not, and would not, grant the required license,” proclaims the complaint.
“In 2020 Young sued another corporation formed by Trump, Donald J. Trump For President, Inc., for copyright infringement of Rockin’ in the Free World along with another song written by Young,” the document by lawyers Scott Simmons and Robert Besser against Trump 47 Committee Inc. adds. “Donald J Trump For President, Inc. asserted no defense and immediately settled shortly after it was served, promising that it would never again use Rockin’ in the Free World without a license and permission from Young.”
The White House did not respond to Deadline’s request for comment on the complaint. But, with 80-year old Trump posting fast and furiously for struggling GOP candidates, don’t be surprised if the octogenarian barbs starting flying like Tomahawk missiles soon-ish.
On the other hand, the Neil Young, or at least his lawyers couldn’t resist a bit of wit, or at least a legalese laugh at Trump’s expense — and maybe even their own. “Young has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J. Trump in any way,” the filing says in a statement that literally no one anywhere would ever think. Keep on rockin’ that in the free world.

On September 29, 2015, a memo went out from Swasthya Bhawan, the West Bengal Health Department’s headquarters in Salt Lake, to every medical college principal and every district’s chief medical officer of health. Its subject was a concern the Union Health Ministry had raised about rising Caesarean sections rates, especially where the operation was not medically needed.
The memo enclosed a statement the World Health Organization (WHO) had issued that April. It suggested that chief medical officers, who license private clinics, carry out periodic “prescription audits” of Caesareans in private and government facilities.
At the time, the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4, 2015-16) had found that about one in four births were Caesareans in West Bengal (23.8%). The latest sixth round (NFHS-6, 2023-24) puts the figure at 44.5%, close to double that level, against 27.2% for India. In Kolkata and North 24 Parganas it was found to be 67.5%, meaning about two of every three babies were born via a C-section.
Why the concern
A Caesarean section saves mothers and babies when labour goes wrong. It is also, however, major abdominal surgery, with slower recovery rates and higher risks of infection and bleeding, and it leaves a scar that can complicate later pregnancies.
The WHO statement said that across a population, Caesarean rates above 10% are not associated with fewer deaths of mothers or newborns. While the WHO does not recommend a specific rate, the increasing numbers of Caesarean births in West Bengal, and more widely in India, deserve attention.
The opening of the gap
The NFHS’s first three rounds, from 1992-93 to 2005-06, found West Bengal close to the national average when it came to C-sections, at 10.2% against 8.5% by the third NFHS round.
The State then pulled away. Its rate reached 32.6% in NFHS-5, for which West Bengal was surveyed in 2019-21, and by NFHS-6 (2023-24) the gap with India had widened from 1.7 percentage points in 2005-06 to 17.3.
The climb has also grown steeper. The rise of 13.6 points between 2005-06 and 2015-16 took a decade, while the latest 11.9 points came in four to five years.
The data cannot reveal how many of West Bengal’s operations were necessary, though it does show when and where the rise happened.
Prevalence of C-section delivery, West Bengal
| Survey Round | West Bengal (%) | India (%) | Difference (% points) | Change in WB (% points)) | Change in India (% points) | 
| NFHS-1 (1992–93) | 3.3 | 2.5 | +0.8 | — | — | 
| NFHS-2 (1998–99) | 10.3 | 7.1 | +3.2 | +7.0 | +4.6 | 
| NFHS-3 (2005–06) | 10.2 | 8.5 | +1.7 | −0.1 | +1.4 | 
| NFHS-4 (2015–16) | 23.8 | 17.2 | +6.6 | +13.6 | +8.7 | 
| NFHS-5 (2019–21) | 32.6 | 21.5 | +11.1 | +8.8 | +4.3 | 
| NFHS-6 (2023–24) | 44.5 | 27.2 | +17.3 | +11.9 | +5.7 | 
Source: NFHS reports
Private vs. government
Of every 10 women who give birth in a private facility in West Bengal, 9 nine now have a C-section (87.7%). In 2015-16, the year of the memo, the figure was 70.9%. West Bengal’s numbers are also significantly higher than current the national private-sector rate, 54.1%.
While numbers in the government sector are lower, they are also on the rise: government facilities performed C-sections in 28.8% of the births they handled, up from 18.8% in 2015-16 and 1.7 times the national public-sector figure of 16.9%. In Kolkata, the share of births in government facilities delivered by C-section rose from 32.4% in NFHS-5 to 59.1% in NFHS-6.
The move to private care
Births are also increasingly moving to private facilities. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 their share of the total rose from about 19% to about 29%, even as the public share fell from 72.4% to 65.8%.
These private facilities now perform almost 6 in 10 of the State’s Caesareans (57%). Had births stayed where they were at NFHS-5, the same arithmetic would give a rate of about 38%. The move into private care accounts for more than half of the 11.9-point rise, about 6.6 points, and higher rates in government facilities for most of the rest, about 4.1 points.
The pattern holds outside cities as well. In rural West Bengal, 88.1% of births in private facilities are Caesareans, slightly more than the urban figure of 86.8%.
A belt around Kolkata
On a district map, the highest rates form one contiguous belt in the south of the State. Kolkata and North 24 Parganas are at 67.5% each, Hooghly at 66.6%, Nadia at 62.9%, Purba Medinipur at 59.1% and Howrah at 58.5%.
Urbanisation alone does not account for the belt. Purba Medinipur, a coastal district where 11.6% of people lived in towns at the 2011 Census, has a higher rate than industrial Paschim Bardhaman (48.1%), where 81.6% did.
Purulia, on the Chota Nagpur plateau in the West, has the State’s lowest rate at 21.6%, followed by Jhargram (27.4%), South 24 Parganas (28.5%), Maldah (29.9%) and Bankura (30.1%). Every district except Purulia is above the national average of 27.2%.
A low district average, however, can also obfuscate women in remote blocks who need an emergency Caesarean and cannot get one. Almost every birth in the two districts with the lowest C-section rates now takes place in a health facility (95.7% in Purulia and 97.7% in Jhargram, against 94.9% for the State), so what matters here, is whether those facilities can perform a Caesarean when one is needed. Block-level hospital records would show how often they do.
Behind the rise
Explanations for the rise need records the survey does not hold. The first concerns money.
Swasthya Sathi, the State’s health insurance scheme, was launched in 2016 and opened to every resident on December 1, 2020. It covers up to ₹5 lakh per family a year in government and empanelled private hospitals. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6, the share of households with at least one member covered by a health insurance or financing scheme rose from 33.7% to 88.2%.
The timing matches the shift to private care. West Bengal was surveyed for NFHS-5 before the scheme became universal, and the births counted in NFHS-6 straddle the change. A scheme that pays for care in private hospitals would be expected to move births into them. The same years brought the COVID-19 pandemic. By May 2020 the State had set aside 69 hospitals for COVID-19 patients, 16 government-run and 53 privates. The disruption fell on both sectors, and the survey cannot separate its effect from the scheme’s.
Whether the scheme’s payments also tilt private hospitals towards surgery is a question its claims records could settle. They would show what share of delivery claims are Caesareans and how package rates for normal and Caesarean births compare.
Another explanation feeds on itself. A woman with a previous Caesarean can safely try labour only where an emergency operation can follow at once, which most district hospitals in India cannot promise. Each first operation therefore tends to bring a second, and the rate keeps rising over years.
Additionally, more women of childbearing age today are overweight or obese (34.6%, up from 22.7%), and more have 10 or more years of schooling (40%, up from 32.9%). An analysis of NFHS-5 data links both to higher odds of a Caesarean.
What the memo asked for
The 2015 memo already proposed periodic audits by the officials who license private clinics. The WHO statement it enclosed put forward a common method for such audits, the Robson classification. It sorts women into 10 groups by details such as how labour began and the baby’s position, so that hospitals can be compared fairly.
Published for each hospital, including every private hospital empanelled under Swasthya Sathi, the results would show where Caesareans are common among low-risk women, the group most likely to have unnecessary operations.
Fewer unneeded operations also require labour wards that can manage a normal birth safely at any hour, and protocols that let suitable women attempt a vaginal birth after a Caesarean. In Purulia and Jhargram the task would have to run the other way, to keep emergency surgery within reach.
What is needed now
The first step is for the State to say whether the audits suggested in 2015 were ever carried out, and what they found. Caesarean audits must then become routine in government and private hospitals alike, under the health department’s supervision. Swasthya Sathi can check each Caesarean claim against the medical reason recorded for it and devise methods to ensure hospitals are given no reason to prefer surgery.
Every woman who needs a Caesarean should get one without delay, and no woman should have one when there is no compelling medical reason behind it.
(Dr. Margubur Rahaman is a public health researcher with the MAMTA Health Institute for Mother and Child, New Delhi. margubur48@gmail.com Ankit Mishra is an ICSSR Doctoral Fellow at the Govind Ballabh Pant Social Science Institute, Prayagraj. ankitmishrakoraon@gmail.com)
