U.S. President Donald Trump held a series of October rallies across battleground and deeply conservative states in an attempt to bolster the Republican Party's chances in the 2026 midterms.
The former reality television star's raucous rallies have long been a defining feature of his political career. According to The New York Times, they usually feature policy proposals, insults against the president's opponents, routines he likes to return to — such as the recitation of an anti-immigrant poem — and, of course, misinformation.
The president often likes to boast about the crowd sizes at his rallies, which leads both his supporters and his satirists to share fake images and videos that supposedly show massive audiences at Trump's events. Snopes has also looked into other rumors aimed at ridiculing these rallies, including jokes about an actual situation where attendees wore diapers.

A group of 21 news publishers has reportedly challenged India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act in the Supreme Court (SC), arguing that the law could undermine investigative journalism and expose journalists’ sources. The lawsuit, filed on October 6, argues that the law’s provisions on consent, data erasure and government access to information could restrict news reporting and force publishers to remove factual stories. The case is scheduled to be heard on October 27, according to a Reuters report. The challenge comes nearly a year after the Centre notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 in November last year. The broader DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules establish a framework governing how organisations collect, process and protect individuals’ digital personal data. The Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which represents the publishers, has argued that the law does not provide a specific exemption for journalistic activities. According to the confidential filing, the association reportedly said that the absence of such safeguards could compromise press freedom and investigative reporting. The DNPA’s members include Mukesh Ambani-owned Network18, Gautam Adani-owned NDTV, the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group. Publishers Vs The DPDP Act A key concern raised by the publishers is the requirement to obtain consent before processing personal data. The DNPA has argued that requiring journalists to notify the subjects of investigations and seek their consent could allow them to destroy evidence or intimidate witnesses. The association has also flagged provisions allowing individuals to withdraw consent and request the erasure of their personal data. According to the filing, the absence of a public-interest safeguard could force publishers to remove or substantially redact factual news reports. The publishers have further raised concerns about provisions empowering the government to seek information from organisations handling personal data. They argue that these powers could expose confidential journalistic sources and discourage whistleblowers from sharing information about corruption, corporate wrongdoing and electoral malpractice. The filing also challenges the government's power to restrict access to information in the public interest, arguing that the provisions could curtail press freedom. The DNPA has sought the quashing of several contentious provisions of the law, most of which are scheduled to come into effect from May 2027, Reuters reported. The association has also argued that the government has granted broad exemptions to the state without extending corresponding protections to the press. What The DPDP Framework Provides The DPDP Act, enacted in August 2023, establishes obligations for processing digital personal data. The later DPDP Rules, notified in November 2025, provide a phased implementation framework, giving organisations up to 18 months to comply with specified requirements. The framework requires platforms to obtain consent for processing personal data, provide clear information about its use and implement security safeguards. It also gives individuals rights to access, correct, update and seek the erasure of their personal data, subject to the applicable provisions. The latest case marks one of the most prominent challenges to the DPDP framework so far, raising questions about how India’s data protection requirements will interact with press freedom and investigative reporting. The Act provides for financial penalties of up to ₹250 Cr for failing to implement reasonable security safeguards. Other violations, including certain breaches of obligations relating to children’s personal data, can attract penalties of up to ₹200 Cr. However, the publishers argue that the framework does not adequately account for the requirements of investigative journalism, particularly when reporting involves personal information collected in the public interest. The government has maintained that the framework protects citizens’ privacy while supporting responsible data processing.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to another working week. We hope the weekend respite was relaxing and invigorating because that oh-too-familiar routine of meetings, deadlines, and the like has returned with a vengeance. But what can you do? The world, such as it is, continues to rotate. To nudge it in a better direction, we are brewing another cup of stimulation. Our choice today is butter pecan with a dash of raw honey. Bristol Myers Squibb reported that one patient died after receiving its investigational CAR-T therapy in an early autoimmune trial, adding to safety concerns about a growing field of research, STAT notes. In a Phase 1 trial that tested the therapy in multiple sclerosis, the patient experienced motor symptoms that did not resolve with standard autoimmune treatments. They were then given a potent immunosuppressant, but developed septic pneumonia and died, Bristol said in a press release. In a subsequent statement, Bristol said this patient was treated for a series of other complications prior to receiving the CAR-T therapy, “confounding our ability to determine the root cause of the issue.”
A Roche drug billed as a potential blockbuster helped patients with a form of lung cancer that had spread live almost six months longer than two competitive medicines, Bloomberg News says. The experimental treatment, called divarasib, fared better than similar drugs from Amgen and Bristol Myers Squibb in a late-stage study. The drug was given to patients with non-small cell lung cancer that had spread, in part because of a genetic mutation, after other treatments, including chemotherapy. The findings could help divarasib become the treatment of choice for this type of lung cancer, in which a mutation called KRAS G12C drives the tumor cell growth.

My father, John Staley, who has died aged 88, was field director for Oxfam in south India and Sri Lanka during the late 1960s and early 70s, when he was responsible for Oxfam’s funding of several hundred local, national and international voluntary agencies.
His role included aid administration, policy formulation, project appraisal, recommendations for funding, disaster relief and liaison with government and non-government organisations. He led Oxfam’s response in India to a drought in Maharashtra in 1973, which fed more than 20,000 people as part of a work-for-food programme, and was made MBE in 1974 for services to the Indian people.
 
John was born in Epsom, Surrey, the only child of Robert, a doctor, and Sylvia, a housewife. He went to Marlborough college in Wiltshire, and then, after national service, to Cambridge University, where he studied natural sciences and economics (1957-61).
At Cambridge he met Elizabeth Pott, and they discovered a shared love of travelling on an overland expedition to Pakistan with friends. They married in 1962 and did PhDs together at the University of the Punjab in Lahore, studying the economics and geography of mountain communities in northern Pakistan.
In 1966 they returned to the UK, where they finished their PhDs and where John did some freelance lecturing at the Commonwealth Institute, the Pakistan Society and the Royal Central Asian Society before taking up his field director post at Oxfam in 1967.
John eventually became research director for Oxfam in India (1975-76), and during that time discovered the concept of experience-based training, by which small groups of people learn about the behaviour of groups and organisations from their own analysis of their experience of the group.
In 1976 he and some Indian colleagues founded Search, an organisation that developed and used these experience-based training methods to train people in development work in India. He was seconded by Oxfam to Search from 1976 to 1980, and then, in 1982, returned to the UK to become a lecturer and later senior lecturer in development studies at Selly Oak Colleges in Birmingham – remaining there until his retirement in 1999.
 
Thereafter he wrote, travelled, took part in his local U3A in Great Malvern, Worcestershire, and cared for his garden and a small local wood that he and Elizabeth bought as a retirement project. Over the years John wrote three books, Words for My Brother (1982), People in Development (also 1982), and Enticing the Learning (2008).
 
Elizabeth died in 2019. John is survived by their children, Eleanor, Joanna and me, and grandchildren Isabelle and Freddie.

On 22 October 2026, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur admitted that “face-offs” with Chinese forces had taken place at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border. Following the ITBP chief’s remarks, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated on 23 October 2026 that the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) becomes “disturbed” when Chinese troops diverge from established patrolling patterns.
In this context, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming to show Chinese soldiers confronting and inspecting Indian soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing a confrontation in Arunachal Pradesh, where Chinese soldiers are intercepting and restricting the movement of Indian troops.
Fact: While the reports have confirmed face-offs between Indian and Chinese forces along the Arunachal Pradesh border, this video actually depicts a counter-terrorism mock drill conducted in Karnataka in April 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led to the original footage (archived) uploaded on the ‘Jagdamba Motors’ Instagram page on 30 April 2026.
The full-length video clearly shows shop signboards, such as “Jagdamba Tools” and “Balaji Tiffin, Tea Centre & Chat”, written in Kannada, indicating that the video was shot in Karnataka, not Arunachal Pradesh.
Furthermore, we contacted the phone number displayed on the “Jagdamba Tools” signboard and spoke with the owner, Sohan Singh Rajput. He confirmed that he recorded the video outside his shop near Devanahalli, Karnataka, in late April 2026, and that it actually depicts a mock drill conducted by Indian forces. We also found some other videos (here and here) of Indian forces participating in exercises at this exact location.
Moreover, the official Indian Army Fact-Check handle clarified that the footage shows an old counter-terrorism mock drill conducted near Bengaluru, Karnataka, and is not a confrontation between Indian and Chinese soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh.
To sum it up, an old video of an Indian counter-terrorism mock drill in Karnataka is being falsely shared as a recent confrontation between Indian and Chinese soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh.

What do you need to know—need to know—about Xavier Trudeau? The eldest son of former Canadian prime minister Justin, the teenage Trudeau has recently begun performing R&B under the mononym Xav. But, with all due respect to Xav, do those facts make him a person of note? Should you expect to be able to read about him on Wikipedia? What about Evanescence guitarist Tim McCord, or 2012 Yachtmaster of the Year Rainer Holtorff?
All three have had a biography on Wikipedia; all three of those biographies were considered for deletion this year on the grounds that the subjects were not notable enough to warrant a biography at all. Every day, dozens, sometimes hundreds, of Wikipedia biographies—of child actors turned LA realtors, retired ambassadors, soccer players who have played less than 10 minutes of professional soccer—are purged from the world’s free encyclopedia.
It’s not as though Wikipedia, which hosts over 7 million articles in the English language, doesn’t have the space. But Wikipedia has only so many volunteers to monitor its contents. To this day, Wikipedia editors are discovering hoaxes that have gone undetected for decades. The time it takes to verify the release dates of Xav’s three singles is better spent—the logic goes—by asking whether the American Civil War officer Nathaniel Lyon really drank mustard during battle, as was claimed in his Wikipedia biography for 17 years. Wikipedia removed the mustard claim, not because it was proven wrong, but because there was no reliable evidence for it. “We’re not really looking for what’s true,” Britta Gustafson, who has been editing Wikipedia since 2001, told me. “We’re looking for what’s verifiable.”
Wikipedia editors do not themselves decide that a person is not notable, only that there is a lack of reliable evidence to support the claim. One person who recently lost her Wikipedia biography on notability grounds is Kimberly Small, the CEO of a Nevada nonprofit that supports survivors of sexual assault. The debate occurred in a public page on Wikipedia itself; it’s in that space that the really tricky decisions about what is and what isn’t good enough for the encyclopedia are made. One editor raised a question: “How should we judge not-for-profit executives? By the nature of their job, the focus is, as it should be, on the organization and the work the organization does, not them.” Another editor replied: “I don’t think there is anything wrong with not-for-profit executives being less often individually notable. Wikipedia coverage is not a prize.”
Is it not? “Having an article says something,” Gustafson admitted. “It implies something.” For six weeks over April and May, I reached out to hundreds of people who were about to lose their Wikipedia page, almost all of whom were learning that information from me. “If you want to write something to save the page, I would appreciate it,” a Spanish filmmaker told me. A biography on Wikipedia might not be intended as a prize, but nobody knows its value like the people who’ve had one and then lost it.
Martina Dimoska is a scientist, originally from North Macedonia, who works at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Specifically, Dimoska is an “analog astronaut”—she takes part in missions that simulate a space environment—and a “science communicator.” She posts often about her work in the can-do, aspirational register that is de rigueur on LinkedIn, where she cites her “recognition by … Forbes, Bloomberg, the United Nations … and global innovation networks.” A Facebook reel of hers, filmed during the crew announcement of NASA’s upcoming Artemis III mission, shows Dimoska alongside the text, “When you work hard so you belong in rooms where history gets proactively written.” On TikTok, she’s had paid partnerships with a makeup brand whose products are tested for effectiveness during spaceflight.
On April 29, Dimoska posted on Facebook, “Wait … I’m on Wikipedia now???” She went on: “A few years ago, building a career in space from the Balkans felt impossible. And now … somehow, that journey is part of the public record. I’m incredibly grateful that [the biography] is there … My hope is that through my journey, I will help a new generation to begin to see space as accessible, not distant.”
The next day, Dimoska’s page was nominated for deletion.
Anne Clin, who has edited Wikipedia since 2005 under the name Risker, warned me that it’s folly to celebrate becoming the subject of a Wikipedia article. “Especially if you’re what we call ‘borderline notable,’” she said.
The other taboo is editing information about yourself. You can’t do that—even if the existing facts about you are wrong—without disclosing a conflict of interest. Even then, it’s strongly discouraged. Jimmy Wales, the cofounder of Wikipedia, has been caught editing his own Wikipedia biography multiple times; that he did so is now part of his Wikipedia biography. In 2022, the novelist Emily St. John Mandel, unable to update her biography to reflect her recent divorce, sat for an interview solely to create a secondary source for that information.
Some high-profile Wikipedia editors and volunteers have bio pages about themselves. Clin is occasionally asked if she would want one. She doesn’t merely refuse; she actively sabotages the possibility. “You cannot write a proper biographical article about me, because I don’t give out enough personal information to do that,” she said. “Absolutely not. Absolutely not.”
Among the people reading Martina Dimoska’s Facebook post about her new Wikipedia page was Kiril Simeonovski, an economist in Skopje, Macedonia, and a Wikipedia editor since 2008. Simeonovski found the post self-congratulatory and the biography itself entirely promotional. He also doubted the inherent notability of an “analog astronaut,” a role that he later likened to a lab mouse.
A Wikipedia editor can tag an article for deletion, and unless satisfactory edits are made within a certain timeframe, the page will disappear. Simeonovski didn’t do this—he referred the article for debate among his fellow editors.
Arguing the case for deletion, Simeonovski described the Dimoska biography as “merely [a] chronology of overhyped personal achievements,” each meticulously deflated by Simeonovski, that did not credibly establish Dimoska as a notable individual.
More damningly, in his argument, was the timing of Dimoska’s Facebook post, coming “shortly after the article was approved.” To him, this was a smoking gun as much as anything. How could she have so promptly promoted the page if she were not somehow connected to it?
When an editor proposes a Wikipedia article for deletion, they append a caveat to the marked page: “If you created this page, please don’t take offense.” This courtesy is not extended to the subject of the article. When I reached out to these people, in the hundreds, to ask them how it felt to be considered non-notable, I was not surprised that the response rate to this question was about 1 percent. Maybe lower.
Matthew Songer, a Michigan orthopedist with three decades of experience, had his biography flagged for deletion (“Unlikely to be notable”) in April. Songer was among the 1 percent of respondees. He told me it’s not for vanity that he needs that page. He is often enlisted as an expert witness in trials, he said, because of the extra imprimatur of being on Wikipedia. The page “is a good reference for attorneys.”
Maneli Mirkhan, a French-Iranian adviser on international affairs, agreed that having a Wikipedia biography inspires confidence in her services. Her biography was called out by Wikipedia editors for reading like a résumé.
The biography of Andrew Wyant, a Phoenix-area executive who works in fitness and nutrition, was also deemed insufficiently notable, due to a lack of coverage from secondary sources. Wyant said he blamed himself for failing to “feed” his public persona through self-promotion. “What I know to be true is that I am largely responsible for the growth of the profession of personal trainers and fitness coaches by building the entire category over the last decade,” he told me. “I feel my accomplishments and impact are notable, but I don’t feel the need to promote them in media so I can have a Wikipedia page.”
Wyant’s biography was deleted. Songer’s biography was deleted. Mirkhan’s biography was deleted.
Of those, only Mirkahn’s reappeared, rewritten and with new sources, a few days later. I asked Mirkhan if she had been involved in re-creating the page. No, she said, but she wasn’t surprised. Mirkhan had been, and continues to be, sought out by the French media to comment on events in Iran, and more coverage means more demonstrations of notability. But there’s always that chicken-and-egg problem: Mirkhan thinks that what gave the media confidence in choosing her as a commentator was not just her career and her expertise. It was the fact that she was on Wikipedia.
Kiril Simeonovski did not lead with his suspicions that Martina Dimoska wrote her own Wikipedia biography. He argued, on Wikipedia’s public page for editorial debates, that the biography’s sourcing was weak, relying in part on posts from Dimoska’s LinkedIn page. It promoted Dimoska’s social media accounts, where she posted things like—and this Simeonovski found objectionable enough to cite in his argument for deletion—a picture comparing herself to NASA software engineer Margaret Hamilton. Published three separate times, it became one of her most popular posts, engendering sexist mockery and vicious defense.
To Simeonovski, self-promotion like this suggested that the case for Dimoska’s notability was regularly oversold by Dimoska herself. Though he could not prove a connection, it was difficult to imagine the Wikipedia biography as anything but an extension of that project.
That afternoon, a new Wikipedia user added comments to Simeonovski’s public arraignment, noting three existing articles about other individual analog astronauts. A fair contribution, tempered by a shot across the bow at Simeonovski: The user’s name was “Kiril’s mom.” The user was not Simeonovski’s mom, and the account was subsequently blocked. Hours later, another new user asked Simeonovski, rhetorically, “If I publish a blog post about someone and he finds it amazing and celebrates it does that mean that he/she created it?” Their username was a coded reference to the actual name of Simeonovski’s mother. They also got blocked.
Nine days later, another anonymous user—whose IP address, according to Simeonovski, placed them in Skopje, North Macedonia—said Dimoska’s biography had improved “considerably,” with new sourcing from publications like The Telegraph. The revised article, the user claimed, was superior to “85%” of Wikipedia articles about living Macedonians.
Three days later, Simeonovski dismantled each of the 32 new sources in turn. It wasn’t really the British newspaper The Telegraph that had been cited, for instance, but the Albanian news website Telegrafi. “I fail to find a single independent and reputable English-language source,” he later wrote.
The next day, the anonymous user rebutted Simeonovski point by point. They said it was “strange” that Simeonovski could not seem to find a single appropriate source for Dimoska’s biography but had found “10 sources from non-independent websites” when he wrote an article about the former governor of the National Bank of North Macedonia. The National Bank of North Macedonia, the user added to Simeonovski: Isn’t that where you work?
At one point, Simeonovski said he would report his detractor to the Wikimedia Foundation legal department.
Of Rosemary Bush, a professor at Northwestern University in Illinois, a Wikipedia editor recently wrote: “It will be many years until she qualifies as notable.” Bush herself agreed, to a point, that the Wikipedia page about her did not make a strong case, though she found the biography itself to be strange, possibly AI-generated, and not wholly representative of her career. “The world is fine without a Wikipedia page on me,” she said, but added, “I do think the comment proposing deletion is a bit rude.”
A little rudeness is unavoidable in this line of work. Sonia Jones, a Welsh singer best known for the theme song from the 1979 film Monty Python’s Life of Brian, is indeed best known for the theme song from Monty Python’s Life of Brian; therefore, Wikipedia editors decided that her Wikipedia biography should be deleted and henceforth redirect to the article about the song. Jones, when I asked her for a comment, did not agree that her achievements since 1979 do not merit documentation. “No, I do not want them to remove my page,” she said. “Why would they?”
“Canada has a national dodgeball team? Who would have thought?” wrote one editor in their case to delete the biography of Savannah Burton, the first transgender athlete to compete for Canada’s national dodgeball team. “Even though dodgeball is not considered a mainstream sport, competing at the highest level in any sport is a significant accomplishment,” Burton told me. “Given the ongoing attempts to erase transgender people, along with infringements on our rights and our ability to live normal lives, this action is not surprising.”
There is, when you look for it, a careless and cocky tone that can creep into the verdicts of Wikipedia editors who have been doing the job for a long time. “This guy is a nobody. Delete him.” “I’ve got more followers on Instagram than he does.” “All we have here are stand-up comedy, opinion columns, being a guest or collaborator on some non-notable podcasts … This is more or less every twentieth person who lives in NYC.”
Rosemary Bush’s biography was deleted. Sonia Jones’ biography was deleted. Savannah Burton’s biography was retained. “It was easy to find more sources,” wrote an editor who came to the page’s rescue. Editors’ participation in this process is not mandatory. Articles, once marked for death, can be deleted simply because nobody showed up to debate the matter. That anyone would volunteer their time to save an undeserving article from oblivion is a kindness: a good deed in a rude world.
Kiril Simeonovski never did refer the anonymous editor of Martina Dimoska’s biography to the Wikimedia Foundation’s legal team. Instead, he and his antagonist continued their debate on sourcing and semantics for days, and then weeks.
Per her Wikipedia page, Dimoska’s achievements included the command of two analog astronaut missions in Poland, but Simeonovski argued that while this information was verifiable, the missions themselves did not meet the threshold of notability and therefore neither did Dimoska. The anonymous user pointed to Dimoska’s inclusion in a Macedonian book for schoolchildren about 50 Macedonian women: “The book was subsequently recommended by the Bureau for Development of Education as optional reading material for ninth-grade students nationwide, which gives the subject recurring exposure within the educational system rather than temporary media attention.”
“You’ve apparently regressed to using children’s books to support the notability of the person we’re discussing,” said Simeonovski. “I expect [you] to continue gaslighting with multi-paragraph comments, but that won’t change the observation that the person isn’t notable [enough] for a Wikipedia article.”
“Count your words and then mine … and see who is the one gaslighting with multi-paragraph comments.”
“You seem to mix up ‘prominence’ and ‘notability.’”
“Your argument relies heavily on personal anecdotes and assumptions about how Macedonian media operates.”
Other editors with an eye on the debate pleaded for colleagues to lend their perspective. Most supported Simeonovski, but they didn’t linger long. “At this point the most visible thing about this individual seems to be [this] article,” one said, before bouncing.
As this unfolded, I asked Dimoska what she made of it. “The whole thing has become quite challenging to track,” she said, “and I’m already behind on my social media.” She denied editing the page herself or having any knowledge of the people defending it. She added: “Watching strangers debate your life, work, and credibility in such an intense way is definitely a strange experience to process.”
On April 25, a user named “DavidfromArizona” took to Wikipedia to announce that his friend Sheldon Marks—“the world’s leading vasectomy reversal expert,” per Marks’ own website—wished for his Wikipedia biography to be removed.
“It is inaccurate and does not truly represent his achievements,” David wrote. “[His] ego is hurt by having such a page. He either wants a detailed page or wants this one deleted.” A request from the subject of a Wikipedia article is not grounds for deletion in itself, although it can tip the balance if there is no clear consensus. On examination, Wikipedia editors found the biography lacking in sources that demonstrated notability.
On May 6, a Wikipedia user who 17 years earlier had created a biography for Sophie Aston, a British landscape artist, said that Aston had recently asked that the page be deleted. “She has retrained as a psychotherapist and wishes to forget her career as an artist.”
Having seen how much a Wikipedia page matters to certain people, I asked Marks and Aston why they wanted theirs removed.
“A kind and enthusiastic man made my Wiki page as a surprise for me about 17 years ago,” Aston told me. “We’d been on two dates. I found it a bit embarrassing but sweet. I didn’t see him again; I wasn’t into him. The info on the page was never [very] accurate and is now very out of date.” It was “ostentatious,” she added, for Wikipedia to present her as an artist of note, not least because for the past 10 years she has been a professional psychotherapist. The biography, she said, “makes it sound like I am an important artist, and I am not—it’s inappropriate.”
The Wikipedia editors could not treat Aston’s request with undue favor, but given the chance to cast fresh eyes over the article, they found her biography lacking. “The request to delete her article is not relevant,” one wrote bluntly, “but I don’t view her artistic career as meeting [notability] guidelines regardless of the request.” Aston’s biography was deleted.
Sheldon Marks didn’t respond to me. After receiving my email, however, he fled straight to the debate unfolding on Wikipedia. “I did not request deletion of this article,” he wrote. The statements made by DavidfromArizona, whom Marks did not know, were apparently fabrications. Marks wanted to keep his page. He admitted it could be improved but maintained that he was a notable individual: “I am the author of Vasectomy Reversal: Manual of Vasovasostomy and Vasoepididymostomy (Springer, 2018), translated into Chinese by Springer Nature in 2025; the surgical instrument known as the Marks Vas Cutting Forceps is named for me; I have served as Course Coordinator for the AUA post-graduate course on vasectomy reversal; and I have been a contributor to WebMD since 2005.”
The Wikipedia editors briefly conferred, then replied that they had already voted to delete.
There’s a final twist in the biography of Martina Dimoska: She knew Kiril Simeonovski—the guy trying to get her deleted.
“I had interacted with him on social media before and had crossed paths through mutual friends,” Dimoska said. “One recent example I remember clearly is seeing his post after he was injured by a cyclist who had left the scene.” Dimoska recalled the post in detail, though she had not responded or reacted to it at the time.
Simeonovski said he didn’t remember ever speaking with Dimoska in person but admitted the possibility of “virtual interaction.” Both are active on Facebook, and though they do not follow each other, Simeonovski said they have enough mutual friends in North Macedonia that their respective algorithms often put them in each other’s path. Just as Dimoska saw Simeonovski’s post about his accident, so Simeonovski came across Dimoska’s celebration of inclusion in Wikipedia, which led him to discover Dimoska’s earlier Instagram post comparing herself to Margaret Hamilton, then to a much older Reddit thread asking if Dimoska was the smartest Macedonian woman. (“Isn’t it just all hype about that girl?” one Redditor replied.) Simeonovski didn’t comment on any of those posts. But in Wikipedia he had found an opportunity to contest her notability on surer ground.
“It was somewhat surprising to me, perhaps because I have become accustomed to professional environments where people tend to be more openly supportive of one another’s work,” Dimoska told me. “At the same time, having grown up in North Macedonia, I am aware that recognition within a small community can sometimes generate more scrutiny than one might expect.”
One month after Simeonovski nominated Dimoska’s biography for deletion, he lost. The page was kept. “Given the bludgeoning, canvassing, and sockpuppetry evident here, this is a no consensus closure without prejudice against speedy renomination,” wrote an editor in a determination. “The arguments to delete here are stronger on the merits, but sufficient reasoned opposition exists that I do not see a consensus for deletion.” Obstinacy won the day, though Dimoska’s page now carries a disclaimer that it contains “promotional content.”
Wikipedia pages, for better or worse, matter to people. To be included is a validation of a life. If it were not so desirable, then one of the very first things Kiril Simeonovski did upon joining Wikipedia in 2008 would not have been to create a page about himself. Which he did do. He “wasn’t aware about the notability policies” back then, he told me.
The page was promptly deleted. “If your achievements, etc., are verifiable and genuinely notable and thus suitable for inclusion in Wikipedia,” an editor chided Simeonovski at the time, “someone else will probably create an article about you sooner or later.” To date, nobody has.

No Saliba, no problem - Konsa stepping up for Arsenal
- Published
When Arsenal confirmed in July that William Saliba would miss an "extended period" with a long-term back issue, you can forgive fans for panicking.
The Frenchman has formed a formidable pairing with Gabriel Magalhaes as part of the Gunners' well-drilled backline that conceded just 27 league goals last season as they lifted the Premier League title.
Eight games into the new season and Saliba still hasn't featured, but Mikel Arteta's side have conceded the fewest goals in the Premier League as they sit level on points at the summit.
That form is testament to the performances of Ezri Konsa, who has stepped up in Saliba's absence and been given his chance to shine.
Before Arsenal signed the 29-year-old for £55m from Aston Villa in August, questions were asked. Is it too much money? Do the Gunners need him with Cristhian Mosquera already in the squad? Why bring in Konsa and not a forward?
But now, the debate is whether Konsa and Gabriel are the best partnership in world football, not just the Premier League.
Arsenal already had seven senior defenders on the books when they signed Konsa.
And add in the fact they already had one of the most solid partnerships in world football too, it can be understood why there was confusion about such a big outlay.
Arsenal have changed their recruitment strategy, focusing on signings in the peak of their career as they look to capitalise on their win window and continue to lift silverware.
Konsa is exactly what they are looking for - in his prime.
The defender made 286 appearances for Villa after joining in July 2019 from Brentford and helped them win the Europa League in May, the club's first European trophy since 1982.
He has established himself as a first-choice starter for England and started seven of their eight games at the World Cup.
His former Aston Villa team-mate, Morgan Rogers - who himself made a big-money move this summer when he joined Chelsea for £117m - said at the World Cup that Konsa does not get the credit he deserves and that he is "one of the best centre-backs in football".
Konsa's impressive start
Konsa is an imposing figure, quick across the ground, and his aggression in challenges has impressed supporters.
Having signed on the opening day of the season, Arteta has praised the way the centre-back has settled in as "unbelievable".
"He's gone to a huge club like Arsenal with no pre-season when Saliba is here, with other players that are already here," Arteta added of Konsa's start.
"To position yourself in that manner, with that naturality I would say, and performing at the level that he's doing and building already a chemistry and a balance with Gabi that seems so solid, it's very difficult to do and we are really lucky to have him."
The stats back up Arteta's claim.
Individually, Konsa had the best pass-completion rate of any player in the Premier League last season and he tops the chart again this season with 96% success rate from his 324 passes.
He also ranked top for success rate among all Premier League outfielders to contest 20 or more ground duels during the last campaign and is currently ranked 12th for this in 2026-27.
Arsenal have kept a clean sheet in five of their eight games, with no team keeping more in the Premier League this season.
After joining just hours before their season-opener against Coventry, Konsa has started six of those matches, while he came on for his debut in their second match against former club Villa after Mosquera picked up an injury.
"The two of them [Saliba and Gabriel] were on the Ballon D'or list as the best defenders in world football," Former Arsenal defender Martin Keown said on Match of the Day.
"He has not been overshadowed at all by the people he has played alongside."
And Konsa produced another impressive performance when he scored his first goal for Arsenal against Everton on Saturday.
"I've come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us. It's not surprising to me," Konsa said of Arsenal's strong start to the season.
"We are champions and to be champions you've got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible."
Gabriel and Konsa partnership is flourishing
Nine starts, seven wins, five clean sheets, two goals between them - the partnership of Konsa and Gabriel could not be going much better.
The pair both scored as the Gunners beat Everton and it was the first time that Arsenal had two centre-backs score in a Premier League match since February 2024, which coincidentally also came against a David Moyes team (Gabriel and Saliba against West Ham).
Konsa has also started all three of Arsenal's games alongside Gabriel in the Champions League and the Gunners are unbeaten as the formidable partnership continues to flourish.
The England international has said that Gabriel made "my life easy since I've joined the club and it's been a pleasure playing alongside him".
Gabriel's regular partner Saliba still has no date for a return but is currently doing individual training work on grass.
When asked whether there is less pressure on Saliba rushing to get back, Arteta was keen to remind everyone of his quality.
"William is not fit and we are desperate to have him back because we know what he offers," he said.
"We are really lucky to have that and I'm sure when Mosquera plays that he will be the same because they have something special those boys.
"The way we train them, the way they want to improve as well and how they look after each other. That's the beauty of our team."
The next challenge for Konsa will be when Saliba returns.
But with his ability to play right-back too, he doesn't only have one route into the starting XI.

In late October, with Election Day less than two weeks away, a post on Threads (archived) about the purported experience of a volunteer at the polls captured social media users' attention. According to the post, the volunteer's training focused on what to do if federal agents, such as officials with U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement or the Department of Justice, intimidate voters at election sites.
The post read:
I've been volunteering at the polls for the last 6 years and I just finished the training for Nov. 3rd.
Six years ago the training covered what to do if some MAGA instigators tried to disrupt voting. Training for this election focused on what to do if DHS, DOJ, ICE, or the Military attempted to intimidate voters.
In 6 years we went from random private citizens to our very own government trying to block our constitutional right to vote.
That is f…ing horrifying.
Users shared the post on other social media sites, such as Facebook (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent us emails asking whether the claim was true.
There are nonprofit, voting-oriented organizations that have been training polling-site volunteers on what to do if federal agents are present and intimidate voters. Therefore, we've rated this claim true.
We attempted to reach out to the Threads user who made the original post to ask more about her experience, but were unable to direct-message her via the social media platform.
To be clear, someone does not have to be an election worker — such as someone who counts votes — to volunteer at the polls. Republicans and Democrats alike have volunteers who monitor polling sites, and nonprofit organizations, particularly those focused on voting concerns, also have volunteers active at voting locations.
For example, Hands Off Our Vote, which is supported by various civil rights organizations and community groups, keeps a toolkit for people and groups to use to host trainings that will "equip volunteers with the skills to handle federal interference (including ICE/ feds at the polls)."
In a report detailing ways it and other organizations may handle armed federal agents at polling sites, the Brennan Center for Justice — a nonprofit group focused on democracy and criminal justice — said civic engagement organizations are providing guidance to volunteers monitoring polling sites on what to do, "such as documenting and reporting agents' activity while avoiding confrontation."
Civic engagement groups in the Chicago area prepared volunteers for potential federal immigration action during the primaries, according to local news reporting from March.
The Save America Movement, which has previously documented ICE operations in various American cities, is participating in Vote Safe, a project between multiple organizations designed to decrease voter hesitancy in minority groups intimidated by the potential of federal agents at polling sites. According to the Save America Movement, it plans to train and have "teams of local activists, volunteers, veterans, and faith leaders stand alongside voters at polling locations, serving as a visible deterrent against intimidation."
According to reporting from NPR, Living United for Change in Arizona has trained what the organization has called "constitutional observers" to monitor polling sites. NPR reported that the group wants people on the ground in the case ICE agents are at polling sites.
Snopes reached out to the group through Facebook Messenger to confirm the group has been training volunteers on what to do if federal agents are at polling sites. We'll update this story if we receive a response.
For further reading, Snopes has fact-checked a number of rumors about voting ahead of the midterms, including a claim that voting machines in Illinois were flagging Republican picks as unpopular.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023), with effect from October 17. The move has raised questions about how violations by medical colleges will be penalised, and how compliance with prescribed standards will be verified under the remaining regulatory framework.
The MSMER-2023 was withdrawn with immediate effect through a notification dated October 14, published in the Gazette on October 17. There is no single new regulation replacing MSMER 2023. Instead, the requirement for medical colleges to submit Annual Disclosure Reports (ADRs) will continue under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and other applicable regulations, the NMC said.
Rules on penalties, enforcement removed
The withdrawal comes close on the heels of a nationwide agitation for greater accountability in the undergraduate medical entrance examination.
Healthcare activists and medical education experts have raised concerns about three key areas that may fall through the gaps with the withdrawal of these regulations: the alleged removal of specific penalties under MSMER-2023, including fines of up to ₹1 crore for specified violations and personal fines of up to ₹5 lakh for faculty and administrators submitting false records; the verification of colleges’ annual disclosures on faculty, infrastructure, clinical facilities, and patient load; and the removal of the specific procedures and timelines for enforcement and appeals laid out in the MSMER-2023.
‘Patients at risk’
Bejon Kumar Misra, consumer rights activist and founder-director of the Patient Safety and Access Initiative of India Foundation (PSAIIF), said the withdrawal raised concerns about transparency, accountability, and the quality of medical education.
While the NMC Act, 2019, provides statutory powers for inspections and enforcement, Prof. Misra said that withdrawing a detailed regulatory framework without clarifying equivalent safeguards creates uncertainty over how institutional deficiencies and false disclosures will be addressed.
“Medical colleges cannot be judged merely by their buildings, equipment, or number of approved seats. The real measure of medical education is the competence of graduating doctors, the availability of qualified faculty, adequate supervised clinical exposure, and their ability to deliver safe and ethical patient care,” he said.
Prof. Misra has also written to the Union government, warning that misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk. He urged the Union Health Ministry and the NMC to clarify the enforcement mechanisms that will remain in place and to ensure that medical education standards are independently verifiable.
‘Dilution of regulatory oversight’
Babu K.V., an ophthalmologist and medical activist, said the withdrawal could dilute the penalty framework. He explained that by denotifying the stronger MSMER 2023 September regulation and retaining the June regulation, some clauses have been deleted.
“Like the clause 8(2)c, which states that monetary penalty not exceeding ₹5 lakh [will be imposed] for the faculty/Head of the Department (HoD)/Dean/Director/doctor submitting false declaration/documents/records (including patients’ records). Further, they can also be charged or penalised for misconduct under the Registered Medical Practitioner (Professional Conduct) Regulations in vogue,” he said.
“This is the key regulation ,where the individual doctors are made accountable and hence deleting it is dilution of regulatory oversight,” Dr. Babu explained, refuting the NMC’s argument that there is no dilution of regulatory oversight.
‘Eliminates duplication’
However, a senior NMC official told The Hindu that the decision had been “misinterpreted”. The withdrawal followed a review by the Commission’s legal team, which recommended streamlining regulatory powers and removing overlapping responsibilities, the official said.
The Commission functions through four autonomous boards, of which two set standards for undergraduate and postgraduate medical education. Another assesses and rates medical colleges and undertakes institutional inspections and regulatory action, while the fourth oversees medical registration, professional conduct, and ethics.
The NMC maintains that the move eliminates duplication without diluting standards, and that its inspection and verification powers remain intact.
Not retrospective
The Gazette notification provides that the withdrawal will not affect actions already taken, approvals granted, or rights, obligations and liabilities accrued under MSMER-2023. Applications, proceedings, appeals and inquiries pending before the withdrawal will continue to be dealt with under the regulations, insofar as applicable. Matters arising after the withdrawal will be governed by the NMC Act and the statutory and regulatory provisions then in force.
India had 846 medical colleges, 1,39,864 MBBS seats and 86,360 postgraduate medical seats, according to government data cited in August 2026. “With medical education expanding, the key question is whether the regulatory framework that remains can ensure that colleges meet prescribed standards and face effective action when they fail to do so,’’ Dr. Babu said.

Mumbai, October 27, 2026: In a temporary relief for actor Imran Khan, the Bombay High Court on Tuesday kept the ‘Leave India’ notice issued to him in abeyance till November 2, when it will hear his plea.
A bench of Chief Justice MC Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna granted relief to Khan while hearing a petition filed by the actor, through advocate Zulfiquar Memon of MZM Legal, challenging a notice directing him to leave India by October 28 for allegedly violating immigration laws by participating in a protest in Mumbai.
On Monday, Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Anil Singh urged the court to adjourn the case till November 2. Singh, representing the Centre, also assured the court that no coercive action would be taken against Khan till then.
However, senior counsel Venkatesh Dhond, appearing for Khan, pointed out that the notice asked him to leave India by October 28, Wednesday. “But I have to leave tomorrow (according to the FRRO directive),” said Dhond.
To this, Singh replied: “(Court) may keep it on Monday. Nothing will happen. That is an oral assurance.”
The court, in turn, agreed to adjourn the case and added that the FRRO’s order be kept on hold till then.
“ASG seeks time. Matter stands over to November 2 at 3 pm. The order under challenge shall be kept in abeyance till the next date,” the court noted in its order.
Notice Follows October 10 Detention
The notice follows Khan’s detention on October 10 during a demonstration at August Kranti Maidan in Mumbai. The protest was held in solidarity with an agitation in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Following the demonstration, a complaint was lodged at Gamdevi police station alleging that Khan had violated the Foreigners Act by participating in a political protest despite being a US citizen. The police subsequently forwarded the complaint to the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO), which issued the notice directing him to leave India.
Khan, who has appeared in several Bollywood films, is the nephew of actor Aamir Khan.
OCI Status And Legal Provisions
As an OCI cardholder, Khan is entitled to certain privileges, including a lifelong visa to visit and reside in India. However, OCI status does not confer Indian citizenship or political rights such as voting or contesting elections.
Under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, the Central government has the power to direct a foreign national not to remain in India or in any specified area. Khan’s proposed challenge is expected to question the legal basis for the action taken against him over his participation in the protest.
Actor Denies Violating Any Law
According to Khan, no gathering was underway when he reached the spot. He claimed that he neither entered a restricted or barricaded area nor disobeyed any police instruction to leave. He further alleged that he was apprehended only after media personnel surrounded him while he was returning to his vehicle.
The actor argued that he had not violated any provision of the Immigration and Foreigners Act or the Citizenship Act. He also highlighted that he had lived in India since the age of two and had deep familial, marital, educational and professional ties to the country, with no criminal antecedents.

A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this summer from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Dolomites, the Italian army has said.
The devices, which included Italian artillery shells and French mortar bombs, were removed and defused by the army’s Julia Alpine brigade, according to a statement.
The weapons originated from the white war, a battle between the Austro-Hungarian army and Italian troops across treacherous and bitterly cold terrain between 1915 and 1918.
More than a century later, hikers reported several sightings of bombs during the summer, mostly in the area of Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley in eastern Trentino. The soldiers then conducted an extensive sweep there and across other high-altitude and glacier locations in the Trentino Alto Adige region of the Dolomites.
They recovered and neutralised 250 explosives, including “18 Italian 75mm artillery shells and 37 Thevetot mortar shells – a French-made device that was also supplied to the Italian royal army during the first world war”, the Julia Alpine brigade.
It is not the first time that relics of the white war have emerged from melting glaciers, whose retreat has accelerated over more than decade.
“It is very much a consequence of global heating,” said Stefano Morosini, a professor at the University of Bergamo and the coordinator of heritage projects at Stelvio national park, where some of the explosives were also found.
“In recent years, at the end of each summer, these dangerous artefacts emerge and each year there is a higher number. They have been conserved by the ice for more than 100 years. Some had already exploded but many hadn’t, so now when they re-emerge, they are very, very dangerous.”
The advice to hikers and mountaineers is to “never touch any type of explosive device you might find, regardless of where it is located” and to promptly report any discovery to police.
Fought mainly in the Dolomites of Trentino Alto-Adige and the Alps of the Lombardy region, the white war was a period of history frozen in time until the 1990s, when global heating started to reveal an assortment of perfectly preserved relics, including weapons, sledges, letters and diaries.
A wooden barracks that had been dug into a cave on the top of Mount Scorluzzo, a 3,095-metre (10,154ft) peak overlooking the Stelvio pass, reappeared in 2015 after the ice which had sealed it off for almost a century completely melted.
The shelter had been hastily locked up when the first world war ended in November 1918, and the soldiers abandoned most of their belongings. Beds made of straw as well as clothes, lanterns, newspapers, postcards, coins, and tinned food were found well preserved inside.
A white war museum to host the relics is scheduled to open in Bormio in June 2027.
The white war is thought to have claimed more than a million lives, although the majority of soldiers were believed to have been killed by avalanches, falling down mountains or hypothermia.
Dozens of corpses, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice over the past 15 years.
The relatives of an Italian soldier were able to bury him in 2017 after documents revealing his identity were found with his body on Presena glacier.
Morosini said the intense summer heat was making access to the glaciers in the Dolomites less safe. Eleven people died when a huge mass of the Marmolada glacier broke off in 2022.
“It is becoming more and more impossible to access the glaciers during the summer because of the very long heatwave at high altitude,” he said.
“If you come to the area, you can see how fast the glaciers are retreating and how strong the impact of climate change is.”

Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.
After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.
The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.
Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.
Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.
However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.
In a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.
Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.
“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said.
The SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.
Mahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.
“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”
Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”
Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.
The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.

Tata Communications plans to invest $400-450 Mn (around ₹4,350 Cr) to build 10,000 km of AI-ready connectivity infrastructure across India in a bid to capitalise on rising demand for data centre connectivity and compute infrastructure. The investment will be used to build a new high-speed fibre network connecting major data centres and AI hubs, allowing transfer of large amounts of data faster with minimal delays. The network will also connect to Tata Communications’ existing global network. The company plans to add around 6 petabits per second (pbps) of network capacity under the programme, taking its total capacity to approximately 7.25 pbps once the expansion is completed. The proposed capacity addition is scheduled between FY30-36 and will be financed via operating cash flows. Its existing network capacity utilisation stands at around 70%-80%. Tata Communications said the investment will help it cater to demand from hyperscalers, AI platforms, cloud providers, global capability centres (GCCs), enterprises and digital-native businesses. The network is designed to support the high capacity, reliability and low latency required to move data between computing infrastructure and data centres. The first phase will focus on the Mumbai-Pune-Hyderabad-Chennai corridor, one of India’s key AI and hyperscale growth routes. Subsequent phases will extend connectivity to emerging data centre clusters in other parts of the country as well. The expansion is expected to connect India’s key AI and data centre hubs with international cable landing stations, strengthening connectivity between domestic infrastructure and global AI hubs and allowing for large volumes of data to be shared quickly and reliably between computing facilities. “The AI economy needs more than compute. It needs a network built for speed, scale and resilience,” said Tata Communications’ CPTO Rupesh Chokshi. E2E Networks To Add Compute Capacity The announcement comes as Indian infrastructure providers step up investments to support growing demand for AI training and inference workloads. Earlier today, cloud and AI infrastructure provider E2E Networks announced plans to expand its AI factory capacity by nearly 59%, adding around 5.4 megawatts (MW) of capacity through NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and other Blackwell GPUs. The proposed expansion will take E2E Networks’ AI factory capacity to approximately 14.6 MW. The company said the additional capacity will support large-scale model training, post-training, production inference, agentic AI and multimodal applications. The company is seeing demand from foundation model builders, AI-native startups, enterprises, higher education and research institutions, and public-sector programmes. It also highlighted growing demand for AI infrastructure hosted in India, particularly among organisations operating in regulated and data-sensitive environments. “India’s AI builders are moving beyond the pilot stage. They now are actively consuming AI tokens in production at previously unheard of scales,” said Tarun Dua, founder and managing director of E2E Networks. This capacity expansion comes on the back of heightened demand for E2E Networks’ GPU services. Its operating revenue jumped 411% to ₹223.8 Cr in the second quarter of FY27 from ₹43.8 Cr in the year-ago quarter. It posted a consolidated net profit of ₹72.7 Cr during the quarter under review, reversing a net loss of ₹13.5 Cr a year earlier. It also signed a multi-year cloud GPU contract worth approximately ₹1,000 Cr during the quarter.

What to know about China's plenum as Xi seeks stronger party discipline
HONG KONG — China's political leaders and elites began a four-day meeting Monday to discuss strengthening the ruling Communist Party's discipline, as Chinese President Xi Jinping pushes for greater loyalty and reliability from officials while deepening his yearslong campaign against corruption.
This week's closed-door gathering, known as the fifth plenum of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, comes roughly a year before Xi is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader and personnel changes to key leadership bodies.
Xi began the meeting by delivering a work report and speaking about a draft policy decision on advancing "full and rigorous party self-governance," according to China's official Xinhua News Agency. The policy aims to make cadres more disciplined, effective and less corrupt.
While Xi has consolidated his grip on power, analysts say the plenum will offer him an opportunity to further align what Chinese officials do with what Beijing wants.
"The plenum is a chance to ensure the new generations rising the ranks share Xi's assessment of the opportunities and risks China faces," said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London's Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.
Here's what to know about one of Beijing's most significant political meetings this year.
Xi targets underperforming cadres and corruption
Xi's anti-graft drive has been a defining feature of his rule since he came to power in 2012. Purges of officials — including some viewed as his political rivals — have been carried out on a scale that led critics to argue the campaign was also used to consolidate his power.
But his focus has expanded to cracking down on underperforming cadres too. In recent years, the number of officials punished for "formalism" and "bureaucratism" — misconduct such as dereliction of duty, inaction and reckless acts that seriously hinder development — has surged.
Xi's policy proposals reflect his emphasis on the party's "self-revolution," a concept centered on the party reforming itself through efforts such as rooting out corruption and building ideological commitment, analysts say.
Osman said the disciplinary crackdowns are now aimed more at institutional longevity.
"It's less about purging elite rivals and more about building a disciplined system that can sustain Xi's political priorities across leadership cycles," she said.
Record-high disciplinary campaigns also do not necessarily mean a rebound in corruption, but rather that Xi has been steadily raising the bar for the party's expectations of officials, she added.
Mingda Qiu, senior analyst of Eurasia Group's China practice, said Beijing has been building its agenda for months.
"The message is clear: the anti-corruption campaign is not winding down. Officials are not only tested for loyalty, but also for compliance and action," he said.
Xi said in a January meeting that while decisions by the party's top leadership were smoothly implemented in general, inspections and audits found problems such as failures to comply and improper execution, according to an October article in the Qiushi Journal, a publication of the central committee.
Xi warned against "two-faced people" who might profess political loyalty while privately defying orders and doing as they please.
"During leadership transitions, we must keep our eyes sharp, elevate good cadres who are truly loyal and reliable, consistent in word and deed, and willing to take responsibility, and never allow 'two-faced people' or those driven by self-interest to slip through," Xi was quoted as saying.
Xi's purges of top army officials will be put on display
The number of empty seats in the conference hall this week will help observers gauge how widespread Xi's purges have been.
Neil Thomas, senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, and his colleagues Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang noted that while Xi's civilian purges are record-breaking, 42 out of 44 officials affiliated with the military elected as full central committee members in 2022 have also been purged or disappeared.
The central committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 full and alternate members. Thomas and his colleagues estimated turnout this week could be less than 80%, potentially setting a record low at any plenum since the end of former leader Mao Zedong's rule in 1976.
Attention will also be on new demands on the officials who remain.
Thomas expects tighter scrutiny of public spending and major projects, more use of technology to uncover corruption, and tougher consequences for officials who fail to deliver on Xi's priorities.
New personnel appointments are possible, though Xi may wait until a once-in-five-years Communist Party Congress next year to anoint his picks, said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London. If he does fill any openings, it will be with loyalists, he added.
Hints at a Xi successor are unlikely
The underlying theme of the fifth plenum is that it will be another opportunity for Xi to position himself for an unprecedented fourth term in office.
Xi, who removed presidential term limits in 2018, is viewed by some as the most powerful Chinese leader since Mao. He is widely expected to be confirmed as party leader for the next term in the fall of 2027.
Ahead of that, Thomas said new ideological language reinforcing Xi's authority might emerge at this week's meeting.
He said the plenum should prepare the ground for Xi's fourth term and reinforce expectations of political and policy continuity.
"After Xi has purged so many of the people that he promoted at the last congress, watch for tougher scrutiny of the officials competing to join his next leadership team," he said.

Jay-Z picks himself to headline the Super Bowl halftime show in Southern California
LOS ANGELES — The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself.
The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he had one request when the league first reached an agreement with Roc Nation: that Jay-Z take the stage himself "whenever the moment felt right to him."
"From 'Reasonable Doubt' to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey," Jay-Z said in a statement. "Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."
After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his celebration of the 30th anniversary of "Reasonable Doubt," the mogul's 1996 debut album. The concerts included three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium and sold-out performances in London and Paris ahead of a stop at SoFi Stadium over the weekend.
Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told Goodell, "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."
Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.
Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog also includes the albums "The Blueprint" and "The Black Album," and hit songs such as "Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)," "99 Problems" and "Empire State of Mind," his collaboration with Alicia Keys.
Last year, "Reasonable Doubt" was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
His recent concerts brought out a rotating cast of guests. At SoFi Stadium, his daughter Blue Ivy played piano on "The Story of O.J." and "Dead Presidents," while Scarface, John Legend and DJ Khaled joined him on opening night. Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too $hort appeared during Saturday's finale.
Earlier in the run, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and Nas were among the guests at Yankee Stadium.
Jay-Z has built a career as an executive and entrepreneur. The Brooklyn rapper co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.
Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021. He is also a four-time Emmy winner.
Roc Nation will executive produce the halftime show, with Hamish Hamilton directing.
The halftime show has collected Emmys in recent years. Bad Bunny's performance in February won a record seven, including best variety special (live), while Kendrick Lamar's show last year won for music direction.
