The Operator Question How can pop-up shops at festive carnivals (Durga Puja/Diwali/Christmas melas) help unconventional new-age lifestyle brands? What is the cost involved? Is it worth the investment? How should brands measure the ROI? Speaking to Inc42, Cure By Design founder Daanish Matheen spoke about the pop-up shop aspect of D2C retail. The startup offers hemp-based CBD oils, balms and pain-relief solutions, alongside personal care and nutrition products such as shampoos, face washes, serums and food items. For unconventional lifestyle brands like Cure By Design, festive pop-ups offer an opportunity to reach new audiences, build trust, and increase brand awareness. Since cannabidiol (CBD) is still an emerging category in India, these events allow the brand to educate consumers, address misconceptions, and encourage first-time purchases. Costs vary depending on the event, location, and footfall, with expenses including stall rentals, staffing, logistics, and branding. We've participated in pop-ups occasionally but have reduced them significantly since opening our retail stores in Bengaluru and Chennai. Permanent stores provide better customer engagement, stronger credibility, and more consistent conversions. For us, ROI goes beyond immediate sales. We evaluate customer acquisition costs, leads generated, repeat purchases, and long-term customer value. Ultimately, pop-ups are worthwhile when they attract the right audience and build lasting customer relationships rather than simply generating footfall.

- The claim that illegal votes cast on behalf of dead people still listed on voter rolls have swayed U.S. elections is historically false.
- U.S. President Donald Trump helped popularize the claim as part of his "Stop the Steal" rhetoric before and after he lost the 2020 presidential election.
- Multiple studies, including one Trump reportedly paid a research group to conduct, found that though instances have occurred, the number of votes actually cast in the names of dead people and counted is too small to sway election results.
- Not all instances of dead people voting involve intentional fraud, either, though fraud is a factor in a fraction of cases. Sometimes, votes attributed to dead people have been counted due to clerical errors or simply because of a timing issue; e.g., a voter submits a mail-in ballot, maybe early, and then dies before Election Day (although several states deem such votes legitimate).
The long-standing claim that U.S. election results have been swayed by votes illegally cast on behalf of dead people resurfaced during the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections.
The rumor is recirculated every election cycle but gained new momentum before and after the 2020 presidential election thanks to President Donald Trump's "Stop the Steal" rhetoric, which also played a role in sparking the insurrection at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.
In recent months, Trump again floated the idea that dead people were voting in droves.
"Hundreds of thousands of noncitizens and dead people are listed and active on the voter rolls, and yet we still have elections with no voter ID, no proof of citizenship and tens of millions of ballots floating aimlessly through the mail," he said during a July news conference (at 35:45).
We found this claim to be false.
This fact check builds on and updates reporting Snopes initially conducted ahead of the 2024 presidential election. Below, we break down how we determined that the claim widespread election fraud has taken place in the form of dead people voting is false:
How often are dead peoples' ballots cast?
The short answer: Though it can sometimes happen, studies show the rate of dead people voting is insignificant and is not enough to sway election results.
As mail-in voting has become increasingly accessible — particularly spurred by the COVID-19 pandemic — the public's trust in the electoral system has declined, according to a 2020 study by the Pew Research Center.
Every U.S. state offers some form of absentee or mail-in voting, meaning that voters have the option to mail in their vote instead of voting in person. Some states require voters to initiate the mail-in process by ordering a ballot, and some require voters to provide a reason they're unable to vote in person, such as illness or disability, in order to receive a mail-in ballot. Eight states — California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington — have an automatic mail-in ballot system.
(ballotpedia.org)
Despite assertions that mail-in voting makes it easier for nefarious actors to vote on behalf of dead people, a 2020 study by Stanford University based on data from Washington state — one of the most prominent mail-in states in recent decades — found that between 2011 and 2018, there were only 14 dead people whose ballots were cast "suspiciously long" after their deaths. That represents 0.0003% of Washington voters for that time period. They identified these 14 people by matching birthdates and their full names to ballots, including middle names.
The study said:
Even these few cases may reflect two individuals with the same name and birth date, or clerical errors, rather than fraud. If we relax requirements for matching middle names to accommodate people who may not have middle names, we estimate that there are an additional 43 cases of potential fraud, but these are more likely to be false positives. On the whole, the results suggest that it is extremely rare for dead people's ballots to be counted as votes in Washington's universal vote-by-mail system.
The study noted that because Washington has had years to perfect its mail-in process, other states could potentially have a higher rate of dead people voting.
Following Trump's loss in 2020, he contested the outcome of six battleground states in particular: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. In 2021, The Associated Press conducted a review of every potential case of voter fraud in those states, including cases where ballots were cast in the names of dead people.
The AP found fewer than 475 cases of fraud in those six states — a number that would not have had a significant effect on the 2020 presidential election results.
In 2023, The Washington Post reported that Trump's campaign had paid researchers $600,000 to investigate potential fraud in that same election. According to the Post, there was "no reason to believe the final vote totals in five key states were fraudulent." (The Trump-commissioned report has not been made public, as of this writing, and only reportedly surfaced after the Justice Department obtained it through a subpoena.)
Why might a state count a dead person's vote?
Not all instances of dead people voting are the result of intentional fraud, though that does make up a fraction of cases. Sometimes, dead people's votes are counted simply because of a timing issue; e.g., a voter submits a mail-in ballot, maybe early, and then dies before Election Day (although several states permit this).
Clerical errors, though rare, can either result in dead peoples' votes being mistakenly counted or votes cast by people who are alive being mistakenly marked as cast by a dead person.
Intentional fraud
There have been recorded cases in which someone intentionally committed voter fraud by submitting a ballot in the name of a dead person. In some cases, the ballot for a deceased family member showed up in the mail and a member of the household submitted it on their behalf.
Russel Hobbs, a 56-year-old man from Washington state, illegally signed and submitted a ballot in his wife's name in the 2020 election. She had died about three months earlier. "I think [Hobbs] just tried to honor his deceased loved one," his attorney said to the Tacoma News Tribune. He was sentenced to 80 hours of community service.
In another 2020 case, a man from Pennsylvania cast a vote on behalf of his dead mother, but the state caught the illegal ballot and sentenced him to five years of probation. "I was isolated last year in lockdown," Bruce Bartman told the court by way of explanation. "I listened to too much propaganda and made a stupid mistake."
But despite the existence of such recorded cases of fraud — whether it was grief, propaganda or something else that motivated the acts — the number of those cases is so low so as to not have an effect on national elections.
Clerical and data errors
People who verify ballots aren't immune to mistakes, and in some cases clerical errors have resulted in a living person being mistakenly marked as deceased.
Jason Roberts, a political science professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, reportedly told the AP in 2022 that "election integrity groups scouring voter files often mistake a living voter for a deceased voter if they have similar names, birthdays or hometowns, resulting in false fraud claims."
For example, according to The Brennan Center for Justice — an independent, nonpartisan law and policy organization at the New York University School of Law — "a 2007 investigation of about 100 'dead voters' in Missouri revealed that every single purported case was properly attributed either to a matching error, a problem in the underlying data, or a clerical error by elections officials or voters."
What if someone mails in their vote then dies before Election Day?
As of this writing, 10 states specifically allow the votes of deceased persons who filled in ballots before they died to be count. Twelve states explicitly prohibit such votes from being counted, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures,a bipartisan policy research organization. The report reads:
- Ten states—Arkansas, Florida, Hawaii, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Montana, North Dakota, Tennessee and Virginia—have statutes that explicitly permit counting absentee ballots cast by voters who die before Election Day. California permits counting these ballots through administrative regulation rather than statute. One state—Connecticut—only counts these ballots if the deceased voter is a member of the armed services.
- Twelve states—Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, South Dakota and Wisconsin—have statutes that explicitly prohibit counting absentee ballots cast by voters who die before Election Day. Missouri law states that such ballots be rejected only if sufficient evidence is shown to an election authority that the voter has died before the opening of the polls on Election Day, and the deceased voter's ballot is still sealed in the ballot envelope. Michigan requires that a clerk make their "best effort to remove the absent voter ballot" and spoil that voter's ballot.
- At least two states—Kentucky and Mississippi—also prohibit counting deceased voters' ballots, but through attorneys general opinions, rather than statute.
Other states either don't have explicit guidance or stipulate that absentee ballots can be challenged on the grounds that a voter died before the day of the election.
What countermeasures exist?
With a combination of punishments for illegal voting and efforts to monitor the legitimacy of ballots, states work to combat votes "cast" by dead people, whether intentionally or accidentally.
Legal penalties for intentionally casting a vote on behalf of a dead person may include probation, a fine or even prison time, depending on the specific charges and the state.
Also, election offices take steps to keep voter lists accurate, such as regularly checking death records, obituaries and driver's-license cancellation records. The Help America Vote Act of 2002 requires states to work with the state agency in charge of recording deaths (most often a bureau of vital statistics or the health department) to keep registration records up to date.
Other acceptable methods for voter verification vary by state, such as notification by a funeral director or the military, family reports, obituaries and other forms of record.

Australia to tighten sunscreen testing after popular products fail protection claims
Tests found that 16 of 20 popular products failed to deliver the protection promised on their labels

Australia is proposing tougher rules for sunscreen manufacturers after tests found that 16 of 20 popular products failed to deliver the sun protection factor (SPF) advertised on their labels.
The findings came to light in 2025, when consumer group Choice tested popular sunscreens and found that some products offered nowhere near the protection promised on their packaging.
Ultra Violette’s Lean Screen SPF 50+ Mattifying Zinc Skinscreen, for instance, returned an SPF rating of just four. The product was later withdrawn, along with other sunscreens made using the same base formula.
The company’s co-founders, Ava Chandler-Matthews and Bec Jefferd, apologised to customers last year, offered them refunds, and asked them to stop using the product, according to reports.
Now, Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) wants manufacturers to test the finished products they sell, rather than relying on results from tests of their base formulas alone. Brands would have to submit their results to the regulator before putting products on sale and repeat testing throughout their shelf life.
The proposed changes state that the results would remain confidential, and the TGA would not routinely check the data before products reached shop shelves, according to ABC News.
Until now, manufacturers have not had to provide SPF test results unless the regulator specifically requested them.
Andy Kelly, Choice’s director of consumer impact, welcomed the proposals but said the regulator needed to go further. In a statement on Tuesday, the consumer group called for test results to be made public and for the TGA to carry out its own compliance testing.
“In the interest of transparency and public safety, we believe these results should be made available to everyone and that the TGA should routinely monitor test results, as well as conduct its own compliance testing program,” Choice said in a statement.
The TGA considered publishing the results but decided against it, citing concerns about commercial confidentiality, intellectual property and the risk that consumers might misinterpret technical data.
Robyn Langham, the TGA’s chief medical adviser, said: “This is about making SPF claims more reliable, reinforcing suppliers’ responsibility for their products, and giving the TGA faster access to evidence when concerns arise.”
Some foundations and other cosmetics sold in Australia can advertise SPF 50+ even though sun protection is not their primary purpose.
The TGA wants to limit the SPF claims these products can make, making it easier for consumers to distinguish them from sunscreens designed primarily to protect against ultraviolet radiation.
The reforms are not yet in force.
The TGA received 119 submissions during a consultation held between March and May 2026, and says some changes could be introduced in the short term, while others will require further consultation or legislative amendments.
Australia has the highest rate of skin cancer in the world, with two in three Australians expected to be diagnosed during their lifetime. Around 2,000 people die from the disease each year, according to Cancer Council Australia.

World champion Jepchirchir fails drugs test
- Published
Olympic and World Championships marathon gold medallist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO.
Kenyan Jepchirchir provided the sample prior to winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026.
The 33-year-old clocked a time of two hours, 18 minutes and 31 seconds to win in Sydney.
EPO, or erythropoietin, is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.
If injected, it is only detectable in the urine or blood for a short window of time, and increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream.
Jepchirchir became the Olympic women's marathon champion at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and returned to the Japanese capital to win the World Championships in September 2025.
She broke the women's half-marathon world record in 2017 and on three occasions in 2020.
In addition to Sydney, her other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.
Jepchirchir won the Sydney race, which became the seventh world major in 2025, by more than three minutes from compatriot Irene Chepet Cheptai.
She provided the sample which tested positive for EPO while in Kenya prior to the race.

Fitbit Edge review: Google strikes the right balance
Want a beautiful tracker with a screen but don’t want AI on your wrist? This is perfect for you.
In the ten years since I reviewed the original Fitbit Alta, I've noticed a pattern. Try as it might to create an activity tracker that looks attractive, Fitbit has never quite delivered. When the Fitbit Alta was launched in 2016, the company had been working with Tory Burch on accessories to make the device "super-chic." But with its rigid cuff-like band and generic appearance, the Alta didn't come off fashionable or pretty. It was just another fitness tracker in a smaller frame.
Fitbit later unveiled the Alta HR, which retained a similar appearance, and the more recent Luxe, with a shinier stainless steel case and softer, nicer-looking bands. And yet, despite the company's proud proclamation that the Luxe was one of its "most fashionable and comfortable devices yet," I found its small size more impressive than its style.
We live in a world of oblongs, and the Fitbit Edge is admittedly just a curvier and wider oblong than the Luxe and the Alta. Yet it packs quite a punch compared to those before it, thanks to a bright, navigable touchscreen, a more attractive array of straps and an updated feature set that makes the Edge feel as modern as it looks.
Design and display
A lot of what I like about the Fitbit Edge, especially compared to the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5 (and other modern smartwatches), lies entirely in its design. While I loved the simplicity of the Fitbit Air's screenless design, its lack of a display did have drawbacks. I always had to whip out my phone to start logging workouts, and it didn't have a readout of my heart rate for me to see if I should push harder or slow down. I'd have to keep my phone nearby so I could look at it for that data.
Meanwhile, though smartwatches like the Pixel Watch 5 and the Apple Watch have larger screens that enable all that, they tended to get in the way when I was doing pushups or moving planks, for instance. Thanks to its narrower shape, the Fitbit Edge stayed mostly tucked out of the way. I was pleasantly surprised to find that I could bend my wrist quite a generous angle without ever triggering its side button, and didn't have to turn it so its face was on the inside of my wrist. On wider-faced wearables like Apple, Pixel and Galaxy watches, their buttons would protrude too far and inadvertently get pushed.
Of course, similarly shaped activity trackers have existed for years as well, but what the Fitbit Edge brings is a shiny case, thinner bezels and a screen that elevates its functionality. I complained about the Luxe's display being small and hard to read. The Edge does not have that issue. Its display was consistently bright and easy to see in various lighting conditions, and it mostly recognized my taps and swipes promptly. Is it the most responsive touchscreen on a wearable? No — I occasionally found myself waiting for something to happen after I swiped to find a tile. But in those cases it was usually that the Edge was still in a sleep state. Most of the time when I was certain it was awake, the screen felt as responsive as the Pixel Watch's.
That's a significant step up from the lackluster and laggy displays on previous Fitbits, which took a lot of prodding to work. The physical button on the Edge's side is also easy to use, and frankly a relief when compared to the touch-sensitive faux button on the Inspire 3 and the haptic one on the Charge 6.
Speaking of the latter, in many ways the Fitbit Edge feels like its spiritual successor — a Charge 7, shall we say. The Edge has a similarly sized case, just a bit bigger and more rounded. Both share a lot of features, including Google Maps support and the ability to take ECG readings. But the Edge has a nicer, larger screen with adjustable brightness, an altimeter to measure elevation gain or steps climbed, GPS tracking for outdoor runs or walks and an IP68 certification for dust and water-resistance (in addition to the 5 ATM rating they both have). Not to mention, the Edge has a proper button and greater media playback support as well. The list of differences between the two models is long and complicated so I'll just point out that the Edge doesn't have NFC for contactless payments while the Charge 6 does. And finally, the new device costs about $20 more.
A word on Fitbit Edge straps (and the Fitbit Air's new metal mesh band)
One of the reasons the Edge is so appealing is its appearance, which is further enhanced by the bands you use with it. Google sent along two straps in addition to the silicone one that came in the box, and both of them really made the Edge look better. I also found it easy to swap out bands — just pushing down the catch on the device's underside and pulling away from the case would remove a strap. Connecting one was as simple as pushing it into the groove.
At first, I struggled to close the Magnet band that snapped together with, well, a magnetic clasp. But once I got the hang of it, I began to appreciate its appearance thanks to its narrow width and stainless steel lugs.
I also loved the Metal Links band that Google sent. The one I received was in gold and it matched my Edge's case so seamlessly that you wouldn't know it was a detachable accessory. My sweet naive gym friend told me they thought it looked like a Rolex. While I think the regulars at r/Rolex would scoff at that assessment, I agree that there is a premium vibe to the Metal Links band. That said, I have to warn you it costs $150, which is about the same price as a whole Fitbit Charge 6, and just $30 shy of the Fitbit Edge itself.
While we're on the topic, Google also sent me a sample of the new Metal Mesh band for the Fitbit Air, and I am a big fan of how it elevates the tracker's appearance. But I also have to point out that at $70, the Metal Mesh Band is just $30 shy of the Air's retail price. You can find cheaper options elsewhere, but I do think Google's offering looks classier in comparison.
What can the Fitbit Edge do?
At the same time it launched the Fitbit Edge, Google also announced that it was updating the model behind its automatic activity detection. For a device like the Fitbit Air, which as I've already explained is highly dependent on its linked smartphone due to its lack of a screen, passive tracking is extremely important.
After a week with the Fitbit Edge and my months with the Fitbit Air, I can confidently say that the new model is certainly more sensitive and, at least so far, more accurate. I didn't get the chance to tap at the Fitbit Edge to log a bunch of walks and bike rides in the city over the weekend, and while I would previously worry that my activity wasn't being accounted for, I soon learned to trust the device. A few minutes after I finished cycling or strolling, I'd see a notification from Google Health on my phone that some exercise had been detected "with low confidence." The app prompted me to confirm and name my activity to help improve its assessments, which I gladly did.
In time, the Edge did seem to understand and correctly recognize when I had been on my e-scooter for a quick grocery run. I still manually started my morning cross training sessions at the gym, because I've been conditioned by the F45 app to do so. (It's horrible at logging your workout metrics if you don't time it to the second.) But the fact that Google was able to improve its system well enough that I learned to relax and trust in the Edge was not only impressive but satisfying. I'd like to spend more time with this to feel more confident, though, because in my experience AI-powered systems tend to randomly forget things over time, resulting in a lot of long-term frustration.
Outside of the automatic activity tracking, the Fitbit Edge's functions are fairly basic. You can swipe through tiles to look at your progress throughout the day, and depending on how you've set up your selection of cards, you can keep swiping sideways to see things like the weather, sleep score, heart rate, cycle health, media playback and so on. Swiping up from the home screen shows your accumulated notifications, while dragging down from the top brings up a control panel of shortcuts.
I found this section the most helpful, as it contains a toolkit that I've come to consider essential to any smartwatch. You can adjust your screen brightness from here, see battery levels, launch do not disturb or bedtime modes, enable the water lock, broadcast your heart rate to nearby machines or ping your connected phone. You can also activate the flashlight, making the Edge so bright that it can illuminate dark purses or closets in a pinch to help find a missing earring or key, for instance.
Finally, pushing the button on the side opens the app drawer, where you can find functions like ECG readings, a stopwatch, media playback controls and more. There's a very small selection of available apps at the moment, and you'd have to set this up from the Google Health app on your phone to make sure the ones you need are installed on the Edge.
Almost everything here worked as expected. I took an ECG reading, which involved pressing my fingers to either side of the Edge's case. Thirty seconds later, I was told my signs were normal. I played Adéla's "Nicole Kidman" on repeat, and the Edge's media controls helped take me back to the start of the track quickly.
I also had the relatively rare opportunity to compare my data to the readings taken by the equipment in a primary care clinic, as I had to see a doctor during my testing period. According to the oximeter, my pulse rate was 65 beats per minute. Looking back at my data as tracked by the Fitbit Edge, the Google wearable said my heart rate was 75 bpm. Meanwhile, the Apple Watch Series 12 I had on at the same time said my range was between 63 bpm and 77 bpm.
I don't generally expect wearables to be extremely accurate, as I prefer to analyze my readings as trends over time rather than as a snapshot. So I didn't find this one-time comparison to be too concerning.
What I did find a bit odd was the Google Maps integration. After I followed all the instructions on setting this up, which involved going into the Health app and enabling the Maps integration for the Edge, I was disappointed when it didn't seem to work. You're supposed to be able to start a navigation from your phone, and the Edge will show you directions while tracking a running or biking workout in the background. I opened Google Maps on my phone, started navigating to nearby businesses, and the Edge would show that Maps has started. But I kept getting a message saying to make sure the Maps app was running on both devices, and then nothing would happen.
I've reached out to Google to troubleshoot this issue, and will update this review when this gets resolved. For now, though, I'm willing to bet this had a lot to do with fact that I had multiple Fitbit devices connected to multiple iPhones (and a Pixel) on my Google Health app. It's such a niche scenario that I'm not going to consider docking points from the Edge for now, but if I see it happening to more people, we will certainly revisit the score and this review.
Speaking of, during my testing period, I used the Fitbit Edge with both a Pixel 11 Pro and an iPhone 17 Pro Max (yes I'm still stuck on last year's model for now). The experience was largely similar across both pairings, with the main feature difference being that you can't reply to notifications from the Edge when paired with an iPhone. I did encounter some weird connection issues, like the Edge randomly switching to my iPhone 18 Pro instead of the iPhone 17 Pro Max, but again, I'd chalk that up to connectivity issues. And again, it's a pretty uncommon scenario that's mostly exclusive to reviewers like myself.
Google Health app and AI Coach
Thanks to the Fitbit Edge's screen, you actually don't need to spend too much time in Google's Health app if you don't want to. After you've set up your watch faces, tiles and apps, you could probably get by with the on-device summaries of your daily metrics.
But since I'd been using the Fitbit Air since I reviewed it in May, I've had to integrate the Health app into my daily routine. And because I'm an unnecessarily competitive person, I obsess over whether I've hit my cardio load targets every week. At a basic level, the app functions just fine. A customizable panel at the top lets you keep track of your favorite stats, and you can dive deeper into your workout and sleep through the different tabs.
But because I'd been using the Premium experience with the AI Health Coach, I've found it just a bit more convenient and, oddly, comforting.
I've been sick for a few days during my testing, so I ended up with a higher resting heart rate than usual. At first, I thought the Fitbit Edge wasn't calibrated correctly or was misreading my data, but on a hunch I asked the AI Health Coach if my illness could be contributing to the poorer cardio performance. I could have Googled that, sure, but it was nice for me to get that assurance from something that actually knew my heart rate over time.
Over the last few months, I've also gone to the coach with questions about random headaches, cycle symptoms and form checks on complicated movements, and I've generally felt mollified by what it said. Plus, my chat history with the system is a good way to remember things that came up in that time frame, which helped me gather my thoughts and concerns when seeing a doctor at a checkup.
Google's AI still is a bit stupid at times. I once asked if it thought I should go out for a walk, since it had just told me to take things easy after realizing I was sick. In response, the coach told me to check the weather, which was odd since it had mentioned in my morning summary that the conditions that day were great for a walk. I pointed out that it knew what the weather was and that it knew from previous chats how I felt that day. After a bit more back and forth with the AI, it finally recognized that "you're totally right, your sleep score landed at a solid 81 today" but remained unable to extract local weather information.
All that is to say – the AI Health Coach experience is nice if you like to consistently get congratulations or encouragement on your progress. It's a decent source of information if you're a bit too lazy (or sick) to Google, and it certainly will tell you to go see a doctor in person. When I told it that it "feels like my throat is closing up," it said that as an agent, it could not provide "the kind of help a human professional can, and I cannot offer advice on how to handle this situation yourself." Then it listed a couple of options like calling 911 or seeking a doctor or "qualified healthcare provider right away, or going to the nearest emergency room."
I felt like it panicked a bit, but I was glad to see it didn't try to offer bad advice.
Battery life and charging
I could give you a time sheet of the random times I checked the power level on my Fitbit Edge over the last week, but in general, it would make it through just over two days before needing a charge. That's with the Always On Display activated, and leaving it off certainly extends runtime. One day, after I forgot to turn off the bedtime mode that dimmed the screen, the Edge's battery levels barely dipped at all.
I ended Tuesday with about 49 percent of the battery left, and managed to make it to Wednesday night with 16 percent remaining. The next morning, the Edge still had about 8 percent left in the tank, but that's without overnight sleep tracking.
Shortly after, a quick 6-minute top-up via an in-car USB-C port took the device to 28 percent. And 24 minutes after that, it had gotten to 90 percent. Google promises you'll go from 0 to 100 percent in 90 minutes, and in my experience that promise held up. When I sat next to a charger one evening and watched the battery level every ten minutes, the numbers went up about 11 to 12 percent each time, and slowed down slightly after the 90 percent mark. (That decrease in charge speed at top levels is typical of modern charging systems as a way to preserve battery longevity.)
Since the Pixel Watch 4 and the Fitbit Air, Google has proven that its ability to deliver such impressive charging speeds has made battery life almost a non-concern. However, I did panic a little when I realized I had left my charger at home mid-commute one day, since I had fallen out of an overnight recharge routine and my Edge was only 50 percent full. I was still able to get through my work day, and I certainly will be making sure to pack a travel charger from now on.
Slightly off topic, but somewhat related: I do wish there was a more universal smartwatch charging standard, or that more wearables had USB-C ports. I understand that sophisticated devices like the Fitbit Edge already pack a lot of components into tiny frames so carving out space for a port is a nearly impossible task. But, say, if all MagSafe chargers also worked with wearables, that would be lovely.
To that end, I'm glad Google uses the same charger for the Fitbit Edge and Air. If you happen to own both, you can have at-home and travel chargers that work with either device.
Wrap-up
Allow me to indulge, for a moment, in characterizing the Google and Fitbit partnership as a romantic relationship. The Fitbit Edge, Fitbit Air and parts of the Google Health experience all feel like the offspring of a couple that finally went to marriage counseling. The two major brands have set aside their differences and consolidated their strengths to produce these truly compelling wearables.
At $180, the Fitbit Edge is significantly cheaper than the Pixel Watch 5 (or even the Apple Watch Series 12) and works with both iOS and Android. It delivers just enough features to be useful for those who care most about their fitness and health, while also allowing you to stay connected to your phone without overwhelming you. Its two-plus-day battery life is respectable, and goes for days longer if you don't need the Always On Display. In my time with the Fitbit Edge, I've really only missed the gesture support and some assistant functions that the Pixel Watch 5 offers. But it was easy enough to swipe one tile away to start a five minute timer or find the weather forecast.
The Edge feels like the first successful attempt in Fitbit's history to deliver a good-looking yet minimal activity tracker, thanks not only to solid hardware but an easy-to-use and fairly refined operating system. With the Fitbit Edge and Fitbit Air, it feels like Fitbit is back to reclaim the activity tracker space that it became synonymous with. And I, for one, am glad Google didn't ditch the Fitbit name.

The Madhya Pradesh Government has constituted a five-member committee to investigate claims that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas district, officials said on Sunday (October 25, 2026).
The panel will submit its report within 15 days, they said.
Ujjain divisional Commissioner constituted the committee after conflicting claims over the deaths.
Some villagers have claimed that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Dewas district between September 27 and October 16.
The district administration had earlier dismissed the claims as false and misleading. It later said viscera samples of two deceased persons have been sent to a forensic science laboratory (FSL) for examination. The cause of death would become clear after the reports are received, it added.
The administration said 10 persons died in Chandana village between October 1 and 15, but denied that any of the deaths was caused by spurious liquor. It attributed the deaths to old age, common illnesses, brain haemorrhage and "deterioration of health due to excessive alcohol consumption".
Ujjain Additional District Magistrate Pratham Kaushik will head the probe committee, which includes Mandsaur Additional Superintendent of Police Ramsanehi Mishra, Ratlam Sub-Divisional Police Officer Lekhraj Meena, Ujjain divisional flying squad Deputy Excise Commissioner Harshvardhan Rai and Regional Director of Public Health and Medical Education Dr Deepak Kumar Pippal.
The panel will conduct a detailed and impartial inquiry into the causes and circumstances of the deaths, along with the related technical and administrative aspects, and submit a factual report within 15 days, according to the Ujjain divisional Commissioner's order.
Madhya Pradesh Congress president Jitu Patwari has claimed that 22 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Chandana, Binjana and adjoining areas over the past month, while at least 40 people suffered damage to their eyesight.
The Opposition party leader has accused the administration of concealing the deaths and shielding the "liquor mafia".

Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.
Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.
Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.
NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.
Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported.
While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported.
A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”.
“She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.”
Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.
Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.
A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.
US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.
There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.
After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.
During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.
Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.
A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

On Oct. 21, U.S. President Donald Trump was speaking at a campaign rally in South Carolina for Republican Sen. Darline Graham when a video (archived) clipped from the speech began circulating in which he appeared to emit a strange, guttural vocalization midsentence: "And I'd say 90% of the reason I took the governor — EHHH! — I took the governor, I put her over at the United Nations, because I wanted this guy to become governor."
People spread the clip — which was easily authenticated via the original C-SPAN footage — on various social media platforms. It's anybody's guess whether it was a burp (or another involuntary noise), or purposeful expression of dislike or disapproval for the person he was talking about.
The moment in question takes place at the 19:40 mark in the C-SPAN video. In the middle of praising South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, he brought up appointing then-Gov. Nikki Haley as ambassador to the United Nations in 2017 "because I wanted this guy to become governor" (emphasis ours):
They allowed 25 million people to pour across our borders from all over the world. And if they ever won, they are going to do it all again, they're going to do it again. You remember the hell we lived in? It was like a dark period. The proud people of South Carolina, Henry, will never let that happen. Please, Henry, you're gonna be watching, Henry is going to be watching. He's great, he's great. You know he was the lieutenant governor. And I'd say 90% of the reason I took the governor — EHHH! — I took the governor, I put her over at the United Nations, because I wanted this guy to become governor.
Spirited debates took place online, with some people taking the position Trump simply burped, while others called it a sign of "advance dementia" or a "mini-stroke." We asked spokespeople at the White House if they could explain it but have not yet received a reply.
As president, Trump has often made verbal gaffes, for example misstating placenames, but he has claimed he does this on purpose. Trump also has made other odd vocal noises during his speeches, for example mimicking the sound of bombs dropping as "Bing, bing!" in 2025.
For further reading, Snopes has also reported on authentic statements Trump has made over the years.

Special ed diaries: Teachers tell NPR about their most joyous, most difficult moments
One of Kathleen Tejeda's students began freshman year just trying to get by. High school can be tricky for any teenager, but she was navigating it as a blind person.
By the end of her junior year, with support from Tejeda and other school staff, the student had gone from getting by to going big: She made the cheerleading squad and the school choir. She even sang the national anthem in front of the whole school.
Tejeda, who has been a special educator for 20 years in Riverside County, Calif., said that kind of advocacy is just as much a part of her job as teaching her students. But teachers like her can be hard to find.
There is a shortage of special educators in 45 out of 50 states, according to the Learning Policy Institute, an education research organization. That shortage is growing because the number of special education students is climbing: It's now more than 8.2 million — about 1 out of 6 public school students.
While turnover worsened sharply after the COVID-19 pandemic, the shortage isn't new. It has existed since special education became embedded in federal law with the passage of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act in 1975. Half a century later, a fundamental question remains: Why is this shortage of special education teachers so persistent?
Myths and realities about teaching special education
Let's start with a common misconception: The kids are hard to work with, so teachers don't want to do the job. "That is not the case," said Liz Bettini, a former special education teacher who is now a researcher and professor at Boston University. "That has not borne out in our research at all."
Loading...
What Bettini's research does show: Special educators can feel isolated from other school staff and feel they have too many student needs to manage. The volume of required paperwork can be crushing. These educators are often responsible for teaching across several subjects and grade levels. Many feel they don't get paid enough to do this essential work.
"That's a very heavy weight to carry as a teacher," Bettini said.
NPR set out to hear directly from about a dozen special educators from around the United States' public schools to learn what it takes to do their jobs day to day. They have been sharing snippets of their lives through voice memos since the start of the school year, and some will open their classroom doors to NPR in the coming months.
"No teacher does this for the paycheck," said third-year high school teacher Diana Swanson, who works in Vail, Ariz., as she sat at her desk the day before her school year began in July. "Just the students, that fulfillment, seeing them fill their cup a little bit, seeing them smile, be a member of society and part of their community. That's what fulfills me."
"I feel like I was coming into this school year more prepared this time around," fourth-year elementary school teacher Danalyn Garcia said late one school night from her living room in Chicago. "Yet, I feel the needs are even greater than the year before."
"Honestly, I had no life outside of school and outside of being a teacher," said Kaori Anderson-Walker, looking back on his first year of teaching middle school in Philadelphia. Now in his fourth year, he said he has finally learned to manage his time more effectively but said the work is still never-ending. "When my students aren't performing where I want them in the classroom, my mind is just constantly moving."
Much of the day isn't spent on teaching
Being an educator of any kind is demanding and requires immense skill. Research shows that burnout among all kinds of public school teachers is high, but it's even more acute for special educators. These teachers work with students who have an incredibly diverse set of needs, including those with autism, learning disabilities such as dyslexia, developmental delays and physical disabilities.
Special educators also do a lot more than teach — in fact, one study found that they spent only about a third of their day on instruction. They spend the rest of their time tracking student goals, coordinating specialized services for students (say, speech therapy or extra reading help), training support staff and writing individualized education programs (IEPs), which are legal documents that track each special education student's needs at school.
In many states, that means teachers must have specialized certification and training, but they typically aren't paid more. In 32 states, teachers get no extra pay for the hardest-to-staff positions, including in special education, according to a recent study.
While all 13 special educators NPR has spoken to said building relationships with students is their favorite part of the work, they also described the realities of those students' needs being more complex than those of many general education students.
"Special educators have reported, 'I can't teach this kid and respond to the student's crisis simultaneously. So I'm abandoning instruction because the crisis has to take priority,'" Bettini said.
For example, Grace Fitzgerald, who teaches elementary school in Peoria, Ill., shared on a drive home from school that one of her students had an emotional crisis that forced her to evacuate the rest of her class for their safety. "It's been challenging mentally and emotionally to kind of go through that at the very end of the first quarter, my first year of teaching," she said. "No one gets a road map to deal with that kind of situation."
Several teachers shared that behavioral challenges with individual students can make it harder to meet the needs of their many other students.
Loading...
"Our school doesn't have walls. So we have six classes per grade level in one ginormous room, and it's separated by dividers," Garcia, in Chicago, said. "So when one kid is screaming and crying and begins to escalate, it disturbs the whole pod and then other kids react to it." Getting students back on track can be difficult in these kinds of situations, she said.
Essential but time-consuming paperwork
Individualized education programs are a key part of special education. These written plans, required by federal law, are managed by teachers and other school staff and serve as a kind of road map for each special education student. IEPs outline the student's unique needs and their annual goals. For example, a goal of a student with autism may be to maintain eye contact for a certain period of time.
IEPs help families hold schools accountable, and they also help enforce a primary aim of special education: to teach students in the "least restrictive environment," meaning students with disabilities are taught alongside students without disabilities as much as possible. But IEPs also require regular meetings with families, an understanding of special education law and time spent away from teaching students — time that teachers often don't have.
Then there's the work of putting the IEP into practice in the classroom. Tejeda, of Riverside County, said when she's "pushing in" to other teachers' general education classrooms, she provides targeted support without singling out special education students. "We're going to walk the classroom and check in with everybody, but at the back of our minds, we know that we need to make sure we're [making] accommodations for that particular student."

For Anderson-Walker, in Philadelphia, "the biggest struggle" was feeling like he had to juggle IEP paperwork with teaching duties. Then, last year, his school, Boys' Latin of Philadelphia, hired staff members who are responsible for the paperwork part of IEPs, leaving teachers more time for the classroom. "Not having that stress is amazing," Anderson-Walker said.
Searching for solutions
In addition to the workload, at the core of the special education teacher shortage are pay and the sheer number of qualified people. Research shows that paying teachers more can help attract and retain them.
For example, in 2020, Hawaii raised special education teacher salaries by $10,000 annually. That cut the state's vacancies by 35%, but it wasn't enough to keep many special education teachers in their jobs. Seventeen states now pay teachers additional money to work in hard-to-staff subjects, including special education. That's down from four years ago, when 22 states did so.
The pipeline of qualified special educators is another big problem. According to education policy researcher Chad Aldeman's analysis of federal data a few years ago, about 46,000 special ed teachers leave public schools every year, while teacher preparation programs train fewer than 30,000 annually to replace those teachers.
Aldeman calls it a crude estimate but said that the rapid increase in demand for special education teachers is outpacing the supply of people trained to do those jobs. Many schools end up resorting to hiring teachers who aren't fully qualified for the work.
But research has found that "grow-your-own" programs that focus on recruiting people who already live in the community may be effective at filling special education jobs. Bettini and her research partners also found that supportive administrators and adequate planning time can help make the work feel more sustainable for teachers.
For example, Fitzgerald, the first-year teacher in Illinois, said she was feeling overwhelmed by her workload at the start of the year. So she worked with her school leadership to build more dedicated planning time into her day.
"I think that's going to be very beneficial and will hopefully lead to a decrease in time spent after school," Fitzgerald said. She uses that time to focus on lesson plans, logging data and writing IEP goals.
It allows her to be more present in the classroom, working with her students.

Cyclone Arnab has intensified into a ‘very severe cyclonic storm’ over the Bay of Bengal and is braced to make landfall along the eastern coast of India on Wednesday, October 18.
However, during such extreme weather events, a common question arises: Where does a cyclone get its name, and how exactly does the global naming process work?
The name 'Arnab' was officially proposed by Bangladesh.
Quick answers to key questions
Arnab was the next available name on the North Indian Ocean cyclone list and was proposed by Bangladesh. In Bengali, “Arnab” means “ocean” or “sea”; the name does not indicate the cyclone’s intensity or where it will make landfall.
The IMD, based in New Delhi, assigns names to cyclonic storms in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea. The names come from a pre-approved list submitted by 13 participating countries and are used in sequence.
A system is named after it reaches cyclonic-storm strength, with maximum sustained surface winds of at least 34 knots—about 62 kmph. Forming over the sea alone is not enough.
Short, distinctive names help avoid confusion, especially when multiple weather systems develop at the same time. They also make warnings, evacuation orders and public information easier to communicate.
No. Under the system described by the IMD, a name is permanently removed from the list after it is used.
According to the IMD's official cyclone naming list, the word "Arnab" translates to "ocean" or "sea" in Bengali. However, meteorological experts emphasised that the naming of a cyclone has nothing to do with its intensity, direction, or the specific country it is expected to hit.
According to IMD protocols, the name for any cyclone is simply the next available entry on a pre-approved, rotational list of tropical cyclone names designated for the North Indian Ocean region.
Therefore, even though Bangladesh contributed the name, the cyclonic storm is currently tracking toward the coastlines of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
Globally, tropical cyclones are named by Regional Specialised Meteorological Centres (RSMCs) and Tropical Cyclone Warning Centres (TCWCs) under the aegis of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), according to the UN agency's guidelines.
For the North Indian Ocean region—which includes the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea—this critical responsibility falls on the IMD based in New Delhi.
The WMO mandates that the IMD serve as the RSMC for this geographical zone and officially assign names to developing weather systems once they reach a specific intensity.
According to the IMD, a weather system is not assigned a name merely because it forms over the sea; it must reach a maximum sustained surface wind speed of at least 34 knots (approximately 62 kmph) to be officially classified and named as a cyclonic storm.
The formal naming protocol for the North Indian Ocean began in September 2004.
In April 2020, an official release by the Ministry of Earth Sciences detailed that the WMO/ESCAP (United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific) Panel on Tropical Cyclones expanded the operational list to include 13 participating nations: Bangladesh, India, Iran, Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Yemen.
According to IMD’s established framework, each of the 13 member countries submitted 13 names, resulting in a consolidated master list of 169 names. These names are arranged column-by-column in alphabetical order by the contributing countries and used in strict sequential order.
When countries propose these names, they must adhere to strict WMO guidelines. The panel mandates that the names must be short (a maximum of eight letters), easy to pronounce, and strictly neutral—meaning they must not hurt the religious, political, or cultural sentiments of any community.
Unlike the Atlantic hurricane system, where names of exceptionally destructive storms are retired and others are recycled, the North Indian Ocean system never reuses a name. Once a name is used, the IMD permanently strikes it from the list.
Assigning short, distinctive names to cyclones is vital for effective crisis management, the WMO states. It eliminates the confusion of using complex technical geographic coordinates, especially when multiple weather systems develop over the ocean simultaneously.
According to disaster management authorities, a clear name makes it significantly easier for them to issue evacuation orders, for the media to report on the trajectory, and for the general public to understand and prepare for the impending danger.

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
- Published
Kenya is grappling with its first ever outbreak of Ebola, a disease which neighbouring countries, such as Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, are used to dealing with.
Nine cases have now been confirmed including its first patient, who travelled from DR Congo and died two weeks ago.
Four relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner have now tested positive, meaning they are all linked to him.
But concerns are rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government has sought to assure citizens.
The US has warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Should Kenyans be concerned?
Kenyans have been expressing their concerns that the disease could spread more widely.
More than 4,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. He died days after his arrival in Kenya.
As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading is a big concern.
The doctors' union in Kenya has expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.
Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.
However, Health Director-General Patrick Amoth on Tuesday evening sought to reassure people, saying that the eight patients were all improving and responding well to treatment.
What is being done to stop it spreading?
When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.
Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.
In Kenya, 134 out of 135 people listed as contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. That means about 99% of the contacts have been traced and isolated, in order to prevent Ebola from spreading to the wider population.
That all of those infected so far had links to the first victim shows Kenya's early response is working, according to the International Rescue Committee.
The government is also working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.
A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.
Is Kenya prepared in case it starts spreading further?
Amoth said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Despite that, Kenya's health ministry says nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.
The ministry has urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It has also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.
The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."
In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.
Is enough being done to protect health workers?
Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).
With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.
Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Dennis Miskellah, the KMPDU deputy secretary general, told the BBC that protective equipment must be provided to hospitals so that they are fully protected, especially in case patients with symptoms do not declare that they have been in areas with Ebola.
He suggests the government ought to conduct proper health education to destigmatise the virus, so that people do not seek to hide their symptoms.
The International Rescue Committee has also called for continued funding for contact tracing, border screening and training of frontline health workers in Kenya.
Will there be any restrictions, like a travel ban?
Kenya remains open with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.
Despite confirming the eight cases, the authorities have explicitly ruled out a national lockdown or general travel ban for Kenyans.
The US on Monday issued an advisory asking citizens to reconsider travelling to the country over Ebola concerns. Other countries have issued health alerts, including the UK, which warned its citizens that they may encounter enhanced health screening, and Canada, which has asked citizens to monitor their health for 21 days.
No country has issued an outright ban against their nationals visiting Kenya, nor have Kenyans been blocked from entering other countries over Ebola fears.
Has business and tourism been affected?
Analysts have raised concerns over the potential impact of public health fears on international travel and tourism but there is no evidence this has happened yet.
But the situation could change if the outbreak were to spread into the wider population.
How many Kenyans are there in DR Congo?
The exact number of Kenyans living in the DR Congo is not clear.
A report authored last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think-tank put the number of Kenyans living in eastern DR Congo at about 2,500, including about 50 investors. It also noted that there were about four times as many Congolese living in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, alone.
The Kenyan embassy in the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, which represents Kenya's interests in four countries - DR Congo, Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville and Gabon - has in the past urged Kenyans living in the region to formally register so that it is able to serve them better.
How have neighbouring countries responded?
Several countries in the region have announced tightening of surveillance measures and enhanced screening for visitors.
One man who came into contact with the man who died in Kenya is under quarantine in Somalia and samples have been sent to Kenya for testing.
Somalia has also said it was taking precautionary measures, including enhancing surveillance measures at border points "given the evolving regional situation and the movement of people between countries".
The suspected case in Somalia had travelled through Ethiopia, which has also said it had tightened surveillance to prevent an outbreak
In Tanzania, visitors are expected to undergo daily health monitoring for 21 days, through an automated tracking system, which was announced after Kenya confirmed multiple cases of Ebola infections.
Uganda said after Kenya's first Ebola case that it was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
The Kenyan businessman had travelled through Uganda on his way home from DR Congo.
Uganda had reported two Ebola deaths shortly after the outbreak was reported in DR Congo, but the WHO has since declared it to be free of the disease.
On Tuesday, Nigeria confirmed a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda to Abuja. Nigeria is the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East and Central Africa.
Ugandan health officials say the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.
The health ministry stressed she did not have symptoms while transiting through Uganda and only developed them after arriving in Abuja.

London’s Oxford Street bans traffic as city tries to revitalize shopping district
London's Oxford Street is closing to cars, buses, and bicycles starting Monday
LONDON -- London’s Oxford Street will be closed to cars, buses and bicycles starting Monday as authorities seek to revive the city’s main shopping street, where the proliferation of souvenir shops and candy sellers has dimmed the allure of what was once the heart of British consumer culture.
From now on, nearly a kilometer of Oxford Street between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street will be traffic-free, with vehicles diverted onto surrounding roads. The move is the first step in a makeover of the storied shopping precinct, with plans to plant trees, install seating and add two new public squares.
Oxford Street still sees about half a million visitors a day, with shoppers bustling between retailers such as Selfridges, Zara and John Lewis.
But city officials say turning it into a pedestrian street will put it back into the league of top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla.
“This is a momentous day for London, a momentous day for Oxford Street,’’ London Mayor Sadiq Khan told the BBC. “It’s a new era.’’
While local officials began discussing the idea of pedestrianizing Oxford Street more than a decade ago, momentum began to build over the last two years when the mayor’s office created the Oxford Street Development Corporation to shepherd the project. That helped overcome opposition from local residents who complained that diverting vehicles from Oxford Street would clog their neighborhoods with traffic.
A public consultation later determined that removing traffic would attract new shops and visitors to Oxford Street, making it “an iconic destination.”
The project also got a boost from the new Elizabeth express train line, which runs through the heart of the city, with a stop on Oxford Street.
Further work on the makeover will begin in the new year, with city officials refining their plans based on feedback from visitors, Khan told reporters Monday on a rain-soaked Oxford Street.
“In advance of Christmas, you know, I want people to come here and shop and enjoy the experience,'' he said.

'The smell of freedom': Serbia's student movement celebrates election triumph
Student-backed movement leads to political shakeup in Serbia
BELGRADE, Serbia — There are no Monday morning blues in Serbia's capital, Belgrade. Cars driving past the green-domed National Assembly sound their horns in celebration. Broadly smiling pedestrians cheer and wave a three-fingered salute in response. This has long been viewed as a nationalist gesture — but now it is the symbol of the Student List.
The group of candidates selected by Serbia's long-running, youth-led protest movement was No. 3 on the ballot in Sunday's parliamentary elections but very much top of the pile when it came to the outcome. The Student List claimed more than half the votes, pushing Serbia's long-serving populist leader, Aleksandar Vučić, and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) into a distant second place.
In the park opposite the National Assembly, hundreds of volunteers are cleaning up the mess left behind by a pro-government camp that had made the area a no-go zone for most citizens.
"Yesterday was a big victory, so today is the smell of freedom," says one of the volunteers, Radomir Delic, who has been painstakingly picking cigarette butts from the grass. "We are in garbage, but it's the smell of freedom."
Most of the country's opposition parties had stood aside to allow the Student List a clear run. When Vučić conceded defeat, shortly after the polls closed, the crowds on the streets erupted in celebration. Champagne corks popped, fireworks crackled and motorbike engines revved to mosquito pitch. Since then, the revelry has barely paused.
It now seems hard to believe that with no reliable opinion polls, the result had been difficult to call before the election. The Student List was an entirely new proposition, with no hierarchy, no leader and no political experience. It was up against a wily and experienced operator in Vučić. He had served as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since his SNS took power in 2012, but it had always been clear that he was the man in charge.
Vučić was also adept at currying international favor. He maintained Serbia's long-standing friendship with Russia, exchanging multiple official visits with Russian President Vladimir Putin. But he also opened membership talks to join the European Union and pushed for closer relations with the United States.
The latter resulted in considerable controversy when Vučić struck a deal with President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner to build a Trump International Hotel on the site of government buildings bombed by U.S. warplanes in 1999. The legal fallout led to Kushner's withdrawal.
Vučić had cast himself as the strong leader who was taking Serbia forward. But that image sustained an irreparable blow in November 2024, when a concrete canopy collapsed at a recently renovated railway station in Novi Sad, killing 16 people.
The facility had been part of Vučić's signature infrastructure project: the high-speed railway line linking Belgrade with neighboring Hungary's capital, Budapest. The disaster triggered protests, with demonstrators accusing him of presiding over endemic corruption — and led to the creation of the Student List.
Its new members of parliament range from academics to athletes, with a smattering of economists and engineers. But there is still a big question mark over how they might govern.
"The danger of a broad coalition like this is that the fissures will show soon after victory," warns Kurt Bassuener, the co-founder of the Democratization Policy Council, a regional think tank. He adds that "it is far from clear to me who's going to be in what position" in the new government.
That, perhaps, is a problem for another day. For now, the smell of victory is still in the air, and the party in Belgrade continues.

Localized Russia-Ukraine ceasefire takes effect to aid occupied town of Oleshky in deal brokered by Melania Trump

A regional ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has come into force to let a humanitarian operation begin in Oleshky, a town in southern Ukraine under Russian occupation.
The ceasefire was agreed in coordination with US First Lady Melania Trump.
Both sides announced the truce on Tuesday, but strikes have continued elsewhere, including in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv.
The halt in fighting is intended to open the way for aid deliveries and evacuations from the frontline town, which is grappling with acute shortages of food and medicine.
Dmytro Lubinets, the parliamentary commissioner for human rights, confirmed Russia's timing of its halt in a Facebook post: "As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments,"
Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram that it stopped shelling in the direction of the city of Kherson from 4 a.m. Moscow time (0100 GMT) to prepare for the effort in Oleshky, which faces Kherson across the Dnipro River.
Mr Lubinets added that the deal was reached with US First Lady Melania Trump in cooperation with Russia's commissioner for human rights, Yana Lantratova.
Where is Oleshky?
Oleshky sits on the eastern bank of the Dnipro in Ukraine's southern region of Kherson, opposite the city of Kherson, which is held by Ukrainian forces.
Russian troops have controlled the town since seizing it during the first days of their February 2022 invasion.

White House envoys have spoken to both sides in recent days in an attempt to find a solution, as the US looks to mediate a peace deal to end the war, Europe's deadliest conflict since the World War Two.
On Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said peace negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to meet at a technical level in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi to continue the talks.
Fighting has continued despite the ceasefire arrangement.
New strikes on Tuesday hit the Southern Bridge and subway infrastructure in Kyiv, forcing a suspension of traffic, city officials said.
A Reuters witness heard explosions in the capital.
A Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 15, including students in a dormitory, since Monday evening.
The attacks also killed and injured people in the cities of Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
On the Telegram messaging app, the Russian defence ministry said it had hit transport infrastructure in Kyiv and a logistics hub in the Kharkiv region.
It also said it had struck industrial facilities and cargo vessels elsewhere that it cited as being put to military use.
A drone attack in the western Russian city of Bryansk, close to the border with Ukraine, killed a man and wounded six people.
In the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine's southeastern region of Zaporizhzhia, a drone hit a bus, killing one person and injuring 30, local officials said.
Reuters could not immediately independently verify the reports.
Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
